text:
Date: 2026-11-19

Generated by qwen3.8-27b-sglang, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 5 of 5: Evaluate. Decide and justify your verdict before you read the answer; the criteria are the ones given in class.

1. Docker Desktop and pre-lecture pulls (Download the images before you start)
00:00:14–00:01:41

Q: A teammate plans to run the three pre-lecture docker pull commands on a laptop while Docker Desktop is closed, because they want to download the images before class. Is that plan acceptable for the class setup? A: No, the instructor says Docker Desktop must be open before running these commands; otherwise Docker may report that it cannot be found and tell you to turn it on. The pre-lecture pulls are meant to have the images ready while the class is checking the environment. (00:00:33)



2. Project scope: keep it simple and correct
00:01:41–00:06:05

Q: A group project plan replaces the required simple regression with a neural network because the team wants a more impressive portfolio model in this course. Would you approve that plan? A: No, the instructor’s biggest tip is to keep the analysis simple and technically correct, and if the model is fitting a straight line, fit the straight-line model. DSCI 522 is not a model-fitting course, and over-complicating the analysis now is the mistake that can backfire later. (00:02:03)
Q: A teammate proposes fitting logistic regression to predict a numeric outcome because the outcome scale is 0 to 1. Is that acceptable according to the class’s correctness criterion? A: No, the instructor explicitly says you should not be fitting logistic regression when you are trying to predict a numeric outcome. The class cares that the data science and machine-learning technique is technically correct, not that the model has a high accuracy score. (00:05:24)



3. Branch, commit, and push for the pull-request task
00:06:05–00:09:50

Q: A branch plan edits README.md, runs git add README.md and git commit while git status shows main, then creates the today branch after the commit. Is that acceptable for the class’s branch workflow? A: No, in a branch workflow you should check the branch with git status right before git add and definitely before git commit. The demonstrated workflow creates the branch with git switch -c today before committing the README.md change. (00:08:08)
Q: A plan skips git pull origin main before creating a branch because the local repository was just cloned. Is that acceptable in an actively collaborating environment? A: No, the instructor says to make sure main is pulled so your work is not based on something out of date. That matters when multiple people are actively working in multiple branches. (00:08:27)



4. Issues as a project board
00:09:50–00:16:17

Q: A teammate argues that the demo repository’s issue #1 and issue #2 require two separate pull requests, one for each issue, even though the today branch changes the same README.md. Is that required by the class? A: No, the class says one extreme is one issue, one branch, and one pull request, but one pull request is allowed to deal with all of your issues. The requirement is to have three issues and practice the project-board system, not to split every issue into its own pull request. (00:14:23)



5. Pull-request descriptions, checkboxes, and auto-close keywords
00:16:17–00:22:18

Q: A pull request’s first comment only says “update README”; the necessary fixes #2 is added in a later comment after discussion. Would you approve that description? A: No, the class says the first comment should carry the references and context because people look there rather than the whole conversation. A strategic first comment can use closes or fixes so that merging the pull request auto-closes the referenced issues. (00:16:40)



6. Merging the pull request and cleaning up branches
00:22:18–00:25:29

Q: A team rule says a merged pull request is not finished until the remote branch and local branch are deleted. Is that a requirement in this course? A: No, the class explicitly says it is not requiring branch deletion; you may keep branches as a record, and other teams may use different Git practices. git fetch --prune and git branch -d today are cleanup steps, not a course rule. (00:23:16)



7. Why containers: a stable, shareable compute environment (27.1 Documenting and loading dependencies)
00:25:29–00:33:21

Q: For a team project where members use Macs and Windows machines with different CPU architectures, a teammate says the uv.lock file alone is enough because it pins package versions. Is that sufficient? A: No, lock files pin package versions but do not capture the tooling or system environment. The class’s criterion is a shareable compute environment that can run the same code across different operating systems and architectures, which a container provides as a virtual computer. (00:38:46)



8. Containers versus virtual machines (27.3 Contrasting containers with virtual machines)
00:33:21–00:36:47

Q: Two setup options are a full Windows virtual machine with a graphical interface and a container with only R and the analysis stack. Which would you recommend for sharing a command-line reproducible analysis, and why? A: Recommend the container, because the class contrasts virtual machines as full operating systems that can take 50 to 80 GB with containers as stripped-down environments that are lighter in disk, memory, and compute. A container can still run the full computational stack while fitting the command-line workflow. (00:36:01)



9. Running the R container: docker pull and docker run (28.1 Launching containers using Docker at the command line)
00:36:47–00:45:01

Q: A teammate proposes running docker run -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 for a short practice and keeping the stopped container because they might need it later. Is that the class’s preferred practice? A: No, the class uses --rm so the container is deleted automatically when it stops, avoiding stopped containers piling up. Without --rm, you would have to manually delete the container afterward. (00:40:55)
Q: A plan says library(tidyverse) should work in rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 because it works in the host terminal. Is that reasoning acceptable? A: No, the container is a separate virtual computer, and the bare R image does not include tidyverse. The class showed that library(tidyverse) fails in the container while it works on the host, using the prompt as the cue that you are typing in a different machine. (00:43:54)



10. Web-app containers: RStudio and browser-first tools (27.2 What is a container?)
00:45:01–00:54:10

Q: A plan says the RStudio container is useless unless the end user also installs RStudio locally. Is that acceptable according to the class’s discussion of browser-first tools? A: No, the class treats RStudio as a web application that runs inside the container and is opened through a browser. That is the same browser-first idea shown for JupyterLab and VS Code, so the container can provide the application interface without a local install. (00:48:04)



11. Port mapping the RStudio container (28.1.3 Mapping ports to containers with web apps)
00:54:10–00:59:14

Q: A teammate proposes running a second RStudio container with docker run --rm -p 8788:8788 rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 because the local port must be 8788. Is that command acceptable? A: No, the class’s -p host:container mapping requires the container side to be the port RStudio listens on, 8787. To run a second instance on a free local port, map that port to 8787, for example -p 8788:8787. (00:57:05)



12. Environment variables and running dashboards in containers (27.2 What is a container?)
00:59:20–01:03:00

Q: A teammate proposes omitting -e PASSWORD="apassword" and using whatever random password the first RStudio container prints. Is that the better approach for reproducible team use? A: No, the class shows you can pass the PASSWORD environment variable with -e so the container uses a known password instead of a generated one. The demonstrated command is docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 -e PASSWORD="apassword" rocker/rstudio:4.4.2. (01:00:05)
Q: A plan claims that mapping -p 8787:8787 makes the RStudio web app available to anyone on the local network. Is that the class’s conclusion? A: No, the class checked that if a person cannot log into the physical machine, the mapped localhost port is not available to them. The demonstrated point is that the container is reached locally after mapping the host and container ports. (01:00:28)



13. Building interactively: base image and the cowsay package (29.1.1 Workflow for building a Dockerfile)
01:03:00–01:08:46

Q: A teammate installs cowsay in a running rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 container, exits, and tells the team to use that same container later because it now has the package. Is that acceptable? A: No, the class showed that a container has no save state: after exiting and starting the image again, the runtime-installed package is gone. The reproducible alternative is to document the working install command in a Dockerfile and build an image. (01:07:04)



14. Writing the Dockerfile: FROM, RUN, and CMD (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:08:46–01:15:01

Q: A Dockerfile line says RUN install.packages("cowsay") because that is the R command used interactively. Is that line acceptable? A: No, RUN runs a Bash command during the image build, so the R expression must be executed through the command-line interface. The class used RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')" because Rscript -e runs the R expression for the build step. (01:12:44)



15. Building and running the hello-cowsay image (29.1.2 Build your first image)
01:15:01–01:18:44

Q: A plan runs docker build --tag hello-cowsay . from inside a subdirectory while the Dockerfile is in the repository root. Is that acceptable? A: No, the . tells Docker to use the current directory as the build context where it looks for the Dockerfile. The class assumes you run this from the directory containing the Dockerfile, which is the repository root for milestone-one style instructions. (01:15:38)



16. Version pinning and wrap-up (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:18:44–01:20:39

Q: A Dockerfile installs Quarto with a command that always takes the latest version instead of pinning a version. Would you approve it for a reproducible group project? A: No, the class’s warning is to hard-pin tool versions so a build does not silently change when something updates. The instructor’s unpinned example broke after an overnight update, turning the work into hours of fixing an unexpected tool change. (01:19:50)

title: Git pull requests and an introduction to Docker containers: review questions, tier 5 — Evaluate
text:
Date: 2026-11-19
Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 5 of 5: Evaluate. Decide and justify your verdict before you read the answer; the criteria are the ones given in class.

1. Project advice: keep the analysis simple
00:01:41–00:05:57

Q: At the first group meeting, a teammate argues that the project should use a neural net instead of a straight-line model, so the report stands out. Judge the proposal. A: Reject it. This is a workflows course, not a model-fitting course, so the report is not the point and model performance does not affect your grade. The instructor warned that a complicated model means “a very bad time in about two weeks,” when the workflow work arrives. If the straight line fits, fit the straight line model. (00:02:16)
Q: To keep the project simple, a group decides to predict a numeric outcome with logistic regression, which they already know well. Is that an acceptable kind of simple? A: No. Simple models are not penalised, but they must be technically correct. The instructor said that fitting logistic regression to predict a numeric outcome is “just wrong.” Simplicity never excuses an incorrect technique. (00:05:24)
Q: A student wants the group project to double as a polished portfolio piece, with a more elaborate analysis. Recommend whether to do that inside the assignment. A: Don’t do it inside this assignment. If you really want a portfolio piece, build it separately and in parallel. A lot happens in this course, and you don’t want a complicated report on top of it. (00:03:27)



2. Git review: working on a branch
00:06:16–00:09:50

Q: In the 2026-11-19-docker repository, a teammate edits README.md and runs git add and git commit straight away, without checking the branch or pulling main first. Critique this habit for a group project. A: It falls short of the standard set in class. In a branch workflow you should look at which branch you are on right before git add, and definitely before git commit. When collaborating actively, you should also pull main first, so you are not changing something out of date. The instructor only escaped committing on main because nothing was committed yet, which let git switch -c today carry the edit onto a new branch. (00:08:08)



3. GitHub issues as a project board
00:09:50–00:16:17

Q: A group creates the three issues the lab requires, then resolves all three in a single pull request. A teammate objects that every issue needs its own branch and pull request. Who is right? A: The group is right. One issue, one branch, one pull request is only one extreme, and that is not always how work divides. The instructor said explicitly that it is okay for one pull request to deal with all three issues. The point is experience with the project board system. (00:14:23)
Q: A group plans to keep its meeting notes and task assignments in a shared Google Doc instead of in GitHub issues. Assess the plan. A: Issues are the better choice. They record who is responsible for what, and meeting-notes issues can spawn separate action-item issues. Issues and pull requests also cross-reference each other with two-way # links. The instructor presented this as a very good way to track what is happening with your team “and you’re not relying on a Google Doc of notes.” (00:15:48)



4. Pull request descriptions, checkboxes and closing keywords
00:16:17–00:22:18

Q: A team makes a major design decision halfway through a pull request’s comment thread but leaves the opening description unchanged, reasoning that the decision is recorded in the conversation. Judge this. A: Not good enough. The first comment should be kept up to date. People reading the pull request want to know “why does this thing exist?” from the top, and won’t read the whole conversation. Comments are editable precisely because pull requests evolve, and project owners can usually edit them. (00:16:56)
Q: A teammate puts fixes #2 only in a commit message, never in the pull request description. Is that the better place for it? A: It works, but it is the weaker choice. The instructor said you could put the keyword in a commit message, “but it’s harder to see.” Writing it in the pull request message makes the link visible to the team, and merging still closes the issue automatically. (00:19:55)
Q: Before submitting, a group plans to close every open issue, including stretch-goal ideas, because they believe open issues will cost them marks. Is that necessary? A: No. The course does not grade on whether all your issues are closed by the end. Creating issues for stretch goals and longer-term ideas is encouraged, and the instructor said it is “totally fine” to leave them open. (00:21:50)



5. Cleaning up after a merge
00:22:18–00:25:19

Q: After pull request #3 merges, a teammate insists that the today branch must be deleted on GitHub and locally, or the workflow is wrong. Judge the claim. A: The claim is too strong. In this course, deleting branches is optional, and you may keep them as a record. The merge history stays either way: git fetch --prune and git branch -d today only remove the shortcut names. Some people keep the branch because git switch today is easier than switching to 3c6d82a. (00:23:16)



6. Why data science workflows need stable environments
00:25:29–00:30:13

Q: To avoid “missing package” errors, a teammate proposes installing every library anyone might want into the project environment. Critique the proposal. A: Reject it. The package list should be the bare minimum the project needs. Installing everything wastes disk space. Packages also update on different cycles, so a large environment can reach a point where it can no longer all be installed together. (00:28:04)



7. What a container is (27.2 What is a container?)
00:30:13–00:34:28

Q: A collaborator doesn’t use uv and doesn’t want to install it, because it might disrupt their setup. You plan to send them only your uv.lock file. Is that enough? A: No. A lock file still requires them to install uv and to have a similarly set-up computer. The instructor’s easier route is a container: a virtual computer you build and hand over, so everyone works on the same computer even on different physical machines. (00:31:17)
Q: The admins of a shared remote machine won’t let you install Python on it directly. You propose running your work in a container there instead, accepting the extra layer. Defend or reject the proposal. A: Defend it. There is a performance hit from the extra layer, but a container gives you a sandbox where you can install what you need without touching the machine itself. If you mess it up, you restart it and get a fresh sandbox. (00:32:34)



8. Containers versus virtual machines (27.3 Contrasting containers with virtual machines)
00:34:31–00:36:40

Q: To share the project’s computing environment, a teammate proposes distributing a full Windows virtual machine instead of a container. Recommend one. A: Recommend the container. A Windows virtual machine can take 50–80 GB, and it carries a full operating system and graphical interface. The containers used in class are a couple of gigabytes or less, yet still run the full computational stack. They are lighter on disk, memory and compute. (00:36:16)



9. Pulling and running a container (28.1.1 Launch and run containers)
00:36:40–00:45:01

Q: For a multi-year clinical trials analysis that must be submitted to a regulator, a team plans to submit only its code and an renv.lock file. Assess whether that meets the standard described in class. A: It does not. Regulators want to reproduce the work with the full compute environment, and R itself updates every six months. Lock files track only the packages, not the version of R or the system tools. Handing over the container that ran the analysis, such as one built on rocker/r-ver:4.3.2, pins those as well. (00:38:46)



10. Know which machine you are typing on
00:45:01–00:46:44

Q: A teammate has a container shell and a laptop terminal open side by side, and runs a destructive cleanup command without first checking the prompt. Critique the habit. A: It is risky. With containers and remote machines, the prompt is often your only visual cue to which machine you are typing on, so check it every time. Commands such as whoami exist to confirm you are on the machine you think you are. (00:45:04)



11. Running RStudio in a container and mapping ports (28.1.3 Mapping ports to containers with web apps)
00:54:10–00:58:59

Q: While practising, a student drops --rm from docker run -p 8787:8787 rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 and starts several containers through the afternoon. Judge the practice. A: Avoid it. Without --rm, containers aren’t removed when they stop, and leaving several running means each one keeps taking up RAM. The instructor warned that you end up asking why your computer isn’t working, because you turned on five computers. (00:55:17)
Q: A student wants two RStudio containers at once and plans to start both with -p 8787:8787. Is that plan sound? A: No. Both containers can listen on 8787 inside, but each needs a different port on your machine. Change the left-hand (host) number of -p for the second container. Running things on different host ports is what lets several run at the same time. (00:56:38)



12. Passing environment variables into a container (27.2 What is a container?)
00:59:20–01:02:53

Q: The instructor ran docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 -e PASSWORD="apassword" rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 with the password in plain view. Was that acceptable in that setting? A: Yes, by the criterion given in class. Port 8787 was only reachable on his own machine, so anyone without access to his laptop could not reach the container at all. The visible password therefore didn’t expose anything. (01:00:16)
Q: For a future dashboard, a team weighs two options: users follow renv setup instructions, or users docker run a container with the dashboard already installed. Recommend one for end users. A: The container. The installation is already done inside it, so users skip the whole process of installing renv and restoring the snapshot. As long as they have Docker, docker run with some flags starts the application. You’ve given them a computer you built from scratch. (01:02:20)



13. Starting from a base image and working inside it (29.1.1 Workflow for building a Dockerfile)
01:03:00–01:08:19

Q: A project README tells users to start rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 and run install.packages() for every package each time before running the analysis. Assess this approach. A: It is poor. A container has no saved state: packages installed by hand disappear when it restarts, so users repeat the installs every time. The instructor called that extremely painful, for example a 15-minute tidyverse install for a 30-second analysis. Those steps belong in a Dockerfile. (01:08:19)
Q: A student wants to learn Linux by running risky commands, but is afraid of breaking their laptop. Is docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash a reasonable place to try them? A: Yes. Restarting a container gives a clean machine, as if you had never run the command. That makes containers a safe place to try new packages or muck around with the command line. (01:07:25)



14. The Dockerfile: FROM, RUN, CMD (29.1.2 Build your first image)
01:10:18–01:15:01

Q: A reviewer rejects a Dockerfile that starts FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2. They argue it should start from a bare-minimum Linux image, with R installed by hand, to keep the image small. Judge the rejection. A: The rejection is too strict. A bare-minimum start is possible and a good learning exercise, but the instructor said disk space is relatively cheap, so starting from a beefier machine is acceptable. rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 already has R and the pieces R needs, which skips steps. (01:12:02)



15. Building and running your own image (29.4.3 3. How do I build an image locally on my laptop?)
01:15:01–01:18:44

Q: A milestone README tells users to cd into a subfolder before running docker build --tag hello-cowsay ., then cd back for the next step. Does that meet the standard set for milestone instructions? A: No. Instructions should assume every command runs from the root of the repository. That way they can be copy-pasted without changing directories in the middle. docker build --tag hello-cowsay . is meant to run from the root, where the Dockerfile lives. (01:16:11)



16. Pinning versions, and what comes next
01:18:44–01:20:39

Q: A project Dockerfile installs Quarto and the analysis packages without specifying any versions, “so we always get the latest.” Would you approve it in a pull request? A: No. Things that update without you knowing can break everything. The instructor restarted an unpinned container in another class and nothing worked, because something had updated the day before. Hard-pin the versions so they change only when you edit that line. (01:19:55)

title: Introduction to Containers and Git Workflow Review: review questions, tier 4 — Analyze
text:
Date: 2026-11-19

Generated by qwen3.6-35b-a3b, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 4 of 5: Analyze. Take each one apart yourself before you read the answer; tiers 1 to 3 cover the facts, reasons and steps it relies on.

1. Project Advice and Course Logistics
00:00:14–00:05:43

Q: Break down the instructor’s advice on the project assignment: which specific components of a data science project are explicitly required, and how do their relative importance and grading weight relate to each other? A: The instructor requires code for downloading data, cleaning, EDA, modeling, and producing figures or tables, but explicitly states that model accuracy does not matter as long as the techniques are technically correct. The written report is secondary to the underlying workflow, meaning students should prioritize reproducible practices over complex analytical choices like neural networks. This hierarchy exists because the course evaluates workflow management rather than statistical sophistication, so overcomplicating the analysis would unnecessarily burden the reproducibility pipeline. (00:01:56)



2. Git Branching and Pull Requests
00:06:05–00:25:29

Q: Trace the lifecycle of a feature branch in the demonstrated Git workflow: which local and remote actions correspond to each stage, and how does cleaning up the local references relate to the state of the remote repository? A: The workflow begins locally by creating and switching to a new branch, committing changes, and pushing them to the remote. Once merged via a pull request on GitHub, the instructor demonstrates that the remote branch can be deleted via the UI, but local tracking references remain until git fetch --prune removes the remote pointers. Finally, git branch -d removes the local branch reference, leaving only the merged history in git log. These steps ensure that local metadata aligns with the remote repository’s actual state, preventing confusion from stale branch pointers. (00:22:25)



3. Introduction to containerization (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:25:33–00:46:44

Q: Differentiate between virtual environments, containers, and virtual machines based on their isolation levels and resource overhead: how does the architectural layer each strategy virtualizes determine its portability and disk usage? A: Virtual environments isolate only application-level dependencies like programming languages and packages, making them extremely lightweight but porous to OS-level conflicts. Containers virtualize the operating system user space, allowing them to capture system-level dependencies and different software versions while remaining significantly smaller and faster than full virtual machines. Virtual machines emulate entire hardware and operating systems, providing maximum isolation at the cost of heavy disk and memory usage. This architectural progression explains why containers are preferred for sharing reproducible compute environments across different host machines. (00:28:50)



4. Using and running containers (28 Using and running containers)
00:46:47–01:03:00

Q: Examine the docker run command used to launch RStudio Server: how do the port mapping flag and the environment variable flag interact to make the containerized application accessible and configurable from the host machine? A: The -p flag maps a local port on the host machine (e.g., 8787) to the corresponding port inside the container, allowing a web browser on the host to route requests to the application running in the isolated environment. The -e flag passes configuration parameters, such as a custom password, directly into the container’s environment variables before the application starts. Together, these flags bridge the network and configuration boundaries of the container, enabling interactive access without modifying the underlying container image. (00:56:31)



5. Customizing and building containers (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:03:00–01:20:39

Q: Break down the three primary instructions in the demonstrated Dockerfile and explain how each contributes to transforming a base image into a self-contained, executable container: A: The FROM instruction establishes the base operating system and software layer, providing a known starting point for the build. The RUN instruction executes commands during the image build phase, permanently baking dependencies like the cowsay package into the image’s layers so they persist across future container runs. The CMD instruction defines the default command that executes automatically when a container launches, replacing the base image’s original startup behavior. Together, these instructions convert a temporary shell session into a reproducible, standalone application environment. (01:05:43)

title: Git workflow review and Docker containers: review questions, tier 3 — Apply
text:
Date: 2026-11-19

Generated by qwen3.8-27b-sglang, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 3 of 5: Apply. Work each situation through before you read the answer; tiers 1 (Remember) and 2 (Understand) cover the facts and reasons it relies on.

1. Pre-lecture setup: Docker Desktop and the docker pull commands (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:00:14–00:01:41

Q: You open a new terminal, type docker pull rocker/r-ver:4.3.2, and get an error saying Docker cannot be found. What is the most likely cause, and what do you do before re-running the command? A: The Docker Desktop application is not running. On macOS and Windows, Docker commands require the Docker engine managed by Docker Desktop; you need to open Docker Desktop (the application called Docker) so the engine is available, then re-run the docker pull command. (00:00:33)
Q: You are preparing for the day’s container exercises and have four actions in front of you: (a) run docker pull rocker/r-ver:4.3.2, (b) open Docker Desktop, (c) run docker pull quay.io/jupyter/datascience-notebook:2025-03-14, and (d) run docker pull rocker/rstudio:4.4.2. A: Add a RUN line that installs uv at a specific version, then a RUN uv sync line to install packages from the lock file, then a RUN line that installs Quarto at a specific version. Each tool is pinned to the version you tested, so the image is reproducible and a floating update cannot silently change the environment. (01:19:02)
Q: The session recounted a case where a container was restarted without hard-version-pinning any of the tool versions, and an overnight update broke the build, costing hours of debugging. Your project’s Dockerfile currently uses FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 (pinned) but the RUN lines install the latest renv and Quarto without version constraints. What should you change, and what is the consequence of not changing it? A: Pin the versions of renv and Quarto in the RUN lines (for example, install renv and Quarto at specific tested versions). If you do not, a future rebuild may pull in updated tool versions that are incompatible with your pipeline, and you will spend time fixing the update instead of doing the actual work. The session’s warning: an un-pinned update can break everything overnight. (01:19:50)

title: Git pull requests and an introduction to Docker containers: review questions, tier 3 — Apply
text:
Date: 2026-11-19
Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 3 of 5: Apply. Work each situation through before you read the answer; tiers 1 (Remember) and 2 (Understand) cover the facts and reasons it relies on.

1. Project advice: keep the analysis simple
00:01:41–00:05:57

Q: Your group is planning its project and a teammate wants to fit a neural net, though a straight line would describe the data. Which model do you choose, and why? A: Fit the straight line model. This is a workflows course, not a model fitting course, and an ambitious model will eat the time the workflow work needs. As the warning goes, “You’re going to have a very bad time in about two weeks” if you go for the neural net. (00:02:16)
Q: Your project’s outcome is a numeric quantity, and your group proposes logistic regression because it is simple. Will simplicity save you here? A: No. Simple models are not penalised, but the technique still has to be correct. Fitting logistic regression to predict a numeric outcome is just wrong, so choose a model that suits a numeric outcome, such as linear regression. (00:05:24)
Q: Your simple, correctly fitted model reaches only about 60% accuracy, and you are tempted to keep tuning it before you move on. What should you do? A: Move on. The results of the model do not matter, as long as the data science and machine learning techniques are technically correct. The time belongs to the workflow parts of the project. (00:03:08)
Q: You want the group project to double as a portfolio piece with a more elaborate analysis. How do you handle that? A: Don’t do it in this assignment. If you really want the portfolio version, build it separately and in parallel, because this class has a lot happening and a complicated report would get in the way. (00:03:27)



2. Git review: working on a branch
00:06:16–00:09:50

Q: In the 2026-11-19-docker repository you have added a line to README.md, and git status says On branch main. You haven’t committed anything yet. How do you get this work onto a new branch called today? A: Run git switch -c today. Nothing has been committed, so the uncommitted edit comes with you to the new branch. git status then shows On branch today with README.md still modified. (00:08:57)
Q: You realise you have already made commits on main that should have been on a branch. Where do you turn? A: The textbook has a cheat sheet with a set of commands for moving those commits onto a branch. Avoid this situation by checking your branch before you commit. (00:07:44)
Q: You are on branch today with an edited README.md. In order, which commands review the change, commit it and send the branch to GitHub? A: Run git diff to review the added line, then git add README.md, then git commit -m "today we are talking about containers", then git push origin today. The push output gives a link for creating a pull request for today on GitHub. (00:09:25)
Q: You and your teammates are all actively working on the project, and you are about to start a new change. What do you run first, and why? A: Pull the main branch with git pull origin main, so that everything is up to date. Otherwise you may be making changes to something that is out of date. (00:08:27)
Q: You are working in a branch workflow and are about to run git add, then git commit. What do you check right before each one? A: Check which branch you are on, for example with git status. With several people working on several branches, committing on the wrong branch is the common mistake. Check before add, and definitely before commit. (00:08:08)



3. GitHub issues as a project board
00:09:50–00:16:17

Q: Your repository has issue #1 and issue #2, and nothing else. You now open a pull request. What number will it get? A: Number 3. Issues and pull requests share one counter on GitHub; they are not counted separately. (00:12:07)
Q: While writing issue #2, you type “meeting from #1”. What happens on issue #1? A: The #1 becomes a link to issue #1, and issue #1 automatically shows a reference back to issue #2. The reference works in both directions, so related items link to each other without extra work. (00:13:34)
Q: Your lab asks for three issues, and one pull request ends up dealing with all three. Do you need to split the work into three branches and three pull requests? A: No. One issue, one branch, one pull request is only one extreme. It is fine for a single pull request to deal with all three issues; the point is to get experience with the project board. (00:14:23)
Q: You open a pull request and want a teammate to look over your work before it is merged. Who goes where in the pull request’s sidebar? A: Assign yourself, since it is your pull request and you are claiming it. Add your teammate in the separate reviewer section. Some projects block changes until someone has actually reviewed the work. (00:14:47)
Q: Halfway through a task you have a stray idea, such as trying a neural net later, that you don’t want to lose. What do you do with it? A: File it as an issue. The issues board is a good place to dump ideas and stretch goals. You can even ask a coding agent to file the issue, so you don’t have to switch to a browser and lose track. (00:13:24)
Q: Your group keeps meeting notes in an issue, and the meeting produces action items for different people. How do you track them? A: Write the action items in the notes issue, then create a separate issue for each one, spawned out of the notes issue and referencing it. Each issue documents who is responsible for what. (00:11:14)



4. Pull request descriptions, checkboxes and closing keywords
00:16:17–00:22:18

Q: Your pull request #3 resolves issue #2. What do you write so the issue closes itself, and when does it close? A: Write a sentence such as fixes #2 in the pull request’s description. When the pull request is merged, GitHub closes issue #2 automatically. This is a GitHub feature, not a feature of Git. (00:19:30)
Q: One pull request resolves three of your issues. How do you avoid going back and closing each issue by hand? A: Write the message strategically: put a closing keyword with each issue number, such as fixes #N, in the pull request description. Merging the pull request then closes all three, and your issues tab gets smaller without any extra clicks. (00:21:02)
Q: You put fixes #2 in a commit message instead of the pull request description. Will that work, and is it a good choice? A: It can work in a commit message, but it is harder to see there. Writing it in the pull request message makes it visible to everyone reviewing the work. (00:19:55)
Q: You wrote closes #1 fixes #2 in pull request #3 and you are unsure which keyword to rely on. Which one do you choose? A: Both closes and fixes are closing keywords. fixes is the one to rely on, because it is the one used almost all the time. The demo repository shows issues #1 and #2 both closed by #3. (00:19:55)
Q: Your pull request is open but not finished, and you want teammates to see what is left to do. What can you put in it? A: Add Markdown checkboxes such as - [ ] item 1 to the description, and check them off as you go. Unchecked boxes show teammates the work isn’t done yet. You can also use these in addition to, or instead of, the draft button. (00:17:49)
Q: A big decision is made halfway down the comment thread of your pull request. Where should that decision end up? A: Edit it into the first comment. Readers want to know what is happening and why the item exists from the top, not by reading the whole conversation. The first comment is editable because it evolves over time. (00:16:56)
Q: Your group’s project ends with several stretch-goal issues still open. Is that a problem for grading? A: No. Issues don’t all need to be closed by the end; that is not what is graded. Creating issues for longer-term ideas is fine practice. (00:21:50)



5. Cleaning up after a merge
00:22:18–00:25:19

Q: Pull request #3 from today has just been merged on GitHub, and locally you are still on today. What do you run to bring your local main up to date? A: Run git switch main, then git pull origin main. The pull fast-forwards main to the merge commit made on GitHub. (00:22:25)
Q: You want to delete the merged today branch on GitHub, but you have already left the pull request page. Where can you delete it? A: Go to the branches view, find today (it shows pull request #3 as merged), and click the trash can. From the pull request page itself, you can use the delete-branch button that appears after merging. (00:22:53)
Q: You have deleted today on GitHub, but git log --oneline --graph --all still shows (origin/today, today) next to commit 3c6d82a. What do you run to drop the remote reference? A: Run git fetch --prune. It removes the origin/today reference to the branch that no longer exists on GitHub, so afterwards the commit is labelled (today) only. (00:24:30)
Q: After git fetch --prune, commit 3c6d82a is still labelled (today). How do you remove that label, and what does the graph look like afterwards? A: Run git branch -d today to delete the local branch. The graph still shows 3c6d82a and the merge commit d25ddfa, but 3c6d82a has no label. You lose only the shortcut name, not the history. (00:24:30)
Q: You expect to return to a merged branch’s commit often and would rather not type its hash. What do you do? A: Keep the branch instead of deleting it, so that git switch today works instead of switching to 3c6d82a. Deleting branches is optional in this course, and you may keep them as a record. (00:25:05)



6. What a container is (27.2 What is a container?)
00:30:13–00:34:28

Q: You give a collaborator your uv.lock file, but they don’t use uv and worry that installing it will disturb how their computer is set up. What do you give them instead? A: Give them a container: a virtual computer built from scratch with everything installed. They do their work on that virtual computer, so everyone effectively shares the same computer, even on different physical machines. (00:31:17)
Q: You prototype on your laptop, but the full analysis must run on a bigger machine that holds all the data. How do you make sure both machines have exactly the same compute environment? A: Run the analysis in the same container on both machines. Expect a small performance hit from the extra layer; there is no way around that. (00:32:15)
Q: The administrators of a remote server won’t let you install Python on it directly. How can you still run your analysis there? A: Use a container. The administrators can give you a sandbox to play in without you installing software on the machine itself. If you mess it up, it is restarted and you get a fresh sandbox. (00:32:34)



7. Containers versus virtual machines (27.3 Contrasting containers with virtual machines)
00:34:31–00:36:40

Q: You need to share your analysis environment with your group, and you are choosing between a virtual machine and a container. Which do you pick? A: A container. A Windows virtual machine can take 50–80 GB, while a container can run a full computational stack in less than two gigabytes. Containers are lighter on disk, memory and compute. (00:36:16)
Q: On your Mac, you need to check that installation instructions work for Windows users, including the Windows graphical interface. Which tool fits? A: A virtual machine. It runs a full-blown operating system such as Windows, with all its buttons and windows, so you can test as if you were on a Windows machine. (00:36:01)
Q: You open a shell in a container and want to browse its folders. How do you get around? A: Type commands such as cd and ls. A container is stripped down and typically has no graphical interface, so you can’t double-click through a folder structure. (00:35:00)



8. Pulling and running a container: R 4.3.2 beside local R (28.1.1 Launch and run containers)
00:36:40–00:45:01

Q: You already downloaded rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 before class and run docker pull rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 again. What do you expect to see? A: Docker checks the registry, prints a Digest: sha256:... line, and reports Status: Image is up to date for rocker/r-ver:4.3.2. If a newer version had been published, the pull would download it. (00:39:51)
Q: R --version on your laptop reports R 4.6.2. You run docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2. Which R do you get? A: R 4.3.2 starts, running inside the container, not the R on your laptop. You can have both versions at once, because the container is effectively a different machine. (00:42:38)
Q: Inside the rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 container, you run library(tidyverse), which works fine in R on your laptop. What happens? A: It fails with there is no package called 'tidyverse'. The image has only R installed, and nothing has told it to install tidyverse. (00:43:49)
Q: You run docker run with an image name you have never pulled. What does Docker do? A: It downloads the image first and then runs it. Pulling ahead of time just saves waiting at the moment you run it. (00:42:16)
Q: You start a container with docker run -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2, leaving out --rm. What happens to the container when you quit? A: It isn’t deleted, so you have to delete it manually. With --rm, the container is removed automatically when it stops. (00:40:55)
Q: You want to type commands at R’s prompt inside the container. Which flags make that possible, and what does each one do? A: Use -it, which is two single-letter flags chained together. -i makes the session interactive, so what you type goes in, and -t gives you a terminal (TTY) to interact with. (00:41:48)
Q: Your multi-year clinical trial analysis must be reproducible for a regulator, while R updates every six months. Your renv lock file pins the packages. What else do you hand over? A: The container that ran the full analysis, which fixes the version of R itself. Lock files only track packages, not the tools installed on the system. (00:38:46)
Q: You want everyone on a project to use an old version of Git, so that nobody can run git switch. How could you enforce that? A: Give everyone a container with that version of Git installed, for example one from 2019. A container pins system tools like Git, not only the packages that a lock file covers. (00:39:02)



9. Know which machine you are typing on
00:45:01–00:46:44

Q: You type q() in R inside a container, and the prompt now reads dan@Heartsbane 2026-11-19-docker %. Where are your next commands going to run? A: On your own laptop. The prompt is back to your computer’s own prompt, and that prompt is your visual cue for which machine you are on. (00:45:04)
Q: Your prompt reads root@95765251a970:/#. Are you on your laptop? A: No. You are in a shell inside a container, whose prompt shows the root user and the container’s ID. The prompt changes when you enter the container, which tells you where you are typing. (01:05:20)
Q: You connect to a remote machine and are given little more than a blinking cursor. How do you confirm you are on the machine you think you are? A: Read the prompt for the machine’s name and run whoami, which reports your username on that computer. Check before running commands, because sometimes these are the only cues you have. (00:46:08)



10. Running RStudio in a container and mapping ports (28.1.3 Mapping ports to containers with web apps)
00:54:10–00:58:59

Q: You want RStudio Server from rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 in your browser. What do you run, and how do you log in? A: Run docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 rocker/rstudio:4.4.2, then go to localhost:8787. The username is rstudio, and the password is the generated one printed in the start-up output. (00:57:42)
Q: One RStudio container is already using port 8787 on your laptop, and you want to start a second one. What do you change in the -p flag? A: Change the left number, which is the port on your machine, and keep the right number at 8787, the port inside the container. Both containers then run side by side on different host ports. (00:56:38)
Q: You have been starting containers all afternoon and your laptop has become sluggish. What is the likely cause, and how do you prevent it? A: Each running container takes up RAM, so you may have “five computers” running at once. Use --rm so a container shuts down and is deleted when you exit it, and stop the ones you don’t need. (00:55:17)
Q: You press Ctrl+C in the terminal running your RStudio container, and it prints [s6-finish] waiting for services. without exiting. What do you do? A: Press Ctrl+C again. After repeated presses the log shows got 3 SIGTERM/SIGINTs, forcefully exiting. Because the container was started with --rm, it is still cleaned up. (00:57:51)
Q: Your desktop RStudio uses R 4.6.2. You log into the RStudio Server from rocker/rstudio:4.4.2. Which R version does it run? A: R 4.4.2, the version installed in that container. It is effectively a different machine from both your laptop and the rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 container. (00:58:51)



11. Passing environment variables into a container (27.2 What is a container?)
00:59:20–01:02:53

Q: The generated RStudio password, such as ooph3Aef2Ohcahcu, is a pain to retype each time. How do you choose your own? A: Run docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 -e PASSWORD="apassword" rocker/rstudio:4.4.2, then log in at localhost:8787 as rstudio with apassword. -e passes an environment variable into the container, and this image reads PASSWORD. (01:00:05)
Q: You pass -e PASSWORD=... to a different image, and it has no effect. What went wrong? A: Environment variables are container-specific: a container uses only the variables it was built to read, and not every container has this one. Check that image’s documentation for the variables it supports. (01:01:08)
Q: Your docker run command shows the RStudio password in plain text on your screen. Is that a security problem? A: Not in this setting. The container’s port is only reachable from your own machine, so someone who can’t log into your laptop can’t reach localhost:8787. (01:00:28)
Q: You built a dashboard and want someone to run it without installing your language, renv and packages. How do you deliver it? A: Put the dashboard code in a container. Anyone with Docker can docker run it with the right flags and open the port in their browser. They skip the whole installation process because you have given them a computer you built from scratch. (01:02:20)



12. Starting from a base image and working inside it (29.1.1 Workflow for building a Dockerfile)
01:03:00–01:08:19

Q: You want a shell in rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 to try install commands, but starting it drops you straight into R. How do you change that? A: Add bash after the image name: docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash. The image’s default command, R, is replaced by a shell, and the prompt changes to the container’s. You can still type R there to start R. (01:05:20)
Q: You are choosing a starting machine for your own R container: rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 or a bare-minimum Linux image. Which saves you work? A: rocker/r-ver:4.6.2. Whoever built it already installed R and the system pieces a new computer needs to run R, much like the compiler tools you installed on your laptop. A bare image means installing every single thing by hand. (01:04:00)
Q: Inside a container started with docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash, you run install.packages("cowsay") in R and the cow appears. You exit, start the container again the same way, and run library(cowsay). Predict the result. A: It fails with there is no package called 'cowsay'. A container has no saved state: each start resets to how its image was built, so anything installed by hand is gone. (01:07:10)
Q: You want to experiment with risky Linux commands without endangering your laptop. Where do you do it? A: In a container. Even a command that deletes the whole computer only damages the container, and when you turn it back on it is as if you had never run that command. (01:07:25)
Q: You are designing a container and aren’t sure your install steps will work. In what order do you go? A: Go through the steps interactively in a shell inside the base image first. Once they work, document them as the instructions for building the machine from scratch. (01:05:48)



13. Running R from the command line with Rscript -e (29.1.2 Build your first image)
01:08:19–01:10:18

Q: You are at the Bash prompt in a rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 container and want to install cowsay without opening R. What do you type? A: Type Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')". Rscript runs R code from the terminal, and -e tells it you are giving it an R expression. (01:09:27)
Q: You are writing the Rscript -e install command and need a quoted package name inside the quoted expression. How do you quote it? A: Use double quotes on the outside and single quotes on the inside: "install.packages('cowsay')". Pay attention to the quotes, so the inner quotes don’t end the outer string. (01:09:41)
Q: You install cowsay with Rscript -e at a container’s prompt, confirm library(cowsay) works, then exit and start a new container from the same image. Is cowsay there? A: No, it is gone again. Running the install from the shell doesn’t change the image, so the command needs to be saved somewhere that rebuilds the machine. (01:10:01)



14. The Dockerfile: FROM, RUN, CMD (29.2 Dockerfile command summary)
01:10:18–01:15:01

Q: You have confirmed that Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')" works at a container’s prompt. How do you make that install permanent? A: Write it into a file named Dockerfile as a RUN line: RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')". RUN holds the bash commands the container runs during the build, so the package is part of every machine built from it. (01:12:44)
Q: Write a Dockerfile that starts from R 4.6.2, installs cowsay, and by default prints a cow saying “Hello from my first image!”. A: FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 comes first, naming the starting machine. Next is RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')", then CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "cowsay::say('Hello from my first image!')"]. CMD is written as a list rather than space-separated words, and it is the last thing the machine runs. (01:13:40)
Q: Your image’s Dockerfile ends with a CMD that prints the cow message. You start it with docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay bash. Does the CMD run? A: No. CMD is only the default, used when you don’t give another command. Adding bash overrides it and gives you a shell instead. (01:14:05)
Q: Your project is in Python and managed with uv. What goes between the FROM line and the CMD line of its Dockerfile? A: Commands that install uv, a COPY of your lock files into the image, and a RUN of uv sync. All the packages are then installed in the container, so the machine has your compute environment ready. (01:14:15)



15. Building and running your own image (29.1.2 Build your first image)
01:15:01–01:18:44

Q: You have just written the Dockerfile in the root of 2026-11-19-docker. In order, what do you run to build an image named hello-cowsay, confirm it exists, and run it? A: Run docker build --tag hello-cowsay ., then docker images, which should list hello-cowsay:latest, then docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay. (01:17:01)
Q: You type docker build --tag hello-cowsay and stop. What is missing, and what does it mean? A: The final ., which tells Docker where to look for the file named Dockerfile: the current directory. This may be the first time a lone dot is something you actually have to type. (01:15:38)
Q: Your project’s milestone instructions include docker build --tag hello-cowsay ., and a teammate runs it from a subfolder. Where should it be run? A: From the root of the repository, where the Dockerfile lives. The instructions assume every command runs from the root, so commands can be copy-pasted without changing directories. (You can give a full path to a Dockerfile, but this command assumes the root.) (01:16:11)
Q: You run docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay with no extra command. What appears? A: An ASCII cow saying “Hello from my first image!”. With no command given, the container runs the CMD line from the Dockerfile. (01:17:14)
Q: You run docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay bash, start R, and run library(cowsay). Predict the result, and contrast it with the bare rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 image. A: It loads without error, because the RUN line installed cowsay when the image was built. In a fresh container from the base rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 image, library(cowsay) fails. (01:17:52)
Q: You add a new RUN line to your Dockerfile, then go straight to docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay, but the new software isn’t there. What did you skip? A: Rebuilding the image with docker build --tag hello-cowsay .. The Dockerfile only holds the instructions: you must build the machine from them before turning it on. (01:17:52)



16. Pinning versions, and what comes next
01:18:44–01:20:39

Q: Your project’s analysis must still run on the same R version a year from now. Which line of your Dockerfile controls that, and how? A: The FROM line, for example FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2. The tag pins the version of R, so that part of the environment is now stable. (01:18:53)
Q: Quarto 1.11 is current, but you want your project’s container to stay on Quarto 1.10. How do you arrange that? A: Install that explicit version in the Dockerfile’s install command. As long as you don’t change that line, the container stays on the same version a year from now. (01:19:25)
Q: You restart a project container whose Dockerfile installs software without pinned versions, and suddenly nothing works. What most likely happened, and how do you prevent it? A: Something upstream updated, perhaps the day before, and the unpinned install pulled in the new version. Hard-pin your versions so nothing changes until you update that line yourself; otherwise you spend hours fixing an update instead of doing the work. (01:19:55)

title: Git Workflow and Docker Containers: review questions, tier 2 — Understand
text:
Date: 2026-11-19

Generated by qwen3.6-35b-a3b, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 2 of 5: Understand. Explain each answer in your own words before you read it; tier 1 (Remember) covers the facts, tiers 3 to 5 put them to use.

1. Project Advice and Course Logistics
00:00:14–00:05:43

Q: Why does the instructor strongly advise keeping the group project analysis simple, such as fitting a straight line if it is statistically appropriate? A: The course focuses on teaching reproducible workflows and trustworthy practices, not on model fitting or statistical novelty. Using a complex model like a neural net would create unnecessary complications in managing the pipeline, making it significantly harder to ensure the code is technically correct and reproducible by the assignment deadline. (00:02:16)
Q: What does the instructor mean when he says that the model’s accuracy or results do not matter for this assignment? A: Grading evaluates whether the data science pipeline is technically sound and properly documented, not the predictive performance of the algorithm. A straightforward model that correctly downloads, cleans, analyzes, and documents data scores just as well as a complex one, because the learning objective is mastering the workflow tooling rather than optimizing statistical outcomes. (00:03:08)
Q: Why is the final written report not considered the main point of the coursework in this class? A: DSCI 522 teaches the underlying infrastructure that keeps data analysis reproducible, which includes writing code for data downloads, cleaning, exploratory analysis, and modeling. The report is merely one output of a much larger pipeline, and the core skill being assessed is the ability to build and share a reliable computational environment. (00:02:41)



2. Git Branching and Pull Requests
00:06:05–00:25:29

Q: Why are GitHub issues useful for tracking a group project, and how does their shared numbering system support team collaboration? A: Issues act as a built-in project management board to document tasks, meeting notes, and assign responsibilities to specific team members. Because issues and pull requests share a single numbering sequence, team members can easily cross-reference them using the # symbol in descriptions or commit messages, creating automatic two-way links that keep all project activities connected. (00:10:28)
Q: How does using keywords like fixes or closes in a pull request description automate project management? A: These special keywords tell GitHub to automatically close the referenced issue(s) the moment the pull request is merged. This saves time by removing the need to manually close multiple tickets and keeps the project board up to date, allowing the team to quickly see which tasks have been completed without navigating away from the main repository view. (00:18:33)
Q: Why is it important to edit and keep the first comment of a pull request or issue up to date as work progresses? A: The first comment serves as the primary summary of what the task is, why it exists, and how it was resolved. Reviewers and future team members typically skim the conversation and rely on this initial description to understand the context, so it must remain accurate and complete even if later comments discuss minor details or troubleshooting steps. (00:16:40)
Q: Why does the instructor recommend running git fetch --prune and git branch -d <branch> after merging a pull request? A: Merging a pull request deletes the remote branch, but local Git still retains stale tracking references to it. Running these cleanup commands removes the deleted remote branch references locally and deletes the local branch name, which prevents visual clutter in the repository history and avoids confusion when switching between branches. (00:24:30)



3. Introduction to Containers and Docker (Introduction to containerization)
00:25:33–00:46:44

Q: How do containers differ from virtual environments like uv or renv in terms of what they isolate? A: Virtual environments only isolate the packages for a specific programming language on the host machine. Containers go further by isolating the entire operating system user space, meaning they also capture system-level dependencies, other installed software, and the OS itself, ensuring the environment is fully reproducible regardless of the host’s configuration. (00:26:11)
Q: Why is a Docker container considered much more lightweight and performant than a traditional virtual machine? A: A virtual machine emulates full hardware and runs a completely separate guest operating system, which consumes gigabytes of disk space and significant memory. A container shares the host’s operating system kernel and only packages the necessary application and dependencies, making it significantly smaller, faster to start, and more efficient to share across teams. (00:34:48)
Q: What specific problem does running a pinned version of software inside a Docker container solve for long-term projects? A: Software tools and packages have frequent update cycles that can change behavior or break compatibility over time. By running a container with a strictly pinned version, a researcher guarantees that the exact same computational environment remains available years later for regulatory submissions or reproducibility audits, independent of updates on the host machine. (00:37:58)



4. Running Web Applications in Containers (Using and running containers)
00:46:47–01:03:00

Q: Why do modern data science tools like JupyterLab and RStudio Server need to be run inside a container and accessed through a web browser? A: Many of these tools are built as web-first applications so they can run on remote or cloud machines while providing a consistent user interface. Running them in a container isolates the compute environment, and port mapping allows the local browser to securely interact with the application running inside the isolated container without requiring local installation of heavy software stacks. (00:47:39)
Q: How does the -p flag in docker run allow multiple containers to run simultaneously without conflicting? A: The -p flag maps a specific port on the host machine to a corresponding port inside the container. By assigning different host ports to different containers (e.g., mapping one instance to 8787 and another to 8788), users can access multiple isolated container instances concurrently, even if the applications inside them all default to the same internal port. (00:56:38)
Q: Why and how can you pass environment variables like PASSWORD when launching a container? A: Many pre-built containers are configured to read environment variables at startup to customize their initial behavior, such as overriding default login credentials. Using the -e flag allows users to inject custom settings directly into the container environment, enabling secure or memorable configurations without needing to rebuild or modify the underlying container image. (00:59:45)



5. Building Custom Containers with Dockerfile (Customizing and building containers)
01:03:00–01:20:39

Q: Why is it necessary to save installation steps in a Dockerfile instead of just installing packages interactively inside a running container? A: Containers are ephemeral and reset to their initial state when stopped; any packages or changes made during an interactive session are completely lost upon exit. A Dockerfile captures these instructions permanently in the image layers during the build process, ensuring that every time the image is launched, the environment is identically configured without requiring manual setup. (01:08:10)
Q: What is the specific role of the RUN instruction in a Dockerfile? A: The RUN instruction executes shell commands during the image build process rather than at runtime. It is used to install software, download files, or configure the system in a way that becomes a permanent part of the container image layers, so the installed components are automatically available to every container launched from that image. (01:12:52)
Q: How does the CMD instruction in a Dockerfile control the default behavior of a container when it starts? A: CMD sets the default command that runs automatically when a container is instantiated from the image, replacing any startup command set by the base image. This ensures the container performs a specific, predefined task immediately upon launch, unless a user explicitly overrides it by appending a different command to the docker run command line. (01:13:52)
