Q: State the habit the instructor said to build in a branch workflow before running git add and git commit. A: Check which branch you are on right before you run git add, and definitely before you run git commit. (00:08:08)
Q: State what the instructor said to do with main when you are actively collaborating, before you start making changes. A: Pull main so everything is up to date, so you aren’t making changes to something out of date. (00:08:27)
Q: Name the command the instructor used to create and switch to the new branch today. A: git switch -c today. (00:08:57)
Q: Name the command the instructor ran to see his changes to README.md before staging them. A: git diff. (00:09:25)
Q: Quote the commit message the instructor used on the today branch. A: “today we are talking about containers”. (00:09:25)
Q: Name the command that pushed the today branch to GitHub. A: git push origin today. (00:09:44)



4. GitHub issues as a project board
00:09:50–00:16:17

Q: What did the instructor say GitHub issues are for? A: Tracking what is happening in your project. They act as a very simple project board. (00:10:08)
Q: Which later MDS course did the instructor say will cover issues in more depth? A: DSCI 524. (00:10:08)
Q: What did the instructor say you should document as issues in a group project? A: Who is responsible for what. (00:10:28)
Q: State how the MDS team uses the issue board of one of its internal repositories. A: To keep meeting notes. Action items from the meeting are then created as separate issues that spawn from the notes issue. (00:10:49)
Q: Name the topics of issue #1 and issue #2 in the 2026-11-19-docker demo repository. A: Issue #1 asked what today’s topic is (“what are we doing today?”), and issue #2 was “edit the readme with today’s topic”. (00:11:37)
Q: State how GitHub numbers issues and pull requests in a repository. A: They share one numbering sequence. If you create an issue and then a pull request, the pull request gets the next number. (00:12:07)
Q: What do you type in an issue or pull request to refer to another item, and what kind of link does it create? A: A hash followed by the number, such as #1. It creates a two-way reference, so the other item links back automatically. (00:13:34)
Q: What did the instructor name as one of the reasons GitHub, as opposed to Git, became so popular? A: Issues and pull requests that link to each other automatically, so you can track everything as a project management system. (00:13:47)
Q: What does the instructor ask a coding agent to do when he has a random idea while working? A: File an issue for it, so he doesn’t have to tab over to a browser and lose track. (00:13:24)
Q: How many issues does the lab ask for, and how many pull requests may deal with them? A: Three issues, and it’s okay if one pull request deals with all three. (00:14:23)
Q: Who do you typically assign to your own pull request, and where do teammates go? A: You assign yourself, because it is your pull request. Teammates go in the separate reviewer section. (00:14:47)
Q: Who did the instructor assign as a reviewer on the demo pull request? A: Copilot. (00:15:14)



5. Pull request descriptions, checkboxes and closing keywords
00:16:17–00:22:18

Q: Which comment of an issue or pull request did the instructor say must be kept up to date? A: The first comment. People reading it want to know what is happening and why the thing exists, not read the whole conversation. (00:16:56)
Q: Who did the instructor say can typically edit other people’s comments on an issue? A: You, as the project owner. (00:16:51)
Q: Name the Markdown feature the instructor used in a pull request to track items still to do. A: Checkboxes, written with Markdown checkbox notation such as - [ ] item. (00:17:49)
Q: Besides checkboxes, which pull request button did the instructor mention for showing that work isn’t finished? A: The draft button. (00:17:49)
Q: Name the two pull request keywords the instructor said he knows for referring to issues. A: closes and fixes. (00:18:33)
Q: Is the closing-keyword behaviour a Git feature or a GitHub feature? A: A GitHub feature, not a feature of the Git version control system. (00:18:54)
Q: What happens when a pull request whose description says fixes #2 is merged? A: GitHub automatically closes issue #2. (00:19:30)
Q: Which closing keyword does the instructor almost always use? A: fixes. (00:19:55)
Q: Besides the pull request description, where else did the instructor say you can write a closing keyword, and what is the drawback? A: In a commit message, but it is harder to see there. (00:19:55)
Q: Quote the first line of the description of pull request #3 in the 2026-11-19-docker demo repository. A: “this is the fix for #2”. (00:14:14)
Q: Name the title of the pull request that merged the today branch in the 2026-11-19-docker demo repository, and give its number. A: Pull request #3, “today we are talking about containers”. (00:22:53)
Q: Will you be graded on having all your issues closed by the end of the course? A: No. Open issues for stretch goals or longer-term ideas are fine. (00:21:50)



6. Cleaning up after a merge
00:22:18–00:25:19

Q: Name the two commands the instructor ran to bring local main up to date after the pull request was merged. A: git switch main, then git pull origin main. (00:22:25)
Q: Name the two places on GitHub where you can delete a merged branch. A: The delete-branch button on the pull request after merging, or the trash can next to the branch in the branches view. (00:22:53)
Q: Is deleting merged branches required in this course? A: No. You can keep them as a record if you want to. (00:23:16)
Q: Name the command the instructor used to view the commit graph with all branches. A: git log --oneline --graph --all. (00:23:56)
Q: Quote the message of the top commit in the git log --oneline --graph --all output after main was pulled. A: “Merge pull request #3 from chendaniely/today” (commit d25ddfa). (00:23:56)
Q: Name the command that removed the local reference to the today branch that had been deleted on GitHub. A: git fetch --prune, which reported origin/today as [deleted]. (00:24:30)
Q: Name the command that deleted the local today branch, and quote what it printed. A: git branch -d today, which printed “Deleted branch today (was 3c6d82a).” (00:24:30)
Q: What hash did the instructor say you would have to type instead of the branch name if you deleted the today branch? A: 3c6d82a, as in “git switch three c six d eighty two a” instead of git switch today. (00:25:05)



7. Why data science workflows need stable environments (27.1 Documenting and loading dependencies)
00:25:29–00:30:13

Q: What is the title of DSCI 522, as stated in class? A: Data Science Workflows. (00:25:48)
Q: Name the three Python plotting libraries the instructor listed as examples of different project package choices. A: Altair, Plotly and Matplotlib. (00:27:06)
Q: State the rule the instructor gave for a project’s package list. A: Keep it to the bare minimum you need, instead of installing everything. (00:27:38)
Q: List the two problems the instructor named with installing far more packages than you use. A: It wastes disk space. Packages also have different update cycles, so updating everything can leave you unable to install it all. (00:28:04)
Q: Name the two kinds of chips the instructor said Windows machines now come with. A: ARM and Intel. (00:28:53)
Q: Quote the phrase the instructor said doesn’t really work when a teammate can’t run your code. A: “This works on my machine.” (00:29:39)
Q: State the two things the instructor said the course’s tooling is about. A: Creating a stable computing environment, and building modular data science pipelines. (00:29:55)



8. What a container is (27.2 What is a container?)
00:30:13–00:34:28

Q: Which two tools from DSCI 521 did the instructor say already handle keeping packages consistent? A: uv and renv. (00:30:13)
Q: What does a uv lock file let someone else do, according to the instructor? A: At least install the same Python packages. (00:30:40)
Q: Define a container in the instructor’s words. A: A virtual computer built from scratch and given to everyone, so you all do your work on the same computer even on different physical machines. (00:31:49)
Q: Name the workflow the instructor said containers make possible across a laptop and a bigger machine. A: Doing prototype work locally, then running on a bigger machine that has access to all the data, with exactly the same compute environment. (00:32:15)
Q: State the cost of using a container that the instructor mentioned. A: A performance hit, because there is an extra layer on top. (00:32:34)
Q: What happens if you mess up a container used as a sandbox? A: You restart it and get a new sandbox. (00:33:05)
Q: Besides Docker, name the container tools the instructor listed. A: LXC, LXD and Podman. He added that Amazon probably has its own. (00:34:01)
Q: What did the instructor say a cloud provider such as Google gives you when you get an “instance”? A: A container on one of their servers, not an actual machine. Pretty much all cloud compute runs on some version of containers. (00:33:30)



9. Containers versus virtual machines (27.3 Contrasting containers with virtual machines)
00:34:31–00:36:40

Q: Define a virtual machine as the instructor described it. A: A full-blown operating system, such as all of Windows, that you log into with all its buttons and graphical interface. (00:34:48)
Q: What does a container typically not have, compared with a virtual machine? A: A graphical interface. It holds only the bare minimum set of things you install. (00:35:00)
Q: How much disk space did the instructor say a Windows virtual machine takes, and how large are the containers used in class? A: A Windows virtual machine takes about 50 to 80 GB. The containers used in class are less than two gigabytes, or even less than one. (00:36:16)
Q: List the three resources in which the instructor said containers are lighter than virtual machines. A: Disk space, memory usage and compute usage. (00:36:32)
Q: What does the instructor still use virtual machines for? A: Testing the MDS installation instructions, where he has to pretend to be on a Windows machine. (00:36:01)



10. Pulling and running a container: R 4.3.2 beside local R (28.1.1 Launch and run containers)
00:36:40–00:45:01

Q: Name the command the instructor used to download the R 4.3.2 container image. A: docker pull rocker/r-ver:4.3.2. (00:36:55)
Q: What is rocker, and what is installed in its r-ver machines? A: An organization that builds container machines, and these only have R installed. (00:37:22)
Q: Which version of R did R --version report on the instructor’s laptop? A: R 4.6.2. (00:37:32)
Q: What did docker pull rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 print when the image was already on the laptop? A: A Digest: sha256:... hash and “Status: Image is up to date for rocker/r-ver:4.3.2”. (00:39:47)
Q: Name the industry the instructor gave as a real use case for keeping an old R version for years. A: Pharmaceutical companies, for clinical trials research, where the regulator wants your code and the full compute environment. (00:37:58)
Q: How often does R release an update, according to the instructor? A: Every six months. (00:38:10)
Q: What example did the instructor give of a system tool, rather than a package, that a container can pin? A: Git. A container with a Git version from 2019 would prevent anyone from running git switch. (00:39:02)
Q: Which Git command did the instructor say docker pull resembles? A: git pull, because both pull something onto your computer. (00:40:33)
Q: Name the command that started R 4.3.2 in a container in class. A: docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2. (00:40:38)
Q: What does the --rm flag of docker run do? A: It deletes the container when you turn it off. Otherwise you have to delete it manually. (00:40:55)
Q: State what a double dash and a single dash mean in front of a command-line flag. A: A double dash marks a flag that is multiple letters long. A single dash marks single-letter flags, which can be chained together. (00:41:20)
Q: State what each letter in ls -alh stands for, as given in class. A: a for all, l for list, and h for human-readable sizes. (00:41:20)
Q: What do the -i and -t in docker run -it stand for? A: -i is interactive, and -t stands for TTY, which gives you a terminal you can interact with. (00:41:48)
Q: What does docker run do if the image you name is not on your computer yet? A: It downloads the image first. (00:42:16)
Q: What do you type to start R in a terminal? A: A capital letter R. (00:42:38)
Q: Quote the error that library(tidyverse) gave inside the rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 container. A: “there is no package called ‘tidyverse’”. (00:43:49)



11. Know which machine you are typing on
00:45:01–00:46:44

Q: What did the instructor call the main visual cue for knowing which machine you are typing on? A: Your terminal prompt. (00:45:04)
Q: Where was the remote computer whose terminal the instructor showed in class? A: In his closet at home. (00:45:48)
Q: What warning did the instructor give about working in containers and on remote machines? A: Sometimes you are given nothing but a blinking cursor, so you must know where you are typing and check you’re on the machine you think you are. (00:46:08)
Q: Which command did the instructor recall from DSCI 521 for checking which machine you’re on, and what does it report? A: whoami, which reports the username on that computer. (00:46:08)



12. Why so many data science tools run in a browser
00:46:44–00:49:11

Q: Name the framework the instructor said shows up constantly in how applications are built. A: Electron, an application that runs in a browser: they made the browser the application. (00:47:39)
Q: For what kind of machine did the instructor say Jupyter Lab was designed? A: A remote container that can have far more cores and memory than your laptop, while keeping the same browser interface. (00:48:04)
Q: How did the instructor describe VS Code? A: As essentially a giant browser application, which can also run in a container or in a browser. (00:48:33)
Q: Which GitHub button gives you VS Code in a browser? A: The Codespaces button. (00:48:49)



13. Running RStudio in a container and mapping ports (28.1.3 Mapping ports to containers with web apps)
00:54:10–00:58:59

Q: Name the image the instructor used to run RStudio in a container. A: rocker/rstudio:4.4.2. (00:55:06)
Q: What warning did the instructor give about running containers without --rm? A: Each running container takes up RAM, so you can end up with five computers running and a computer that stops working. (00:55:24)
Q: Which port does RStudio use inside the container? A: 8787. (00:55:56)
Q: How did the instructor describe the port numbers that tools choose? A: As very arbitrary: you can pick whatever you want, and 8787 is just the number RStudio picked. (00:56:19)
Q: In -p 8787:8787, which number is the port on your computer and which is the port in the container? A: The left number is the port on your local computer, and the right number is the port inside the container. (00:57:05)
Q: How did the instructor say you can run two RStudio containers at the same time? A: Map each one to a different port on your machine. (00:56:38)
Q: Name the full command that started RStudio in a container in class, before a password was set. A: docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 rocker/rstudio:4.4.2. (00:57:42)
Q: What address did the instructor type in the browser to reach RStudio running in the container? A: localhost:8787. (00:57:51)
Q: What did the RStudio container’s startup output print about passwords? A: A generated password (“The password is set to ooph3Aef2Ohcahcu”), followed by a note that you can set your own with the PASSWORD environment variable. (00:57:51)
Q: What username logs in to the rocker/rstudio container? A: rstudio. (00:58:29)
Q: Which R versions ran in RStudio desktop on the laptop and in the rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 container? A: The desktop ran R 4.6.2 and the container ran R 4.4.2, which also differs from the 4.3.2 r-ver container. (00:58:51)



14. Passing environment variables into a container (27.2 What is a container?)
00:59:20–01:02:53

Q: Which docker run flag passes an environment variable into a container? A: -e. (01:00:05)
Q: Name the environment variable that sets the login password in the rocker/rstudio container. A: PASSWORD, in all caps. (01:00:05)
Q: Name the full command the instructor used to run RStudio with a password he chose. A: docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 -e PASSWORD="apassword" rocker/rstudio:4.4.2. (01:00:39)
Q: Do all containers accept the same environment variables? A: No. It depends on how the container was set up, and not every container has these. (00:59:45)
Q: Who did the instructor say can reach the RStudio running on his 8787 port? A: Only someone with access to his physical machine. If you can’t log into his machine, 8787 is not available to you. (01:00:16)
Q: For which later MDS course and kind of app did the instructor say you can hand people a container to run? A: DSCI 532, where you put your dashboard code in a container that anyone with Docker can run and open at its port. (01:01:47)



15. Starting from a base image and working inside it (28.1.4 Changing the containers default command)
01:03:00–01:08:19

Q: What must you still choose first when you build your own container? A: A starting machine, which can be someone else’s container, such as the rocker/r-ver image that already has R installed. (01:03:51)
Q: Name the command that opened a shell, instead of R, in the R 4.6.2 container. A: docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash. (01:04:44)
Q: What does the rocker/r-ver container run by default when it starts, without a command after the image name? A: R: the R prompt comes up. (01:05:20)
Q: What did the prompt look like inside the rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 container started with bash? A: root@ followed by the container’s ID and :/#, for example root@95765251a970:/#. (01:04:53)
Q: What did the instructor say you should do with install steps that work when tried by hand in a container? A: Start documenting them, so you have the instructions for building the machine from scratch. (01:05:48)
Q: What does the R package cowsay do? A: It draws ASCII art of a cow saying some text. (01:06:08)
Q: Why did the instructor not install tidyverse in the demo container? A: Because it is a super long install. (01:06:03)
Q: Name the two dependencies that install.packages("cowsay") also installed in the container. A: crayon and rlang. (01:06:15)
Q: Name the R call that drew the cow saying hello inside the container. A: cowsay::say('hello'). (01:06:41)
Q: What happened to library(cowsay) after the instructor exited the container and started it again? A: It failed with “there is no package called ‘cowsay’”: the package was gone. (01:07:04)
Q: Does a container keep a saved state between runs? A: No. When you turn it back on, it resets to how it was set up. (01:08:11)
Q: How long did the instructor say tidyverse can take to install on a Linux machine that isn’t set up right? A: About 15 minutes, which is painful when the project itself runs in 30 seconds. (01:08:19)



16. Running R from the command line with Rscript -e (29.1.2 Build your first image)
01:08:19–01:10:18

Q: What did the instructor say saving an install step comes down to? A: Whether you know the terminal command you need to write to make it happen. (01:08:54)
Q: Name the command that lets R run code from the terminal. A: Rscript. (01:09:23)
Q: What does the -e in Rscript -e stand for? A: Expression: you are giving it an R expression to run. (01:09:27)
Q: Name the command that installed cowsay from the container’s shell. A: Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')". (01:09:47)
Q: Which quotes go on the outside and which on the inside in Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')"? A: Double quotes on the outside and single quotes on the inside. (01:09:41)



17. The Dockerfile: FROM, RUN, CMD (29.2 Dockerfile command summary)
01:10:18–01:15:01

Q: Name the special file that holds the instructions for setting up a container, and state its naming convention. A: Dockerfile, which begins with a capital D. (01:10:22)
Q: Which instruction is normally the first line of a Dockerfile, and what does it name? A: FROM, in all caps, which names the starting-point machine. (01:11:17)
Q: Quote the FROM line of the Dockerfile written in class. A: FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2. (01:11:30)
Q: What did the instructor say about starting from an even smaller base image? A: There are bare-minimum Linux containers, but then you have to install every single thing by hand. (01:11:49)
Q: What does the RUN instruction in a Dockerfile hold? A: The bash commands the container runs during the build process. (01:12:44)
Q: Quote the RUN line of the Dockerfile written in class. A: RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')". (01:12:52)
Q: Which Dockerfile instruction did the instructor say is pretty rare, compared with CMD? A: ENTRYPOINT. (01:13:36)
Q: How is a CMD instruction written, compared with a normal bash command? A: As a list of terms instead of words separated by spaces. (01:13:40)
Q: What does CMD set in a Dockerfile? A: The default last thing the machine runs when it starts, which you can override by giving another command such as bash. (01:14:05)
Q: Quote the message the class’s CMD line makes the cow say. A: “Hello from my first image!” (01:13:52)
Q: For a Python project, what did the instructor say the Dockerfile would do to install packages? A: Install uv, copy in the lock files with a copy command, and run uv sync. (01:14:15)
Q: Name the tool, besides your language and packages, that your project container will have to install next week. A: Quarto, which is not installed on the machine. (01:14:40)



18. Building and running your own image (29.1.2 Build your first image)
01:15:01–01:18:44

Q: Name the command the class used to build its first image. A: docker build --tag hello-cowsay .. (01:15:11)
Q: What does the . at the end of docker build --tag hello-cowsay . mean? A: The current directory, where Docker should look for the Dockerfile. (01:15:38)
Q: Which file does docker build look for by default? A: A file named exactly Dockerfile, with a capital D. (01:15:38)
Q: From which directory are milestone commands assumed to be run? A: The root of the repository, so commands can be copy-pasted without changing directories. (01:16:11)
Q: What full image name did the docker build --tag hello-cowsay . output say it was naming the image? A: docker.io/library/hello-cowsay:latest. (01:16:39)
Q: Which command lists every image on your computer? A: docker images. (01:17:01)
Q: How much disk usage did docker images report for hello-cowsay:latest? A: 1.45GB. (01:17:01)
Q: Name the command that ran the new image, and state what it printed. A: docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay, which printed an ASCII cow saying “Hello from my first image!” (01:17:14)
Q: Name the command that opened a shell inside the hello-cowsay image. A: docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay bash. (01:17:28)
Q: What happened when the instructor ran library(cowsay) in R inside the hello-cowsay image? A: It loaded, because the build had installed the package. (01:17:52)
Q: List the kinds of instructions the instructor said fill the middle of a typical Dockerfile. A: Many RUN and copy commands, and port commands where relevant, such as opening 8787. (01:18:07)



19. Pinning versions, and what comes next
01:18:44–01:20:39

Q: Do you need to build containers for this week’s lab assignment? A: No, this week’s lab doesn’t need it. You need it for next week. (01:18:48)
Q: What did the instructor say goes in the placeholder section of a project Dockerfile? A: Your renv setup, which installs, snapshots and loads the packages, or the equivalent for Python. (01:19:02)
Q: What failure did the instructor recall from another of his classes a few weeks earlier? A: He restarted a container without hard-pinned versions, something had updated the day before, and nothing worked. (01:19:55)
Q: How long does a pinned version stay the same in a Dockerfile? A: Until you update that install line yourself. (01:20:27)
Q: What container topic did the instructor say comes next week? A: More on containers, including how to string multiple containers together. (01:20:39)

1. Class setup: Docker Desktop and the pre-lecture docker pull commands (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:00:14–00:01:41

Docker Desktop must be running: on macOS and Windows, open Docker Desktop before running any docker command; if you get an error like “can’t find Docker”, install Docker (the application called Docker) and start it, or the commands will tell you to turn it on.
Pre-lecture pulls: run the three docker pull commands posted in Slack before class so the images are downloaded by the time the session begins — pulling takes a while.

The three images: rocker/r-ver:4.3.2, rocker/rstudio:4.4.2, and quay.io/jupyter/datascience-notebook:2025-03-14 (the Jupyter image is the largest, around 9 GB).

The exercise for the day: practice making a branch, creating a pull request, and merging it, plus working with pull requests and issues.
Why it matters: this is the same workflow you will reuse for every assignment moving forward.

section: 2. Project advice: keep the analysis simple and correct
text:
2. Project advice: keep the analysis simple and correct
00:01:41–00:06:05

Do not make the analysis difficult: the single biggest tip — if your model is a straight line, fit a straight line; resist the urge to add a neural network “to make it your time to shine.”
This course is not model fitting: DSCI 522 is about workflows, so almost no machine-learning code appears in the lectures.
The report is not the point: there is a lot more to do than write a report; keep the analysis short, but still include data-download code, some cleaning, EDA, modelling code, and figures and tables.
Accuracy does not matter, correctness does: a 60%-accurate model is fine, but the data science and ML techniques must be technically correct — for example, do not fit logistic regression to a numeric outcome.
Portfolio projects later: if you want a portfolio piece, build it in parallel, not inside this assignment.
Timeline: it is the same project you build on for three or four weeks; you need a machine-learning project to start with even though no ML code is shown in class; this week’s individual focus is getting everything on Git, next week’s is containers.


[!WARNING]
Over-scoping the project is the common mistake that backfires: the instructor warned that if you turn a simple task into a complicated model now, “you’re going to have a very bad time in about two weeks.” Keep it simple and correct.

text:
3. Git review: branch, commit, and push for the pull-request task
00:06:05–00:09:50

The task: create a repository, bring it onto your local machine (git clone the demo repository), then create a pull request.
Check your branch before committing: in a branch workflow, run git status right before git add and definitely before git commit to confirm which branch you are on; a cheat sheet in the textbook lists commands for moving commits if you accidentally commit on main.
Pull main before you start: in an actively collaborating environment, make sure main is up to date so you are not changing something stale.
The live sequence: edit README.md, git switch -c today to create the branch, git status to confirm you are on today, git diff to show the added line, git add README.md, git commit -m "today we are talking about containers", then git push origin today.
Why this is new since 521: what was single-user in DSCI 521 now matters with multiple people actively working on multiple branches.

title: Containers: Running and Building a Shareable Compute Environment
text:
4. Issues as a project board
00:09:50–00:16:17

Issues track what is happening: a simple view of who is responsible for what; the issue board can even double as meeting notes (MDS keeps meeting notes in the issue board of an internal repository).
Action items spawn issues: write a meeting note, then create separate issues for each to-do and assign them.
Shared numbering: issues and pull requests share one counter (issue #2, then PR #3), so you can reference any item with a hash number, e.g. #1.
Two-way references: referencing #1 from another item creates a back-link automatically; this cross-linking is a big reason GitHub (as a service) became popular.
Ideas and agents: use issues as a dump for random ideas or stretch goals; when working with an agent, you can ask it to file an issue so you do not lose track.
One pull request can close several issues: the class requires three issues, but one pull request is allowed to deal with all three.
Assignment and review: you can assign people to issues and to pull requests; the assign section claims responsibility, while the reviewer section requests a look-over (larger projects can block a merge until a reviewer approves).
Demo repository items: issue #1 what are we doing today? and issue #2 edit the readme with today’s topic.

title: Containers: Running and Building a Shareable Compute Environment
section: 5. Pull-request descriptions, checkboxes, and auto-close keywords
text:
5. Pull-request descriptions, checkboxes, and auto-close keywords
00:16:17–00:22:18

Keep the first comment current: the first comment on an issue or pull request should hold all the context, because people read that and not the later conversation; project owners can edit others’ comments to keep it up to date.
Markdown checkboxes: use - [x] item 1 and - [ ] item 2 in a pull request to track what is done; with the draft button, teammates can see status at a glance.
closes and fixes keywords: a sentence ending in closes #1 or fixes #2 references those issues; when the pull request merges, GitHub auto-closes the referenced issues.
GitHub, not Git: this auto-close is a GitHub service feature, not part of the Git version-control system; you can reference multiple issues or the same one multiple times.
Strategic messages: write the description so that merging the pull request closes all the issues at once instead of clicking close several times; the instructor’s own textbook workflow does this (“fixes #N” in the message closes the issue on merge).
Stretch goals as issues: you can create issues for future ideas; the class does not grade on all issues being closed.
The demo pull request is #3 today we are talking about containers, whose description uses closes #1 fixes #2.

title: Containers: Running and Building a Shareable Compute Environment
section: 6. Merging the pull request and cleaning up branches
text:
6. Merging the pull request and cleaning up branches
00:22:18–00:25:29

Finish on main: after the pull request merges, git switch main and git pull origin main to bring the merge down locally.
Delete the remote branch: on GitHub, after merging there is a “delete branch” button; or use the branches view and click the trash can. This is not required in the class — you may keep branches as a record.
Teams differ: the way shown here is one valid way to work with Git; other teams and companies do it differently.
Clean up local references: git log --oneline --graph --all still shows the branch tip; run git fetch --prune to drop the remote-tracking reference, then git branch -d today to delete the local branch.
Why keep or delete: deleting loses the quick git switch today shortcut, but the merge commit still records that it happened; some keep branches so they do not lose the reference.

title: Containers: Running and Building a Shareable Compute Environment
section: 7. Why containers: a stable, shareable compute environment (27 Introduction to containerization)
text:
7. Why containers: a stable, shareable compute environment (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:25:29–00:33:21

From homework to projects: 522 moves from short, instructor-supplied package files to data-science projects that can last days to years and are often team-based.
Different package needs: each project (R or Python; Altair, Plotly, or Matplotlib) has its own package requirements; you now manage your own list instead of the instructor’s, and keep it to the bare minimum.
Stable for you and others: uv and renv (from 521) keep packages consistent on one machine; Docker goes further so a teammate on a different operating system or CPU architecture (Intel vs ARM, Mac vs Windows) can run the same environment.
“Works on my machine” fails: the goal of the course is a compute environment you can share and run all of your code through, not a private one.
A virtual computer: instead of handing over your machine, build a virtual one (a container) and give everyone that; you can prototype locally and then run the identical environment on a bigger machine.
Sandbox and performance: there is a performance hit from the extra layer; if you break the sandbox you just restart it; it is a safe place to learn to muck around an operating system.
Instances and other tools: cloud “instances” are often containers; besides Docker there are LXC, LXD, Podman, and cloud-specific variants.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Containers: Running and Building a Shareable Compute Environment
section: 8. Containers versus virtual machines (27 Introduction to containerization)
text:
8. Containers versus virtual machines (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:33:21–00:36:47

Virtual machine: a full operating system (for example, a complete Windows install with a graphical interface) that you log into; the instructor still uses VMs, e.g. to test the MDS install while pretending to be on Windows.
Container: a stripped-down environment containing only what you install plus a terminal; it has no graphical interface, which fits the 521 habit of working at the command line.
Size difference: a virtual machine can take 50–80 GB; the containers used in class are under about 1–2 GB and still run a full computational stack.
Performance: containers are lighter in disk, memory, and compute because there is less to run; think of a container as a virtual machine with the full operating system and visual bits removed.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Containers: Running and Building a Shareable Compute Environment
section: 9. Running the R container: docker pull and docker run (27 Introduction to containerization)
text:
9. Running the R container: docker pull and docker run (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:36:47–00:45:01

docker pull rocker/r-ver:4.3.2: the name looks like user/repo:tag; rocker is an organization that builds R-only images, and the tag picks R 4.3.2. Pulling downloads the image, or reports it is up to date and shows a content hash.
Two versions of R: the host has R 4.6.2 (check with R --version), while the container runs R 4.3.2. A real case is a pharmaceutical or clinical-trial analysis where the R version must stay fixed for years, and a drug submission requires the code plus the exact compute environment.
Lock files vs system tools: uv/renv lock files pin package versions but not the tooling itself (for example, the installed version of git); a container pins the system tools too.
docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2: docker run starts a container, pulling the image first if needed; --rm deletes the container when it stops so stopped containers do not pile up; -i keeps input open (interactive) and -t attaches a TTY so R runs interactively; single-letter flags can be chained (-it).
Proof it is a different machine: the container opens R 4.3.2 while the host has 4.6.2; library(tidyverse) fails in the bare container (there is no package called 'tidyverse') but works on the host — two terminals on one computer doing different things.
Know where you are typing: the only cue is the prompt (the container’s prompt looks different from the host’s); this mirrors working on a remote or cloud machine, and is why 521 taught whoami-style checks.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Containers: Running and Building a Shareable Compute Environment
section: 10. Web-app containers: RStudio and browser-first tools (28 Using and running containers)
text:
10. Web-app containers: RStudio and browser-first tools (28 Using and running containers)
00:45:01–00:54:10

Browser-first applications: many data-science tools — JupyterLab at localhost:8888, VS Code, GitHub Codespaces — are built as browser apps (often via Electron) so the same interface can run on a remote machine or in a container.
RStudio as a web app: the rocker/rstudio image runs RStudio Server, which you reach from a browser; it is an easier one to teach than a plain terminal.
Why it matters for 532: a dashboard is a browser app; you can containerize it so an end user only needs Docker to run it.
Same interface, different machine: connecting to the container’s web app is the same idea as connecting to cloud compute.
The class took a five-minute break at this point before continuing with the RStudio container.

title: Containers: Running and Building a Shareable Compute Environment
section: 11. Port mapping the RStudio container (28 Using and running containers)
text:
11. Port mapping the RStudio container (28 Using and running containers)
00:54:10–00:59:14

docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 rocker/rstudio:4.4.2: the RStudio image listens on port 8787; -p host:container maps a local port to the container’s port.
Running it more than once: the container side is fixed at 8787, but you can map it to a different local port (up to roughly 60,000 ports) so multiple RStudio containers run at the same time.
Open it in the browser: go to http://localhost:8787; sign in with username rstudio and the password printed in the terminal (a generated one on the first run).
Confirm it is the container, not the host: local RStudio runs the host’s R (4.6.2), while the containerized RStudio runs a different version (the rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 image) — two independent machines.
Resources: each running container uses RAM; leaving several open can make the machine sluggish, which is why --rm is used.

title: Containers: Running and Building a Shareable Compute Environment
section: 12. Environment variables and running dashboards in containers (28 Using and running containers)
text:
12. Environment variables and running dashboards in containers (28 Using and running containers)
00:59:20–01:03:00

-e PASSWORD="apassword": pass environment variables at run time; the rocker/rstudio image reads PASSWORD to set the login password instead of generating a random one.
Not every container exposes the same variables: behavior depends on how the image was built; more is covered when building containers.
Is the port reachable by others?: the instructor checked that localhost:8787 is only reachable by someone who can log into the host machine — a good habit for verifying what a port mapping actually exposes.
Dashboards in 532: put dashboard code in a container; the end user installs nothing but Docker and runs docker run with the right flags, so all the heavy installation (environment, Quarto, etc.) is already done inside.

title: Containers: Running and Building a Shareable Compute Environment
section: 13. Building interactively: base image and the cowsay package (29 Customizing and building containers)
text:
13. Building interactively: base image and the cowsay package (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:03:00–01:08:46

Start from a base image: even when customizing, pick a starting point; here rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 already has R and the tooling a fresh install would otherwise need (like the compiler setup that Windows and Mac users had to do by hand).
Get a shell, not R: docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash starts bash instead of the image’s default R, so you can run the install commands you plan to document.
Try before you write: run the steps interactively first (install cowsay with install.packages("cowsay"), then cowsay::say('hello')), and only document what actually works.
No persistence: exit the container and any package you installed is gone the next time you start it — a container has no save state and resets to the image; that is also a safe place to run destructive commands or experiment with new packages without harming the real machine.

title: Containers: Running and Building a Shareable Compute Environment
section: 14. Writing the Dockerfile: FROM, RUN, and CMD (29 Customizing and building containers)
text:
14. Writing the Dockerfile: FROM, RUN, and CMD (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:08:46–01:15:01

The Dockerfile: a plain-text file (capital D, no extension) holding the instructions to build the machine; it is version-controlled like a pyproject.toml or lock file (see the Dockerfile the class committed).
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2: the first line sets the base image; you can choose an even smaller, near-bare Linux image and install everything by hand.
RUN: bash commands to run during the build, e.g. RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')"; mind the quoting (double quotes on the outside, single quotes on the inside), because Rscript -e runs an R expression from the command line.
CMD: the default command when the container starts; here CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "cowsay::say('Hello from my first image!')"] so the image prints the message; ENTRYPOINT is the rarer alternative for fixed commands.
COPY + uv sync: for a Python image you would COPY in your lock files and run uv sync so the packages are installed at build time; next week you will install the language, Quarto, and packages the same way.

section: 15. Building and running the hello-cowsay image (29 Customizing and building containers)

15. Building and running the hello-cowsay image (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:15:01–01:18:44

docker build --tag hello-cowsay .: --tag (or -t) names the image; the . is the build context / current directory where Docker looks for the Dockerfile.
Run from the repository root: the . convention assumes you run commands from the directory root — the same assumption used in the milestone-one instructions.
Check it built: docker images lists local images, including hello-cowsay:latest and its disk size (about 1.45 GB).
Run it: docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay executes the CMD (the cowsay message); docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay bash drops you into a shell where library(cowsay) now works, proving the RUN step baked the package into the image.

section: 16. Version pinning and wrap-up (29 Customizing and building containers)
text:
16. Version pinning and wrap-up (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:18:44–01:20:39

Pin your tooling: add a placeholder for the uv/renv setup and pin the Quarto version (or any tool version, e.g. an older Quarto) so the image installs exactly those versions.
Control what updates: as long as you do not change the install line, a year from now you are still on the same tool versions.
The Dockerfile as the control point: you say “here is the version I want; it will not change until I update that line.”
Next time: this was an introduction to containers (using and building them); the next class builds on it, including stringing multiple containers together and the sections listed as not reached.


[!WARNING]
Do not let tool versions float. The instructor recounted restarting a container without hard-version-pinning its tools, where an overnight update broke everything and hours were spent fixing the update instead of doing the work. Pin the versions in the Dockerfile so an unexpected update cannot silently break a validated build.

section: 2. Project advice: keep the analysis simple
text:
2. Project advice: keep the analysis simple
00:01:41–00:05:57

The biggest tip: do not make your analysis difficult. If a straight line fits, fit the straight line model. Don’t treat the project as your “time to shine” with a neural net.
This is not a modelling course: the course is about workflows, and there is almost no machine learning code in the lectures. The report is not the point of the class.
What the project still needs: code that downloads the data, possibly cleaning code, EDA code, modelling code, and figures and tables. All of it should stay very simple.
Correctness still counts: model performance doesn’t matter (60% accuracy is fine), but the techniques must be correct data science. Fitting logistic regression to predict a numeric outcome, for example, is simply wrong.
Portfolio ambitions: if you want a portfolio piece, build it separately and in parallel, not in this assignment.
Schedule: this week’s work is getting everything onto Git, and next week is containers. It is the same project, built up over three or four weeks.

section: 4. GitHub issues as a project board
text:
4. GitHub issues as a project board
00:09:50–00:16:17

What issues are for: tracking what is happening in a project, as a simple project board. The course practises them now, and DSCI 524 covers them further.
Who does what: document who is responsible for what as issues.

The MDS team uses an internal repository’s issues for meeting notes.
Action items from a meeting become separate issues spawned from the notes issue.

Demo issues:

Issue #1 what are we doing today? asked “what is today’s topic?”.
Issue #2 edit the readme with today’s topic referred back with “meeting from #1”.

Shared numbering: issues and pull requests use one counter. After two issues, the next pull request is number 3.
Two-way references: typing #1 in an issue or pull request links to item 1, and item 1 automatically shows a link back. This automatic linking is a big part of why GitHub became popular, beyond Git itself.
Idea dump: issues are a fine place for stray ideas such as “maybe a neural net later” or stretch goals.

The instructor sometimes asks a coding agent to file an issue for a passing thought, so he doesn’t have to switch to a browser and lose focus.

Assignees and reviewers: you can assign people to issues and to pull requests.

You normally assign yourself to your own pull request, which claims it as your responsibility.
Teammates go in the separate reviewer section. Some projects block merging until someone has reviewed.
In the demo the instructor added Copilot as a reviewer.

One pull request, many issues: it doesn’t have to be one issue, one branch, one pull request. The lab asks for three issues, and one pull request may deal with all three.

title: Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers
section: 5. Pull request descriptions, checkboxes and closing keywords
text:
5. Pull request descriptions, checkboxes and closing keywords
00:16:17–00:22:18

Keep the first comment current: edit the opening comment as decisions are made. Readers want to know “why does this exist?” from the top, not by reading the whole conversation. Project owners can usually edit others’ comments too.
Markdown checkboxes: - [ ] item lists track what is still to do. They show teammates the work isn’t finished, as an alternative or complement to marking the pull request as a draft.
Closing keywords: a sentence with closes #1 or fixes #2 in a pull request makes merging that pull request auto-close those issues. This is a GitHub feature, not a Git feature.
The demo pull request: #3 today we are talking about containers had this description:
this is the fix for #2

- [x] item 1
- [ ] item 2

closes #1 fixes #2
Did closes work? In class the instructor wasn’t sure closes had taken effect. He usually uses fixes. The demo repository shows both #1 and #2 closed by #3.
Commit messages work too: keywords also work in commit messages, but they are harder to see there.
The payoff: the issues tab shrinks as work merges. The instructor’s textbook workflow is to file an issue, work, write “fixes #N” in the pull request, then pick the next issue from the list.

One textbook refactor of the containers and virtual environments chapters fixed several issues in a single pull request.

Grading: you won’t be graded on closing all your issues. Open stretch-goal issues are fine.

text:
6. Cleaning up after a merge
00:22:18–00:25:19

Update local main: git switch main, then git pull origin main, which fast-forwarded to the merge commit.
Delete the remote branch: after merging, click the delete-branch button on the pull request. Alternatively, go to the branches view, find the merged branch (it shows pull request #3, merged) and click the trash can.
Optional in this course: you don’t have to delete branches, and you may keep them as a record. Teams and companies differ a lot in how they use Git; this is one way, and others are variations on it.
Remove stale references locally:

git fetch --prune drops the origin/today reference to the branch deleted on GitHub.
git branch -d today deletes the local branch.

The history stays: the merge commit and its parent are still in the graph. You only lose the shortcut name. That is why some people keep branches: git switch today is easier than switching to 3c6d82a.

title: Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers
section: 7. Why data science workflows need stable environments (27.1 Documenting and loading dependencies)
text:
7. Why data science workflows need stable environments (27.1 Documenting and loading dependencies)
00:25:29–00:30:13

What changes now: until now, assignments came with a ready-made package list. Projects last longer than a homework assignment and involve other people.
Each project differs: groups choose their own language and libraries, such as Python or R, and Altair, Plotly or Matplotlib. You adapt the environment to the project, as you would at a company.
Bare-minimum package lists: don’t install everything.

It wastes disk space.
Packages update on different cycles, so a big environment can become impossible to install all at once.

Two stability goals:

Keep your own environment stable over days, weeks, months or years.
Make it reproducible on a teammate’s machine that may run a different OS, or even a different chip. Macs and Windows machines differ, and Windows itself now ships on both ARM and Intel.

“It works on my machine” isn’t enough: the course’s tooling is about stable computing environments and modular pipelines that others can run.

title: Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers
section: 8. What a container is (27.2 What is a container?)
text:
8. What a container is (27.2 What is a container?)
00:30:13–00:34:28

Where uv/renv stop: DSCI 521 covered uv and renv, which keep package versions consistent. A uv.lock file lets someone install your Python packages, but they still need uv installed and a similarly set-up computer.
The container idea: “here’s my computer”. You build a virtual computer from scratch, give it to everyone, and everyone runs their code on it, even on different physical machines. See 27.4 Contrasting common computational environment virtualization strategies and 27.5 Virtualization strategy advantages and disadvantages for reproducibility.
Prototype locally, run big: the same environment can run on your laptop and on a larger machine that holds all the data.
Cost: there is a performance hit from the extra layer.
Sandboxing: remote machines’ admins may not let you install software directly, but they can hand you a container to play in. If you break it, you restart it and get a fresh sandbox. It is the safe place to muck around with an operating system.
Tools: the course uses Docker. LXC, LXD and Podman are alternatives, and cloud providers have their own.

title: Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers
section: 9. Containers versus virtual machines (27.3 Contrasting containers with virtual machines)
text:
9. Containers versus virtual machines (27.3 Contrasting containers with virtual machines)
00:34:31–00:36:40

Virtual machine: a full-blown operating system, such as all of Windows, with its graphical interface and buttons.
Container: a stripped-down version with typically no graphical interface. It holds only the bare minimum you install. This is why DSCI 521 pushed typing commands, since sometimes the terminal is the only interface you get.
Size and performance: a Windows VM can take 50–80 GB. The containers used in class are a couple of GB or less yet run a full computational stack. They are lighter on disk, memory and compute.
VMs still have uses: the instructor uses one to test the MDS install instructions as if on Windows.

title: Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers
section: 10. Pulling and running a container: R 4.3.2 beside local R (28.1.1 Launch and run containers)
text:
10. Pulling and running a container: R 4.3.2 beside local R (28.1.1 Launch and run containers)
00:36:40–00:45:01

docker pull rocker/r-ver:4.3.2: downloads an image. The name looks like a GitHub user/repo because it works similarly. rocker is the organisation, and these images have only R installed. The tag 4.3.2 picks the R version. If the image is already present, the output says “Image is up to date” and shows a digest hash.
Two R versions at once: R --version on the laptop shows R 4.6.2, and the container gives R 4.3.2.
Real-world case: in pharmaceutical work, clinical trials research runs for years while R updates every six months. Regulators can ask for your code and the full compute environment, so you hand over the container that ran the analysis.
Beyond lock files: lock files pin packages; containers pin the tools themselves, such as R or Git. A container with an old Git could even prevent anyone from using git switch.
Similar names across tools: docker pull echoes git pull because tools borrow each other’s vocabulary.
docker run flags:

--rm: a double dash marks a multi-letter flag. When the container stops, it is deleted automatically; otherwise you delete it by hand.
-it: single-letter flags can be chained, as in ls -alh. -i is interactive and -t allocates a terminal (TTY). You’ll see -it everywhere.
The image name comes last. docker run also downloads the image if it isn’t present.

Isolation shown: in the container, library(tidyverse) fails because the image has only R. In a local terminal, tidyverse loads fine. Two terminals on one laptop behave like two different machines.

section: 11. Know which machine you are typing on
text:
11. Know which machine you are typing on
00:45:01–00:46:44

Read your prompt: after quitting the container, the laptop’s own prompt returns. The prompt is often your only visual cue.
Same idea remotely: the instructor opened a terminal on a machine in his closet at home. The only clue was the hostname he’d given it.
Why whoami exists: it reports the username on that computer, which is another way to confirm you’re on the machine you think you are.
Applies everywhere: the same habit matters in containers and on remote cloud systems.


[!WARNING]
With containers and remote machines you are sometimes given nothing but a blinking cursor. Check your prompt (or whoami) before running commands, so you don’t run something on the wrong machine.

section: 12. Why so many data science tools run in a browser
text:
12. Why so many data science tools run in a browser
00:46:44–00:49:11

Applications as browsers: many desktop apps are built on Electron, which is essentially a browser packaged as an app.
Why: a browser-first application can run inside a container or on a remote machine while you view it in your local browser.
Jupyter Lab: you open it at a localhost address because it was designed to run on remote machines with more cores and memory but the same interface.
VS Code: it is effectively a big browser app. GitHub’s Codespaces button gives you VS Code in a browser, running on a machine whose whole compute environment someone has set up.

section: 13. Running RStudio in a container and mapping ports (28.1.3 Mapping ports to containers with web apps)
text:
13. Running RStudio in a container and mapping ports (28.1.3 Mapping ports to containers with web apps)
00:54:10–00:58:59

Jupyter users too: projects are written in Quarto, but the same setup applies if you prefer a Jupyter interface.
Keep --rm: each running container uses RAM. Without it you can end up with “five computers” running and a laptop that grinds to a halt.
Ports: like Jupyter Lab on 8888, RStudio Server listens on 8787 inside the container. The numbers are arbitrary choices by the tool’s developers.
-p host:container: the left number is the port on your machine and the right is the port in the container. -p 8787:8787 puts the container’s 8787 on the laptop’s 8787. To run RStudio twice, map the second container to a different host port.
Open it: go to localhost:8787 in the browser. The username is rstudio, and the start-up output prints a generated password.
Different machines again: this RStudio runs R 4.4.2 in the container. The desktop RStudio runs the laptop’s R 4.6.2, and the earlier r-ver container ran R 4.3.2.


[!WARNING]
Running containers without --rm, or leaving several running, keeps using your computer’s RAM. Use --rm so a container is cleaned up when you exit.

title: Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers
section: 14. Passing environment variables into a container
text:
14. Passing environment variables into a container
00:59:20–01:02:53

-e NAME=value: passes an environment variable into the container. rocker/rstudio reads PASSWORD, so -e PASSWORD="apassword" replaces the hard-to-remember generated password (see the RStudio exercise in 27.2 What is a container?).
Container-specific: not every container supports the same variables. It depends on how the image was built, so check its documentation.
Showing the password is fine here: the port is only reachable from the instructor’s own machine. If you can’t log into his laptop, his 8787 isn’t available to you.
Looking ahead to DSCI 532: a dashboard runs in a browser. Put the dashboard code in a container and anyone with Docker can docker run it and visit the port. They skip the whole install process (renv, snapshots and so on) because you’ve given them a computer you built from scratch.

section: 15. Starting from a base image and working inside it (29.1.1 Workflow for building a Dockerfile)
text:
15. Starting from a base image and working inside it (29.1.1 Workflow for building a Dockerfile)
01:03:00–01:08:19

Start from someone else’s machine: when building your own container you still pick a starting machine. rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 already has R plus the system pieces R needs, the equivalent of the compiler tools students installed on their laptops. That saves steps.
Override the default command: docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash gives a shell instead of R. The prompt changes to the container’s (root@<id>:/#), and you can still type R to start R (see 28.1.4 Changing the containers default command).
Try first, then document: test install steps interactively, and once they work, write them down as the build instructions.
Demo: install.packages("cowsay") in the container’s R, then cowsay::say('hello') drew an ASCII cow. The instructor used cowsay instead of tidyverse because tidyverse takes far too long to install.
No saved state: after exiting and starting the container again, library(cowsay) failed with “there is no package called ‘cowsay’”. A container resets to how its image was built every time.
A good place to experiment: even destructive commands from DSCI 521 are safe in a container, because restarting gives a clean machine.
The problem this creates: making users follow README install steps inside a container every time is painful, for example a 15-minute tidyverse install for a 30-second analysis.

16. Running R from the command line with Rscript -e (29.1.2 Build your first image)
01:08:19–01:10:18

The key question: do you know the terminal command that makes the install happen? Build steps have to be shell commands.
Rscript: runs R code from the shell. -e means “here is an R expression”.
The command: Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')". Note the quoting: double quotes outside and single quotes inside.
Confirmed, then lost: R in that container could library(cowsay) afterwards. Exiting and re-entering lost it again, so the information has to be saved somewhere.

section: 17. The Dockerfile: FROM, RUN, CMD (29.2 Dockerfile command summary)
text:
17. The Dockerfile: FROM, RUN, CMD (29.2 Dockerfile command summary)
01:10:18–01:15:01

Dockerfile: a special file named with a capital D. It holds the instructions for installing and setting up the computer. The rocker images have their own Dockerfiles, which is how RStudio comes installed with its port open. See also 27.6 Container usage workflow.
FROM (all caps): normally the first line. It names the starting machine, here rocker/r-ver:4.6.2.

You could start from a bare-minimum Linux and install everything yourself. That is a good learning project for a break.
Disk space is relatively cheap, so a beefier base image is acceptable.

RUN: the shell commands the image runs during the build, here the same Rscript -e line tested by hand.
CMD: what a container from the image runs by default.

It is written as a list instead of space-separated words.
It runs only if you don’t give another command such as bash, which overrides it.
ENTRYPOINT also exists, but the instructor called it rare.

The class’s file (Dockerfile):
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2

RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')"

CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "cowsay::say('Hello from my first image!')"]
For a Python project: the RUN section would install uv, COPY in the lock files and run uv sync. Next week, project containers also install the language and Quarto.

title: Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers
section: 18. Building and running your own image (29.1 Building container images from Dockerfile’s)
text:
18. Building and running your own image (29.1 Building container images from Dockerfile’s)
01:15:01–01:18:44

docker build --tag hello-cowsay .: --tag names the image.

The . is the directory to build from, the current one. It may be the first time a lone . is something you must type.
Docker looks for a file named exactly Dockerfile there.

Run from the project root: you can point docker build at another path. Milestone instructions assume every command runs from the repository root, so commands can be copy-pasted without changing directories (see 29.4 Dockerfile FAQ).
docker images: lists every image on your machine, including the new hello-cowsay.
Run it: docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay prints the cow message from CMD.
Shell access: docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay bash gives a shell inside the image, which is useful when something “works on my machine but not in the container”. There, library(cowsay) now loads, because the build installed it.
Typical shape: one FROM, a middle section of many RUN and COPY lines (and port instructions where relevant), and a CMD. Writing it all depends on knowing shell commands.

section: 19. Pinning versions, and what comes next
text:
19. Pinning versions, and what comes next
01:18:44–01:20:39

Next week: this week’s lab doesn’t need any of this. Next week’s work does.
Pin the language: the FROM line pins the R version. A placeholder section would then hold the renv or uv setup that installs the packages.
Pin the tools: you can choose a specific, even older, Quarto version. A year later you are still on the same versions, as long as you don’t touch that install line.
A real failure: in another class a few weeks earlier, the instructor restarted a container without hard-pinned versions. Something had updated the day before, and nothing worked. Hours of fixing an update instead of doing the real work is why you control what updates and when.
Coming up: more on building containers, and stringing several containers together.


[!WARNING]
If you don’t pin versions in your container, an upstream update can break everything overnight, as it did in the instructor’s other class. Install explicit versions and change them only when you mean to.

27.7 Image vs container?
Analogy: The program Chrome is like a Docker image, whereas a Chrome window is like a Docker container.

You can list the container images on your computer that you pulled using Docker via docker images. After pulling the images for this chapter, the list includes these three, and any other images you have:
Terminal
docker images
Output
IMAGE                                             ID             DISK USAGE   CONTENT SIZE   EXTRA
quay.io/jupyter/datascience-notebook:2025-03-14   bf25d19758c0       9.06GB         2.17GB        
rocker/r-ver:4.3.2                                4e32addfc4da       1.11GB          313MB        
rocker/rstudio:4.4.2                              6bfc87fb66d0       3.16GB          734MB        
DISK USAGE is how much space an image takes on your computer, and CONTENT SIZE is about how much was downloaded.
You can list the states of containers that have been started by Docker on your computer (and not yet removed) via docker ps -a. Here, the R container from the first exercise and the RStudio container from the second are both running:
Terminal
docker ps -a
Output
CONTAINER ID   IMAGE                  COMMAND   CREATED        STATUS                  PORTS                                         NAMES
adf3ea77f63f   rocker/rstudio:4.4.2   "/init"   1 second ago   Up Less than a second   0.0.0.0:8787->8787/tcp, [::]:8787->8787/tcp   objective_hoover
adca5933388b   rocker/r-ver:4.3.2     "R"       1 second ago   Up Less than a second                                                 hardcore_swartz

text:
27.8 What is a container registry?
A container registry is a remote repository, or collection of repositories, used to share container images. This is similar to remote version control repositories for sharing code. Instead of code, however, it is container images that are pushed and pulled to/from there. For this course we will focus on the widely used Docker Hub container registry: https://hub.docker.com/.
However, there are many container registries that can be used, including:

https://github.com/
https://quay.io/
https://aws.amazon.com/ecr/

In the examples above, we have used the rocker/rstudio container, which comes from Docker Hub, and the Jupyter server comes from quay.io.
Exercise
Exploring container registries
Let’s visit the repositories for the two container images that we used in the exercise earlier in class:

rocker/rstudio
quay.io/jupyter/datascience-notebook

Question: you pulled these images with docker pull before you started. What would docker run ... have done if you had not?
Answer: docker run ... will first look for images you have locally, and run those if they exist. If they do not exist, it then attempts to pull the image from the registry named in the image (Docker Hub, if the image name does not name a registry).

28.1.2 Mounting volumes to containers
Oftentimes, we want to use the software made available to us in containers on files on our computers. To do this, we need to explicitly tell Docker to mount a volume to the container. We can do this via: -v <path_to_local_computer_directory>:<absolute_path_to_container_directory>.
Often, we want to mount the volume from our current directory (where we are working), and we can do that with $(pwd), which prints the current directory, in place of the path to our computer’s directory. This is a useful shorthand command when you work with multiple people, so the same command will work on different computers since you are not hard-coding the local computer path.
To mount our current directory at /workspace in a container from the ubuntu:24.04 image, we type the following on our laptop:

macOS and Linux
Windows (Git Bash)
Windows (PowerShell)

Terminal
docker run --rm -it -v "$(pwd):/workspace" ubuntu:24.04
Terminal
docker run --rm -it -v "/$(pwd):/workspace" ubuntu:24.04
docker run --rm -it -v "${PWD}:/workspace" ubuntu:24.04
Then, at the container’s prompt, go to the directory where you mounted your files and list them:
Terminal
cd /workspace
ls
Output
hello.R
Here, the current directory on the laptop held one file, hello.R.
Why /$(pwd) in Git Bash?
Git Bash turns command-line arguments that start with / into Windows paths, so /workspace could reach Docker as C:/Program Files/Git/workspace. Doubling the first slash stops that (see “Known issues” in the Git for Windows release notes). /$(pwd) does it for the mount, and a path inside the container, such as /workspace/hello.R below, is written //workspace/hello.R in Git Bash.
Note
If you are mounting volumes to a container from a Docker image that runs a web app, be sure to read the documentation to see where you should mount that volume. Usually, the web apps are only exposed to certain directories, and you will only be able to access the files in the mounted volume if you mount them to the correct place. For example, in the rocker/rstudio image that we loaded earlier, volumes need to be mounted within /home/rstudio/ to be able to access them via the RStudio Server web app.

Windows notes for mounting volumes

Windows machines need to explicitly share drives with Docker. This should be part of your computer setup!
On Windows, the laptop path depends on what shell you are using. Here are some details:

If you are going to run it in Windows terminal, then the command to share the current directory should be:

Terminal
docker run --rm -it -v /$(pwd):<PATH_ON_CONTAINER> <IMAGE_NAME>

If you are going to run it in PowerShell, then the command should be:

Terminal
docker run --rm -it -v <ABSOLUTE_PATH_ON_YOUR_COMPUTER>:<PATH_ON_CONTAINER> <IMAGE_NAME>
(pwd and variants do not seem to work). And the path must be formatted like: C:\Users\tiffany.timbers\Documents\project\:/home/project




28.1.5 Use a container to execute a script
What if, instead of running the container interactively, we wanted to run a script? Let’s take this R script, named hello.R, shown below, which prints the version of R that runs it, and a summary of a column of R’s built-in mtcars data:
# hello.R
cat("Hello from", R.version.string, "\n")
summary(mtcars$mpg)
Assuming that script is in our current working directory, we can mount the directory and then run the script with Rscript in a container from the rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 image:

macOS and Linux
Windows (Git Bash)
Windows (PowerShell)

Terminal
docker run --rm -v "$(pwd):/workspace" rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 Rscript /workspace/hello.R
Terminal
docker run --rm -v "/$(pwd):/workspace" rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 Rscript //workspace/hello.R
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/workspace" rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 Rscript /workspace/hello.R
This should result in:
Output
Hello from R version 4.3.2 (2023-10-31) 
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  10.40   15.43   19.20   20.09   22.80   33.90 
The script ran with R 4.3.2, the version in the image, whatever version of R your computer has.
Now, that was a small example, but the same docker run command can run a whole analysis non-interactively. Python and R in one image uses it to render a project’s reports in Python and R.

28.2 Docker command-line commands
The table below summarizes the Docker commands we have learned so far and can serve as a useful reference when we are using Docker:

28.2.1 Docker commands







command/flag
What it does




pull
Downloads a Docker image from Docker Hub


images
Tells you what container images are installed on your machine


rmi
Deletes a specified container image from your machine


ps -a
Tells you what containers are on your machine, including stopped ones


stop
Stops a specified running container


rm
Removes a specified stopped container


run
Launches a container from an image


exit
Exits a Docker container





28.2.2 Docker run commands







command/flag
What it does




-it
Tells Docker to run the container interactively


--rm
Makes a container ephemeral (deletes it upon exit)


-v
Mounts a volume of your computer to the Docker container


-p
Specifies the ports to map a web app to


-e
Sets environment variables in the container (e.g., PASSWORD=“apassword”)





29.1.3 Layer caching
Docker saves each step’s result as a layer, and reuses a layer when nothing in its step, or in the steps above it, has changed. To see this, change only the message on the CMD line of the Dockerfile:
CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "cowsay::say('Moo! Only my message changed.')"]
Then build again:
Terminal
docker build --tag hello-cowsay .
Output

This is why a Dockerfile puts the steps that change least often, such as installing software, near the top, and the steps that change most often near the bottom. A change to one step rebuilds that step and every step below it.
docker image ls lists the image, and docker history lists its layers, newest first (head -5 keeps the first five lines):

docker image ls hello-cowsay

The top two rows are the layers our Dockerfile added. The RUN layer holds the 4.17MB of R packages, and it shows that Docker ran the command with /bin/sh -c. The CMD layer adds no files, only the default command, so its size is 0B. The rows below come from rocker/r-ver:4.6.2, including its CMD ["R"], which our CMD replaces.
More information
Docker runs RUN commands with the shell /bin/sh, not Bash, unless the Dockerfile picks another shell with the SHELL instruction (see Docker’s Dockerfile reference). For commands like these, the two shells behave the same.


29.1.4 Guidelines for RUN commands
Each RUN command creates a new layer in the Docker image. Each layer in a Docker image takes more disk space. As a consequence, we want to minimize the number of layers where reasonably possible. How can we do this?
Install everything that can be installed by a tool (e.g., apt-get, or install.packages() in R) at once (i.e., when installing 5 programs via apt-get, do not call apt-get five times; instead do: apt-get install tool1 tool2 tool3 tool4 tool5, and in R, install.packages(c("pkg1", "pkg2"))). However, doing this can lead to long lines. In response, we can break a single command across lines in the shell by using the \ character. For example, to reduce the long line below, which uses apt-get to install the programs Git, Tiny Nano, Less, and wget:
Terminal
apt-get install --yes git nano-tiny less wget
We can use \ after each program to break the long command across lines and make the command more readable (especially if there were even more programs to install). Similarly, we indent the lines after \ to increase readability:
Terminal
apt-get install --yes \
    git \
    nano-tiny \
    less \
    wget
We can also group together related commands that depend upon each other. When doing this, we need to be careful, though, as sometimes we don’t want to run a command if the command that was run immediately before it failed. We can specify this in the shell using &&. For example, if we want to not run apt-get installation commands if apt-get update failed, we can write:
Terminal
apt-get update && \
    apt-get install --yes git


29.2.1 CMD or ENTRYPOINT?
Both set what a container runs when it starts. They differ in what docker run can replace. A command after the image name in docker run replaces CMD. For example, this runs R --version in the hello-cowsay image in place of its cowsay message (head -1 keeps the first line):
Terminal
docker run --rm hello-cowsay R --version | head -1
Output
R version 4.6.2 (2026-10-29) -- "Diversified Portfolio"
ENTRYPOINT is not replaced this way. Anything after the image name is passed to it as arguments, and replaces only CMD. With both, ENTRYPOINT holds the part that always runs, and CMD holds the default arguments. For example, this Dockerfile, in a folder of its own, always runs Rscript -e, with cowsay R code as the default:
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2

RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')"

ENTRYPOINT ["Rscript", "-e"]
CMD ["cowsay::say('Hello from my first image!')"]
Terminal
docker build --tag cowsay-entrypoint .
docker run --rm cowsay-entrypoint
Output
 ____________________________ 
< Hello from my first image! >
 ---------------------------- 
      \
       \

        ^__^ 
        (oo)\ ________ 
        (__)\         )\ /\ 
             ||------w|
             ||      ||
Passing different R code replaces the default, but still runs it with Rscript -e:
Terminal
docker run --rm cowsay-entrypoint "cowsay::say('Only the R code changed.')"
Output
 __________________________ 
< Only the R code changed. >
 -------------------------- 
      \
       \

        ^__^ 
        (oo)\ ________ 
        (__)\         )\ /\ 
             ||------w|
             ||      ||
The images in this book, rocker/r-ver among them, set only CMD, so that a command such as bash after the image name replaces it, as in step 3 of the workflow.

29.3.1 Good base images to work from for R or Python projects!



Image
Software installed




rocker/r-ver
Ubuntu Linux and R; the base of this book’s R examples


rocker/rstudio
R, RStudio


rocker/tidyverse
R, R packages (including the tidyverse), RStudio, Make; ARM-based computers need tag 4.5.1 or later


ubuntu

python
Debian Linux and Python; the -slim tags leave out software most projects do not need

Use rocker/tidyverse:4.5.1 or later
rocker/tidyverse images before 4.5.1 were built only for Intel and AMD computers (amd64). From 4.5.1 on, they are also built for ARM computers (arm64), such as Macs with Apple silicon. On an ARM computer, pulling an older tag fails:
Terminal
docker pull rocker/tidyverse:4.5.0
Output
Error response from daemon: no matching manifest for linux/arm64/v8 in the manifest list entries: no match for platform in manifest: not found
So use 4.5.1 as the minimum version. The rocker/tidyverse tags page lists each tag with the platforms it was built for (linux/amd64, linux/arm64), so you can check a tag before you use it.
