text:
33.1 Docker Compose to launch containers
It can be fiddly and error-prone to type long commands into the terminal, or a GUI every time you want to launch a container. Even if you are copying and pasting commands, it can be difficult to make changes to long commands because you cannot click to a location to make edits.
A better approach is to use Docker Compose to specify how you want to launch the container. This way, all the parts of your command are saved in a file. This helps document how to run the Docker image, and it can be version controlled as part of a project.
Docker Compose uses a YAML file, specifically named docker-compose.yml, to record how the container should be launched. This file can include details such as:

the Docker image and version to use, or how to build it
how to mount volumes
what ports to map
what environment variables to set

docker run commands are interchangeable with the parameters specified in docker-compose.yml; the compose file makes it easier to manage all the docker run parameters. See this resource that can convert a run command to a compose file: https://www.composerize.com/
Here is the docker-compose.yml file of docker-uv-renv, the project from Python and R in one image:
services:
  analysis-env:
    build: .
    image: docker-uv-renv
    ports:
      # 2222 on your computer, 22 in the container.
      # "127.0.0.1:2222:22" stops others on the same Wi-Fi from reaching it.
      - "2222:22"
    volumes:
      - .:/workspace
      # ro: read-only
      - ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub:/root/.ssh/authorized_keys:ro
Without Docker Compose, building the image and starting the container takes these two commands, from the project folder:
Terminal
docker build --tag docker-uv-renv .
docker run --detach -p 2222:22 -v "$(pwd):/workspace" -v ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub:/root/.ssh/authorized_keys:ro docker-uv-renv
Each part of the docker run command is a line of the file:

services: lists the containers the project runs. This project has one, which it calls analysis-env.
build: . builds the image from the Dockerfile in this folder, like docker build ..
image: docker-uv-renv names the image, like --tag docker-uv-renv.
ports: maps port 2222 on your computer to port 22 in the container, like -p 2222:22. Port 22 is where the container’s ssh server listens. The file uses 2222 on your computer, because your computer may already use 22.
volumes: mounts two things, like the two -v options. .:/workspace mounts the project folder at /workspace. The second line mounts your ssh public key as the list of keys that may log in to the container as root, and ro makes it read-only inside the container. The key is the one from SSH for authentication.

No ssh key yet?
To check that you have the key, list it:
Terminal
ls ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
If ls says No such file or directory, make a key as in SSH for authentication:
Terminal
ssh-keygen -t ed25519
Press Enter to save it in the default place, ~/.ssh/id_ed25519. Make the key before you start the container. If the key is missing when the container starts, Docker makes a folder at ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub instead, and you cannot log in to the container.
Docker Compose reads the paths in the file itself, so the same file works on macOS, Linux and Windows, without the Git Bash /$(pwd) change from the earlier chapters.

title: Docker Containers and Workflow Practices
text:
1. Git Workflow and Project Management

GitHub Issues: Used for tracking tasks, meeting notes, and ideas. Issues and pull requests share a single sequential numbering system.
Auto-closing with Keywords: Writing fixes #N or closes #N in a pull request description automatically closes the corresponding issue when the PR is merged into the target branch.
Branch Cleanup: After merging a pull request, the branch should be deleted on GitHub. Locally, run git fetch --prune to remove stale remote-tracking references, then git branch -d <branch> to delete the local branch.
Keep Analysis Simple: The course prioritizes reproducible workflows over complex statistical modeling. A technically correct, simple analysis is preferred over an over-engineered one that complicates the pipeline.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Docker Containers and Workflow Practices
text:
2. Containerization Fundamentals

What is a Container?: A lightweight, isolated computing environment that virtualizes the operating system user space. Unlike virtual machines, containers share the host OS kernel, lack a graphical interface, and are significantly smaller and faster to start.
Solving “Works on My Machine”: Containers guarantee that everyone uses the exact same versions of programming languages, packages, and system-level dependencies. This eliminates compatibility issues across different host operating systems (macOS, Windows, Linux) and architectures.
Ephemeral State: By default, interactive containers discard all changes upon exit. To persist an environment or installed software, it must be baked into a new container image.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Docker Containers and Workflow Practices
text:
3. Running Containers with Docker

docker run: Launches a container instance from an image.
--rm: Automatically removes the container instance when it stops, preventing stopped containers from piling up and consuming disk space.
-it: Two combined flags. -i keeps standard input open (interactive), and -t allocates a pseudo-TTY terminal.
Port Mapping (-p): Routes network traffic from the host to the container. Format is -p <host_port>:<container_port>. Essential for running web-based IDEs like RStudio or Jupyter inside containers.
Environment Variables (-e): Pass configuration into the container at runtime using -e KEY="VALUE". Commonly used to set passwords or toggle features.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Docker Containers and Workflow Practices
text:
4. Building Custom Images with Dockerfiles

Dockerfile: A plain-text configuration file that instructs Docker on how to build a container image. It builds in layers, starting from a base image.
Key Instructions:

FROM: Specifies the base image to build upon (e.g., rocker/r-ver:4.6.2).
RUN: Executes shell commands during the image build process (e.g., installing packages).
CMD: Sets the default command that runs when a container is launched from the new image.

Building and Caching: Use docker build --tag <name> . to build an image from the Dockerfile in the current directory. Docker caches each layer; if a RUN command hasn’t changed, Docker reuses the cached layer, making rebuilds extremely fast.

docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2    # Run interactively; --rm cleans up after exit

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 5 of 5: Evaluate. Decide and justify your verdict before you read the answer; the criteria are the ones given in class.

1. Why branches exist: escaping the pull-before-push friction (8 Git branches)
00:06:49–00:09:43

Q: A teammate proposes that your group skip branches this semester and just all commit to main directly, the way the DSCI 521 shared slide-deck exercise worked, to keep things simple. Judge this plan using the class’s reasoning about collaboration friction. A: Not acceptable. The class standard is that branches let each person work in their own parallel stream, pushing and pulling without the constant “I have to pull before I push” friction that two people editing the same branch create; the instructor identified that friction as a problem that “always” exists in a project and said the group project moves to branches specifically so you “want to work in parallel streams.” (00:08:41)



2. Local repository versus remote origin (8 Git branches)
00:09:46–00:11:11

Q: A student has finished writing their data-cleaning script and saved the commit locally, but has not pushed to GitHub. A teammate asks whether that work counts toward the group’s project milestone. Give a verdict. A: No, it does not count. The class criterion is that the remote repository is what gets graded and published; work that exists only on your local computer “effectively doesn’t really exist” for grading or project purposes, so the student must push to origin for the work to be recognized by the team or by the graders. (00:10:48)



3. main, origin/main, HEAD, and what belongs on the default branch (8 Git branches)
00:11:11–00:16:05

Q: A teammate wants to push their exploratory, half-finished plots directly to main so the whole group can see them immediately. Is that consistent with the class’s standard for what belongs on main? A: No. The class defined main as the stable, production-like branch where “at least the code works”; exploratory analysis that is still being tested and is “not ready yet” belongs on a branch until it is finished and reviewed, so pushing unfinished plots to main violates that standard. (00:15:10)



4. Branches are useful even when working alone (8 Git branches)
00:16:05–00:17:54

Q: A solo developer has made a dozen experimental commits directly on main in a personal repository and now wants to undo them. A peer criticizes the approach, saying they should have used a branch. Assess that criticism using the reasoning the instructor gave. A: The criticism is valid. The instructor’s criterion is that a branch makes abandonment cheap: if the experiment fails, you just delete the branch and return to main, whereas undoing a tangled sequence of commits on main means going through git history and “start[ing] copying and pasting all the bits that are actually relevant,” which is much harder. (00:16:51)



5. Creating a branch with git switch -c (8 Git branches)
00:17:54–00:23:46

Q: A student begins a new milestone by running git switch -c milestone-branch without first synchronizing with the remote. They build two days of work on it and then discover their starting point was missing a teammate’s earlier push. What is wrong with this plan per the class standard? A: The student skipped the sync step the class requires before coordinated branch work: running git pull origin main so the starting point includes everything everyone has pushed. The instructor warned that starting from a stale local state wastes time, using the multi-laptop example where the student “could have saved myself a bunch of time if I had literally synced up my work before I started to begin with.” (00:18:39)



6. Switching between branches: switch versus the older checkout (8 Git branches)
00:23:46–00:28:26

Q: An AI coding assistant suggests the command git checkout main to switch to the main branch. The student is not comfortable with checkout and is working in the group codebase where losing work is a risk. Should they run it, or is there a class-endorsed alternative? A: They should not run it as-is; the class-endorsed alternative is git switch main. The instructor’s criterion is that checkout also performed the behavior of revert and restore, so if you don’t know what it does and you are “really scared about losing work,” you should prompt the tool to use switch instead, which only moves HEAD and does nothing else. (00:27:34)



7. Pushing a branch to origin (8 Git branches)
00:28:31–00:33:40

Q: A student is on branch dan-b1 with two unpushed commits and types git push origin main, expecting their work to appear on GitHub. The command reports “Everything up-to-date.” Diagnose what is wrong with this approach. A: The student pushed the wrong branch name. The class standard is that git push takes the branch you are actually on as its last argument; since they are on dan-b1, the correct command is git push origin dan-b1. Pushing origin main only syncs main, which had no new commits, so nothing from dan-b1 was sent to GitHub. (00:30:44)



8. Opening a pull request and reviewing the changed files (9 Pull requests)
00:33:40–00:39:56

Q: A pull request’s “Files changed” tab shows the intended README.md edit, a .DS_Store file, and a notebook.ipynb_checkpoints directory. Would you approve this pull request for merging? A: No. The class standard is that the reviewer checks the changed files for things that don’t belong in the repository—temporary checkpoint files, hidden files like .DS_Store, Word backup files—and that in this course visible unwanted files “will take points off”; the .gitignore file is the first line of defense and the pull-request review is the second, so this pull request should not be merged until those files are excluded. (00:38:44)
Q: After pushing a second commit to the same open pull request, a student adds a new conversation comment reading “I also added the long git log command now” instead of editing the original pull-request description. Is that acceptable per the class standard for pull-request communication? A: No. The instructor’s criterion is that all of the changes should be “defined and explained in the very first comment,” and when you make additional changes you should edit that first comment rather than just appending new notes, because “that’s what people are going to read.” (00:40:48)



9. Pull request conversation, code review, and updating the same branch (10 Code review on GitHub)
00:39:56–00:45:41

Q: A reviewer on a pull request sees a bug in the code and commits a fix directly to the author’s branch, then merges the pull request themselves. The author was not involved in the fix. Is that consistent with the class’s code-review standard? A: No. The class standard is that “if it’s your pull request, it is your job to fix it all”; the reviewer’s role is to point out the problem (“rewrite this or this doesn’t look right”), and it is the author’s job to go back to the branch, make the fix, commit, and push to the same branch so the pull request updates. (00:42:17)
Q: After receiving review comments, the pull-request author closes the PR, makes the fixes locally, and opens a brand-new pull request with the corrected code. Is that the correct workflow per the class? A: No. The instructor explicitly stated you do not need to close and recreate the pull request; you go back to the branch the PR was working from, run git add, git commit, and git push to the same branch, and the existing pull request updates automatically with the new commits. (00:43:02)



10. Draft pull requests, merging, and deleting the remote branch (9 Pull requests)
00:52:11–00:58:51

Q: A student opens a pull request for a feature that will take three weeks to finish. They leave it as an open, non-draft pull request with the green merge button active, reasoning that teammates can see progress. A teammate suggests converting it to a draft. Which approach is better per the class guidance, and why? A: The draft is better. The class criterion is that for work that will last more than a day, you should use a draft to signal it is not ready; the gray bar and disabled merge button prevent someone from “actually accidentally merge[ing] something that is very explicitly saying this not working or this not ready yet.” The instructor has kept draft pull requests open for “three or four months” as a standing signal to the team. (00:53:50)
Q: After merging pull request #1 from dan-b1 on GitHub, a student leaves the remote branch in place, saying they might want to reference it later. A teammate says they should delete it. Who is right per the class guidance? A: The teammate is right in this course’s context. The instructor’s criterion is to delete the remote branch after merging so the branch dropdown does not accumulate into a “giant list,” and the commits are not lost because they remain in history including the separate merge commit. The only exception the instructor noted was a compliance law requiring retention, which does not apply to the group project. (00:56:08)
Q: A student receives five AI-generated review comments on their pull request and merges without reading or responding to any of them, treating the AI’s suggestions as binding. Is that appropriate per the class standard? A: No. The instructor’s criterion is that AI review comments are not automatically mandatory: “It doesn’t mean that every single comment that the LLM is making is a comment you have to keep. Sometimes you can push back on it. Sometimes you can just reject it. Sometimes you can accept it.” A person reviews and decides whether to merge; the AI assists but does not replace human judgment. (00:52:30)



11. Local cleanup after a merge: git fetch --prune and git branch -d (8 Git branches)
00:58:53–01:03:51

Q: A student runs git branch -D dan-fetch to clean up their local branch after it was merged on GitHub. An AI tool had suggested the capital -D flag. Is that safe per the class standard? A: No, it is not the safe choice. The class standard is to use lowercase git branch -d <branch> for normal cleanup, because lowercase -d only allows deletion if the branch has been merged, protecting unmerged work. The instructor specifically warned that a copied-and-pasted AI suggestion of capital -D (force delete) “could delete the commits that you’re working on,” so the student should have used -d. (01:02:46)
Q: After merging a pull request on GitHub, a student switches to local main and sees none of the merged commits. They conclude the merge failed and open a new pull request to re-apply the changes. Assess this conclusion per the class guidance. A: The conclusion is wrong. The class stated that local main does not update automatically when a pull request is merged on GitHub; the student needs to run git pull origin main to synchronize the local main with the remote. The merge did succeed on GitHub; the local copy was simply out of date, so no new pull request is needed. (01:00:08)



12. Creating a merge-conflict scenario with two branches (8 Git branches)
01:03:51–01:10:51

Q: A student is reviewing two open pull requests side by side in the demo repository and sees both are green and mergeable into main. They conclude that merging both will not cause a conflict. Is that conclusion valid per the class demonstration? A: No, it is not valid. The class demonstrated that two pull requests can both appear green and mergeable when viewed separately, yet a conflict is not visible until one of them is actually merged; after the first merge moves main, GitHub rechecks the second pull request and only then reports the conflict. The instructor explicitly said “Nothing here actually tells you that a merge conflict is going to happen” when looking at the two pull requests side by side. (01:09:28)



13. Resolving the conflict locally with git rebase main and git push --force-with-lease (8 Git branches)
01:10:51–01:20:42

Q: After resolving the <<<<<<< markers in README.md during a rebase by keeping only their side of the change, a student runs git rebase --continue and considers the conflict “fixed.” A teammate runs the notebook and gets an error on line 50 because the other side’s variable definition was needed. Who is right per the class standard for what “fixing” a conflict means? A: The teammate is right. The class standard is that fixing a conflict does not just mean removing the markers; “your code needs to work from top to bottom again.” The instructor explicitly warned that just because a conflict appears on one line “doesn’t mean that’s the only place your code is going to affect,” so the student is still responsible for making the entire notebook run correctly. (01:11:09)
Q: After resolving the conflict and running git rebase --continue, a student types git push origin dan-delete to update the remote branch. Git rejects the push. What is wrong with this approach, and what is the class-endorsed command? A: A plain push fails because rebase rewrote the commit history of the branch; the previous commit the remote has no longer matches the local history. The class-endorsed command is git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete, which force-updates the branch while still checking that no one else has pushed to it in the meantime; the instructor said “you can’t get around not force pushing” after a rebase changes history. (01:19:23)

title: Git branches, pull requests and rebasing to fix conflicts: review questions, tier 5 — Evaluate
text:
Date: 2026-11-17
Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 5 of 5: Evaluate. Decide and justify your verdict before you read the answer; the criteria are the ones given in class.

1. Course logistics: lab groups, attendance and interview week
00:00:01–00:04:04

Q: A group plans to send one representative to each 522 lab while the others work from home, because the project lives on GitHub anyway. Assess this plan. A: The plan isn’t acceptable. Lab attendance is mandatory because this is a group project. The TAs go around and talk to every group, and each member should be there when the TA arrives. (00:02:19)
Q: Before interview week, a student says they don’t need to understand one module in their group’s code base, because an AI tool wrote it and a teammate merged it. Judge this position. A: It’s a poor position. The interview covers your group’s actual code base, and anything in it is “fair game” to be talked about, “especially in the world of AI.” You are expected to know the code you’re working in, just as you would at work. (00:03:15)



2. Why branches: escaping the 521 push/pull friction (8 Git branches)
00:06:49–00:09:43

Q: Once each teammate owns a self-contained part of the project, the group proposes that everyone keeps committing and pushing directly to main all week, as in the 521 shared slide-deck exercise. Would you recommend this? A: No. When everyone pushes to the same place, you keep hitting the friction from 521: you can’t push until you pull what someone else pushed first, even when there’s no conflict. Working in parallel streams on branches puts each person in “your own little world.” You can push and pull freely, and the work gets coordinated at review time. (00:08:46)
Q: On the first day of the project, a group splits into four branches and starts four parallel pieces of work before anything shared exists. Critique this plan. A: It’s unrealistic. Not every project can start with four parallel pieces of work. Early on, everyone is bound by one or two people getting the basics in place, so that friction will exist somewhere in a project no matter what. Parallel branches pay off once each person has a part that is solely their responsibility. (00:07:50)



3. Review: the local–remote picture
00:09:46–00:11:47

Q: On the night of a milestone, a teammate says their section is done: it’s committed on their laptop, but they haven’t pushed. Judge whether their part is submitted. A: It isn’t. What’s on GitHub is the thing that matters: it’s what gets graded and what gets published. Work that exists only on a local computer “effectively doesn’t really exist” for grading or project purposes, like a product that can’t ship because the code isn’t anywhere. (00:10:53)



4. What a branch is: main, HEAD and origin/main (8 Git branches)
00:12:03–00:17:54

Q: A teammate commits their half-finished exploratory plots straight to main so that everyone can see them. Would you accept that? A: No. Treat main as the stable “production” version: even if the project isn’t finished, the code on it should work. Exploration that isn’t ready belongs on the teammate’s own branch. main holds shared, finished pieces, such as the cleaned dataset that everyone builds from. (00:15:24)
Q: A student working alone says branches are pointless for them, because they can always undo a mistake with git reset or git revert. Assess this argument. A: It’s technically true but a weak argument. The instructor uses branches even when he’s the only one working, so he can section off work and test it before main changes. If an idea fails, deleting the branch and switching back to main is easy. Untangling one commit that did twenty things means digging through history. Reset and revert work, but branches make this easier. (00:17:22)



5. Creating and switching branches (8.1 Creating a branch using the command line)
00:17:54–00:26:29

Q: Two days after last pulling, a teammate opens their laptop and immediately runs git switch -c to start a new feature for the group project. Critique this sequence. A: They skipped a step. If your work builds on coordinated work, first confirm you’re on main and run git pull origin main, so your starting point includes everything others have pushed. Otherwise you can waste time redoing or conflicting with work that already exists. The instructor described doing exactly that when he forgot he had done half the work on another laptop. (00:18:09)



6. git checkout and git branch versus git switch (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:26:40–00:28:26

Q: ChatGPT gives you a git checkout command to fix something in your group repository, and you aren’t sure what it will do. You have uncommitted work you don’t want to lose. Is it reasonable to run it as given? A: No. checkout doesn’t only move HEAD: it also does what restore and revert do. If you don’t know what a command does, prompt the AI for the switch version instead. When you’re scared of losing work, think about the commands you type rather than pasting a working answer. (00:27:41)



7. Pushing a branch and viewing it on GitHub (8.2 Useful things you can do with branches on GitHub)
00:28:31–00:33:40

Q: After committing on dan-b1, a student switches to main, runs git push, sees Everything up-to-date, and concludes the branch is on GitHub. Judge this conclusion. A: It’s wrong. Pushing from main sent nothing from dan-b1. With branches, where and what you push matter. You need to be on the branch and name it: git push origin dan-b1. (00:29:34)
Q: A teammate finishes their branch and plans to merge it into main on their own laptop and push main, skipping GitHub. Would you recommend this? A: No. The easiest way to combine a branch with main is to not do it on your local computer at all. Do it through a review process, where you push the branch and merge it through a pull request. (00:28:58)



8. Opening a pull request (9.1 Creating a pull request)
00:33:40–00:41:16

Q: A pull request’s file list includes a .DS_Store file and an .ipynb_checkpoints folder alongside the real changes. Should it be created and merged as is? A: No. Files that don’t belong in the repository, such as checkpoint files, .DS_Store and Word backup files, lose points even when the instructions don’t mention them. Checking the file list on the pull request page is your second line of defence. Remove them and keep your .gitignore up to date. (00:38:44)
Q: As a pull request grows, its author leaves the original description untouched and adds a new comment each time (“now I’m also doing…”). Critique this habit. A: It’s the wrong habit. The first comment is what people read, so all the changes should be defined and explained there. Edit the opening description instead of appending updates. (00:40:55)
Q: A teammate never looks at the line at the top of the “Open a pull request” page, because in this course it always says main. Defend or critique this. A: Critique it. main is probably the target in this class, but it’s still a good idea to look and make sure the words make sense: your branch, then the branch you’re merging into. In 524 the target won’t always be main, and with forks you must make sure you’re sending code to the right place. (00:36:50)



9. Code review and updating a pull request (10 Code review on GitHub)
00:41:16–00:45:41

Q: While reviewing a teammate’s pull request, a reviewer finds a bug and decides to rewrite the code themselves. Is that the right division of work? A: No. The rule of thumb is that if it’s your pull request, it’s your job to fix it. The reviewer’s job is to say “rewrite this” or “this doesn’t look right” in a comment, and the author makes the change. (00:42:17)
Q: To address review comments on PR #1, a student plans to close it and open a fresh pull request with the fixes. Assess this plan. A: It’s unnecessary. You don’t need to close the pull request and create a new one. Go back to the branch it was opened from (dan-b1), then add, commit and push to that same branch, and the pull request updates. (00:43:09)



10. AI reviewers and draft pull requests (9.2 Draft pull requests)
00:52:11–00:55:41

Q: A group requests a Copilot review on every pull request and agrees to apply every comment it makes. Judge this policy. A: Requesting the review is fine, because more eyes on something is never really a bad idea. Applying every comment is not. You don’t have to keep every comment an LLM makes: you can push back, reject it or accept it. (00:52:30)
Q: A teammate opens a pull request on day one for work that will take two weeks and leaves it as a normal open pull request. Would you recommend converting it to a draft? A: Yes. A draft shows a grey bar that tells everyone “you can look, but it isn’t ready yet.” It also greys out the merge button, so nobody can accidentally merge unfinished work. The instructor believes it also stops an agent from merging everything that’s green. (00:54:30)



11. Merging and deleting the branch on GitHub (8.2 Useful things you can do with branches on GitHub)
00:55:41–00:59:07

Q: After PR #1 is merged, a student refuses to click “Delete branch” on dan-b1, worried that this will erase its commits. Is the worry justified? A: No. Deleting the branch removes only the name. main’s history still shows the branch’s two commits plus the merge commit, so you can still find and undo the feature later. Cleaning up keeps the branch list from growing into a giant, stale list. (00:58:19)
Q: A data team at a regulated workplace adopts “always delete branches after merging” from this class. Is the rule appropriate there? A: Not necessarily. If there is a legal or compliance requirement, don’t delete branches; some places don’t allow it. The team’s workflow decides. Where nothing forbids it, at least clean up your own branches. (00:57:00)



12. Syncing and cleaning up locally after a merge (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:59:07–01:03:51

Q: ChatGPT suggests git branch -D dan-b1 to tidy up after a merge. Would you run it? A: Use lowercase git branch -d dan-b1 instead. Lowercase -d refuses to delete a branch that hasn’t been merged, because Git makes it harder to lose work. Capital -D force-deletes regardless. The two differ by one character, so be very careful copying commands from ChatGPT, because you could delete commits you’re still working on. (01:03:21)
Q: After PR #1 is merged on GitHub, a student runs git switch main and starts a new branch right away, assuming local main now includes the merge. Critique this. A: The assumption is wrong. Local main doesn’t update itself, so you need a synchronisation step: git pull origin main while on main. In class, that step brought in the merged lines of README.md. (01:00:17)
Q: A student wants their local view of the remote to drop the deleted origin/dan-b1, but doesn’t want any files on disk to change. Is git pull or git fetch --prune the better choice? A: git fetch --prune. git pull runs fetch and then a merge, which changes your files. fetch alone only coordinates the history, and --prune removes local references to branches that were deleted on GitHub. (01:01:52)



13. Setting up two conflicting pull requests (8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?)
01:04:00–01:10:00

Q: To practise conflicts on their own, a student opens a pull request from dan-fetch and merges it immediately, then creates dan-delete from main to edit the same line. Will this plan produce the conflict they want? A: No. The key is not to merge the first pull request right away. Leave it open while you create the second branch from the same main commit, so both edit the same line in parallel. If the first is merged before the second branch exists, the second starts from the updated file and there’s nothing to conflict. (01:06:07)
Q: PRs #2 and #3 both show green and say they can be merged into main, so a teammate plans to click every green button without coordinating. Assess this plan. A: It’s risky. Nothing on a pull request warns you that another one edits the same line. Once one is merged, main changes and GitHub rechecks every other pull request targeting main, so the second one can turn into a conflict. (01:10:08)



14. When a merge creates the conflict: resolving on GitHub (8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?)
01:10:00–01:12:44

Q: A teammate resolves a conflict on line 13 of an analysis script by deleting the <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> markers. A variable they renamed there is still used under its old name on line 50. Is the conflict resolved? A: No. In this class, fixing a conflict means the code works from top to bottom again, not just that the markers are gone. A change at the conflicting line can break code elsewhere, and that’s still the author’s problem to deal with. (01:11:39)
Q: A group rule says every conflict must be resolved locally, never in GitHub’s web editor. Is that rule justified? A: Not for every case. Simple conflicts can be resolved in the web editor, and that’s fine. The instructor showed the local route because it’s more involved, not because the web route is wrong. (01:12:19)



15. Resolving the conflict locally with rebase (8.3.2 Using rebase)
01:12:44–01:20:42

Q: To fix the conflicting PR #3, a student runs git switch dan-delete and git rebase main without first updating local main. Critique this sequence. A: It skips step one. The commit that was merged into main on GitHub has to be on your computer first: git switch main, then git pull origin main. Only then switch back and run git rebase main, so your commits are replayed on top of the change you conflict with. (01:13:42)
Q: After a successful git rebase --continue on dan-delete, a student expects a plain git push origin dan-delete to update PR #3. Will it work? A: No. The rebase changed the commit’s history: its parent is now the updated main. A plain push won’t go through, and you can’t get around force pushing. In class, git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete worked, and GitHub then recorded the force push, since you’ve “mangled history.” (01:19:34)
Q: Halfway through a rebase with a conflict, a nervous teammate wants to delete the project folder and re-clone. Is that a sensible response? A: No. Let git status guide you: it tells you to git add the resolved file and then run git rebase --continue. If you’re scared something got messed up, git rebase --abort returns you to where you started. (01:18:20)
Q: A teammate who knows Git well says rebasing to fix conflicts is wrong and insists on another method. Is your rebase therefore incorrect? A: No. There are many ways to fix a conflict on your computer. The instructor uses rebase and expects people who know their way around Git to have opinions, “and that’s okay.” What counts is that the conflict is properly fixed and the branch can merge. (01:12:48)

title: Branches, Pull Requests, and Conflict Resolution: review questions, tier 4 — Analyze
text:
Date: 2026-11-17

Generated by qwen3.6-35b-a3b, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 4 of 5: Analyze. Take each one apart yourself before you read the answer; tiers 1 to 3 cover the facts, reasons and steps it relies on.

1. The problem with parallel work on main (8 Git branches)
00:04:04–00:09:43

Q: Break down the coordination friction caused by pushing directly to main versus using branches: how does the required step change for collaborators before pushing, and how does the HEAD pointer behave differently in each workflow? A: Pushing directly to main forces every collaborator to execute a pull before every push to coordinate changes, creating constant friction that bottlenecks parallel development. In a branch workflow, the HEAD pointer is detached and moved to a new branch using git switch -c, allowing commits to accumulate independently without altering origin/main. This structural separation means developers can work in isolated environments until a deliberate merge step intentionally combines the lines of development. (00:07:50)



2. Creating and managing branches locally (8.1 Creating a branch using the command line)
00:09:43–00:25:12

Q: Examine how git switch -c <name> and the legacy git checkout -b <name> command manipulate the Git repository state: which component does each command move, and why does the instructor advise prioritizing switch for learners? A: Both commands create a new branch and immediately move the HEAD pointer to it, establishing an independent line of development. However, checkout historically handled multiple roles, including switching branches and restoring files, which creates ambiguity about what each part of the command actually modifies. The instructor recommends switch because it isolates branch navigation into a dedicated command, reducing the risk of accidentally overwriting local changes or misusing the command when safety is a concern. (00:26:53)



3. Pushing branches and initiating Pull Requests (9 Pull requests)
00:25:12–00:46:00

Q: Trace how a Pull Request on GitHub stays synchronized with ongoing local work: what happens to the PR interface and the “Files Changed” tab when you make additional commits on the same branch, and how does this relate to the review process? A: A Pull Request is tied directly to a remote branch, so any new commits pushed to that branch automatically update the PR’s commit count and visual state on GitHub. The “Files Changed” tab continuously reflects the diff between the base branch and the latest commits on the feature branch, meaning the diff grows dynamically as you push updates. This allows the PR to serve as a living review document where peers can track progress and leave comments without needing to close and reopen the request. (00:44:43)



4. Merging, cleanup, and local synchronization (8 Git branches)
00:52:17–01:03:51

Q: Separate the post-merge cleanup workflow into its remote and local components: which actions manage the remote repository, and which commands synchronize the local machine to fully reflect that deletion? A: On the remote repository, the merge operation automatically closes the Pull Request, and the instructor manually deletes the branch via the GitHub UI dropdown to clear the visual list. On the local machine, git pull origin main fast-forwards the local main branch to include the newly merged commits. Following that, git fetch --prune removes the remote tracking reference for the now-deleted branch, and git branch -d <name> finally removes the local branch pointer, ensuring the local and remote states are completely aligned. (00:56:27)



5. Resolving merge conflicts via rebase (8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?)
01:03:51–01:21:43

Q: Differentiate how git rebase resolves a conflict compared to a standard merge workflow: what structural change does it apply to the commit history, and why does this necessitate a --force-with-lease push afterward? A: Instead of creating a new merge commit to join two divergent histories, git rebase replays the feature branch’s commits sequentially on top of the updated main branch, effectively rewriting the commit history to be linear. Because the commit hashes change during this replay, the local branch no longer matches the remote branch’s history. This structural change requires git push --force-with-lease to overwrite the remote branch safely, as a standard push would be rejected for having diverged history. (01:19:34)

title: Git branches, pull requests, and merge conflicts: review questions, tier 3 — Apply
text:
Date: 2026-11-17

Generated by qwen3.8-27b-sglang, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 3 of 5: Apply. Work each situation through before you read the answer; tiers 1 (Remember) and 2 (Understand) cover the facts and reasons it relies on.

1. Review Git basics in the demo repository (8 Git branches)
00:04:07–00:06:49

Q: You are in the demo repository after cloning it, on main, and you have edited README.md. Put the commands in the order you would run them to make that edit visible on GitHub for a teammate. A: Run git status to confirm the file is modified, then git diff to inspect the change, then git add README.md, git commit -m "intro and review", and git push origin main. The commit makes the change part of local main, but the push is what sends it to origin. Your teammate can only see it after it exists on the remote. (00:06:38)
Q: You have edited README.md in the demo repository and want to know whether Git sees the file as changed before you stage anything. Which command shows the current changes? A: Use git status; it reports modified: README.md and states that no changes are staged. It also tells you the current branch and whether the working tree is clean. It is the first check before git add. (00:06:13)
Q: You want to read the exact added text in README.md before committing. Which command shows the text difference? A: Use git diff to compare the working tree to the staged or last committed version. In the demo, it showed the added branch link and review sentence. It lets you verify the edit before git add. (00:06:13)



2. Why branches exist for parallel work (8 Git branches)
00:06:49–00:09:43

Q: You own a self-contained analysis task in a group project, and no one else is editing that part yet. What Git workflow should you use before committing to main? A: Create a feature branch for your own work stream. That gives you a separate place to commit and push without moving main for your teammates. You can wait for review before the work is merged. (00:08:46)
Q: Two people are working on the same project file, and a teammate has already pushed a new commit to main. What must you do before your own main push can succeed? A: Synchronize with the remote first, typically by running git pull origin main. That brings their new commit down to your local main before you push. Without that step, your local state is behind the shared remote. (00:07:06)
Q: You finish your branch work early, but your group does not schedule review until Friday. What can you do with your branch while waiting? A: Keep committing to, pushing, and pulling from your branch without depending on your teammates’ branches. Your work stays in its own branch until the review happens. This is the parallel-stream benefit of branching. (00:09:19)



3. Local repository versus remote origin (8 Git branches)
00:09:46–00:11:11

Q: You finish a feature on your laptop, but a teammate says they cannot find it on GitHub. What step did you skip? A: You skipped pushing the work to origin. Work that exists only on a local computer is not available for grading or project coordination. The remote repository is the shared state teammates see. (00:10:53)
Q: You need to start working in the demo repository on your computer and want a local copy connected to GitHub. Which one-time command do you use? A: Use git clone with the repository URL. It creates a local repository and sets up the remote reference to origin. After cloning, you use ordinary push and pull commands for ongoing synchronization. (00:11:25)
Q: A teammate pushes a commit to origin/main, and you need that commit on your local main. What command brings it down? A: Run git pull origin main while on main. It fetches the remote state and merges the new commit into your local branch. This keeps your local main coordinated with the remote. (00:11:47)



4. main, origin/main, HEAD, and branch state (8 Git branches)
00:11:11–00:16:05

Q: You are on main, create dan-b1, and make one commit without pushing. What will git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all show about main and dan-b1? A: It will show local dan-b1 one commit ahead, with HEAD -> dan-b1, while main and origin/main remain at the older commit. The new commit moved the branch name you are on, not main. The remote reference has not changed because nothing was pushed. (00:14:06)
Q: You need to know which branch will move when you make the next commit. How can you check from Git history? A: Look for HEAD in the output of git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all; the arrow shows the branch HEAD is attached to. You can also use git status to see On branch <name>. That current branch is the one that increments on your next commit. (00:13:17)
Q: You are making exploratory plots that may not work and you do not want teammates’ main to become unstable. Where should that exploratory work live? A: Put it on a feature branch, not on main. Keep main as the stable, working state for the shared project. The exploratory branch can be reviewed or discarded without disturbing the default branch. (00:15:49)



5. Branches when working alone (8 Git branches)
00:16:05–00:17:54

Q: You are the only person working in a repository, but you want to test a large change without immediately changing the stable main branch. What workflow should you use? A: Create a branch with git switch -c <branch-name> and do the testing there. This sections off the work so main only changes after you review and merge it. Branching is useful even when there is only one collaborator. (00:16:25)
Q: You tried a branch, it did not work, and you do not want to dig through many commits to undo them. What is the easier recovery? A: Switch back to main with git switch main and leave or delete the bad branch. The failed work remains isolated on that branch instead of tangling main. Deleting a branch is easier than reversing a tangled commit on main. (00:17:22)
Q: You have finished work on dan-b1 but have not merged it. What does main contain after you switch back to main? A: It contains only the commits that were already on main, not the new dan-b1 commits. The working files revert to the state stored at main. The branch-specific changes remain available when you switch to dan-b1. (00:16:25)



6. Creating a branch with git switch -c (8.1 Creating a branch using the command line)
00:17:54–00:23:46

Q: Before creating a branch for coordinated group work, what two checks should you perform? A: Run git status to confirm you are on main and your working tree is ready. Then synchronize with the shared remote, for example with git pull origin main, so the branch starts from an up-to-date state. This avoids building on an old local state. (00:18:09)
Q: You type git switch -c dan-b1 in the demo repository. What immediately happens to the repository state? A: Git creates the new branch dan-b1 and moves HEAD to it. git status now says On branch dan-b1. No new commit is created; the new branch starts at the same commit as main. (00:21:03)
Q: You edit README.md on dan-b1 and want to record the branch-creation note. Put the commands in order after the edit. A: Run git add README.md, then git commit -m "define swtich -c", and then use git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all to confirm dan-b1 moved. The commit moves dan-b1 while main and origin/main stay where they were. (00:22:43)



7. Switching branches and inspecting state (8.1.1 Switching to branches that already exist)
00:23:46–00:28:26

Q: You are on dan-b1 and need your working files to match the state stored on main. What command do you run? A: Run git switch main. That moves HEAD back to main and restores the files to the main state. Your dan-b1 commits remain on that branch. (00:25:22)
Q: Your branch names do not appear in git log --oneline --graph --decorate. What flag did you omit? A: Add --all to the command, as in git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all. That tells Git to show references for all branches, including local and remote branches. Without it, some branch names may be missing from the graph. (00:25:38)
Q: A tool suggests git checkout dan-b1 for switching to an existing branch. What command should you use instead in this workflow? A: Use git switch dan-b1. The session taught switch as the modern command for moving HEAD to an existing branch. If you are unsure about checkout, ask the tool to use switch instead. (00:27:41)



8. Pushing a branch to origin and viewing it (9 Pull requests)
00:28:31–00:33:40

Q: You are on dan-b1 and have one local commit that GitHub does not have. What command pushes that branch? A: Run git push origin dan-b1. The final word is the branch name, not main, so the commit is sent to the remote dan-b1 branch. Afterward, git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all shows origin/dan-b1. (00:30:36)
Q: You are on main in the demo repository and run a bare git push after main is already synchronized with origin/main. What will Git report? A: It will report Everything up-to-date. There are no new local main commits to send. A bare push only pushes the current branch if there is something new to send. (00:29:50)
Q: Your teammate wants to read the code on your pushed dan-fetch branch before a pull request is merged. Where can they look on GitHub? A: They can use the branch selector in the repository interface to view the dan-fetch branch. That lets them inspect the branch’s files without merging it into main. It is not the same as accepting or merging the branch. (00:32:24)



9. Opening a pull request and reviewing changed files (9 Pull requests)
00:33:40–00:39:56

Q: You pushed dan-fetch, but the GitHub pop-up for creating a pull request has disappeared. How do you start the pull-request process? A: Go to the repository’s branches view, find dan-fetch, and choose the option to create a new pull request. That reaches the same pull-request page as the pop-up. This is useful when you want to open the review process early. (00:35:00)
Q: You are about to create a pull request from dan-delete to the demo repository. What should you check at the top of the page before proceeding? A: Check the target branch, which should be main for this project. Also confirm the branch being merged is the one you are working on. In larger projects, the target may not always be main, so the words must make sense. (00:36:08)
Q: While reviewing the Files Changed tab of your pull request, you see .ipynb_checkpoints or .DS_Store files. What does that tell you, and what should happen before merging? A: Those temporary or hidden files do not belong in the repository. You should keep them out of the commit, for example by ensuring .gitignore handles them. In this project, visible unwanted files in the repository can cost points. (00:39:16)
Q: Your pull request diff does not include a file you thought you had changed. What likely went wrong? A: You probably did not complete git add, git commit, and git push for that file on the branch. The pull request only shows commits that were actually pushed to the branch. Check the branch history and working tree to find the missing step. (00:39:37)



10. Code review and updating the same branch (10 Code review on GitHub)
00:39:56–00:45:41

Q: A teammate comments on your pull request that a section should be rewritten. Who is responsible for making the code change? A: You are, because it is your pull request. The reviewer points out the problem, but you fix it by returning to the branch, editing the code, committing, and pushing to the same branch. The pull request updates automatically. (00:42:17)
Q: You need to add a new line to README.md after pull request #1 is already open. Put the commands in order to include that change in the same pull request. A: First make sure you are on dan-b1 with git switch dan-b1, then run git add README.md, git commit -m "show you the long git log command", and git push origin dan-b1. The pull request is tied to that branch, so the new commit appears there. Refresh the pull-request page if it does not update immediately. (00:43:58)
Q: Where on a GitHub pull request do you add a line-specific review comment? A: Use the Files Changed tab and the plus button beside the diff line. That comment is tracked in the conversation tab. It is how reviewers point at specific code without rewriting the whole pull request description. (00:41:34)
Q: You edit the exact line that a teammate previously commented on. What may happen to that old comment? A: GitHub may collapse it as outdated because the line changed. It does not mean the comment was ignored; it indicates the original context may no longer be relevant. You can still reply or address it in the conversation. (00:45:02)



11. Draft pull requests, merging, and remote cleanup (9.2 Draft pull requests)
00:52:11–00:58:51

Q: You open a pull request for work that will take more than a day. What GitHub control signals that it is not ready for review? A: Click the control to convert it to a draft. The pull request then shows a gray bar instead of a green one. It tells teammates that the work is in progress and not ready to merge. (00:53:52)
Q: A teammate wants to merge your draft pull request by accident. What visual or interface cue prevents that? A: The merge control is grayed out on a draft pull request. The draft state explicitly signals that the branch is not ready. This prevents someone from merging work that is still in progress. (00:54:30)
Q: Your draft pull request is finished and ready for merge. What do you click to make it open again? A: Click Ready for review at the bottom of the pull request conversation. That turns the draft back into an open pull request. The normal green merge controls become available. (00:55:28)
Q: After you merge pull request #1 from dan-b1, what cleanup step do you perform on GitHub? A: Delete the remote dan-b1 branch. The commits are still in main’s history, including the merge commit. Deleting the branch keeps the branch list from growing with finished work. (00:56:27)



12. Local cleanup after a merge (8 Git branches)
00:58:53–01:03:51

Q: Pull request #1 was merged on GitHub, but your local main does not yet have those changes. What commands update your local main? A: Run git switch main and then git pull origin main. The first command moves HEAD to main; the second brings the merged changes down from origin. Afterward, main matches the remote state. (01:00:27)
Q: After deleting dan-b1 on GitHub, git branch -a still shows origin/dan-b1. What command removes that stale local reference? A: Run git fetch --prune. It synchronizes your local knowledge of remote branches and deletes references to branches that no longer exist on GitHub. After it runs, origin/dan-b1 is gone from the local reference list. (01:01:30)
Q: You want to delete local dan-b1 after it has been merged. What command should you use, and why is it safe? A: Use git branch -d dan-b1 with a lowercase d. Git allows that deletion only when the branch has been merged. It protects you from accidentally deleting unmerged work. (01:02:46)
Q: You are on an unmerged local branch and an AI suggests git branch -D <branch>. What is the danger? A: Capital D force-deletes the branch even if it has unmerged commits. That can permanently remove work you were still testing. Use lowercase d for normal cleanup unless you are certain the branch can be discarded. (01:03:21)
Q: You type git pull main and Git says main does not appear to be a git repository. What is the problem, and what is the corrected command? A: The command is missing the remote name; main is a branch name, not a remote. Use git pull origin main to fetch and merge from the origin remote. This is the command used to synchronize local main with GitHub. (01:00:27)



13. Creating a merge-conflict scenario (8 Git branches)
01:03:51–01:10:51

Q: You create two branches, dan-fetch and dan-delete, from the same main state, and both edit the same lines in README.md. What event makes the second pull request conflicted? A: Merging the first pull request moves main forward. GitHub then rechecks the open pull requests against the new main. The second pull request can become conflicted even if it looked mergeable before. (01:10:08)
Q: You want to practice a merge conflict by yourself. After you create and push the first branch, what must you do before creating the second conflicting branch? A: Do not immediately merge the first pull request. Switch back to main and create the second branch from that same base, then push it. This sets up two open pull requests based on the same starting point. (01:06:07)
Q: You look at two open pull requests side by side and both seem mergeable. Why may the conflict still not be obvious? A: Each pull request is compared to main as it existed before the other one merges. The conflict appears only after one branch changes main and GitHub rechecks the other. The Files Changed view does not necessarily show the future merge conflict. (01:09:48)



14. Resolving the conflict locally with git rebase and force-with-lease (8.3.2 Using rebase)
01:10:51–01:20:42

Q: Pull request #3 from dan-delete is conflicted after pull request #2 was merged. Put the local commands in the order used to resolve it. A: Run git switch main, then git pull origin main, then git switch dan-delete, and then git rebase main. When the conflict appears, fix README.md, run git add README.md, and run git rebase --continue. Finally, update the remote branch with git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete. (01:16:25)
Q: During git rebase main, Git stops with CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in README.md. What are the next Git commands after you edit the file? A: Mark the resolution with git add README.md, then run git rebase --continue. git status can guide you by saying all conflicts are fixed. Use git rebase --abort if something is wrong and you want to return to the pre-rebase state. (01:18:32)
Q: After rebasing dan-delete, why is a plain git push origin dan-delete not enough? A: Rebase rewrote the commit history of a branch that was already pushed to GitHub. A normal push would not replace the old remote branch. You must use git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete to update the remote branch safely. (01:19:47)
Q: You type git push --force-with-leasse origin dan-delete and get an unknown option error. What is wrong, and what is the corrected command? A: The flag has a typo: leasse is not a Git option. The correct command is git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete. This is the force-push variant used after rewriting a pushed branch. (01:20:17)
Q: You resolve the conflict markers in README.md, but the report still fails later in a code chunk. What does “fixing the conflict” require in this course? A: It requires the whole report or code to work from top to bottom, not just removing the markers. A conflict on one line can affect variable names or later code. You remain responsible for making the resulting branch run as expected. (01:11:39)

title: Git branches, pull requests and rebasing to fix conflicts: review questions, tier 3 — Apply
text:
Date: 2026-11-17
Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 3 of 5: Apply. Work each situation through before you read the answer; tiers 1 (Remember) and 2 (Understand) cover the facts and reasons it relies on.

1. Review: the local–remote picture
00:09:46–00:11:47

Q: Your part of the group analysis is committed on your laptop but never pushed. The milestone is graded tonight. Predict what the graders see, and say what you must run. A: They see nothing of your work. Whatever is on GitHub is what gets graded and published, and work that exists only on your local computer “effectively doesn’t really exist.” You must push the commits to the remote. (00:10:53)
Q: You cloned your group’s repository yesterday. Today you want to keep working in it. Do you run git clone again? A: No. Clone is a one-time command that brings the repository down to your computer. From then on you sync with push and pull. (00:11:25)
Q: A teammate tells you they just pushed a commit you need. Which direction does the work have to move, and which command moves it? A: The commit is on the remote and has to come down to your computer, so you pull it. push only sends your own commits up. (00:11:47)



2. What a branch is: main, HEAD and origin/main (8 Git branches)
00:12:03–00:17:54

Q: You are on main. You make two commits but don’t push, then run git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all. Predict where main and origin/main sit. A: HEAD -> main sits two commits ahead of origin/main. origin/main is what your computer thinks GitHub’s state is, and it doesn’t move until you sync with GitHub. (00:13:39)
Q: You run git switch -c dan-b1 and then git add and git commit a change. Which branch label moves forward, and which stays put? A: dan-b1 moves forward with HEAD, and main stays where it was. The add and commit workflow is unchanged. The only difference is that your commits now drag your branch along instead of main. (00:14:25)
Q: Your group has a cleaned dataset that everyone builds on. You are halfway through exploratory plots that don’t work yet. Where should each one live? A: The cleaned dataset belongs on main, which should be the stable version where at least the code works. Your unfinished EDA stays on your own branch until it is ready. (00:15:24)
Q: You tried an idea on its own branch, and none of it worked. Choose the easiest way back to your starting point, and say why it beats having made one big commit on main. A: Switch back to main, and delete the branch or just leave it behind. Undoing one commit that did twenty things would mean digging through the history and copying back the relevant bits. git reset and git revert also work, but a branch makes the undo easier. (00:17:22)



3. Creating and switching branches (8.1 Creating a branch using the command line)
00:17:54–00:26:29

Q: You are about to start your own part of the group project, and teammates have pushed work since you last synced. In order, what do you run before your first commit on a new branch? A: Run git status to confirm you are on main, then git pull origin main, then git switch -c <name>. Pulling first means your branch starts from everything the team has already pushed. Otherwise you may redo work that already exists. (00:18:39)
Q: In the demo repository, you run git switch -c dan-b1 and then git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all before editing anything. Predict the output. A: The top commit shows HEAD -> dan-b1 alongside main and origin/main, all on the same commit. No new commit was made. Only the name HEAD is attached to has changed, and git status now says On branch dan-b1. (00:21:15)
Q: You run git log --oneline, but your branch dan-b1 doesn’t appear. What do you add to the command? A: Add the --all flag, as in git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all. Without it, you may not see your other branch names. (00:25:38)
Q: You commit a new line to README.md on dan-b1, then run git switch main and open README.md. What do you see? A: The new line is gone. The file shows main’s version, because switching moves HEAD and your files follow it. dan-b1 stays where you left it, and switching back brings the line back. (00:25:46)
Q: You are creating a branch in a repository you share with others. Choose a naming convention that helps your teammates. A: Start the branch name with your own name, such as dan-b1. Then anyone who finds something odd on that branch knows whom to talk to. (00:20:31)



4. git checkout and git branch versus git switch (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:26:40–00:28:26

Q: You type git switch -b dan-delete. Predict what happens, and fix it. A: Git fails with error: unknown switch `b', because -b belongs to the older git checkout -b. Run git switch -c dan-delete instead. (01:06:40)
Q: You run git branch my-feature and then start editing and committing. Which branch gets the commits? A: The branch you were already on. git branch creates the branch but doesn’t move you to it, so you still have to run git switch my-feature (or check it out) before committing. (00:28:13)
Q: An AI assistant tells you to run a git checkout command you don’t understand, in a repository where losing work would hurt. What do you do? A: Ask it for the git switch version instead. checkout does more than move HEAD: it also has the behaviour of the newer restore and revert commands. If you don’t know what it will do, think before you type it. (00:27:44)



5. Pushing a branch and viewing it on GitHub (8.2 Useful things you can do with branches on GitHub)
00:28:31–00:33:40

Q: You committed on dan-b1, switched back to main, and ran a bare git push. Predict the output, and fix it so your branch reaches GitHub. A: It prints Everything up-to-date and sends nothing, because the new commit is on dan-b1, not main. Run git switch dan-b1, then git push origin dan-b1. The last word names the branch you are pushing. (00:29:34)
Q: Right after git push origin dan-b1, you run git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all. Which labels sit on your latest commit, and where is origin/main? A: Your commit shows HEAD -> dan-b1, origin/dan-b1, meaning GitHub now has the branch at the same place. origin/main hasn’t moved and is still one commit behind. (00:31:19)
Q: You push your branch and refresh the repository’s GitHub page, but your changes aren’t there. Where do you look? A: The page shows main. Use the branch dropdown in the top left, which says main, to switch the view to your branch. The branch button next to it lists every branch. (00:32:21)
Q: A teammate made a great figure on their unmerged branch. You want to read the code without running it. What needs to happen? A: They push their branch to GitHub, and you select it in the branch dropdown to read the code. You can look at their work even though it isn’t merged into main or reviewed yet. (00:32:36)



6. Opening a pull request (9.1 Creating a pull request)
00:33:40–00:41:16

Q: You pushed a branch two days ago, and the “Compare & pull request” pop-up has gone. How do you open the pull request, and how could you have avoided the problem? A: Go to the Branches tab, find your branch, open its menu and choose “New pull request”. You land on the same page the pop-up would have opened. To avoid the problem, push a small change and start the pull request right away, even before the work is done. (00:34:32)
Q: You are opening a pull request from your branch. Before writing anything, what do you check in the line at the top of the page? A: Check that it names your branch as the one being merged and main as the branch it merges into. In this course the target is main. In DSCI 524 it won’t always be, and with forks you must also check the code is going to the right place. (00:36:00)
Q: The changed-files list at the bottom of your new pull request includes .DS_Store and .ipynb_checkpoints. What do you do before clicking “Create pull request”? A: Get those files out of the branch and make sure your .gitignore keeps them out. Files that don’t belong in the repository lose points even if nobody explicitly told you so. The file list is your second line of defence for catching them. (00:39:16)
Q: A script you worked on is missing from the pull request’s file list. Diagnose it. A: You probably forgot to add, commit or push it, or you typed something wrong. Commit and push it to the same branch, and it will appear. (00:39:37)
Q: Your pull request keeps growing as you add more work. Where do you describe the new changes? A: Edit the first comment, the pull request’s description, rather than adding “now I’m also doing…” comments. The first comment is what people read, so every change should be explained there. (00:40:55)



7. Code review and updating a pull request (10 Code review on GitHub)
00:41:16–00:45:41

Q: You are reviewing a teammate’s pull request and want to question one line, such as why they used switch and not checkout. Where do you go, and what do you click? A: Open the “Files changed” tab, which shows the diff between the original and new code. Hover over the line and click the + to leave a comment. The comment is also tracked in the Conversation tab. (00:41:34)
Q: A reviewer comments “this doesn’t look right” on your pull request from dan-b1. Who changes the code, and what do you run? Do you close the pull request? A: You fix it, because the author of a pull request fixes it, not the reviewer. Don’t close the pull request or open a new one. Go back to dan-b1 locally, then git add, git commit and git push origin dan-b1, and the open pull request updates. (00:43:15)
Q: You pushed a new commit to your pull request’s branch, but the pull request page doesn’t show it. What do you try? A: Refresh the page. The pull request is tied to the branch and tracks every commit you push, but sometimes it only shows up after a refresh. (00:45:00)
Q: You change a line that a reviewer commented on and push. Predict what happens to their comment. A: It doesn’t disappear, but GitHub may collapse it and mark it as outdated. The line it referred to has changed, so the comment probably no longer applies. (00:45:02)



8. AI reviewers and draft pull requests (9.2 Draft pull requests)
00:52:11–00:55:41

Q: You opened a pull request early and will keep pushing to it for a week. You don’t want anyone, or an agent, to merge it by accident. What do you do, and what changes on the page? A: Click “Convert to draft”. The pull request gets a grey bar instead of a green one, and the merge button is greyed out, so it can’t be merged by accident. It signals that people can look but the work isn’t ready. (00:54:30)
Q: Your draft pull request is finished and you want it merged. What do you click? A: Scroll to the bottom, where it says the pull request is a work in progress, and click “Ready for review”. It becomes an open pull request again, with green merge buttons. (00:55:28)
Q: You request a Copilot review, and one of its comments seems wrong. Do you have to make the change? A: No. More eyes on your code is never a bad idea, but you don’t have to keep every comment an LLM makes. You can push back, reject it or accept it. (00:53:01)



9. Merging and deleting the branch on GitHub (8.2 Useful things you can do with branches on GitHub)
00:55:41–00:59:07

Q: Your project has run for weeks, and the branch dropdown has become a giant list. What should you do each time a pull request is merged? A: Click “Delete branch” on GitHub right after the merge. The branch count drops (two to one in the demo) and the list stays manageable. At the very least, clean up your own branches. (00:57:42)
Q: You merged pull request #1 and deleted dan-b1 on GitHub. A teammate worries its commits are gone. Predict what main’s history shows. A: The branch’s two commits are still there, plus a merge commit, “Merge pull request #1 from chendaniely/dan-b1”. Deleting the branch only removes the label, so you can still find those commits and undo the feature later. (00:58:10)
Q: You work somewhere with a legal compliance requirement on code history. Do you delete merged branches? A: No. Where compliance rules apply, you can’t delete them, and the branch list just gets long. Otherwise your team’s workflow decides. (00:57:00)



10. Syncing and cleaning up locally after a merge (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:59:07–01:03:51

Q: Pull request #1 was merged on GitHub. You run git switch main locally, but README.md doesn’t have the merged lines. Diagnose it and fix it. A: Your local main doesn’t update itself. Run git pull origin main, which fast-forwarded main in the demo and added the pull request’s 6 new lines to README.md. (01:00:17)
Q: You type git pull main. Predict the result, and fix it. A: It fails with fatal: 'main' does not appear to be a git repository, because Git reads the first word as the remote. Run git pull origin main. (01:04:28)
Q: The branch was deleted on GitHub, but git branch -a still lists remotes/origin/dan-b1. What do you run? A: Run git fetch --prune. It syncs your history with origin and removes references to branches deleted there. It printed [deleted] (none) -> origin/dan-b1. (01:01:30)
Q: You want your local history to match GitHub, but you don’t want any files in your working directory to change. Do you run git pull or git fetch? A: Run git fetch. git pull is a fetch followed by a merge, which changes your files. Fetch alone only coordinates the history. (01:02:07)
Q: Your pull request from dan-b1 was merged and the branch was deleted on GitHub. In order, what do you run locally to finish cleaning up? A: Run git switch main, then git pull origin main, then git fetch --prune, then git branch -d dan-b1. The lowercase -d deletes the local branch because it has been merged. (01:03:21)
Q: You abandoned an experiment branch that was never merged, and git branch -d refuses to delete it. ChatGPT suggests git branch -D. What happens if you run it, and what is the risk? A: Capital -D force-deletes the branch even though it is unmerged, and its commits are lost. Lowercase -d refused precisely to stop you losing work. It is a one-character difference, so be very careful when copying commands that may hand you -D. (01:03:21)



11. Setting up two conflicting pull requests (8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?)
01:04:00–01:10:00

Q: You want to practise a merge conflict on your own in a repository. In order, what do you do, and what must you not do? A: Sync main, then git switch -c dan-fetch, edit a line of README.md, commit, push and open a pull request. Then git switch main, git switch -c dan-delete, change the same line, commit, push and open a second pull request. Don’t merge the first pull request right away, or there will be no conflict to practise on. (01:06:07)
Q: You committed a line on dan-fetch, then ran git switch main and git switch -c dan-delete. Is that line in README.md on dan-delete? A: No. dan-delete was created from main, which doesn’t have the dan-fetch commit, so the line is not there. (01:07:20)
Q: With dan-fetch and dan-delete both pushed, you run git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate. Predict the shape of the graph. A: Two lines leave the same main commit (3851b00): 157c3cd on dan-fetch and cb810d5 on dan-delete. That shows two parallel pieces of work. (01:08:24)



12. When a merge creates the conflict: resolving on GitHub
01:10:00–01:12:44

Q: Pull requests #2 and #3 both target main, edit the same line, and both show as mergeable. You merge #2. Predict what happens to #3. A: Merging #2 changes main, so GitHub rechecks every pull request that targets main. #3 now shows a conflict. Nothing warned you beforehand, because each pull request looked fine on its own. (01:10:19)
Q: The conflict in #3 is simple, and you resolve it in GitHub’s web editor. What do you look for, and when is a conflict in report text fixed? A: Look for the conflict markers, <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>>. Fix them so that the remaining report text is English that makes sense. (01:11:09)
Q: A conflict hits line 13 of your analysis script. You resolve it by keeping a version that renames a variable, delete the markers, and stop. The old name is still used on line 50. Are you done? A: No. Fixing a conflict means your code works from top to bottom again, not just that the markers are gone. The broken reference on line 50 is still your problem to fix. (01:11:39)



13. Resolving the conflict locally with rebase (8.3.2 Using rebase)
01:12:44–01:20:42

Q: #2 (dan-fetch) was merged, and #3 (dan-delete) now conflicts. In order, what do you run to resolve it on your computer and update #3? A: git switch main, git pull origin main, git switch dan-delete, git rebase main. Then fix the markers in README.md, git add README.md, git rebase --continue, and finally git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete. The rebase replays your commit on top of the updated main, which is where the conflict surfaces. (01:17:08)
Q: You skip pulling main and run git rebase main on dan-delete straight away. Why won’t this deal with the conflict GitHub reports? A: The dan-fetch commit was merged on GitHub, but your local main doesn’t have it yet. The rebase replays onto a main without that change. Syncing main first is what brings the merged commit to your computer. (01:13:42)
Q: git rebase main stops with CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in README.md. You have fixed the file and aren’t sure what comes next. How do you find out, and what do you run? A: Run git status, which guides you. It tells you to use git add README.md to mark the conflict resolved. Once all conflicts are fixed, it tells you to run git rebase --continue, which asks you to confirm the commit message. (01:18:32)
Q: You are midway through a rebase, the file looks like a mess, and you are scared you have broken something. How do you get back to where you started? A: Run git rebase --abort. It stops the rebase and returns your branch to its state before git rebase. (01:18:20)
Q: After git rebase --continue, the log shows dan-delete at a new commit (0e16503) on top of main, but origin/dan-delete still at cb810d5. You run a plain push. Predict what happens, and choose the fix. A: The plain push is rejected, because the rebase changed the branch’s history: the commit now has a different parent. Run git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete. GitHub records that a force push happened, so you are rewriting history, which matters in compliance settings. Only do it on your own branch. (01:19:47)
Q: You type git push --force-with-leasse origin dan-delete. Predict the result, and fix it. A: Git fails with error: unknown option `force-with-leasse' and prints its usage text. It is a typo, so re-run it as git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete. (01:19:34)
