Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 2 of 5: Understand. Explain each answer in your own words before you read it; tier 1 (Remember) covers the facts, tiers 3 to 5 put them to use.

1. Parallel work and the role of branches (8 Git branches)
00:04:07–00:09:43

Q: Why did the instructor introduce branches after reviewing basic Git commands? A: He introduced them to solve the constant pull-before-push friction and merge conflicts that happen when multiple teammates push directly to the main branch, allowing individual responsibilities to proceed independently. (00:07:57)
Q: How does the instructor describe the benefit of working on branches instead of main directly? A: Branches act as isolated “playgrounds” or separate worlds where you can explore, test, and develop new features without breaking the stable, working order of the main branch for everyone else. (00:14:34)
Q: Why does the instructor recommend syncing with git pull origin main before creating a new branch? A: To ensure your new branch starts from the most up-to-date coordinated code, which saves time and prevents you from accidentally losing work that a teammate has already pushed to the remote. (00:18:25)



2. Managing branches locally (8 Git branches)
00:09:43–00:25:12

Q: How does git switch -c change the state of the repository compared to just making commits on main? A: It creates a new named branch and moves the HEAD pointer to it, meaning subsequent git add and git commit commands will increment that new branch name instead of moving main. (00:20:09)
Q: Why does the instructor advise using git switch instead of the older git checkout command? A: Because checkout historically handled both branch switching and file restoration/reverting, whereas switch is specialized for moving the HEAD around branches, reducing the risk of accidentally losing work if you are unfamiliar with the command. (00:27:09)
Q: What is the practical benefit of viewing the repository in the VS Code Git interface while working with branches? A: It provides a visual graph that maps out the commit history, clearly showing where main, origin/main, and your local branch HEAD point to confirm that your branch is developing independently. (00:23:51)



3. Pushing branches and initiating Pull Requests (9 Pull requests)
00:25:12–00:46:00

Q: Why should you run git push origin <branch_name> instead of just git push when you are on a new branch? A: Running just git push without a specified branch might not do anything or push to the wrong target; explicitly naming the branch sends your isolated work to the remote so teammates can see it. (00:29:50)
Q: How does creating a Pull Request change how you review your own work or an AI-generated commit? A: It presents a “Files Changed” diff that you can inspect directly on GitHub, allowing you to catch stray temporary files, verify intended changes, and leave inline comments before merging. (00:38:15)
Q: Why does the instructor recommend starting a Pull Request immediately after pushing a branch, even if the work isn’t finished? A: The “Compare & Pull Request” banner tends to disappear after a day, so starting it right away ensures you don’t lose the easy prompt to open the review workflow. (00:35:28)



4. Draft Pull Requests (9 Pull requests)
00:46:59–00:55:41

Q: What visual cues and restrictions does a Draft Pull Request display on GitHub? A: It displays a gray bar instead of a green one and disables the merge button, signaling that the work is explicitly not ready for integration. (00:53:59)
Q: Why is it useful to convert an open Pull Request into a Draft while working on a long-term task? A: It acts as a clear signal to teammates and automated agents that the branch is a work-in-progress, preventing accidental merges and discouraging agents from blindly merging green checks. (00:54:48)
Q: How do you revert a Draft Pull Request back to an open state? A: Scroll to the bottom of the conversation tab, click “Ready for review,” which turns the gray bar green and re-enables the green merge button. (00:55:23)



5. Merging, cleanup, and local synchronization (8 Git branches)
00:52:17–01:03:51

Q: Why is it important to run git fetch --prune after deleting a branch on GitHub? A: It removes the local tracking references for that remote branch, preventing your local branch list from becoming cluttered with inactive markers. (01:01:30)
Q: What is the difference between using git branch -d and git branch -D when deleting a local branch? A: Lowercase -d safely deletes only merged branches to prevent accidental data loss, while uppercase -D force-deletes regardless of merge status, carrying a high risk of permanently losing unmerged work. (01:02:46)
Q: Why must you run git pull origin main after merging a Pull Request on GitHub? A: To fast-forward your local main branch to the remote, updating your local computer with the newly integrated commits that were not present on your machine before the merge. (01:00:17)



6. Resolving merge conflicts via rebase (8 Git branches)
01:03:51–01:21:43

Q: Why does a merge conflict occur when merging a second Pull Request after the first has been accepted? A: Merging the first PR updates the main branch, so when the second PR tries to merge, it rechecks against the new main and finds that both branches independently changed the same lines. (01:10:19)
Q: What is the purpose of running git rebase main on a branch that has fallen behind main? A: It replays your branch’s commits sequentially on top of the updated main branch, triggering the conflict locally so you can fix it and push the resolved version. (01:14:10)
Q: Why does the instructor emphasize that fixing a conflict marker does not guarantee the code will run correctly? A: Resolving the conflict at one specific line (e.g., line 13) might leave broken dependencies elsewhere (e.g., line 50) if variable names or logic shifted, so you must verify the entire file works top to bottom. (01:11:39)
Q: Why must you use git push --force-with-lease instead of a standard git push after rebasing? A: Rebasinrewrites the commit history, so a standard push would be rejected; --force-with-lease safely updates the remote branch only if no new, untracked commits were added by others in the meantime. (01:19:47)

1. Course logistics: lab groups, attendance, and interview week
00:00:01–00:04:04

Q: What did the instructor say DSCI 522 is for the students? A: It is their first big, project-based class where they actually have to work with the other people in their lab section. (00:00:45)
Q: What is the lab-sections repository on GitHub used for? A: Students look up their lab section, and the column they are in gives their group number, which determines who they work with on the project. (00:01:07)
Q: Why did the instructor collect students’ GitHub usernames? A: The usernames form a main list of metadata that is “used everywhere else under the hood” in the rest of the program. (00:02:01)

2. Review of the DSCI 521 Git cycle in the demo repository
00:04:07–00:06:49

Q: What is the name of the demo repository the instructor cloned and worked in during the session? A: chendaniely/2026-11-17-git, cloned from git@github.com:chendaniely/2026-11-17-git.git. (00:05:36)
Q: What change was made to README.md in the demo repository? A: A link to the Git branches chapter of the course textbook was added, with the text “we will review 521 git basics and then go into branches.” (00:05:57)
Q: What commit message was used for the first commit on main in the demo repository? A: “intro and review.” (00:06:32)
Q: What did the instructor say about whether anything new had been presented on screen at that point? A: “There is nothing new that I’ve presented onto the screen so far”; everything was a review of DSCI 521. (00:06:38)



3. Why branches exist: parallel work in a group project
(8 Git branches)
00:06:49–00:09:43

Q: What exercise from DSCI 521 week 3 did the instructor reference to motivate the need for branches? A: A shared slide deck where students collaborated, and even without a conflict they always had to pull before they could push. (00:06:54)
Q: What was the recurring annoyance in the DSCI 521 slide deck exercise? A: You had to pull first because someone else had pushed before you could push your own changes. (00:07:06)
Q: What does a branch give you in the context of the group project, according to the instructor? A: “Your own little world” where you can push and pull until your work is done, waiting for review from your teammates. (00:08:46)



4. Local repository versus remote origin
(8 Git branches)
00:09:46–00:11:11

Q: What two places does the instructor say you do work in Git? A: Your local computer and the remote (cloud) repository, called origin. (00:10:09)
Q: What is git clone described as? A: A one-time command that brings the repository down to your computer. (00:11:25)
Q: Which command sends local commits up to the remote, and which brings others’ work down? A: git push sends local commits to the remote; git pull brings others’ commits down. (00:11:33)
Q: What warning did the instructor give about work that exists only on your local computer? A: If your work exists only on your local computer, it “effectively doesn’t really exist” for grading or project purposes; the remote is what matters. (00:10:48)



5. main, origin/main, HEAD, and what a branch is
(8 Git branches)
00:11:11–00:16:05

Q: What is the main branch described as? A: The default branch that represents the stable, final, or production state of the project; everything in it should be in working order. (00:12:38)
Q: What does origin/main represent? A: What your local computer thinks the state of the remote main branch is on GitHub. (00:13:30)
Q: What is HEAD in Git? A: The pointer to your current position in the commit history; when it points to main, you are on the main branch. (00:19:51)
Q: What is a branch, essentially, according to the instructor? A: Instead of incrementing main when you commit, you increment some other name you give it yourself; it is a way to section off work. (00:13:55)
Q: What kind of work should not be in the main branch? A: Exploratory data analysis, unfinished plots, and work that is still being tested; those belong on a branch until they are ready. (00:15:24)



6. Branches are useful even when working alone
(8 Git branches)
00:16:05–00:17:54

Q: Does the instructor say you need other people to use branches? A: No; the instructor said “You don’t need to do branches to collaborate with other people” and noted that many single-person Git repositories use branches. (00:16:05)
Q: What did the instructor describe doing with the course textbook? A: All the work was done in a sequence of branches so the textbook would not move around during a teaching day; the branches were merged in after lectures and testing. (00:16:37)
Q: Why is a bad idea easier to undo on a branch than on main? A: It is easy to delete a branch and go back to main, whereas undoing a tangled set of commits on main requires going through Git history copying and pasting the relevant bits. (00:16:51)



7. Creating a branch with git switch -c
(8.1 Creating a branch using the command line)
00:17:54–00:23:46

Q: What command creates a new branch named dan-b1 and immediately moves HEAD to it? A: git switch -c dan-b1. (00:20:09)
Q: What does the -c flag in git switch stand for? A: Create. (00:20:09)
Q: What should you check before creating a branch, according to the instructor? A: Run git status to make sure you are on main, and if you are building on coordinated project work, first synchronize with the remote using git pull origin main. (00:18:01)
Q: What does git status show after creating and switching to the dan-b1 branch? A: It says “On branch dan-b1” instead of “On branch main.” (00:21:03)
Q: What did the instructor say about naming branches in a group project? A: He sometimes begins a branch with his name so other people know who to talk to if something looks wrong. (00:20:31)
Q: After committing on dan-b1, which branch moves forward? A: The dan-b1 branch moves forward; main and origin/main remain where they were. (00:22:58)



8. Switching between branches and older commands
(8.1.1 Switching to branches that already exist)
00:23:46–00:28:26

Q: What command switches HEAD back to the main branch? A: git switch main. (00:25:22)
Q: What is the difference between git switch <branch> and git switch -c <branch>? A: git switch <branch> moves HEAD to an existing branch; git switch -c <branch> creates a new branch and moves HEAD to it. (00:22:04)
Q: What is the full command the instructor used to display the Git history with a graph and all branch names? A: git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all. (00:43:36)
Q: What older command did the instructor mention that creates a new branch? A: git checkout -b <branch>; the instructor said git checkout is the older equivalent of git switch. (00:27:09)
Q: What does git branch <name> do differently from git switch -c <name>? A: git branch <name> creates the branch but does not move HEAD to it; you still have to switch or checkout after creating it. (00:28:13)
Q: Did the instructor say the class would test students on git checkout? A: No; the instructor said “I’m not gonna test you on that like this.” (00:26:40)



9. Pushing a branch to origin and viewing it on GitHub
(8 Git branches)
00:28:31–00:33:40

Q: What command pushes the dan-b1 branch to the remote? A: git push origin dan-b1. (00:30:36)
Q: What did a plain git push while on main report? A: “Everything up-to-date.” (00:29:50)
Q: After pushing dan-b1, what new reference appeared in git log? A: origin/dan-b1, meaning the local computer now knows that GitHub has that branch. (00:31:27)
Q: Where on the GitHub repository page can you view another branch without merging it? A: In the branch selector (the little tab in the top-left corner that says main), you can switch to view another branch. (00:32:24)
Q: What did the instructor say about teammates viewing a pushed branch before it is merged? A: A teammate can push their changes to their branch and you can go look at their code on GitHub, even though it is not combined into main yet. (00:32:36)



10. Opening a pull request and reviewing the changed files
(9.1 Creating a pull request)
00:33:40–00:39:56

Q: What button on GitHub starts the pull request process after pushing a new branch? A: The “Compare and Pull Request” button (or the green button that appears in a popup). (00:34:25)
Q: What did the instructor say happens to the “Compare and Pull Request” popup after a day or so? A: It disappears; to get the same process back, go to the branches tab, find your branch, and choose “new pull request.” (00:34:32)
Q: What title did the instructor give to pull request #1 in the demo repository? A: “Learning about branches and PRs.” (00:37:15)
Q: What did the instructor recommend doing when you start work on a branch that may take more than a day? A: Open the pull request right away so the process exists, and keep pushing the branch; the pull request updates as you go. (00:35:15)
Q: What did the instructor say to look for in the Files Changed tab of a pull request? A: Confirm all your intended files and code changes are present, and check that no unwanted files (such as .ipynb_checkpoints, .DS_Store, or Word backup files) are in the repository. (00:38:44)
Q: What did the instructor say about points if unwanted files appear in a repository? A: “If we see it in a repository, even if it’s not explicit, we will take points off.” (00:38:44)



11. Pull request conversation, code review, and updating the same branch
(10 Code review on GitHub)
00:39:56–00:45:41

Q: Which tab in a GitHub pull request is where code review happens? A: The “Files Changed” tab, which shows the diff between the original file and the new file. (00:41:22)
Q: What button appears when you hover over a line in the diff to start a review comment? A: A little plus button; clicking it lets you write a comment on that specific line, which is tracked in the main conversation tab. (00:41:34)
Q: What is the rule of thumb about who fixes issues raised in a pull request? A: If it is your pull request, it is your job to fix all the issues; the reviewer’s job is to say “rewrite this” or “this doesn’t look right,” not to fix the code. (00:42:17)
Q: How does a pull request update when you make additional changes to its branch? A: You commit and push to the same branch; the pull request updates automatically, though you may need to refresh the page. (00:43:15)
Q: What happens to a review comment if you edit the line it was attached to? A: GitHub may collapse the comment as “outdated” because the line it referred to has changed. (00:45:02)



12. Draft pull requests, merging, and deleting the remote branch
(9.2 Draft pull requests)
00:52:11–00:58:51

Q: What button converts an open pull request into a draft? A: The “Convert to Draft” button in the top-right corner of the pull request. (00:53:52)
Q: What visual cue does a draft pull request have compared to an open one? A: A gray bar instead of a green one. (00:54:04)
Q: What happens to the merge button on a draft pull request? A: It gets grayed out (disabled) so no one can accidentally merge something that is not ready. (00:54:30)
Q: What button turns a draft pull request back into an open one? A: “Ready for review,” found at the bottom of the pull request conversation. (00:55:28)
Q: What did the instructor say about deleting a branch on GitHub after merging a pull request? A: The commits are still in the history, including the merge commit; deleting the branch just removes the branch name from the dropdown so the list does not grow forever. (00:56:08)
Q: What did the instructor say about using AI (Copilot) to review a pull request? A: You can request Copilot to do a review, but not every comment from the LLM has to be kept; a person still reviews and decides whether to accept or reject them. (00:52:30)



13. Local cleanup after a merge
(8 Git branches)
00:58:53–01:03:51

Q: After a branch is merged on GitHub, does local main update automatically? A: No; you must run git switch main and then git pull origin main to sync local main with the remote. (01:00:14)
Q: What command lists all branches, including remote-tracking branches? A: git branch -a; the current branch has a star next to it. (01:01:06)
Q: What does git fetch --prune do? A: It synchronizes with the remote and removes local references to branches that have been deleted on GitHub; in the demo it removed the origin/dan-b1 reference. (01:01:30)
Q: What command deletes a local branch that has been merged? A: git branch -d <branch> (lowercase -d). (01:02:46)
Q: What is the difference between lowercase -d and capital -D in git branch? A: Lowercase -d only deletes a branch if it has been merged; capital -D force-deletes a branch even if it has not been merged. (01:02:54)
Q: What warning did the instructor give about capital -D? A: Be very careful if you are copying commands from ChatGPT, because it might say capital -D (force delete), and you could delete commits you are still working on. (01:03:21)
Q: What error did the terminal show when the instructor typed git pull main without specifying the remote? A: fatal: 'main' does not appear to be a git repository; the correct command is git pull origin main. (01:02:57)
Q: What does the instructor say individual assignment 1 requires? A: It has students review merge conflicts again, because you still need to know how to recover from them even when working in branches. (00:59:07)



14. Creating a merge-conflict scenario with two branches
(8 Git branches)
01:03:51–01:10:51

Q: What are the names of the two branches created for the merge-conflict demonstration? A: dan-fetch and dan-delete. (01:04:35)
Q: What is the title of pull request #2 in the demo repository? A: “define fetch –prune,” from branch dan-fetch. (01:05:36)
Q: What is the title of pull request #3 in the demo repository? A: “branch -d and -D,” from branch dan-delete. (01:07:51)
Q: What error did the terminal show when the instructor typed git switch -b dan-delete? A: error: unknown switch 'b'; the correct flag for creating a branch with git switch is -c. (01:06:40)
Q: What happens to open pull requests when one is merged into main? A: GitHub rechecks the remaining open pull requests to see if they can still be merged against the new main. (01:10:19)
Q: What did the instructor say about looking at the two pull requests side by side before the first merge? A: It is “not very obvious” that they will conflict; the conflict only appears after one branch is merged and main moves. (01:09:28)



15. Resolving the conflict locally with git rebase main and force push
(8.3.2 Using rebase)
01:10:51–01:20:42

Q: What command replays the commits of the dan-delete branch on top of the updated main? A: git rebase main, run while on the dan-delete branch. (01:17:08)
Q: What does “fixing” a merge conflict mean in this course, according to the instructor? A: It is not enough to remove the conflict markers; the resulting code or report must work from top to bottom again. (01:11:21)
Q: What command is run after resolving the conflict and staging the file to continue the rebase? A: git rebase --continue. (01:18:54)
Q: Why could a plain git push origin dan-delete not be used after the rebase? A: Because rebase changed (rewrote) the commit history of the branch that was already pushed; a force push is required. (01:19:34)
Q: What command was used to push the rebased branch to GitHub? A: git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete. (01:19:34)
Q: What error did the terminal show when the instructor first typed the force-push command with a typo? A: error: unknown option 'force-with-leasse' (a misspelling of --force-with-lease). (01:19:20)

title: Git branches, pull requests and rebasing: review questions, tier 1 — Remember
text:
Date: 2026-11-17
Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 1 of 5: Remember. Answer each question before you read its answer; tiers 2 to 5 build on these.

1. Course logistics: lab groups, attendance and interview week
00:00:01–00:04:04

Q: Where do you look up your DSCI 522 lab group? A: In the lab sections repository on GitHub. Find your lab section, then the group number column; everyone with the same number is in your group. (00:00:56)
Q: What are the GitHub usernames students submitted used for? A: They build a main list of everyone’s GitHub usernames. That list is a piece of metadata used everywhere else in the program. (00:02:01)
Q: State the attendance rule for 522 labs. A: Lab attendance is mandatory. TAs go around and talk to every group, and you should be there when a TA comes to yours. (00:02:19)
Q: How long is the interview-week conversation, and what is it modelled on? A: About seven minutes, run like a technical interview. (00:02:50)
Q: What two things does the interview-week conversation cover? A: How much you know about Git, and your group’s actual code base. Anything in the code base is fair game. (00:03:15)
Q: Does the interview-week conversation affect your grade? A: No. You get a grade, but it doesn’t affect your course grade. (00:03:02)
Q: What did the instructor say this interview format might become next year? A: The exam. (00:03:48)



2. Git recap: setting up the demo repository
00:04:07–00:06:49

Q: What is the name of the demo repository the instructor created and cloned? A: 2026-11-17-git, named for the day’s date, under chendaniely. (00:04:51)
Q: Which file was the demo repository initialized with, instead of starting empty? A: A README. The instructor noted you could also add a Python .gitignore and a license. (00:05:06)
Q: What did the instructor add to README.md as the first change? A: A line saying the class will review 521 Git basics and then go into branches, plus a link to the textbook’s Git branches chapter. (00:05:57)
Q: What commit message did the instructor use for that first commit on main? A: intro and review. (00:06:32)



3. Why branches: escaping the 521 push/pull friction (8 Git branches)
00:06:49–00:09:43

Q: Which DSCI 521 week-3 exercise did the instructor recall as an example of push/pull friction? A: Creating a shared slide deck together. (00:06:54)
Q: What step was always needed in that exercise before you could push, even when there was no conflict? A: You had to pull first, because someone else had pushed before you. (00:07:06)
Q: What kind of work does the instructor want groups to reach in a project? A: Parallel streams of work, where each person is responsible for their own self-contained part. (00:08:41)
Q: In the instructor’s example timeline, which day did the group review and coordinate everyone’s work? A: Friday, after each person worked on their own part from Tuesday to Friday. (00:08:46)



4. Review: the local–remote picture
00:09:46–00:11:47

Q: What are the two places your work can live? A: Your computer (local) and the cloud (the GitHub remote). (00:10:09)
Q: Which copy of the work is the one that’s graded and published? A: The copy on the GitHub remote. Work that exists only on your computer effectively doesn’t exist for grading or project purposes. (00:10:53)
Q: Which Git command did the instructor call a one-time command? A: git clone. (00:11:25)
Q: Name the command that sends commits up to GitHub and the one that brings teammates’ commits down. A: git push sends commits up, and git pull brings commits down. (00:11:33)



5. What a branch is: main, HEAD and origin/main
00:12:03–00:17:54

Q: What is the main branch? A: The default branch you work on. (00:12:38)
Q: What happens to the main branch each time you commit while HEAD is attached to it? A: main moves forward (increments) with each commit. (00:13:17)
Q: What does origin/main represent? A: The remote: what your computer thinks the state of main on GitHub is. (00:13:30)
Q: Define a branch as the instructor described it. A: A name you choose yourself that moves forward when you commit, instead of main moving. The git add/git commit process stays the same. (00:13:55)
Q: What did the instructor say the main branch should be treated as? A: The production or final version: the stable place where at least the code works. (00:15:10)
Q: Do you need collaborators to use branches? A: No. Branches are useful when working alone too, to section off work. (00:16:05)
Q: What real project did the instructor say he edited entirely in branches, and why? A: The course textbook. Another instructor was teaching from it that day, and he didn’t want pages moving around mid-lecture. (00:16:37)
Q: Which two DSCI 521 commands did the instructor name as another way to undo work, besides using branches? A: git reset and git revert. (00:17:22)



6. Creating and switching branches (8.1 Creating a branch using the command line)
00:17:54–00:26:29

Q: What command did the instructor run first, to confirm he was on main before creating a branch? A: git status. (00:18:03)
Q: Which command syncs your starting point before you create a branch that builds on coordinated work? A: git pull origin main. (00:18:39)
Q: Define git switch. A: The command that moves HEAD around the repository, switching between branches. (00:19:46)
Q: What does the -c flag in git switch -c <name> stand for, and what does the command do? A: -c is for create. The command creates a new branch and moves HEAD to it. (00:20:09)
Q: What name did the instructor give the first branch he created? A: dan-b1. (00:21:31)
Q: What does the instructor put at the start of branch names in shared repositories? A: His own name, so others know whom to talk to about that branch. (00:20:31)
Q: What did git switch -c dan-b1 print? A: Switched to a new branch 'dan-b1'. (00:20:58)
Q: After git switch -c dan-b1, what did git status report? A: On branch dan-b1, with nothing to commit. The only change was the branch name. (00:21:03)
Q: What line did the instructor add to README.md on dan-b1? A: `switch -c <name>`: create and move HEAD to the branch <name>. (00:21:56)
Q: What commit message did the instructor use for the first commit on dan-b1? A: define swtich -c, typed with that spelling. (00:22:31)
Q: Which view in VS Code or Positron shows the same branch picture as the terminal log? A: The graph view in the Git tab. (00:23:51)
Q: What command moved HEAD from dan-b1 back to main? A: git switch main. (00:25:12)
Q: Which flag must you add to git log --oneline to see your other branches? A: --all, as in git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all. (00:25:38)



7. git checkout and git branch versus git switch (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:26:40–00:28:26

Q: Will students be tested on using git checkout instead of git switch? A: No. The instructor said using checkout is fine and he won’t test students on it. (00:26:42)
Q: Roughly when was git switch introduced, replacing part of what git checkout did? A: Around 2019 to 2020. (00:26:59)
Q: Which command does the instructor use himself day to day, and when does he use switch? A: He uses git checkout. He only uses switch when teaching. (00:26:59)
Q: Besides moving HEAD, what else did git checkout do? A: Much of what restore and revert do. Those newer commands came out of checkout, and checkout still has those behaviours. (00:27:09)
Q: What should you ask an AI tool to do if it tells you to run a checkout command you don’t understand? A: Ask it to do the same thing with switch instead. (00:27:44)
Q: Name the git checkout equivalent of git switch -c <name>. A: git checkout -b <name>. (00:28:10)
Q: What does git branch <name> do, and what doesn’t it do? A: It creates the branch but doesn’t move you to it. You still have to checkout or switch afterwards. (00:28:13)



8. Pushing a branch and viewing it on GitHub (8.2 Useful things you can do with branches on GitHub)
00:28:31–00:33:40

Q: What two names did the instructor give for the review process used to get a branch into main? A: A pull request, or a merge request. (00:28:58)
Q: Which command is the only one that links your local work to the remote? A: git push. (00:29:22)
Q: What did a plain git push, run while on main, print in class? A: Everything up-to-date. It didn’t send dan-b1. (00:29:34)
Q: What command pushed the dan-b1 branch to GitHub? A: git push origin dan-b1. (00:30:36)
Q: Besides pushing, what did git push origin dan-b1 print about pull requests? A: A link to create a pull request for dan-b1: https://github.com/chendaniely/2026-11-17-git/pull/new/dan-b1. (00:30:36)
Q: After pushing dan-b1, which new reference appeared in git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all? A: origin/dan-b1, at the same commit as dan-b1. origin/main had not moved. (00:31:19)
Q: Where on a GitHub repository page do you switch to view a branch like dan-b1? A: The dropdown in the top left-hand corner, which says main. (00:32:21)
Q: Which GitHub button lists all of a repository’s branches? A: The branch button next to the branch dropdown. (00:33:16)



9. Opening a pull request (9.1 Creating a pull request)
00:33:40–00:41:16

Q: What does the button say on the pop-up GitHub shows after you push a branch? A: “Compare & pull request”. (00:34:25)
Q: Roughly how long does that pop-up stay before it disappears? A: About a day. (00:34:32)
Q: If the pop-up has gone, where can you start a pull request for your branch? A: In the Branches tab: find your branch, open its menu, and choose “New pull request”. (00:35:00)
Q: In which later course did the instructor say the merge target will not always be main? A: DSCI 524. (00:36:14)
Q: What title did the instructor give pull request #1 in the demo repository? A: “Learning about branches and PRs”. (00:37:15)
Q: What description did the instructor write for pull request #1? A: “We are learning about Git switch and creating PRs.” (00:37:21)
Q: Name two kinds of files the instructor said shouldn’t appear in a pull request’s changed files. A: Jupyter’s .ipynb_checkpoints and the Mac .DS_Store. Microsoft Word backup files are another example. Files like these lose points even when the instructions don’t explicitly mention them. (00:39:16)
Q: If work you expected is missing from a pull request’s file list, what did you probably do? A: Typed something wrong, or forgot to add, commit and push. (00:39:37)
Q: Which green button finishes opening the pull request? A: “Create Pull Request”. (00:39:56)
Q: Where can you find a pull request again after leaving its page? A: The Pull Requests tab at the top of the repository. (00:40:15)
Q: When a pull request grows, which comment should you edit instead of adding new ones? A: The very first comment, because that’s what people read. (00:40:55)



10. Code review and updating a pull request (10 Code review on GitHub)
00:41:16–00:45:41

Q: Which pull request tab is where code review happens? A: The “Files Changed” tab, which shows the diff between the original and new files. (00:41:16)
Q: How do you leave a comment on a specific line in a pull request’s diff? A: Hover over the line and click the little plus (+) button. (00:41:34)
Q: What was the instructor’s example review comment? A: “Why are you using switch and not checkout?” (00:41:34)
Q: In code review, whose job is it to fix the code? A: The pull request’s author. The reviewer’s job is to point out problems, not to fix them. (00:42:17)
Q: How do you update an open pull request with new changes? A: Go back to the same branch locally, add, commit and push to it, and the pull request updates. You don’t need to close it and open a new one. (00:43:15)
Q: What commit message did the instructor use for the second commit on dan-b1? A: show you the long git log command. (00:44:12)
Q: What does GitHub do to a review comment when you change the line it was on? A: It may auto-collapse the comment and mark it as outdated. (00:45:02)



11. AI reviewers and draft pull requests (9.2 Draft pull requests)
00:52:11–00:55:41

Q: Which AI tool can you ask on GitHub to review a pull request? A: Copilot. You don’t have to keep every comment it makes: you can push back, reject or accept. (00:52:30)
Q: Which button turns an open pull request into a draft, and where is it? A: “Convert to Draft”, in the top right corner. (00:53:52)
Q: What colour bar marks a draft pull request? A: Gray instead of green. (00:54:04)
Q: What happens to the merge button on a draft pull request? A: It’s grayed out, so no one can merge it by accident. (00:54:30)
Q: How long has the instructor kept draft pull requests open? A: Three or four months. (00:54:56)
Q: Which button turns a draft back into an open pull request, and where is it? A: “Ready for review”, at the bottom of the pull request where it says the pull request is a work in progress. (00:55:28)



12. Merging and deleting the branch on GitHub (8.2 Useful things you can do with branches on GitHub)
00:55:41–00:59:07

Q: What does the instructor do on GitHub right after a pull request is merged? A: He deletes the branch on GitHub. (00:56:08)
Q: When did the instructor say you should not delete branches? A: When a law or compliance rule requires keeping them. (00:57:00)
Q: After merging #1 and clicking delete branch, what happened to the repository’s pull request and branch counts? A: The open pull request count went down by one, and the branch count went from two to one. (00:57:42)
Q: What message did the merge commit for pull request #1 have? A: Merge pull request #1 from chendaniely/dan-b1. (00:58:10)
Q: Does deleting a merged branch delete its commits? A: No. The commits remain in history, along with a separate merge commit. (00:58:19)



13. Syncing and cleaning up locally after a merge (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:59:07–01:03:51

Q: Which individual assignment has students practise merge conflicts again? A: Individual assignment 1. (00:59:07)
Q: What command updated local main after pull request #1 was merged on GitHub? A: git pull origin main, run while on main. (01:00:27)
Q: What did that git pull origin main report about README.md? A: A fast-forward that added 6 lines to README.md (6 insertions(+)). These were the merged pull request’s changes. (01:00:41)
Q: Which command lists all the branches your computer knows about, including remote ones? A: git branch -a. (01:01:06)
Q: In git branch -a output, what marks the branch you’re on? A: A star (*). (01:01:11)
Q: Which command removes local references to branches deleted on GitHub? A: git fetch --prune. (01:01:30)
Q: What did git fetch --prune print in class? A: - [deleted]         (none)     -> origin/dan-b1. (01:01:30)
Q: Which two commands does git pull run? A: git fetch, then a merge. (01:01:52)
Q: Which command deletes a local branch only if it has been merged? A: git branch -d <branch>, with a lowercase d. (01:02:54)
Q: What does git branch -D (capital D) do, and what warning came with it? A: It force-deletes a branch even if it hasn’t been merged, which can delete commits you’re still working on. Be very careful copying commands from ChatGPT, which may hand you capital -D. (01:03:21)



14. Setting up two conflicting pull requests
01:04:00–01:10:00

Q: What kind of change causes a merge conflict? A: Two different changes to the same line of the same file. (01:04:00)
Q: Name the two branches the instructor created to cause a conflict. A: dan-fetch and dan-delete. (01:04:35)
Q: What commit message did the instructor use on dan-fetch? A: define fetch --prune. (01:05:36)
Q: What did the instructor say is the key to practising merge conflicts on your own? A: Don’t merge the first pull request right away. (01:06:07)
Q: What error did git switch -b dan-delete produce in class? A: error: unknown switch `b'. The working command was git switch -c dan-delete. (01:06:40)
Q: What commit message did the instructor use on dan-delete? A: branch -d and -D. (01:07:51)
Q: Which pull request numbers came from dan-fetch and dan-delete? A: #2 (define fetch --prune) came from dan-fetch, and #3 (branch -d and -D) came from dan-delete. (01:09:11)
Q: What did git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate show after both branches were committed? A: Two lines coming out of the same main commit: two parallel pieces of work. (01:08:19)
Q: Before either pull request was merged, did GitHub warn that #2 and #3 would conflict? A: No. Each pull request on its own showed nothing indicating a merge conflict. (01:09:53)



15. When a merge creates the conflict: resolving on GitHub (8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?)
01:10:00–01:12:44

Q: What does GitHub do to other pull requests targeting main when one of them is merged? A: It rechecks each one to see whether it can still be merged. (01:10:19)
Q: Which GitHub tool can resolve simple conflicts without your local computer? A: The web editor. (01:10:54)
Q: Name the three conflict markers you look for when fixing a conflict. A: Less-than, equals and greater-than markers: <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>>. (01:10:59)
Q: State what “fixing” a conflict means for code in this course. A: Your code must work from top to bottom again, not just have the markers removed. A conflict on line 13 can still break something on line 50. (01:11:21)



16. Resolving the conflict locally with rebase (8.3.2 Using rebase)
01:12:44–01:20:42

Q: Which Git command does the instructor use to fix conflicts on a branch locally? A: git rebase. (01:14:04)
Q: Define what a rebase does, in the instructor’s words. A: It replays your branch’s commits on top of the existing changes. (01:14:31)
Q: What two commands synced main before the rebase? A: git switch main, then git pull origin main. (01:16:25)
Q: What two commands started the rebase of the conflicting branch? A: git switch dan-delete, then git rebase main. (01:17:01)
Q: What did git rebase main print when it hit the conflict? A: CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in README.md, followed by error: could not apply cb810d5... branch -d and -D. (01:17:14)
Q: How did the instructor resolve the README.md conflict? A: He kept both definitions and cleaned up some whitespace. (01:17:46)
Q: In DSCI 521, which command triggered merge conflicts, compared with the one used here? A: In 521 it was git pull origin main. Here it was git rebase main. (01:17:56)
Q: Which option gets you out of a rebase if something goes wrong? A: git rebase --abort. (01:18:20)
Q: After fixing the conflict markers, which two commands completed the rebase? A: git add README.md to mark the resolution, then git rebase --continue. (01:18:32)
Q: What exact command pushed the rebased dan-delete branch? A: git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete. (01:19:34)
Q: What error came from the first attempt at the force push? A: error: unknown option `force-with-leasse' because the option was misspelled. (01:19:34)
Q: What did the successful force push print for dan-delete? A: + cb810d5...0e16503 dan-delete -> dan-delete (forced update). (01:19:47)
Q: After a rebase, can you push without forcing, and what does GitHub show afterwards? A: No. You can’t avoid a force push, because the rebase changed the branch’s history. GitHub then records that a force push happened. (01:20:17)
Q: How did the instructor describe a force push after a rebase, in compliance terms? A: You’ve “mangled history”. (01:20:21)
Q: Which two commands clean up locally after a rebased pull request is merged? A: git fetch --prune and git branch -d. (01:20:35)

text:
2. Review Git basics in the demo repository (8 Git branches)
00:04:07–00:06:49

title: Git branches, pull requests, and merge conflicts
section: 3. Why branches exist: escaping the “I have to pull before I push” friction (8 Git branches)
text:
3. Why branches exist: escaping the “I have to pull before I push” friction (8 Git branches)
00:06:49–00:09:43

DSCI 521 shared slide deck: In week 3 of 521, students collaborated on a shared slide deck and often had to pull before they could push, even when there was no actual conflict.
Collaboration friction: If two people are editing the same thing, there is constant friction around coordinating updates; this problem exists in every project.
Parallel streams: The goal is to reach a part of the project where a student owns a self-contained piece of work and can work on it without constantly waiting for others.
Branch benefit: A branch gives a person “their own little world” where they can commit, push, and pull until their work is ready for team review.

title: Git branches, pull requests, and merge conflicts

text:
4. Local repository versus remote origin (8 Git branches)
00:09:46–00:11:11

Two places work happens: Git work happens locally on a computer and remotely on the cloud/remote, called origin in this session.
Coordination: With teammates, everyone coordinates through the remote; the remote is the shared source of truth.
One-time clone: git clone is a one-time command that brings the repository down to the computer.
Push and pull: Local commits are sent upward with git push; work created by others is brought down with git pull.


[!WARNING]
Daniel Chen stressed that if your work exists only on your local computer, it “effectively doesn’t really exist” for grading or project purposes. The remote repository is what matters.

title: Git branches, pull requests, and merge conflicts
section: 5. main, origin/main, HEAD, and what a branch is (8 Git branches)
text:
5. main, origin/main, HEAD, and what a branch is (8 Git branches)
00:11:11–00:16:05

main: main is the default branch and the place that often represents the stable, final, or production state of the project.
origin/main: origin/main is the local computer’s record of what the remote main branch is at.
HEAD: HEAD is the current pointer into the Git history; when it points to main, you are on the main branch.
Branch as a name: A branch is essentially another name that moves forward when you commit, instead of moving main.
Stable main: In larger projects, main should be stable and working; exploratory work, unfinished analysis, or plots that are still being tested should live on a branch until ready.




The Git review, branches, and pull-request diagrams

title: Git branches, pull requests, and merge conflicts
section: 6. Branches are useful even when working alone (8 Git branches)
text:
6. Branches are useful even when working alone (8 Git branches)
00:16:05–00:17:54

Solo branching: Branches are not only for collaboration; many single-person Git repositories also use branches.
Section off work: A branch lets you test a large set of changes without changing main until you have reviewed and confirmed that everything works.
Easy abandonment: If a branch was a bad idea, it is much easier to abandon or delete the branch than to undo a tangled set of commits on main.
Textbook example: Daniel Chen described working on the course textbook by making a sequence of branch-based changes and merging them after lectures and testing.

section: 7. Creating a branch with git switch -c (8.1 Creating a branch using the command line)
text:
7. Creating a branch with git switch -c (8.1 Creating a branch using the command line)
00:17:54–00:23:46

Check starting state: Before creating a branch, run git status and confirm you are on main.
Sync before coordinated work: If you are building on shared project work, first synchronize with the remote, for example with git pull origin main, so you do not start from an old local state.
Create and move: git switch -c dan-b1 creates a new branch named dan-b1 and immediately moves HEAD to it.
Visible state: After switching, git status says On branch dan-b1, and git log --all shows the new branch at the same commit as main before any new branch-specific commits exist.
Branch naming: In group repositories, Daniel Chen sometimes prefixes branch names with the owner’s name so teammates know who to talk to when something looks odd.
Commit moves the branch: After committing on dan-b1, the branch moves forward while main and origin/main remain where they were.

title: Git branches, pull requests, and merge conflicts
section: 8. Switching between branches and seeing the repository state (8.1.1 Switching to branches that already exist)
text:
8. Switching between branches and seeing the repository state (8.1.1 Switching to branches that already exist)
00:23:46–00:28:26

Editor Git view: In VS Code or Positron, the Git graph shows local main, origin/main, and branch-specific commits; this graph corresponds to the terminal log.
Switch back to main: git switch main moves HEAD back to main, and the working files return to the state stored at main.
Seeing all branches: If branch names do not appear in git log --oneline --graph --decorate, use the --all flag.
switch vs switch -c: git switch <branch> switches to an existing branch; git switch -c <branch> creates and switches to a new branch.
Older checkout command: git checkout is the older equivalent. git checkout -b <branch> created a branch; git branch <branch> creates a branch without moving to it. Daniel Chen uses switch in teaching and suggests that, if you are unsure about checkout, ask tools to use switch instead.

title: Git branches, pull requests, and merge conflicts
section: 9. Pushing a branch to origin and viewing it on GitHub (8.2 Useful things you can do with branches on GitHub)
text:
9. Pushing a branch to origin and viewing it on GitHub (8.2 Useful things you can do with branches on GitHub)
00:28:31–00:33:40

Remote review process: Instead of merging locally, the class workflow is to push the branch and use a GitHub review process.
Check the current branch: Before pushing, confirm which branch you are on; a plain git push while on main may simply report that everything is up to date.
Push the branch: From dan-b1, the command is git push origin dan-b1; this is the same push behavior as before, but the final branch name changes from main to the branch being pushed.
Remote branch appears: After the push, git log --all shows origin/dan-b1, meaning the local computer now knows that GitHub has that branch.
GitHub branch dropdown: On the GitHub repository page, the branch selector can be used to view another branch without merging it into main.
Pre-merge inspection: Teammates can inspect pushed branch code on GitHub even before a pull request is merged.

title: Git branches, pull requests, and merge conflicts
section: 10. Opening a pull request and reviewing the changed files (9.1 Creating a pull request)
text:
10. Opening a pull request and reviewing the changed files (9.1 Creating a pull request)
00:33:40–00:39:56

Compare and pull request: When GitHub recognizes a newly pushed branch, it often shows a “Compare and Pull Request” button or popup.
If the popup disappears: Daniel Chen said the popup can disappear after a day or so; to start the same process later, go to the branches tab, find the branch, and choose the option to create a new pull request.
Open the pull request early: He recommended opening the pull request right away, even while work is in progress, so the process exists and updates as commits are pushed.
Check the base branch: In DSCI 522, the target is usually main, but in 524 the target may not always be main; forks and large open-source projects also require checking that the pull request goes to the right repository and branch.
Title and description: The first pull-request comment should explain the whole set of changes; later edits should update that first comment rather than just appending new notes.
Review the Files Changed tab: Confirm that all intended files are present and that no unwanted files are included.


[!WARNING]
Check the pull request’s changed files for things that do not belong in the repository, such as .ipynb_checkpoints, .DS_Store, Word backup files, or other hidden/temporary files. Daniel Chen said that, in this course, visible unwanted files in a repository can cost points.

The demo pull request created from branch dan-b1 was #1 Learning about branches and PRs.

title: Git branches, pull requests, and merge conflicts
section: 11. Pull request conversation, code review, and updating the same branch (10 Code review on GitHub)
text:
11. Pull request conversation, code review, and updating the same branch (10 Code review on GitHub)
00:39:56–00:45:41

Pull requests tab: Once created, the pull request appears under the repository’s Pull Requests tab and can be revisited later.
Conversation tab: The conversation area is where people discuss the pull request; the original post can be edited, and Daniel Chen recommended keeping the first comment as the definitive explanation.
Files Changed tab: This is where code review happens: GitHub shows the diff between the original file and the proposed new file.
Inline comments: Hovering over diff lines gives a plus button that allows line-specific review comments, which are tracked in the conversation.
Author fixes the code: If it is your pull request, it is your job to fix the issues; reviewers point out problems, but the author updates the codebase.
Push to the same branch: To address review comments, go back to the branch, make the change, commit, and push to the same branch; the pull request updates automatically, though the page may need refreshing.
Outdated comments: If you edit a line that has a comment, GitHub may collapse the comment as outdated.

title: Git branches, pull requests, and merge conflicts
section: 12. Draft pull requests, merging, and deleting the remote branch (9.2 Draft pull requests)
text:
12. Draft pull requests, merging, and deleting the remote branch (9.2 Draft pull requests)
00:52:11–00:58:51

Draft workflow: For work that may take more than a day, open the pull request early and then use “Convert to Draft” to signal that it is not ready for merge.
Visual cue: A draft pull request shows a gray bar instead of a green one, and the merge button is disabled so nobody accidentally merges it.
Ready for review: When the work is ready, use “Ready for review” to turn the draft back into an open pull request.
AI review: Daniel Chen mentioned that you can request AI/Copilot review, but AI comments are not automatically mandatory; a person still reviews and decides whether to accept or reject them.
Merging: After merging, the pull request counter decreases because the pull request is closed.
Remote branch cleanup: He recommended deleting the remote branch after merging so the branch dropdown does not become a long list of finished branches.
Commits remain: Deleting the branch does not delete the commits; they remain in history, including the separate merge commit created by the pull-request merge.

title: Git branches, pull requests, and merge conflicts
section: 13. Local cleanup after a merge: git pull, git branch -a, git fetch --prune, and git branch -d (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
text:
13. Local cleanup after a merge: git pull, git branch -a, git fetch --prune, and git branch -d (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:58:53–01:03:51

Group-project warning: Even when teams use branches, merge conflicts can still happen because agents or teammates may edit the same line, file, or typo.
Individual assignment 1: Daniel Chen noted that individual assignment 1 has students review merge conflicts again, because they still need to know how to recover from them.
Local main is not automatic: After a branch is merged on GitHub, local main does not update by itself; run git switch main and then git pull origin main.
List branches: git branch -a shows local branches and remote-tracking branches; the current branch has a star.
git fetch --prune: This fetches remote state and removes local references to branches that were deleted on GitHub, such as origin/dan-b1.
Safe local branch deletion: git branch -d dan-b1 deletes a local branch only if it has been merged; lowercase -d protects you from deleting unmerged work.
Force local branch deletion: git branch -D <branch> force-deletes a local branch even if it has not been merged.


[!WARNING]
Use lowercase git branch -d <branch> for normal cleanup. A capital -D can permanently delete unmerged work. Daniel Chen specifically warned that copied-and-pasted AI advice might say to use -D, and that can delete commits you were still working on.

title: Git branches, pull requests, and merge conflicts
section: 14. Creating a merge-conflict scenario with two branches (8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?)
text:
14. Creating a merge-conflict scenario with two branches (8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?)
01:03:51–01:10:51

Two competing branches: Daniel Chen created two branches from the same main state: dan-fetch and dan-delete.
Conflicting edits: Both branches made changes to the same region of README.md, so they would conflict if both were merged.
Two pull requests: The two branches produced two open pull requests: #2 define fetch –prune from dan-fetch and #3 branch -d and -D from dan-delete.
First merge changes main: When one pull request is merged, main moves forward.
Other pull requests are rechecked: GitHub rechecks open pull requests against the new main; a pull request that looked mergeable before can become conflicted afterward.
Conflict is not always obvious side by side: Looking at the two pull requests separately did not clearly show that they would conflict; the conflict appears after one branch is merged.

title: Git branches, pull requests, and merge conflicts
section: 15. Resolving the conflict locally with git rebase main and git push --force-with-lease (8.3.2 Using rebase)
text:
15. Resolving the conflict locally with git rebase main and git push --force-with-lease (8.3.2 Using rebase)
01:10:51–01:20:42

Local versus web resolution: Simple conflicts can be resolved in GitHub’s web editor, but Daniel Chen showed local resolution because the command-line process is more general.
What “fix the conflict” means: Fixing the conflict markers is not enough. In this course, “fixed” means the resulting report or code works from top to bottom again.
Sync main first: Switch to main and run git pull origin main so the local main includes the already-merged pull request.
Rebase the conflicting branch: Switch to dan-delete and run git rebase main; this replays the branch’s commit on top of the updated main.
Resolve and continue: When Git stops with a conflict, edit the file, run git add README.md, check git status, and then run git rebase --continue.
Force-with-lease push: Because rebase rewrites the commit history of a branch that was already pushed, a normal push is no longer enough; the session used git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete.
Merge and cleanup: After the force push, the pull request could be merged, and the usual branch cleanup could be done.




Several branches, pull requests, a conflict, and a rebase



[!WARNING]
Resolving the visible conflict markers does not mean the work is done. Daniel Chen stressed that, if changing the conflict affects later code, the student is still responsible for making the whole thing work. Also, after rebase has changed pushed history, use git push --force-with-lease origin <branch>, not a plain push.

3. Why branches: escaping the 521 push/pull friction (8 Git branches)
00:06:49–00:09:43

The 521 problem: in the week 3 shared slide-deck exercise, even without a conflict, you often could not push because someone else had pushed first. You had to pull before pushing again, which is annoying.
Projects start serially: early in a project, everyone is blocked on one or two people getting the basics in place, so not every piece of work can start in parallel. That friction will exist somewhere in every project.
Then move to parallel streams: eventually each person owns a self-contained part. On their own branch, each person can push and pull freely without caring what others are doing.
Coordinating at review time: for example, you work on your part from Tuesday to Friday, and then on Friday the group reviews and merges everyone’s work.

4. Review: the local–remote picture
00:09:46–00:11:47

Two places work lives: your computer (the local repository) and the cloud (the GitHub remote). With teammates, each person’s computer also has to coordinate with that same remote.
The remote is what counts: GitHub is what gets graded and published. Work that exists only on your laptop “effectively doesn’t really exist” for grading or project purposes, just as an unshipped product at work.
The verbs:

clone is a one-time command that brings the repository down.
push sends your commits up to GitHub.
pull brings down commits that teammates pushed.

title: Git Branches, Pull Requests, Code Review and Rebasing to Fix Conflicts
section: 5. What a branch is: main, HEAD and origin/main (8 Git branches)
text:
5. What a branch is: main, HEAD and origin/main (8 Git branches)
00:12:03–00:17:54

main: the default branch. Until now you could ignore why it is called main, but with collaboration you will no longer do most of your work on it.
HEAD: marks where you are. When HEAD is attached to main, each git add and git commit moves main forward.
origin/main: what your computer thinks the state of main on GitHub is. If you commit without pushing, your local main gets ahead of origin/main.
A branch: a name that you choose (drawn as b1). Your commits move that name forward instead of main. The git add/git commit workflow does not change.
main as production: treat main as the stable version, where at least the code works even if the project is unfinished.

For example, the cleaned dataset sits on main, and someone’s exploratory data analysis stays on their branch until it is ready.

Branches help solo work too: Daniel uses branches even in repositories where he is the only contributor.

He made textbook edits on branches while another instructor was teaching from it, so pages would not shift mid-lecture. He merged them only after reviewing and testing.

Easy to throw away: if an idea fails, you can switch back to main or delete the branch. Untangling one 20-change commit from history is much harder. git reset/git revert from 521 also work, but branches make this easier.
These skills work in “single person mode” but scale to multiple people.

title: Git Branches, Pull Requests, Code Review and Rebasing to Fix Conflicts
section: 6. Creating and switching branches (8.1 Creating a branch using the command line)
text:
6. Creating and switching branches (8.1 Creating a branch using the command line)
00:17:54–00:26:29

Check where you are first: run git status and confirm you are On branch main.
Sync before branching: if your work builds on coordinated work, run git pull origin main first. Daniel has wasted time branching from an out-of-date computer when half the work was already done on another laptop.
git switch: moves HEAD around the repository. git switch -c <name> (-c for create) creates a new branch and moves HEAD to it.

In class: git switch -c dan-b1. In shared repositories, Daniel starts branch names with his own name, so others know whom to ask when something looks odd.

Nothing else changes: git status now says On branch dan-b1, and git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all shows HEAD -> dan-b1 on the same commit as main. No new commit was made.
Commit as usual: he documented the command in README.md, then ran git diff, git add README.md and git commit -m "define swtich -c". The log now shows dan-b1 one commit ahead of main and origin/main.
IDE view: the Git tab’s graph view in VS Code and Positron shows the same picture as the terminal log, with origin/main, local main and the dan-b1 commit.
Switching back: git switch main moves HEAD back to main, and the files on disk return to main’s version. The branch you left stays where it was.
You need --all: without the --all flag, git log --oneline may not show your other branches.
Branches are cheap. Create one to try something, then merge it if it works, or switch back and leave it behind if it doesn’t.

title: Git Branches, Pull Requests, Code Review and Rebasing to Fix Conflicts
section: 7. git checkout and git branch versus git switch (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
text:
7. git checkout and git branch versus git switch (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:26:40–00:28:26

git checkout: the older command, used before about 2019–2020, and still what Daniel uses day to day. He uses switch when teaching.
Why it was split: checkout moved HEAD and did much of what git restore (introduced in 521) and git revert do. The newer commands were carved out of it, although checkout still has all those behaviours.
Equivalents: git checkout -b <name> is the old form of git switch -c <name>.
git branch <name>: creates a branch but does not move you to it, so you still need switch or checkout afterwards.
AI advice: Copilot or ChatGPT may tell you to run checkout. If you do not know exactly what that command will do, ask for the switch version instead, especially when you are worried about losing work.

title: Git Branches, Pull Requests, Code Review and Rebasing to Fix Conflicts
section: 8. Pushing a branch and viewing it on GitHub (8.2 Useful things you can do with branches on GitHub)
text:
8. Pushing a branch and viewing it on GitHub (8.2 Useful things you can do with branches on GitHub)
00:28:31–00:33:40

Merging through review: the easiest way to get a branch into main is not to merge locally. Push the branch and merge it through a pull request (called a merge request on some platforms).
No new command: push is still the only link from local to remote, but now where and what you push matter.

On main, a bare git push printed Everything up-to-date. It did not send dan-b1.
Switch to the branch, then run git push origin dan-b1. If you have typed git push origin main for ten weeks, the last word is the branch you are pushing.

After the push: the log shows origin/dan-b1 beside dan-b1, but origin/main has not moved.
On GitHub: the repository’s main view still shows only main’s content. Use the branch dropdown at the top left to view dan-b1, and the branch button next to it to list all branches.
Why that’s useful: you can check that your work really reached GitHub. You can also read a teammate’s pushed code, such as how they made a figure, without running it and before it is merged.
The branch list grows over a project (one branch per person or feature) unless you delete merged branches.

title: Git Branches, Pull Requests, Code Review and Rebasing to Fix Conflicts
section: 9. Opening a pull request (9.1 Creating a pull request)
text:
9. Opening a pull request (9.1 Creating a pull request)
00:33:40–00:41:16

“Compare & pull request”: after you push a branch, GitHub shows a pop-up with this green button.

The pop-up disappears after about a day. You can get the same page from the Branches tab: find your branch, open its menu, and choose “New pull request”.
Daniel opens a pull request right away, even after one tiny commit, so he never loses the pop-up.

Check the base and compare branches: the top line should name your branch and the branch it merges into, which is main in this course. In DSCI 524 the target will not always be main. With forks of open-source projects you must also check that the code is going to the right repository.
Title and description: the pull request is a report of what changed and why. Daniel used the title “Learning about branches and PRs” and the description “We are learning about Git switch and creating PRs.” For small group-project changes, the title and description may be nearly the same. Pull requests written by AI agents can “read like a novel.”
Review your own work here: the bottom of the page lists every changed file and diff relative to main. This is your second line of defence, after reviewing on your own computer.

Check that all the files you worked on are there. If any are missing, you probably forgot to add, commit or push.
Check that no junk is there: .ipynb_checkpoints, macOS .DS_Store, Word backup files and the like. Your .gitignore still matters.

Create pull request: it then appears under the Pull requests tab for everyone with access, and teammates can discuss it in the conversation. The result in class was #1.
Edit the first comment: when the pull request grows, edit the opening description rather than adding “now I’m also doing…” comments. People read the first comment.


[!WARNING]
Files that don’t belong in the repository — checkpoint files, .DS_Store, hidden backup files — lose you points even if the instructions don’t explicitly mention them. Check the file list before creating the pull request.

title: Git Branches, Pull Requests, Code Review and Rebasing to Fix Conflicts
section: 10. Code review and updating a pull request (10 Code review on GitHub)
text:
10. Code review and updating a pull request (10 Code review on GitHub)
00:41:16–00:45:41

Files changed tab: this is what “code review” means. You read the diff between the original file and the new one.
Inline comments: hover over a line and click the + to comment on it. Daniel’s example was “why are you using switch and not checkout?” These comments also appear in the main Conversation tab.
Who fixes it: the author of the pull request fixes the code. The reviewer’s job is to point out problems (“rewrite this”, “this doesn’t look right”), not to fix them. The author can also simply reply to a comment.
Updating a pull request: do not close it and open a new one. Go back to the same branch locally, then add, commit and push, and the pull request updates.

In class he added the git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all command to README.md, then ran git commit -m "show you the long git log command" and git push origin dan-b1. The second commit appeared in #1, sometimes only after a page refresh.

Outdated comments: if you change a line someone commented on, GitHub may collapse that comment as outdated, because it no longer applies.

title: Git Branches, Pull Requests, Code Review and Rebasing to Fix Conflicts
section: 11. AI reviewers and draft pull requests (9.2 Draft pull requests)
text:
11. AI reviewers and draft pull requests (9.2 Draft pull requests)
00:52:11–00:55:41

The progression so far: you can review your own work, so you don’t bother a human, and then teammates can review it too.
Copilot review: GitHub lets you request a Copilot review. More eyes are not a bad idea, but you do not have to keep every comment an LLM makes. You can push back, reject it or accept it.
Convert to draft: Daniel opens a pull request early and keeps pushing to it, so he signals that it is unfinished with “Convert to draft” at the top right.

A draft shows a grey bar instead of green, which tells everyone “you can look, but it’s not ready.”
The merge button is greyed out, so nobody can merge it by accident. Daniel believes this also stops an agent from merging everything that’s green.
He has kept drafts open for three or four months on long pieces of work.

Ready for review: at the bottom of the pull request (“This pull request is still a work in progress”), click “Ready for review” to make it an open pull request again, with green merge buttons.

12. Merging and deleting the branch on GitHub (8.2 Useful things you can do with branches on GitHub)
00:55:41–00:59:07

Merge: clicking the merge button closed #1, and the open pull request count went down by one.
Delete the branch afterwards: Daniel clicks “Delete branch” after a merge, so the branch dropdown does not become a giant list of stale branches. In the demo, the branch count went from two to one.
Team norms decide: some workplaces cannot delete anything for compliance reasons. Otherwise, at least clean up your own branches.
Nothing is lost: deleting the branch label does not delete commits. main’s history shows the branch’s two commits plus a merge commit (“Merge pull request #1 from chendaniely/dan-b1”), so you can still find and undo a feature later.

section: 13. Syncing and cleaning up locally after a merge (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
text:
13. Syncing and cleaning up locally after a merge (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:59:07–01:03:51

Conflicts still happen with branches: even when people split the work, someone, or an agent, may fix a typo in your part. That is why individual assignment 1 has you practise merge conflicts again.
Local main doesn’t update itself: after git switch main, run git pull origin main. In class this fast-forwarded main and added 6 lines to README.md, which were the merged pull request’s changes.
git branch -a: lists the local branches (with * on the current one) and the remote-tracking branches such as remotes/origin/dan-b1.
git fetch --prune: syncs history with origin without changing your files. It also removes local references to branches deleted on GitHub; the output showed [deleted] (none) -> origin/dan-b1.

git pull is git fetch followed by a merge. Run fetch alone when you don’t want your working files to change.

git branch -d <branch>: lowercase -d deletes a local branch only if it has been merged. Git makes it harder to lose unmerged work.
git branch -D <branch>: capital -D force-deletes the branch even if it has not been merged.


[!WARNING]
Use lowercase git branch -d. Capital -D force-deletes a branch even if it was never merged, which can throw away commits you’re still working on. It’s a one-character difference — be very careful when copying commands from ChatGPT, which may hand you -D.

title: Git Branches, Pull Requests, Code Review and Rebasing to Fix Conflicts
section: 14. Setting up two conflicting pull requests (8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?)
text:
14. Setting up two conflicting pull requests (8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?)
01:04:00–01:10:00

What causes a conflict: two changes to the same line of the same file. Daniel created two branches from main that both added text at the same spot in README.md.
First branch, dan-fetch: he documented git fetch --prune, committed with git commit -m "define fetch --prune", pushed, and opened #2. He did not merge it straight away; that is the key to practising conflicts on your own.
Second branch, dan-delete: he switched back to main, created dan-delete, and documented git branch -d and -D. Because he branched from main, the fetch line was not in this version of the file. He committed with git commit -m "branch -d and -D" and opened #3.
The split is visible: git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate shows two lines leaving the same main commit, which means two parallel pieces of work.
GitHub hides it at first: each pull request on its own looks fine and mergeable into main. Nothing warns you that both edit the same line.
crumbs: Nov 17 · Git Branches, Pull Requests, Code Review and Rebasing to Fix Conflicts

title: Git Branches, Pull Requests, Code Review and Rebasing to Fix Conflicts
section: 15. When a merge creates the conflict: resolving on GitHub
text:
15. When a merge creates the conflict: resolving on GitHub
01:10:00–01:12:44

How it appears: when one pull request merges, main changes, and GitHub rechecks every other pull request that targets main. Once #2 was merged, #3 showed a conflict.
Web editor: simple conflicts can be resolved in GitHub’s web editor. Find the conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) and fix them.
What “fixed” means for prose: the remaining report text must be English that makes sense.
What “fixed” means for code: the code must run from top to bottom again. A conflict on line 13 can break line 50, for example if a variable was renamed, and that is still your problem.


[!WARNING]
Resolving a conflict doesn’t just mean deleting the conflict markers. Your code has to work again from top to bottom — a change made at the conflicting line can break code elsewhere in the file.
crumbs: Nov 17 · Git Branches, Pull Requests, Code Review and Rebasing to Fix Conflicts

title: Git Branches, Pull Requests, Code Review and Rebasing to Fix Conflicts
section: 16. Resolving the conflict locally with rebase (8.3.2 Using rebase)
text:
16. Resolving the conflict locally with rebase (8.3.2 Using rebase)
01:12:44–01:20:42

Many valid ways: Daniel uses rebase and noted that people who know Git well will have opinions about it.
The idea: replay your branch’s commits on top of the updated main. The conflict then surfaces on your own computer, where you can fix it.

In the demo, dan-delete’s parent was 3851b00. It needed to sit on top of the merge that contains 157c3cd (the fetch commit).

Step 1, sync main: git switch main, then git pull origin main.
Step 2, rebase your branch: git switch dan-delete, then git rebase main. Git stops on the conflict.
Step 3, fix the file: open README.md in your editor and resolve the markers. Here he kept both definitions and tidied the whitespace. This is the same skill as week 3 of 521; only the trigger differs (git rebase main instead of git pull origin main).
Step 4, let git status guide you: it tells you to git add the file to mark it resolved, and then to run git rebase --continue, which asks you to confirm the commit message. If you are scared, git rebase --abort gets you back to where you started.
Step 5, force-push: the rebased commit has a new parent, so the branch’s history has changed and a normal push is rejected. Daniel used git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete. GitHub then records that a force push happened, and the pull request shows a green merge button again.
Finish up: merge, delete the branch on GitHub, and clean up locally with git fetch --prune and git branch -d.


[!WARNING]
Rebasing rewrites your branch’s history, so you can’t avoid a force push afterwards — and it shows up on GitHub as a force push (“you’ve mangled history”, which matters in compliance settings). Only do this to your own branch.
