title: Git Cheatsheet
text: Run all of these commands in your terminal, from inside your project folder (except git clone, which creates the folder for you). For the full explanations, see the textbook chapters on Git basics, Git history, Git branches, and merge conflicts.

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
1 The Everyday Workflow







Task
Command




Clone a remote version control repository from GitHub.com to your local computer
git clone <URL>


Check the status of the local version control repository
git status


Add a file to the staging area
git add <FILENAME>


Commit staged files to the version control history
git commit -m "Some relevant message about the changes"


Push changes from the local repository to the remote repository on GitHub.com
git push


Pull changes from the remote repository on GitHub.com to the local repository
git pull


View the version control history
git log



The usual loop is: git pull → edit files → git status → git add → git commit → git push.

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
2 Getting a Repository

git clone <URL> — Copy a remote repository from GitHub.com to your computer

Example: git clone https://github.com/UBC-MDS/DSCI_522_dsci-workflows_students.git

This creates a new folder named after the repository. Use cd <folder_name> to go into it.

Do not clone a repository inside another repository.

git init — Turn the current folder into a new, empty Git repository

Only needed when you start a project locally. If you start on GitHub.com and then git clone, you do not need it.

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
3 Checking the Status

git status — Show which files are modified, staged, or not tracked yet

Run it often, especially before git add and git commit.

git diff — Show the changes you made that are not staged yet

git diff --staged — Show the changes that are staged and will go into the next commit

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
4 Staging and Committing

git add <FILENAME> — Add a file to the staging area

git add <FILE1> <FILE2> — Add several files at once

git add <FOLDER>/ — Add everything in a folder

git add . — Add all changes in the current folder (check git status first so you only stage what you mean to)

git commit -m "Some relevant message about the changes" — Commit the staged files to the version control history

Write a short, specific message that says what changed and why.
Only staged files are committed.

git restore --staged <FILENAME> — Unstage a file (your edits to the file are kept)
git restore <FILENAME> — Discard your unstaged edits to a file and go back to the last commit

⚠️ This cannot be undone.

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
5 Syncing with GitHub

git push — Send your local commits to the remote repository on GitHub.com

First push of a new branch: git push -u origin <BRANCH_NAME> (-u stands for --set-upstream). See the branches section below for the difference between this and git push origin <BRANCH_NAME>.

git pull — Get changes from the remote repository on GitHub.com and merge them into your local repository

Pull before you start working, and before you push, to avoid conflicts.

git fetch — Download the latest changes from GitHub.com without merging them into your files
git remote -v — Show the URL of the remote repository your local repository is connected to

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
6 Viewing the History

git log — View the version control history

Press q to exit the log. Use the arrow keys, b, or the space bar to scroll.

Press / + a search term + Enter to search the log; n / N jump to the next / previous match.

git log -n 3 — Show only the last 3 commits

git log <FILENAME> — Show only the commits that changed this file

git show <COMMIT_ID> — Show the changes made in one commit

The commit ID (also called the commit hash, or SHA) is the long string of letters and numbers after commit in git log. It is a hash of the commit’s contents, so each commit has a unique one.

The first 7 characters (the short SHA) are usually enough: git show 238dbcb








TipJust want a look at the past?



On GitHub.com, click the commits link on the repository’s main page to see the history and commit messages. Click the <> button next to a commit to view the state of the whole repository at that point in time.

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
7 Going Back in Time
Use these in your local repository when you want to run or explore files from the past, or bring a past version of a file into the present.

git checkout <COMMIT_ID> . — Move the whole project (all files and directories) back to the state of that commit

The last . is really important, so don’t forget it!

Example: git checkout 9b4af1d .

The files now look like they did at that commit, so you can explore and run them.

git checkout HEAD . — Go back to the future: return to the most recent commit

HEAD is the nickname for the most recent commit.

Run git log afterwards to check you returned safely.

git checkout <COMMIT_ID> <FILENAME> — Bring back the version of a single file from a past commit

Example: git checkout 5837143 doc/count_report.Rmd

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
8 Branches

git branch — List the local branches (the current one is marked with *)

git branch -v — Also show the SHA and message of the last commit on each branch (-v stands for --verbose)
git branch -a — Also list the branches on the remote

git switch -c <BRANCH_NAME> — Create a new branch and switch to it

Same as git checkout -b <BRANCH_NAME>

Use a descriptive name, e.g. patch-docs for a fix to the documentation.

git switch <BRANCH_NAME> — Switch to an existing branch (no -c, since we are not creating one)

Same as git checkout <BRANCH_NAME>

git fetch --all — Download all changes to all branches from the remote, so you can switch to a branch a collaborator created
git push origin <BRANCH_NAME> — Push the changes on a branch to the remote repository (usually named origin)

This pushes once. Git does not remember the connection, so a plain git push on that branch fails with fatal: The current branch <BRANCH_NAME> has no upstream branch, and you have to type git push origin <BRANCH_NAME> every time.

git push -u origin <BRANCH_NAME> — Push and link your local branch to the remote branch of the same name (-u stands for --set-upstream). After this, plain git push and git pull work on that branch, and git status tells you whether you are ahead of or behind the remote.

You only need -u the first time you push a new branch.

git merge <BRANCH_NAME> — Merge the branch <BRANCH_NAME> into the branch you are currently on

If the same lines were changed in both branches, Git stops with a merge conflict. Open the files with <<<<<<< markers, choose what to keep, then git add and git commit.

git branch -d <BRANCH_NAME> — Delete a local branch that has been merged







TipTypical branch workflow




git switch main and git pull — start from the latest main
git switch -c my-new-feature — create a branch
Edit, git add, git commit (repeat as needed)
git push -u origin my-new-feature — push the branch
Open a pull request on GitHub.com, get it reviewed, and merge it there
git switch main and git pull — bring the merged work back to your computer

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
9 Ignoring Files
.gitignore — A text file in the root of the repository listing files and folders that Git should not track
- One pattern per line, e.g. .venv/, *.log, .DS_Store
- Prepend **/ to a file or folder name (e.g. **/.venv/, **/.DS_Store) to also ignore it in subdirectories anywhere within the repository

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
10 Common Problems







Message or situation
What to do




fatal: not a git repository
You are not inside a repository folder. Use pwd and cd to find your project folder.


Your branch is behind 'origin/main'
Run git pull.


rejected ... failed to push some refs
The remote has commits you do not have. Run git pull, fix any conflicts, then git push again.


CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in <file>
Open the file, resolve the <<<<<<< / ======= / >>>>>>> sections, then git add <file> and git commit.


nothing to commit, working tree clean
Nothing has changed since the last commit. Nothing to do.


git commit opens a strange text editor (Vim)
You forgot -m "message". In Vim, type :q! and press Enter to quit, then run the command again with -m.

--name and -n are equivalent

More command line review cheatsheet is available here

title: Conda & Conda-lock Cheatsheet
text:
3 Conda-lock

3.1 Basic Commands








Command
Output
Description




conda-lock lock --file environment.yml
conda-lock.yml
General lock file for all platforms


conda-lock lock --file environment.yml -p linux-64
conda-lock.yml
General lock file for specific platform (Linux)


conda-lock -k explicit --file environment.yml -p linux-64
conda-linux-64.lock
Explicit lock file for one platform (Linux)


conda-lock render -p linux-64
conda-linux-64.lock
Explicit lock file from existing conda-lock.yml





3.2 Comparing conda-lock.yml vs conda-linux-64.lock








Feature
conda-lock.yml
conda-linux-64.lock




Format
Unified YAML (multi-platform)
Explicit (single-platform)


Content
Structured metadata + dependencies for all platforms
Simple list of package URLs


File Size
Larger (contains all platforms)
Smaller (one platform only)


Installation
conda-lock install --name <env_name> conda-lock.yml
conda create --name <env_name> --file conda-linux-64.lock


Use case
Development across multiple platforms
Production deployment, Docker, single platform


Speed
Slightly slower (conda-lock processes it)
Fastest





3.3 Creating Environments from Lock Files
From conda-lock.yml:
conda-lock install --name <env_name> conda-lock.yml
From explicit lock file (e.g., conda-linux-64.lock):
conda create --name <env_name> --file conda-linux-64.lock

title: Milestone 4
text:
NoteThe end-of-course project goal





Your team answers a predictive question with a public data set, in R and/or Python, with a focus on reproducible and trustworthy workflows. By the end of the course, your single Quarto document will have become a project with:

well-documented, modular scripts in R and/or Python
a pipeline automated with GNU Make
a reproducible Quarto report
a Docker container for the computational environment
a GitHub repository for collaboration and sharing

title: Milestone 4
text:
Milestone 4 summary
This milestone ties your project together: one command runs the whole analysis, your code is tested, your report reads like a finished paper, and you fix what reviewers pointed out.

Write a Makefile so make all runs every script, renders the report and publishes it
Move some code into functions (at least one per team member) and write tests for them
Polish your report: no visible code, numbered and cross-referenced figures and tables, citations
Address feedback from the TAs and from the peer review







ImportantSee what a finished Milestone 4 looks like



An example Milestone 4 that corresponds to our expectations is here: Breast Cancer Predictor 3.0.0. Look at its Makefile, src/ and tests/ folders. It uses conda for its environment: ignore that part and keep the uv/renv setup from Milestone 2.








TipReadings for this milestone






Data analysis pipelines with GNU Make and the Makefile cheatsheet
Testing, then pytest (Python) or testthat (R)
Reproducible reports with Quarto and the Quarto cheatsheet (you practised these in Individual Assignment 3)





1. Write a Makefile that runs everything
Put a file named Makefile in the root of your repository, as you did in Individual Assignment 4. It needs:

an all target: runs the whole analysis from top to bottom, including publish
a clean target: deletes everything the pipeline made, so make all can start fresh
a publish target: copies the rendered report to docs/index.html, replacing the steps you did by hand in Milestone 2
real file targets for the other steps, with their dependencies (the data and the script), so Make only reruns what changed. Only all, clean, publish and similar group names may be phony.
comments that explain each rule, and a README section that says how to run it

Your scripts run in the container, so the commands in the rules start with uv run (Python), for example uv run python scripts/download_data.py ... and uv run quarto render .... Run the pipeline with docker compose run --rm analysis-env make all.






TipExample: the publish target





Change the report’s path to your own:


Makefile

publish: docs/index.html

docs/index.html: reports/<your-report>.html
    mkdir -p docs
    cp reports/<your-report>.html docs/index.html
    touch docs/.nojekyll

Because docs/index.html depends on your rendered report, make publish copies it only when the report has changed. Commit and push docs/ after it runs.





2. Write functions and test them
Look for code that repeats (cleaning several columns the same way, many similar plots, tuning several models) or that you would reuse in another project.

Write at least one function per team member, following the textbook’s workflow for writing functions and tests: write the documentation first, then the tests, then the function body.
Put them in their own files: src/*.py (Python) or R/*.R (R). One function per file, or all in one file, both are fine.
Use them in your scripts with import (Python) or source() (R).
Write tests in tests/ with pytest (Python) or testthat (R). Add the test package to your environment, and say in your README how to run the tests in the container.







TipHow your functions are marked






Quality: each function does one thing, and returns a value unless it is meant to write a file or plot.
Usability and readability: clear names and arguments; black (Python) or tidyverse (R) style.
Documentation: a docstring (Python) or roxygen comment (R) saying what it does, its arguments and what it returns.
Tests: they cover expected cases, edge cases and errors.

More functions than the minimum are welcome, but each one is held to these standards.





3. Polish your report
A reader who is not a data scientist should not be able to tell that code made the report. Render it to HTML (that is the version on GitHub Pages); a PDF as well is optional.

A table of contents
Citations from a BibTeX file, with a reference list at the end
Figures with a label and a caption, so Quarto numbers them, at a sensible size
Tables with a label and a caption, so Quarto numbers them
The text refers to figures and tables with cross-references (@fig-..., @tbl-...), never typed numbers
Values in the text (accuracy, sample size…) come from inline code, not typed in by hand
No code shows in the rendered report, only its output



4. Address feedback

From the TAs
Fix what the TAs pointed out in earlier milestones. Then submit a regrade request on Gradescope for that question, with links to the pull requests or commits that show the change. If the TA confirms the fix, you get back 50% of the points you lost on that question. Keep the request easy to follow, or we can’t give points back.


From the peer review
Address at least one peer review item per team member (a team of 4 fixes at least 4). List them in a CHANGELOG.md in the root of your repository: for each item, the feedback, what you changed, and a link to the evidence (an issue, pull request, commit or lines of code). Feedback that the TAs also gave can go in too. See keepachangelog.com for an example.



5. Update your README
Your README must take someone from a fresh clone to the rendered report: pull the image, run make all in the container, and how to run the tests. Also say how to run make clean.






Important5 all-or-nothing points for your README instructions



If someone can’t run your whole pipeline by following your instructions exactly as written, you lose all 5 points. Test them on both Windows and Mac. If your team doesn’t have both, ask another team to test them.

All tests pass in the container
The rendered report shows no code and every item in the polish list above is done
CHANGELOG.md lists at least one peer review item per team member, with links
Someone on Windows and someone on Mac followed your README steps exactly
Your report on GitHub Pages matches your release
You created the 3.0.0 release










TipTeamwork expectations (these are marked)






Everyone contributes equally to code, writing and project management, shown by a roughly equal number of commits, pull request reviews and GitHub issue comments.
Use the GitHub flow: a branch for each feature or fix, reviewed by at least one teammate before the pull request is merged.
Commit and push every time you work on the project, with meaningful commit messages (one or two less meaningful ones are OK).
Talk to your teammates in GitHub issues, not email or Slack: at least 3 issues per person on average in this milestone.
Your question, analysis and visualization should make sense. They don’t have to be complicated.
Your analysis should be correct and run reproducibly from your README instructions.
Follow the black style guide (Python) or the tidyverse style guide (R).
Don’t commit generated files, except docs/, which GitHub Pages needs.
Write your README in full sentences with proper grammar. Keep point form under 10% of it.

title: Milestone 2
text:
NoteThe end-of-course project goal





Your team answers a predictive question with a public data set, in R and/or Python, with a focus on reproducible and trustworthy workflows. By the end of the course, your single Quarto document will have become a project with:

well-documented, modular scripts in R and/or Python
a pipeline automated with GNU Make
a reproducible Quarto report
a Docker container for the computational environment
a GitHub repository for collaboration and sharing

title: Milestone 2
text:
Milestone 2 summary
This milestone is about moving your project into a container.

Run your project’s environment in a Docker container, and work in it from now on
Build the image on GitHub Actions for Intel/AMD and ARM, and publish it on Docker Hub
Update your README and CONTRIBUTING.md so they use the container
Publish your report on GitHub Pages

We give you the Dockerfile, the workflow file and docker-compose.yml (see below). They are adapted from docker-uv-renv.






ImportantYou only lose points once for the same mistake



If you lost points for something in Milestone 1, we won’t take points off again for it in Milestone 2. That would be unfair: you may not get your Milestone 1 grades back before Milestone 2 is due. Still fix it once you get the feedback: later milestones build on this work, and in Milestone 4 you can fix the mistakes you made in previous milestones.








ImportantSee what a finished Milestone 2 looks like



An example Milestone 2 that corresponds to our expectations from this year is here: Breast Cancer Predictor in Python 1.0.0. Use it as your model: compare your repository with it before you submit.








TipReadings for this milestone






Python and R in one image: what each line of the Dockerfile does
uv in a container and renv in a container: adding a package to your image
renv: declaring packages in DESCRIPTION: pinning R package versions
Docker Compose: starting the container with one command
Working in a container over ssh with Positron: editing code inside the container
Building images for several platforms: why the workflow builds for two kinds of computer
Introduction to Quarto and GitHub Pages (DSCI 521): publishing the report in part 3





1. Put your environment in a container

Add the Dockerfile. Copy the version for your project’s language(s) below into a file named Dockerfile in the root of your repository. If you use R, change 4.6.2 on the FROM line to the R version in your renv.lock. Always keep a version tag on the FROM line, never latest.
Check your environment files. The image installs your packages from your lock files, so these must be in your repository and agree with each other:

Python (uv): pyproject.toml with every package pinned with == (not >=), uv.lock and .python-version. It must list ipykernel, nbclient and pyyaml (Quarto needs them to run the Python code in your report).
R (renv): DESCRIPTION with every package pinned with (== x.y.z), renv.lock, .Rprofile and renv/. DESCRIPTION is required, and it must list knitr and rmarkdown (Quarto needs them to run the R code in your report).

Test the build on your computer before you push: docker build --tag my-project . (as in Individual Assignment 2). Fixing errors here is much faster than on GitHub Actions.
Build and publish the image with GitHub Actions.

One team member sets up Docker Hub and the GitHub secrets (see below).
Copy the workflow below into .github/workflows/publish-dockerhub.yml, then commit and push. You don’t need to change anything in it.
It builds for linux/amd64 (Intel/AMD) and linux/arm64 (ARM, such as Apple silicon Macs), and publishes them under two tags: latest and sha- plus 7 characters of the commit ID.
Check that the run succeeds and that your image’s tag on Docker Hub lists both platforms.
Don’t turn on branch protection for main: the workflow commits the new image tag straight to your branches, and branch protection would block it.

Add docker-compose.yml.

Copy the file below into the root of your repository.
Change its image: line to your image, pinned to the commit-SHA tag your workflow pushed, not latest (for example, image: yourname/your-github-repo-name:sha-1a2b3c4, all in lowercase). You only do this once: after that, the workflow updates the tag for you.
Keep the service name analysis-env, so the commands in part 2 work as written.

Work in the container from now on, with Positron over ssh Follow the step-by-step guide below the first time. To add a package:

On a branch, add it with uv or renv, commit the changed files together and push.
GitHub Actions publishes a new image and commits its tag to docker-compose.yml on that branch.
Run git pull and docker compose pull, then merge the branch in a pull request.
The merge builds the image once more and commits a new tag to main. When that run finishes, everyone runs git pull on main and docker compose pull again.








TipThe Dockerfile (step 1)





Pick the tab for your project. All three start the ssh server, so you can work in the container with Positron.

Python onlyR onlyPython and R




Dockerfile

# Adapted from docker-uv-renv by Daniel Chen (MIT License)
# https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv

# Start from Ubuntu Linux (this image also has R, which you can ignore).
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2

# Install the programs the project needs:
# curl downloads files, git/less/nano let you work in a terminal,
# make runs a Makefile, openssh-server lets Positron connect over ssh
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install --yes \
    curl \
    git \
    less \
    make \
    nano \
    openssh-server

# Install Quarto (it comes with Typst for PDFs, so no LaTeX).
# dpkg --print-architecture gives amd64 or arm64, to match the computer.
RUN curl --location --output quarto.deb \
    https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/releases/download/v1.11.9/quarto-1.11.9-linux-$(dpkg --print-architecture).deb \
  && apt-get install --yes ./quarto.deb \
  && rm quarto.deb

# Copy the uv program into the image (0.13.7 pins uv's version)
COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/

# Your project folder is mounted at /workspace,
# so the packages go in /opt instead
WORKDIR /workspace

# Python packages (uv) go in /opt/venv
ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv
# ssh logins don't see ENV, only /etc/environment
RUN echo "UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=$UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT" >> /etc/environment
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version ./
# --locked: stop if uv.lock doesn't match pyproject.toml
RUN uv sync --locked

# On a Linux laptop, remove the # from the next line.
# (sshd wants root to own the key file, but on Linux the mounted one is yours.)
# RUN echo "StrictModes no" > /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/container.conf

# Start the ssh server when the container starts.
# -D keeps it in the foreground, so the container keeps running.
CMD ["/usr/sbin/sshd", "-D"]





Dockerfile

# Adapted from docker-uv-renv by Daniel Chen (MIT License)
# https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv

# Start from Ubuntu Linux with R installed.
# Change 4.6.2 to the R version in your renv.lock.
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2

# Install the programs the project needs:
# curl downloads files, git/less/nano let you work in a terminal,
# make runs a Makefile, openssh-server lets Positron connect over ssh,
# libuv1-dev is needed by the R package fs
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install --yes \

With R only, you render with quarto render instead of uv run quarto render.

TipSetting up Docker Hub and the GitHub secrets (step 4)





One team member:

Creates a public Docker Hub repository with the same name as your GitHub repository, in lowercase (e.g. GitHub Wine_Quality_Predictor becomes Docker Hub wine_quality_predictor).
Creates a Docker Hub access token with Read & Write permissions.
Adds two repository secrets to your GitHub repository (Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions > New repository secret): DOCKER_USERNAME (the Docker Hub username) and DOCKER_PASSWORD (the access token, not the Docker Hub password).










TipThe workflow file (step 4)





Job 1 runs the same docker build and docker push as Individual Assignment 2, on an Intel/AMD and an ARM computer at the same time. Job 2 puts the two images under one tag. Job 3 writes that new tag into your docker-compose.yml and commits it to the branch you pushed. You don’t need to change anything: the workflow names your image from the DOCKER_USERNAME secret and your GitHub repository’s name.


.github/workflows/publish-dockerhub.yml

# Builds the image from your Dockerfile for Intel/AMD and ARM computers,
# and publishes it on Docker Hub.
# Save this file as .github/workflows/publish-dockerhub.yml

name: Publish image to Docker Hub

# When the workflow runs
on:
  # by hand: Actions tab > Publish image to Docker Hub > Run workflow
  workflow_dispatch:
  # on its own: when a push changes one of these files
  push:
    # only branch pushes, not tags: a release creates a tag, and GitHub
    # ignores the paths filter for tag pushes, so it would run every release
    branches:
      - '**'
    paths:
      - Dockerfile
      - pyproject.toml
      - uv.lock
      - .python-version
      - renv.lock
      - .Rprofile
      - renv/activate.R
      - .github/workflows/publish-dockerhub.yml

env:
  # Your image: your Docker Hub username / this GitHub repository's name.
  # Nothing to change here.
  IMAGE_NAME: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}/${{ github.event.repository.name }}

jobs:
  # Job 1: build the image on two computers at the same time,
  # one Intel/AMD and one ARM, and push one tag from each
  build:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        include:
          - runner: ubuntu-latest     # Intel/AMD
            arch: amd64
          - runner: ubuntu-24.04-arm  # ARM
            arch: arm64
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.runner }}
    steps:
      # 1. Docker image names must be lowercase, so save a lowercase copy as IMAGE
      - name: Make the image name lowercase
        run: echo "IMAGE=$(echo "$IMAGE_NAME" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

      # 2. Copy your repository onto the computer
      - name: Check out the repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v7

      # 3. Log in to Docker Hub with your two repository secrets
      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }}

      # 4. Build the image for this computer, tagged for example sha-1a2b3c4-arm64
      #    (sha- plus the first 7 characters of the commit ID, plus the chip)
      - name: Build the image
        run: docker build --tag "$IMAGE:sha-${GITHUB_SHA::7}-${{ matrix.arch }}" .

      # 5. Upload it to Docker Hub
      - name: Push the image
        run: docker push "$IMAGE:sha-${GITHUB_SHA::7}-${{ matrix.arch }}"

  # Job 2: after both builds finish, put the two images under one tag,
  # so each computer downloads the one for its chip
  combine:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      # Docker image names must be lowercase, so save a lowercase copy as IMAGE
      - name: Make the image name lowercase
        run: echo "IMAGE=$(echo "$IMAGE_NAME" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }}

      # Make the tags latest and sha-1a2b3c4, each holding both images
      - name: Combine the two images under one tag
        run: |
          docker buildx imagetools create \
            --tag "$IMAGE:latest" \
            --tag "$IMAGE:sha-${GITHUB_SHA::7}" \
            "$IMAGE:sha-${GITHUB_SHA::7}-amd64" \
            "$IMAGE:sha-${GITHUB_SHA::7}-arm64"

  # Job 3: write the new tag into docker-compose.yml and commit it
  # to the branch you pushed, so your team only has to git pull
  update-compose:
    needs: combine
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # lets this job push a commit to your repository
    permissions:
      contents: write
    steps:
      - name: Check out the repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v7

      # Replace the image: line, e.g. image: yourname/your-repo:sha-1a2b3c4
      # (skipped if you have no docker-compose.yml yet)
      - name: Put the new tag in docker-compose.yml
        if: hashFiles('docker-compose.yml') != ''
        run: |
          IMAGE=$(echo "$IMAGE_NAME" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')
          sed -i "s|^\( *image:\).*|\1 $IMAGE:sha-${GITHUB_SHA::7}|" docker-compose.yml

      # Commit and push the change (does nothing if the file didn't change)
      - name: Commit and push docker-compose.yml
        if: hashFiles('docker-compose.yml') != ''
        run: |
          git config user.name "github-actions[bot]"
          git config user.email "41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"
          git add docker-compose.yml
          git diff --cached --quiet && exit 0
          git commit -m "Use image tag sha-${GITHUB_SHA::7} in docker-compose.yml"
          git pull --rebase
          git push

It runs on its own when a push changes the Dockerfile, a file the Dockerfile copies into the image, or the workflow file. To run it by hand: Actions tab > Publish image to Docker Hub > Run workflow. On Docker Hub you will see four tags: latest, sha-1a2b3c4, and the two halves sha-1a2b3c4-amd64 and sha-1a2b3c4-arm64. Job 3 puts the one without -amd64 or -arm64 in docker-compose.yml for you. Then run git pull to get that commit, and docker compose pull to download the new image.









TipThe docker-compose.yml file (step 5)





Change only the image: line.


docker-compose.yml

# Adapted from docker-uv-renv by Daniel Chen (MIT License)
# https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv

services:
  # the service name: `docker compose run analysis-env ...` uses it
  analysis-env:
    # CHANGE THIS LINE once: your Docker Hub username / your GitHub repository's
    # name in lowercase, with the sha- tag your workflow pushed (not latest).
    # After that, the workflow updates the tag for you.
    image: your-docker-hub-username/your-github-repo-name:sha-1a2b3c4
    ports:
      # 2222 on your computer, 22 (ssh) in the container
      - "2222:22"
    volumes:
      # your project folder, at /workspace in the container
      - .:/workspace
      # your ssh public key, so you can log in (ro: read-only)
      - ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub:/root/.ssh/authorized_keys:ro
      # your Git name and email, so your commits in the container count as yours
      - ~/.gitconfig:/root/.gitconfig:ro

There is no build: . line: everyone downloads the image your workflow published, instead of building their own.









TipConnect Positron to the container over ssh, step by step (step 6)





Your CONTRIBUTING.md walks your teammates through these same steps (see part 2).
Once, before your first connection:

Install Positron on your computer. Its Remote SSH feature, which connects to the container, comes built in, so you don’t need an extension.
Make an ssh key if you don’t have one. In a terminal on your computer, run ssh-keygen -t ed25519 and press Enter at each question. Check that ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub now exists.
Check that Git knows who you are on your computer: git config --global user.email should print the email of your GitHub account. If it prints nothing, set it with git config --global user.name "Your Name" and git config --global user.email "you@example.com". docker-compose.yml shares this with the container, so your commits there count as yours.
Download the image: in your project folder, run docker compose pull.

Each time you work on the project:

In a terminal, in your project folder, start the container in the background:
docker compose up -d
docker compose ps should list analysis-env as running.
In Positron, open the Command Palette (Cmd+Shift+P on Mac, Ctrl+Shift+P on Windows).
Type and run Remote SSH: Show Remote Menu, then pick Connect to Host.
Type root@localhost:2222 and press Enter. A new Positron window opens.

If it asks for the platform of the remote host, pick Linux.
If it asks whether you trust the host (a “fingerprint”), click Continue.
The first time, Positron installs its server inside the container. This takes a few minutes (e.g., took > 5 minutes on Sky’s computer).

Open your project folder. You are connected now (the bottom left corner shows SSH: localhost:2222), but the Explorer says No folder opened, and a terminal starts in /root, the container’s home folder, which has no project files. That is normal.

Click Open Folder in the Explorer. A path box appears at the top of the window.
Delete what is in it, type /workspace, and press Enter (or click OK, you may need to click “ok” a few times before this works).
The window reloads. The Explorer now shows WORKSPACE [SSH: LOCALHOST:2222] with your project files. A file you change here changes on your computer too.

Pick the interpreter. Positron may start a different Python than your project’s, so check this every time. Click the interpreter button at the top right of the window (it shows a Python or R version). The menu that opens, Running Interpreter Sessions, only lists sessions that are already running (such as /usr/bin/python3, the container’s system Python: not this one). Click New Console Session…, then:

Python: pick the one named Python 3.x (uv: your-project-name) with the path /opt/venv/bin/python, the environment built from your uv.lock. The top right button then shows that name. If it isn’t in the list, open the Command Palette, run Python: Select Interpreter, choose Enter interpreter path… and type /opt/venv/bin/python. Don’t pick /workspace/.venv: that is the environment from your own computer, and it doesn’t run in the container.
R: pick the R version in the list. It already uses the packages from your renv.lock.
To check, run import sys; print(sys.executable) in the Console. It should print /opt/venv/bin/python.

Work as usual. The Terminal, Console and Render button all run inside the container.
When you are done, close the Positron window, then stop the container in a terminal on your computer:
docker compose down

If it doesn’t connect:

~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub is a folder: Docker made it because the key didn’t exist yet. Run docker compose down, delete that folder, make the key (step 2 above), and start again.
~/.gitconfig is a folder, or Git in the container doesn’t know your name: the same thing happened with your Git settings. Run docker compose down, delete that folder, set your name and email (step 3 above), and start again.
GitHub asks you to sign in when you push from the container: sign in once in the browser window Positron opens. Positron remembers it.
It asks for a password: the container can’t see your key. Check that your key is named id_ed25519.pub, or change the key path in docker-compose.yml.
“Remote host identification has changed”: you are using a new image. Run ssh-keygen -R "[localhost]:2222", then connect again.
Linux laptops: ssh refuses the key because the file belongs to you, not root. Remove the # from the StrictModes no line in the Dockerfile and push, so the workflow publishes a fixed image.
Port 2222 is already in use: change the first 2222 in docker-compose.yml to another number (e.g. 2223), and connect to that port instead.

More detail: Working in a container over ssh with Positron.





2. Update your README and CONTRIBUTING.md

README: for someone who wants to run your analysis.
CONTRIBUTING.md: for a teammate or contributor who wants to change it.

Keep each set of steps in its own file.
Your README: use the example README.md as your template.






TipWhat your README must include





In this order:

Make an ssh key if you don’t have one: ssh-keygen -t ed25519, pressing Enter at each question. (Without it, Docker makes a folder named ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub, and ssh into the container fails until you delete that folder and make the key.)
Download the image: docker compose pull.
Render the report in the container:

Python, or Python and R: docker compose run --rm analysis-env uv run quarto render
R only: docker compose run --rm analysis-env quarto render
Add your report’s path after quarto render if your project has no _quarto.yml that lists it.

Say how the container stops: with --rm, it is removed by itself when the render finishes. If your README also uses docker compose up -d, add docker compose down to stop and remove it.
Link to your CONTRIBUTING.md for anyone who wants to change the project.




Your CONTRIBUTING.md: use the example CONTRIBUTING.md as your template. It replaces any setup steps from Milestone 1 (such as installing packages on your own computer).






TipWhat your CONTRIBUTING.md must include






Link to your README for the setup steps (ssh key, docker compose pull), instead of repeating them.
Work in the container with Positron over ssh: write the steps from the step-by-step guide in part 1 for your project (the steps the README already covers can be a link), including installing Positron, the Git name and email check, which interpreter to pick, and the fixes for when it doesn’t connect.
Add or update a package: on a branch, add it with your environment manager, commit and push. Wait for GitHub Actions to publish the new image and update the tag in docker-compose.yml, then run git pull and docker compose pull.
Publish the report: after re-rendering, copy it to docs/index.html and push (see part 3).










ImportantReproducibility is worth 20 points



We launch your container and run your analysis by following your README exactly as written. The less of it we can run (a missing package, a wrong file path, a step we had to guess or fix), the more points you lose. Test them on both Windows and Mac. If your team doesn’t have both, ask another team to test them.




3. Publish your report on GitHub Pages
Anyone should be able to read your report online without cloning your repository. You publish it by hand: put a self-contained copy of your rendered report at docs/index.html. If you already published your report in Milestone 1, switch to this setup anyway, because later milestones build on it.

Make the rendered report one self-contained HTML file, in its YAML header (skip this if your _quarto.yml already sets it):
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
If you have only been rendering to PDF, render to HTML as well.
Render your report, then copy it into docs/ as index.html, and add an empty .nojekyll file:
mkdir -p docs
cp <path-to-your-report>.html docs/index.html
touch docs/.nojekyll






TipIf you also render a PDF: fix the “Other Formats” link





When you render more than one format, Quarto adds a link to the others (for example “Typst”) under Other Formats in the HTML report. That link points to a file next to the report, which is not in docs/, so on GitHub Pages it gives a 404. Either remove the link, in your report’s YAML header or your _quarto.yml:
format:
  html:
    format-links: false
or point it to the PDF in your repository:
format:
  html:
    format-links:
      - html   # stops Quarto adding its own link
      - text: PDF
        href: https://github.com/ubc-mds-2026-27/<your-repository>/blob/main/<path-to-your-report>.pdf
        icon: file-pdf



Commit and push docs/. Check that your .gitignore does not ignore docs/ or .html files.
On GitHub.com, go to Settings > Pages > Deploy from a branch, choose the main branch and the /docs folder, and click Save.
After a few minutes, open https://ubc-mds-2026-27.github.io/<your-repository>/ and check that the whole report shows, including its figures.
Put this URL in your README (as the link to your rendered report) and in the About section of your repository.







ImportantKeep the published report up to date



docs/index.html is a copy. Each time you re-render your report, copy it into docs/ again and push. We grade from your 1.0.0 release, and the report on GitHub Pages should match it.








TipWhy this works






GitHub Pages can publish the files in a docs/ folder on main, exactly as they are.
When someone visits your site’s address, the server shows the file named index.html.
With embed-resources: true, the report is one HTML file that holds its figures and styling, so it still works after you copy it.
.nojekyll tells GitHub Pages to serve your file as it is (see Turning off Jekyll with .nojekyll).

Copying by hand is easy to forget, so it is not how you would publish a larger site. In DSCI 524 you will use tools that build and publish a website for you.

title: Individual assignment 4
text:
Instructions

Make the repository. Open the template repository, click Use this template > Create a new repository, and make a public repository under your personal account named data_analysis_pipeline_practice. Clone it and cd into it.
Start the container and run the script. Open Docker Desktop, then start a terminal inside the container and run bash runall.sh (commands below). Look at what it makes in results/ and report/, then run git status to see which files are new.
Write the Makefile in the root of the repository. Turn each command in runall.sh into a rule, listing as dependencies the data file and the script each step uses. Then add two targets:

all: makes everything runall.sh makes, ending with the rendered report
clean: deletes everything the pipeline made (and nothing else)

Test it. Run make clean, then make all. Run make all again: Make should say there is nothing to do. Then change one data file (e.g. touch data/isles.txt) and run make all: only the steps that use it should rerun. Finally run make clean and check with git status that the repository is back to how you found it.
Commit and push the Makefile, but not the files it makes.







TipCommands to start the container (step 2)





From your repository folder:
docker compose run --rm ia4
You land in a terminal inside the container, with Python, Quarto and Make installed. Note this is docker compose run, not docker compose up: there is no browser app, just the terminal. Your repository folder is shared with the container, so files you make there show up on your computer too.
bash runall.sh   # run the whole analysis the old way
make all         # later: run your Makefile instead
exit             # leave the container when you are done









TipWhat a rule looks like (step 3)







Makefile

# target : dependencies
#     command (indented with a TAB)
results/isles.dat : data/isles.txt scripts/wordcount.py
    python scripts/wordcount.py --input_file=data/isles.txt --output_file=results/isles.dat

all and clean don’t make files with those names, so list them as .PHONY:
.PHONY : all clean
The Makefile cheatsheet has more examples.









TipTroubleshooting






Makefile: *** missing separator. Stop.: the command line must start with a TAB, not spaces. Turn off “insert spaces for tabs” in your editor for Makefiles.
make: Nothing to be done or is up to date: that’s Make working: the target is newer than all its dependencies. Run make clean first, or touch a dependency, to make it run again.
A step doesn’t rerun after you edit a script: the script is missing from that rule’s dependencies.
make clean deletes a file it shouldn’t: only delete what the pipeline makes. Keep the README.md files in results/ and report/.

title: Individual assignment 2
text:
This assignment is hands-on practice to help you get reaady for Milestone 2: build a Docker image from a Dockerfile, and publish it to Docker Hub with GitHub Actions.

Make a small uv (Python) or renv (R) project with the two pinned packages listed in step 2
Add a Dockerfile that installs your packages, and test it on your computer
Publish the image to Docker Hub with a GitHub Actions workflow







TipReadings for this assignment






uv: pinning exact versions or renv basics
Python packages with uv in an image or R packages with renv in an image: what each line of the Dockerfile does
uv refresher: DSCI 521 uv lecture notes

title: Individual assignment 2
text:
Instructions

Make the repository. Create a public GitHub.com repository under your personal account, named dsci522-dockerfile-practice, with a README. Clone it; everything below happens in this folder.
Make a small project with uv or renv, whichever you prefer. Install these two packages, each pinned to an exact version (commands below): cowsay and numpy for uv, or cowsay and praise for renv. The test in step 4 loads exactly these two, so it fails if either is missing.

uv: pyproject.toml lists each package with ==, and Python 3.11 or newer is pinned in .python-version. Commit pyproject.toml, uv.lock and .python-version, but not .venv/.
renv: a small script hello.R uses both packages, and a snapshot records their exact versions in renv.lock. Commit hello.R, renv.lock, .Rprofile and renv/ (the .gitignore inside renv/ keeps the installed packages out).

Add the Dockerfile. Copy the uv or renv version below into a file named Dockerfile (no file extension) in the root of your repository. It installs your packages exactly as your lock file records them. The comments explain each line. For renv, change 4.6.2 on the FROM line to the R version in your renv.lock.
Test it on your computer. Build the image, then load your packages in a container from it (commands below). Fix problems now: debugging on your computer is much faster than on GitHub Actions.
Publish with GitHub Actions. Set up Docker Hub and the two secrets (see below). Then copy the workflow below into .github/workflows/publish-dockerhub.yml as it is: no changes needed. Commit and push.
Check that it worked. The run on the Actions tab finishes with a green check mark, and your Docker Hub repository shows two tags: latest and sha- plus 7 characters.







TipCommands to make the project (step 2)





Run these in the terminal, from your repository folder.

uv (Python)renv (R)


# 1. Start a uv project and pin the Python version
uv init --bare
uv python pin 3.14

# 2. Open pyproject.toml to tell uv to pin exact versions
nano pyproject.toml
Add these two lines at the bottom of pyproject.toml, then exit and save the file (in nano: Ctrl+X to exit, then Y to save):


pyproject.toml

[tool.uv]
add-bounds = "exact"

# 3. Install both packages: uv writes them with == in pyproject.toml
uv add cowsay numpy

# 4. Keep the .venv/ folder out of Git
echo ".venv/" >> .gitignore

# 5. Commit and push
git add pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version .gitignore
git commit -m "Add uv project with cowsay and numpy"
git push


# 1. Start an empty renv project
Rscript -e 'renv::init(bare = TRUE)'

# 2. Install both packages
Rscript -e 'renv::install(c("cowsay", "praise"))'
Then create a file named hello.R that uses both packages. renv::snapshot() only records packages your code loads, so without it renv.lock stays empty.


hello.R

library(cowsay)
library(praise)

say(praise())

# 3. Record the exact versions in renv.lock
Rscript -e 'renv::snapshot()'

# 4. Commit and push
git add hello.R renv.lock .Rprofile renv/
git commit -m "Add renv project with cowsay and praise"
git push
If the terminal says Rscript: command not found (common in Git Bash on Windows), run the part inside the quotes in the R console instead, from your repository folder.












TipThe Dockerfile (step 3)






uv (Python)renv (R)




Dockerfile

# Adapted from docker-uv-renv by Daniel Chen (MIT License)
# https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv

# Start from Ubuntu Linux. It has no Python: uv installs it.
FROM ubuntu:24.04

# Copy the uv program into the image (0.13.7 pins uv's version)
COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/

# Work in the /workspace folder inside the image
WORKDIR /workspace

# Put the packages in /opt/venv (not in a .venv folder in /workspace)
ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv

# Copy only the files that list your packages
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version ./

# Install Python and the exact packages in uv.lock
# (--locked: stop if uv.lock doesn't match pyproject.toml)
RUN uv sync --locked





Dockerfile

# Adapted from docker-uv-renv by Daniel Chen (MIT License)
# https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv

# Start from Ubuntu Linux with R installed.
# Change 4.6.2 to the R version in your renv.lock.
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2

# Install curl: renv downloads packages with it
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install --yes curl

# Work in the /workspace folder inside the image
WORKDIR /workspace

# Put the packages in /opt/renv/library (not in renv/library in /workspace)
RUN echo "RENV_PATHS_LIBRARY=/opt/renv/library" >> /usr/local/lib/R/etc/Renviron.site

# Copy the files renv needs to install your packages, and your script
COPY renv.lock .Rprofile hello.R ./
COPY renv/activate.R renv/

# Install the exact packages in renv.lock
RUN Rscript -e "renv::restore()"













TipCommands to test your image (step 4)





Open Docker Desktop first. From your repository folder, build the image and give it a name (--tag):
docker build --tag dsci522-test .
Then start a container, use your two packages, and remove the container when it finishes (--rm). If a cow talks to you, it worked: an error means a package didn’t install.

uv (Python)renv (R)


docker run --rm dsci522-test uv run python -c \
  "import cowsay, numpy; cowsay.cow(f'numpy says 1 + 2 + 3 = {numpy.sum([1, 2, 3])}')"


docker run --rm dsci522-test Rscript -e \
  "library(cowsay); library(praise); say(praise())"



Changed your environment? Run docker build again: Docker rebuilds only the steps that changed.









TipThe workflow file (step 5)





Copy it as it is: it reads your Docker Hub username from the DOCKER_USERNAME secret. The comments explain the rest.


.github/workflows/publish-dockerhub.yml

# Builds the image from your Dockerfile and publishes it on Docker Hub.
# Save this file as .github/workflows/publish-dockerhub.yml

name: Publish image to Docker Hub

# When the workflow runs
on:
  # by hand: Actions tab > Publish image to Docker Hub > Run workflow
  workflow_dispatch:
  # on its own: when a push changes one of these files
  push:
    paths:
      - Dockerfile
      - uv.lock
      - renv.lock
      - .github/workflows/publish-dockerhub.yml

env:
  # The image name: your Docker Hub username (from the secret) / repository name
  IMAGE: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}/dsci522-dockerfile-practice

jobs:
  publish:
    # a fresh Linux computer on GitHub (Intel/AMD)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      # 1. Copy your repository onto that computer
      - name: Check out the repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v7

      # 2. Log in to Docker Hub with your two repository secrets
      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }}

      # 3. Build the image with two tags:
      #    latest, and sha- plus the first 7 characters of the commit ID
      - name: Build the image
        run: docker build --tag "$IMAGE:latest" --tag "$IMAGE:sha-${GITHUB_SHA::7}" .

      # 4. Upload both tags to Docker Hub
      - name: Push the image
        run: docker push --all-tags "$IMAGE"

Steps 3 and 4 are the same docker build and docker push you would type on your own computer: GitHub just runs them for you, from the files in your repository.









TipSetting up Docker Hub and the GitHub secrets (step 5)






Create a free Docker Hub account if you don’t have one.
You don’t need to create the Docker Hub repository: the workflow’s first push creates it. Afterwards, check on Docker Hub that it is public.
Create a Docker Hub access token with Read & Write permissions. Copy it somewhere safe: you can only see it once.
In your GitHub repository, add two repository secrets (Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions > New repository secret), with exactly these names, because the workflow looks for them:

DOCKER_USERNAME: your Docker Hub username (not your GitHub username)
DOCKER_PASSWORD: the access token (not your Docker Hub password)











TipTroubleshooting






Git refuses to push the workflow file: your personal access token needs the workflow scope. On GitHub, go to Settings > Developer settings > Personal access tokens, select your token, and tick workflow.
The workflow didn’t start: it only starts on its own when a push changes the Dockerfile, a lock file or the workflow file. Run it by hand: Actions tab > Publish image to Docker Hub > Run workflow.
The login step fails: check the secret names, and that DOCKER_PASSWORD is an access token with Read & Write permissions.
The push step fails with “denied” or “unauthorized”: the DOCKER_USERNAME secret must be your Docker Hub username, all in lowercase.
The logs show *** instead of your username: that’s normal. GitHub hides every secret value in the logs.

title: Bonus: Project website
text:
This optional bonus turns your whole project into a Quarto website on GitHub Pages, at the same URL as the report you published in Milestone 2.

Make your project’s _quarto.yml a website that renders into docs/
Add a homepage (your README), your report (HTML and PDF), an about page, and a GitHub icon in the menu bar
Make make all build everything, from downloading the data to the website
Publish it on GitHub Pages







ImportantUp to 5 bonus points, for your team



The points go to Milestone 4 unless you tell us otherwise when you submit. They can make up for points lost on that milestone, but can’t take it above its maximum. It is due with Milestone 4 (see the syllabus), and we grade it from the same 3.0.0 release, so your Milestone 4 README instructions must still work exactly as written.








TipReadings for this bonus






Introduction to Quarto and GitHub Pages (DSCI 521): the same setup, read it again first
Quarto: includes and alt text for figures







Edit _quarto.yml in the root of your repository: add type: website and output-dir: docs, list the website’s pages under render, and add a website section with the menu bar (example below). Keep your existing format settings (such as embed-resources and PDF): they still apply to your report.
Give each new page format: html in its YAML header, so Quarto doesn’t also make a PDF of it.
Add an empty .nojekyll file to the root of your repository (Quarto copies it into docs/), and add .quarto/ to your .gitignore.
Clean up the old report: it now renders to docs/reports/<your-report>.html and .pdf, with the website’s menu bar. Delete the old rendered files from reports/, and update your Makefile and README to the new locations.

quarto render now renders the whole website; quarto render reports/<your-report>.qmd still renders just the report, and quarto preview shows the website as you edit.






TipExample _quarto.yml and folder layout (step 1)





Change the title, the report’s file name and the repository URL to your own.


_quarto.yml

project:
  type: website
  output-dir: docs
  render:          # keeps files like CONTRIBUTING.md out of the website
    - index.qmd
    - about.qmd
    - reports/<your-report>.qmd

website:
  title: "Your project title"
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      - href: reports/<your-report>.qmd
        text: Report
      - href: about.qmd
        text: About
    right:
      - icon: github
        href: https://github.com/UBC-MDS-2026-27/<your-repository>
        aria-label: GitHub repository

# Keep your existing `format:` settings below.

Only the new and changed parts are shown:
.
├── _quarto.yml           # now a website: renders everything into docs/
├── .nojekyll
├── Makefile
├── README.md
├── index.qmd             # homepage: includes README.md
├── about.qmd             # the team
├── reports/
│   └── <your-report>.qmd
└── docs/                 # the published website (generated, but committed)
    ├── index.html
    └── reports/
        ├── <your-report>.html
        └── <your-report>.pdf







Homepage (index.qmd): include your README instead of copying it, so the homepage stays up to date. It needs no title: Quarto uses the README’s first heading.


index.qmd

---
format: html
---

{{< include README.md >}}

About page (about.qmd): for each team member, their name linked to their GitHub profile, and a few sentences in their own words (for example, their background and what interests them in data science). The site is public, so each person decides what to share. A photo is optional.
Report: the Report menu item links to its HTML page, and Quarto adds a link to the PDF on that page. Link to both versions from your README too. Give every figure alt text: the fig-alt option on code cells that make figures, or the fig-alt attribute on images:
![Feature densities.](../results/figures/densities.png){#fig-densities fig-alt="Density plots of each feature by class."}







WarningLinks in your README must work on the website too



The website only publishes its pages, not the rest of your repository. A relative link such as CONTRIBUTING.md or src/ works on GitHub but breaks on the website, and Quarto doesn’t warn you. Use the full GitHub URL instead (for example, https://github.com/UBC-MDS-2026-27/<your-repository>/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md).





Extend your Milestone 4 Makefile so that make all, from a fresh clone inside your container, downloads the data, runs your validation checks and the rest of the analysis, then renders the whole website into docs/. make clean removes everything make all creates, including docs/.

Change the rule behind publish so it runs quarto render instead of copying the report (sketch below).
Remove your old rule that renders the report in reports/: the report now renders as part of the website.
List as prerequisites every file the website reads, including your README and the figures and tables your report shows.
Say in your README how to build the website.







TipSketch of the Makefile changes (step 3)





Change the file names to your own:


Makefile

.DELETE_ON_ERROR:

publish: docs/index.html

docs/index.html: _quarto.yml index.qmd README.md about.qmd \
        reports/<your-report>.qmd results/figures/<your-figure>.png
    quarto render

clean:
    rm -rf docs
    # ... and everything else your pipeline creates


quarto render empties docs/ first, so no old pages are left over.
.DELETE_ON_ERROR: deletes docs/index.html if the render fails partway. Without it, the next make would find docs/index.html and say there is nothing to do.










ImportantA clean build, with no warnings



Before you submit, run make clean and then make all inside your container. Everything should rebuild, and Quarto should print no ERROR or WARN messages (for example, about links it could not find). Messages from other tools, such as Jupyter, don’t count. We grade the bonus by doing the same.






Commit docs/, including docs/.nojekyll (check with ls -a docs, and on GitHub.com). It is generated, but GitHub Pages can only publish files in your repository.
Keep the GitHub Pages setting from Milestone 2 (main branch, /docs folder). The homepage is now https://ubc-mds-2026-27.github.io/<your-repository>/, and the report moves to .../reports/<your-report>.html.
Update the report link in your README, and say in your README and in the repository’s About box that the URL is now your project’s website.

About page (about.qmd): for each team member, their name linked to their GitHub profile, and a few sentences in their own words (for example, their background and what interests them in data science). The site is public, so each person decides what to share. A photo is optional.
Report: the Report menu item links to its HTML page, and Quarto adds a link to the PDF on that page. Link to both versions from your README too. Give every figure alt text: the fig-alt option on code cells that make figures, or the fig-alt attribute on images:
![Feature densities.](../results/figures/densities.png){#fig-densities fig-alt="Density plots of each feature by class."}







WarningLinks in your README must work on the website too



The website only publishes its pages, not the rest of your repository. A relative link such as CONTRIBUTING.md or src/ works on GitHub but breaks on the website, and Quarto doesn’t warn you. Use the full GitHub URL instead (for example, https://github.com/UBC-MDS-2026-27/<your-repository>/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md).





Extend your Milestone 4 Makefile so that make all, from a fresh clone inside your container, downloads the data, runs your validation checks and the rest of the analysis, then renders the whole website into docs/. make clean removes everything make all creates, including docs/.

Change the rule behind publish so it runs quarto render instead of copying the report (sketch below).
Remove your old rule that renders the report in reports/: the report now renders as part of the website.
List as prerequisites every file the website reads, including your README and the figures and tables your report shows.
Say in your README how to build the website.







TipSketch of the Makefile changes (step 3)





Change the file names to your own:


Makefile

.DELETE_ON_ERROR:

publish: docs/index.html

docs/index.html: _quarto.yml index.qmd README.md about.qmd \
        reports/<your-report>.qmd results/figures/<your-figure>.png
    quarto render

clean:
    rm -rf docs
    # ... and everything else your pipeline creates


quarto render empties docs/ first, so no old pages are left over.
.DELETE_ON_ERROR: deletes docs/index.html if the render fails partway. Without it, the next make would find docs/index.html and say there is nothing to do.










ImportantA clean build, with no warnings



Before you submit, run make clean and then make all inside your container. Everything should rebuild, and Quarto should print no ERROR or WARN messages (for example, about links it could not find). Messages from other tools, such as Jupyter, don’t count. We grade the bonus by doing the same.






Commit docs/, including docs/.nojekyll (check with ls -a docs, and on GitHub.com). It is generated, but GitHub Pages can only publish files in your repository.
Keep the GitHub Pages setting from Milestone 2 (main branch, /docs folder). The homepage is now https://ubc-mds-2026-27.github.io/<your-repository>/, and the report moves to .../reports/<your-report>.html.
Update the report link in your README, and say in your README and in the repository’s About box that the URL is now your project’s website.

text:
Policies

Academic Integrity
Academic integrity is a commitment to honesty, respect, responsibility, and accountability in academic work. It is foundational to teaching and learning and is a shared value of all members of the UBC community. In a project course, it also means being transparent with your teammates and the teaching team about how your work was produced.
Academic integrity in this course includes:

Submitting individual assignments that reflect your own understanding and intellectual contribution.
Contributing your fair share to your group’s project, and making sure your commits, pull requests, and reviews honestly represent the work you did.
Citing any code, text, or ideas you draw on from elsewhere (classmates outside your group, documentation, Stack Overflow, blog posts, generative AI tools, etc.), following the MDS program policy.
Respecting the licenses of any code, data, or other material you reuse in your project.
Following the generative AI policy below, including disclosing AI use for every deliverable.



Use of Generative AI
This course follows the MDS program’s Academic Integrity and Use of Generative AI policy. Assessment-specific instructions always take precedence over the general guidance below.
AI assistance is allowed. Generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, GitHub Copilot, Cursor) are a real part of modern data science workflows, and you may use them in this course to brainstorm, explain concepts, debug errors, or help write code and documentation. That said, this course is about building your own skills in version control, environments, containers, testing, and pipelines. We strongly encourage you to attempt the work yourself first, and to use AI to support your learning rather than replace it. A useful question to ask yourself is: is this tool helping me understand the problem, or is it doing the thinking I am here to learn to do?
Disclose your AI use. For every milestone and individual assignment, you must state whether generative AI was used, including when it was not. If AI was used, please share:

which tool(s) and model(s) you used;
which parts of the work they were used for, and how; and
the instructions you gave the tool, such as any system prompt or agent configuration file (e.g., CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .cursor/rules/, .github/copilot-instructions.md), or, if you did not use one, a few representative example prompts.

For group milestones, please keep this disclosure in an AI_USAGE.md file or CLAUDE.md (or other file names that indicate AI was used) in the root of your project repository and update it as the project evolves. For individual assignments, include the disclosure with your Gradescope submission. Disclosing AI use is not penalized, and it helps us give you useful feedback.
You remain responsible for everything you submit. Whether code was written by you, a teammate, or an AI tool, everyone in the group is responsible for its correctness, quality, and licensing. You should be able to explain what your code does, why it is designed that way, and how it fits into the rest of your project. Please do not merge code you have not read and understood.
Humans open pull requests and issues, and make the final merge decisions. AI agents may help you review or generate some code, and may help double-check code before pull requests are merged (e.g., an automated review bot such as Cursor Bugbot or GitHub Copilot code review), but a group member must review any generated changes and open every pull request and issue themselves. Ultimately, it is human reviewers who make the final decisions and merge the pull requests. Please do not let an AI agent push to your repository, open pull requests or issues, or merge pull requests on its own. Because GitHub history is used to evaluate teamwork, it should accurately reflect who did the work.
Communicate in your own words. When writing issues, pull request descriptions, code reviews, peer reviews, and team work reflections, please use your own words. AI may help with translation or grammar editing. Much of what you learn in this course comes from these conversations with your teammates.
Weekly check-ins. As described in Deliverables, the teaching team will have a short, ungraded oral check-in with each of you during lab every week, as practice for technical interviews. We may ask you to walk us through any part of your project, including code that was written with the help of AI. If someone is not yet able to explain work they contributed, we will follow up to better understand how the work was produced and to support their learning. Where needed, this may also include steps under UBC’s academic misconduct procedures.
Protect private information. Do not share confidential, private, or sensitive information with AI tools, including personal information about yourself, your teammates, or other students (for example, peer review content or team work reflections).
If you are unsure whether a particular use of AI is appropriate, please ask the teaching team before you submit your work.
Academic misconduct
Violations of academic integrity (i.e., academic misconduct) may lead to serious consequences. For more details, please see UBC’s Academic Integrity website, the Academic Calendar Statement on Academic Misconduct, and UBC’s guidance on Generative AI.
Parts of this AI policy are adapted from the earthaccess AI policy, which is based on the SciPy and SymPy AI policies.


General Program Policies

Please see the general and genAI use policies in MDS policies.
Please review General Lab Instructions
Check the MDS Rubrics for grading criteria.

title: Individual assignment 1
text:
This assignment will provide practice in the context of version control and will prepare you to collaborate on your group projects for this course. Follow the instructions listed below. You will be graded for completion.

Create a new public repository on GitHub.com named learning-about-version-control. Make sure the repository:

Includes a README.md that has a heading that says “Learning about Version Control” and has your name listed as the author.








Importantgithub.com not https://github.ubc.ca/



Make sure you do this in your own personal public GitHub account. Do not make this in the UBC github.



Clone your learning-about-version-control repository to your local computer.
Create and resolve a merge conflict 😱!

On GitHub.com, open your README.md, click the pencil (edit) icon, and add a line that says “Solving merge conflicts is easy!”. Commit the change on GitHub.
On your local computer (without pulling first!), add a line in the same place in the README, but this time write “Solving merge conflicts is soooooo hard!”
Add and commit your local changes to the README.md, then try to push. Git will reject the push, because GitHub has a commit you don’t have locally yet.
Pull the changes from GitHub with git pull --no-rebase. This is when the merge conflict appears. (The --no-rebase tells git to merge the two versions. Without it, newer versions of git stop and ask you how to combine them.)
Resolve the merge conflict on your local computer so that the line reads “Solving merge conflicts takes conscious effort, but I can do it!”. Take a screenshot while you are resolving the conflict (with the conflict markers <<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>> visible) to show you did this.
Add and commit the resolved file, then push to your remote repository on GitHub.com.

Create and accept a pull request!

Create a new Git branch on your local version control repository named opinions and switch to that branch.
Edit your README.md so that you add at least one sentence about what you like most about version control, and add at least one sentence about what you find most challenging/confusing/frustrating about version control (we all have opinions on this one…). Add and commit your changes to local version control.
Push the changes to the README.md that you made on the opinions branch to the remote repository on GitHub.com.
Visit GitHub.com and create a pull request to suggest that the changes on the opinions branch should be merged into the main branch.
Merge the pull request you opened, so your changes from the opinions branch go into the main branch.

text:
Instructions

Make the repository. Open the Python template or the R template, click Use this template > Create a new repository, and make a public repository under your personal account (not under UBC-MDS). Clone it and cd into it.
Start the container. Open Docker Desktop, then run docker compose up in the repository folder. It gives you JupyterLab (Python) or RStudio (R) with everything installed (see below).
Make the figures and table. In the terminal inside JupyterLab or RStudio, run the script (command below). New plots and a .csv file appear in results/.
Make the 7 edits to reports/qmd_example.qmd. The Syntax you need section below has an example of each.

Headers and table of contents: turn the plain section names (Aim, Data, Methods, Results, References) into # headers, and add a table of contents to the YAML header.
References: point the YAML header at references.bib, and replace each hand-typed citation (e.g. “Van Rossum and Drake 2009”) with a citation key.
Figures: give both figures a caption and a #fig- label, and make the second one 60 to 70% wide.
Table: give the table a tbl- label and a caption.
Cross-references: replace every hard-coded “Figure 1”, “Table 1” and so on in the text with a cross-reference such as @fig-horse-pop.
Inline code: replace the ??? in the text with inline code that prints largest_sd.
Hide the code: set echo: false so the rendered report shows figures and tables, but no code.

Render the report to HTML and PDF (commands below) and open both to check your edits. Then commit and push.
Optional bonus: GitHub Pages. Publish the HTML report on the web (steps below).
Clean up. Press Ctrl + C in the terminal where you ran docker compose up, then run docker compose rm.







TipCommands to run (steps 2, 3 and 5)





Start the container from your repository folder:
docker compose up

PythonR


Open the link that starts with http://127.0.0.1:8888/lab?token= from the terminal output. Then open a terminal in JupyterLab and run:
python scripts/generate_figures.py --input_dir="data/00030067-eng.csv" \
    --out_dir="results"

quarto render reports/qmd_example.qmd --to html
quarto render reports/qmd_example.qmd --to pdf


Go to http://localhost:8787 and log in with username rstudio and password password. Then open a terminal in RStudio and run:
Rscript scripts/generate_figures.R --input_dir="data/00030067-eng.csv" \
    --out_dir="results"

quarto render reports/qmd_example.qmd --to html
quarto render reports/qmd_example.qmd --to pdf



The rendered files appear next to qmd_example.qmd in reports/. JupyterLab may not show the figures inside the HTML file: open it from your own file browser instead.









TipSyntax you need (step 4)





YAML header (edits 1, 2 and 7), at the top of qmd_example.qmd. This is what it looks like when you’re done:
---
title: "DSCI 310: Historical Horse Population in Canada"
author: "Tiffany Timbers & Jordan Bourak"
editor: source
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
  pdf:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
bibliography: references.bib
execute:
  echo: false
---
Delete the old format: html line: a setting can only appear once.
Headers (edit 1): # Aim, # Data, # Methods, # Results, # References.
Citations (edit 2): put the key in square brackets after @. Separate several keys with ;.
Horse population data were sourced from the
[Government of Canada's Open Data website](http://open.canada.ca/en/open-data) [@horses1; @horses2].
Only references you cite show up in the reference list.
Figures (edits 3 and 5): caption in the square brackets, label and width in the curly brackets, then refer to the label in the text. Delete the old “Figure 1: …” line under the image.
![Horse populations for all provinces in Canada from 1906 - 1972.](../results/horse_pops_plot.png){#fig-horse-pop width=80%}

We can see from @fig-horse-pop that Ontario, Saskatchewan and Alberta ...
Table (edits 4 and 5): add a label and caption as the first lines of the code cell that makes the table, and delete the old “Table 1. …” line above it.

PythonR


We present the standard deviations in @tbl-horse-sd.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-horse-sd
#| tbl-cap: Standard deviation of historical (1906-1972) horse populations for each Canadian province.

horses_sd_table = pd.read_csv("../results/horses_sd.csv")
largest_sd = horses_sd_table['Province'].values[0]
Markdown(horses_sd_table.to_markdown(index = False))
```


We present the standard deviations in @tbl-horse-sd.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-horse-sd
#| tbl-cap: Standard deviation of historical (1906-1972) horse populations for each Canadian province.

horses_sd_table <- read_csv("../results/horses_sd.csv")
largest_sd <- horses_sd_table$Province[1]
knitr::kable(horses_sd_table)
```



Inline code (edit 6): a single backtick, the language in curly brackets, then the code.

PythonR


we zoom in and look at the province of `{python} largest_sd`, which had ...


we zoom in and look at the province of `{r} largest_sd`, which had ...



Quarto docs if you want more detail: table of contents, citations, figures, tables, inline code, execution options.









TipOptional bonus: publish on GitHub Pages (step 6)






In the root of your repository, create _quarto.yml with:


_quarto.yml

project:
  type: website
  output-dir: docs

Also in the root, create an empty .nojekyll file (touch .nojekyll). It tells GitHub Pages to serve your files as they are.
From the root, run quarto render. The rendered site lands in docs/. Check that docs/ contains index.html and .nojekyll (ls -a docs).
Commit and push, including docs/.
On GitHub, go to Settings > Pages. Under Source pick Deploy from a branch, then pick the main branch and the /docs folder, and click Save.

Wait a few minutes and refresh: the page shows the link to your live report.










TipTroubleshooting






A YAML error when you render: indent with 2 spaces (not 4, not a tab), and put a : after every setting name.
A setting seems ignored: check it appears only once in the YAML header (e.g. no leftover format: html).
The reference list is empty: you haven’t cited anything yet. Add [@key] citations in the text.
@fig-... or @tbl-... shows as “?@fig-…”: labels must start with fig- or tbl- and use -, not _ (fig-horse-pop, not horse_pop).
The PDF fails but the HTML works: read the error message for the line number, and check special characters in your captions.
