text:
Learning Objectives

Use GitHub’s pull requests tool to perform code reviews, with in-line comments and suggested changes.
Accept suggested changes from a code review and merge the pull request.

We very often need to have a conversation to get pull requests into good shape before merging the changes into the main branch. GitHub has a very nice tool we can utilize to do this: GitHub code reviews. This tool allows us to add inline comments to proposed changes, as well as inline suggested changes that can be accepted with a click of a button. These features increase review efficiency and effectiveness!

In the project, you are expected to read and review each other’s code BEFORE accepting a pull request.
Do not expect all (or even most) pull requests to be perfect in their first submission.
Pull requests are opened, reviewed and merged by people. You may use AI tools to help check the code in a pull request, but a person reviews it and decides whether to merge it. Write down how your project uses AI tools in its AI policy.


Exercise
Demo: do a code review
I am going to demo a code review of a pull request. I have set-up a template GitHub repository for you so that you can easily generate a pull request for you to review if you want to try this later.
Steps:

Click the green “Use this template” button in this repository to obtain a copy of it for yourself (do not fork it).
Go to Repository Settings > Actions > General and change two settings:

Under “Actions permissions”, select “Allow all actions and reusable workflows”.
Under “Workflow permissions”, select “Read and write permissions”, and tick “Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests”. A repository made from a template does not keep this box ticked, so you need to tick it yourself.

Click the “Save” button under each section you change. When you are done, the page should look like this:



GitHub’s Settings, Actions, General page for a repository. Under Actions permissions, Allow all actions and reusable workflows is selected. Under Workflow permissions, Read and write permissions is selected and Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests is ticked.


Here are the two “Workflow permissions” settings up close:



The Workflow permissions section, with red arrows pointing to the selected Read and write permissions option and the ticked Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests checkbox.


If you skip this step, the workflow in the next step fails with an error like remote: Permission to <user>/<repo>.git denied to github-actions[bot] and The requested URL returned error: 403. Changing these settings fixes it.
Click on the Actions tab, and then click on the workflow .github/workflows/pr.yml. You then should see a “Run workflow” button with a drop down menu, from that menu select “Run workflow”.
Click on the Pull Requests tab of your copy of the repository, click on the pull request titled “Report most accomplished pilots”, and then click on “Files Changed”. Next click on the star-wars.Rmd file. Review the file and observe the following problems with the R Markdown report that was submitted via the pull request:

Reasoning of the sentence on line 15
Incompatibility with the sentence on line 15 with the code in the code chunk named table-of-most-accomplished-pilots
Incorrect code in code chunk named table-of-most-accomplished-pilots (unnested film instead of starships) leads to naming the wrong pilot as the most accomplished pilot on line 19
Incorrect code in code chunk named table-of-most-accomplished-pilots (unnested film instead of starships) leads to the use of the wrong character’s picture in the image that is sourced in the code chunk named top-pilot (it should be a picture of Obi-Wan Kenobi, you could use this URL for example: https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/images/ewan-mcgregor-obi-wan-1570898048.jpg).

Add comments and suggested changes using the + sign beside the line numbers (the first time you do this will trigger the start of your code review. Need help? See GitHub’s how to on reviewing proposed changes in a pull request.
After you have made all the comments and suggested changes, then add a general comment for the code review, select “Request Changes” and submit your code review.

Exercise
Demo: Accept suggested changes from a code review
Steps:

To accept the code changes that you provided as suggestions, revisit the Pull Requests tab of your copy of the repository and clicking on the pull request titled “Report most accomplished pilots”. Scroll through the pull request comments and find the code suggestions. Then click on the “Commit suggestion button” for each suggestion.
Click on the “Show all reviewers” link beside the red “Changes requested”” text. Then click on the ... beside the reviewer and click “Approve changes”.
Finally click on the green buttons (“Merge Pull Request” & “Confirm merge”) to merge the pull request.

Activity
Discussion
If I didn’t tell you what to review, could you really have done a good job reviewing the code only on GitHub?
Hint: if I didn’t tell you that the top pilot was Obi-Wan Kenobi, how would you have known that?

2. The problem with parallel work on main (00:04:04–00:09:43)

In single-developer or uncoordinated workflows, pushing directly to main causes constant pull-before-push friction and frequent merge conflicts.
Group projects inherently have phases where work cannot be fully parallelized, but branches allow individual responsibilities to proceed independently once isolated.
Branches act as isolated playgrounds for exploration, testing, and feature development, keeping the main branch stable and ready for integration.
The instructor uses the metaphor of house construction: the foundation (main) must be stable before parallel work (walls, floors) can happen on separate branches.

text:
3. Creating and managing branches locally (8 Git branches) (00:09:43–00:25:12)

Before starting new work, run git pull origin main to sync your local repository with the remote, ensuring you branch off the most up-to-date coordinated code.
Use git switch -c <branch_name> to create a new branch and immediately move the HEAD pointer to it, detaching it from origin/main.
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all provides a visual map of the commit history, clearly showing how the HEAD advances on the new branch while origin/main remains static.
In group settings, prefix branch names with your username (e.g., dan-b1) so teammates know who is responsible for that specific line of development.
git checkout is a legacy command that handles both branch switching and file restoration; git switch is the modern, specialized alternative. Use switch to avoid accidental data loss.

text:
4. Pushing branches and initiating Pull Requests (9 Pull requests) (00:25:12–00:46:00)

Push a new branch to the remote using git push origin <branch_name>. GitHub typically prompts you to create a Pull Request immediately after the push.
A Pull Request initiates the code review workflow, presenting a diff of all changes in the “Files Changed” tab for peers to inspect and comment on.
Reviewers should verify that all intended work is present, check for stray temporary files (like .DS_Store or .ipynb_checkpoints), and ensure the .gitignore is functioning.
You can update a PR dynamically by making new commits and pushing them to the same branch; the GitHub interface automatically reflects the new state.
Use the “Convert to Draft” option to open a Pull Request as work-in-progress. Draft PRs display a gray bar, disable the merge button, and signal to the team that the code is not yet ready for review.

section: 5. Merging, cleanup, and local synchronization (8 Git branches) (00:52:17–01:03:51)
text:
5. Merging, cleanup, and local synchronization (8 Git branches) (00:52:17–01:03:51)

Once a Pull Request is approved, click “Merge Pull Request” to integrate the branch’s commits into main. This automatically closes the PR on GitHub.
After merging, delete the branch on GitHub via the UI dropdown menu to prevent the repository from accumulating a cluttered list of inactive branches.
Switch back to your local main branch and run git pull origin main to fetch and fast-forward the local history to include the newly merged commits.
Run git fetch --prune to remove local tracking references for remote branches that were deleted on GitHub, then use git branch -d <branch_name> to delete the local branch.
Use lowercase -d for safe deletion (it refuses to delete unmerged work to prevent data loss); uppercase -D forces deletion but carries a high risk of losing commits.


[!WARNING]
Blindly copying force-deletion commands from AI tools can permanently destroy unmerged work. Always verify the branch state before using -D.

title: Branches, Pull Requests, and Conflict Resolution
section: 6. Resolving merge conflicts via rebase (8 Git branches) (01:03:51–01:21:43)
text:
6. Resolving merge conflicts via rebase (8 Git branches) (01:03:51–01:21:43)

Merge conflicts occur when two branches independently modify the same lines of the same file. The conflict becomes apparent when a second PR attempts to merge after the first has already updated main.
To resolve conflicts locally, switch to the affected branch and run git rebase main. This replays your branch’s commits sequentially on top of the updated main branch, triggering the conflict resolution process locally.
Git halts at the conflicting commit and inserts markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) into the file. Edit the file to keep the correct content, run git add <file> to mark the resolution, and finish with git rebase --continue.
Because rebasing rewrites commit history, a standard push will fail. You must force-push the updated branch using git push --force-with-lease origin <branch_name>, which safely updates the remote only if no new, untracked commits were added by others.


[!WARNING]
Fixing a conflict marker at a specific line does not guarantee the code will run. You must verify that the entire file functions correctly after the merge, as variable names, imports, or logic dependencies may have shifted elsewhere.

title: Summary
text:
2. Git fundamentals and branches

Local and remote repositories

Work takes place on a student’s computer and in the shared remote repository. Cloning brings the repository to a computer; commits record local changes; pushing sends commits to the remote; and pulling brings down work that teammates have committed and pushed.
The shared GitHub remote is the authoritative version for grading and publication. Code that exists only on a local computer is unavailable for grading or delivery.
In the course 521 shared-slide-deck exercise, students sometimes had to pull teammates’ changes before pushing their own. Similar friction can occur when people work on the same project area. Separating work into self-contained streams helps reduce these coordination issues.

Basic repository workflow

The reviewed workflow includes creating a GitHub repository, bringing it to a computer, editing the README, checking the repository with git status, reviewing changes, staging files with git add, and committing them. The demonstration also added a link to the Git branches chapter.
A repository could be initialized with a README, a Python-related option, and a license. The demonstrated commit message was “Intro and review.”
These steps recap material practiced in course 521 over approximately the preceding ten weeks.

What branches are for

main is the default branch and represents the stable, production-like version of a project. Its contents should work or be finished, although course work does not necessarily have to be fully finished to appear there.
Branches let people develop, test, or explore work separately from the shared main line. For example, cleaned data could remain in main as a common starting point while exploratory analysis and plots are developed on a separate branch.
Branches make it easier to set aside or abandon unsuccessful work without disentangling changes from the main project history. The instructor contrasted this with using reset or revert, which were covered in course 521.
Branches also support peer review: work can be developed separately, reviewed and tested, and then merged into the shared project. The instructor’s textbook example used branches for changes made during a class, avoiding disruptive updates while teaching was underway.

Branch references and HEAD

HEAD points to the currently checked-out branch. When working on main, commits advance the local main reference; when working on another branch, commits advance that branch instead.
origin/main represents the remote state of main on GitHub as understood by the local computer. If commits are made locally on main but not pushed, local main moves ahead of origin/main.
Creating and switching to a branch does not create a commit or change project files. It changes the branch that HEAD points to. The existing main branch and remote references remain in place.
A local branch is not automatically synchronized with GitHub. The lecture example remained one commit behind the remote because nothing had been pushed, fetched, or synchronized.

title: Summary
text:
3. Creating, using, and switching branches

Create a branch and switch to it

Use git switch -c <branch-name> to create a branch and move HEAD to it. The -c option means create. Examples included B1 and the local branch Dan-B1.
In group repositories, the instructor sometimes begins branch names with their own name so teammates know whom to contact about the work.
After switching, git status reports the new branch. Before creating a branch, check that you are on main and start from an up-to-date base when the work depends on coordinated project changes. Starting from outdated work can cause duplicated effort.

Continue the usual edit-and-commit workflow

Branching does not change the normal workflow: edit a file, use git status to see what changed, and use git diff to review the changes.
If satisfied, stage the file—for example, with git add README.md—and commit it with a message. One example commit message was define switch -c.
The branch that is checked out is the one that advances when a commit is made.

Inspect branches and move between them

Use git switch <branch-name> to move to an existing branch, such as main. Switching away does not move the branch being left; the working files change to match the branch that is now checked out.
A log view can show where main, remote references, and local branches point. The instructor noted that the --all option is needed to show branch names that might otherwise be absent. The demonstrated one-line log command was git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all.
VS Code and Positron display branch and commit relationships in a graph, corresponding to the relationships shown in the terminal. The example showed three commits, origin/main, local main at the same point, and a later commit on Dan-B1.
Branches are inexpensive to create and can be left in place if an experiment is unsuccessful. Switch back to main to continue other work, or create another branch. Successful work can later be merged into the main line.

Related Git commands

git checkout was commonly used to switch branches before the newer git switch command. The instructor placed the transition to newer commands around 2019–2020, while noting uncertainty about the exact year.
The older branch-creation command is git checkout -b <branch-name>, equivalent to git switch -c <branch-name>. checkout also covered behaviors now associated with revert and restore, which remain available through checkout.
Tools such as GitHub Copilot or ChatGPT may suggest checkout commands. Understand a suggested command before running it, especially when work could be at risk; if unsure, ask for an equivalent using switch.
git branch <branch-name> creates a branch without switching to it. Use git switch <branch-name> or git checkout <branch-name> afterward to begin working on it.

title: Summary
section: 4. Pushing branches and using pull requests
text:
4. Pushing branches and using pull requests

Push the branch containing your work

Check which branch is active and switch to the branch you intend to share, for example, with git switch dan-b1. Switching changes the working files to the state committed on that branch.
Push the feature branch rather than main. The example was git push origin dan-b1: origin is the remote, and the branch name specifies what is being pushed.
After pushing, the log can show an origin reference for the feature branch at the same commit as the local branch, while main remains unchanged. On GitHub, use the branch selector to view the branch and confirm it is available for teammates to inspect. A branch being visible does not mean it has been reviewed or approved.
Branch lists can grow as projects add contributors, features, and projects. Branches can be deleted when they are no longer needed.

Create and configure a PR

After pushing a branch, GitHub may show a Compare and Pull Request button. If the prompt disappears, find the branch under the repository’s branches tab and select New pull request.
The instructor recommends opening a PR early, even while work is in progress, so review can happen as changes are made. The initial prompt may disappear after roughly a day, but the branch menu remains another route.
Verify the base branch that will receive the changes and the source branch being compared. In this class, the destination is generally main; other courses or projects may differ. For forks or large open-source projects, confirm the intended repository and branch.
Write a clear title and description that briefly report what the branch changes. One example title was “Learning about branches and PRs,” with a description about git switch and creating PRs. Keep the original description current by editing it as the work changes, rather than adding disconnected updates that reviewers may miss.

Review changes and collaborate through the PR

The PR displays changes between the feature branch and the base branch, including affected files, code, and commits. Check that all intended work is present; missing changes may not have been added, committed, or pushed.
Check for unnecessary files, such as temporary checkpoint files, Microsoft Word backup or fallback files, Jupyter Notebook .ipynb_checkpoints, and macOS .DS_Store files. Keep .gitignore appropriate; unwanted repository files can cost points in the class.
People with repository access can review the PR and discuss it in the conversation. The Files Changed tab shows a diff, and reviewers can comment on specific lines. Code review means examining that diff and commenting on the changes.
The PR author is responsible for making requested code changes; the reviewer identifies concerns or suggests changes. Review can happen locally or on GitHub. GitHub Copilot can also be asked to review work, but its suggestions can be considered, challenged, rejected, or acted on.
To address feedback or add work, return to the PR’s source branch, make changes, then add, commit, and push to that same branch. The existing PR updates with the new commits; there is no need to close it or create another one.
The example added a line about viewing Git history with git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all, staged the README with git add README, committed it, and pushed it. The instructor recommended pushing regularly, even about every 10 minutes, so work remains available for review. Refresh the PR page to see updates. If a changed line had a review comment, GitHub may collapse the comment and mark it outdated.

Use draft PRs for unfinished work

An open PR can be converted to a draft with Convert to Draft. A draft displays a gray status bar rather than a green one, signals that the work is not ready to merge, and disables the merge control.
Drafts can remain open for extended work; the instructor mentioned drafts lasting three or four months. Draft status communicates the work’s state to the team and may discourage an agent from merging work automatically.

title: Summary
section: 5. Merging pull requests and cleaning up branches
text:
5. Merging pull requests and cleaning up branches

Review and merge completed work

Change a draft PR to Ready for review when it is ready. Once the PR has been reviewed and its checks are green, merge it into the target branch, such as main.
The intended workflow is to develop work on a feature branch, review it through a PR, and merge approved commits into main. A merged PR is closed. The changes should then be present on main, and the commit history can confirm the branch commits and, depending on the merge method, a separate merge commit.

Synchronize local work after a merge

Switching to local main does not automatically update it with changes merged on GitHub. Switch to main and run git pull origin main to bring the remote changes onto the local computer.
git branch -a lists branches known locally, including remote-tracking branches; an asterisk marks the current branch.
git fetch --prune updates the local view of remote history and removes remote-tracking references for branches deleted on GitHub. Use git fetch alone when you want to update your knowledge of remote history without changing local files.
git pull combines fetching with merging fetched changes into the current branch.

Delete branches carefully

Deleting a branch after its work is merged can keep a long-running project’s branch list manageable. Deleting the branch marker does not delete the commits or remove the work from history; relevant commits remain available if the feature later needs to be undone.
Branch deletion depends on the team’s workflow and any compliance or record-retention requirements. Do not delete work that must be retained.
After pruning, use git branch -d <branch-name> to delete a merged local branch. Lowercase -d refuses to delete a branch Git believes contains unmerged work.
Uppercase -D force-deletes a branch even if it has not been merged. Use it cautiously, since it can remove a branch containing work you still need.
A branch can also be deleted on GitHub after merging, removing it from the remote branch list.

title: Summary
section: 6. Merge conflicts and local rebase workflow
text:
6. Merge conflicts and local rebase workflow

Understand how conflicts arise

A merge conflict can occur when two branches based on the same starting point make different changes to the same line in the same file. The demonstration used two branches and PRs with conflicting edits around lines 12–14, including line 13.
When one PR is merged, main changes. GitHub then checks whether other open PRs can still be merged. A later PR may conflict even if it initially appeared mergeable and had green checks.
Conflicts can still occur when work is divided among contributors; another person or an agent might make a small edit in the same area, such as correcting a typo.
Resolve conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>>) by choosing the correct final content and removing the markers. For report writing, the result should read as sensible English; for code, it must work from top to bottom. A conflict can have implications elsewhere in the file, such as a variable name used on another line, so check the broader result.

Resolve simple conflicts on GitHub or locally

Simple conflicts can be resolved in GitHub’s web editor. More complex conflicts can be handled locally.
In the local rebase demonstration, one PR had already been merged into main, while another branch, named DanDelete in the example, remained open.
Update local main first with git switch main and git pull origin main. Then switch to the still-open branch, for example with git switch dan-delete, and run git rebase main. Rebase replays the branch’s commits on top of the updated main, bringing the conflict into the local working files.
Open the conflicted file, remove the markers, choose the correct content, and check the result. The example retained both definitions and cleaned up whitespace.
Use git status to inspect the repository state and Git’s suggested next steps. Stage the resolved file, for example with git add README.md, and run git rebase --continue. Git also provides an abort option if the rebase needs to be abandoned.
After the rebase completes, the branch’s commit appears at the top of the updated history with the conflict resolved.

Force-push a rebased branch

Rebasing rewrites branch history by replaying commits onto a different base, so a normal push is not sufficient to update the remote branch.
Use a force push, such as git push --force origin dan-delete, to update the remote branch and its PR. GitHub indicates that a force push occurred.
Once updated, the PR can be merged if its checks and review allow it. Then synchronize and clean up branches as appropriate, while observing team and compliance requirements.

Q: What is the instructor’s stated reason for making lab attendance mandatory during the group project phase? A: TAs will circulate to talk to every single group and conduct the ungraded technical interviews. (00:02:30)



2. The problem with parallel work on main (8 Git branches)
00:04:04–00:09:43

Q: What command must you run before creating a new branch to ensure your starting point is up to date? A: You should run git pull origin main to sync your local repository with the remote. (00:18:55)
Q: If your work exists only on your local computer and has not been pushed to the remote repository, what is its status for grading purposes? A: It effectively does not exist for grading or project purposes because the code is not shipped or accessible to reviewers. (00:11:11)
Q: What analogy did the instructor use to describe the relationship between the main branch and exploratory work on branches? A: The instructor compared main to the foundation of a house that must be stable before parallel work like building walls or floors (branches) can occur. (00:14:50)



3. Creating and managing branches locally (8 Git branches)
00:09:43–00:25:12

Q: What command and flag are used to create a new branch and immediately switch to it? A: The command is git switch -c <branch_name>, which creates the branch and moves the HEAD pointer to it. (00:20:18)
Q: What older Git command, commonly used before 2020, also handled branch switching but was later split into specialized commands? A: git checkout was the legacy command that handled both branch switching and file restoration before git switch was introduced. (00:27:09)
Q: What visual cue in git status indicates which branch you are currently on? A: The output explicitly states “On branch <branch_name>” instead of “On branch main”. (00:21:03)



4. Pushing branches and initiating Pull Requests (9 Pull requests)
00:25:12–00:46:00

Q: What command is used to push a local branch to the remote GitHub repository? A: You run git push origin <branch_name> to send the branch’s commits to GitHub. (00:30:44)
Q: What is the name of the GitHub UI tab that displays the diff of changes for code review? A: The “Files Changed” tab shows the diff between the original file and the proposed changes. (00:41:22)
Q: What visual indicator does GitHub show to communicate that a Pull Request is still a work-in-progress draft? A: GitHub displays a gray bar at the top of the page instead of a green bar. (00:54:04)



5. Merging, cleanup, and local synchronization (8 Git branches)
00:52:17–01:03:51

Q: What command removes local tracking references for remote branches that have been deleted on GitHub? A: git fetch --prune synchronizes the history and removes local markers for deleted remote branches. (01:01:30)
Q: Which flag for git branch should you use to safely delete a local branch that has already been merged? A: The lowercase -d flag is used for safe deletion, preventing accidental deletion of unmerged work. (01:02:46)
Q: After a Pull Request is merged and the remote branch is deleted, what command must you run on your local main branch to update it with the new commits? A: You run git pull origin main to fast-forward your local main branch to match the remote. (01:00:27)



6. Resolving merge conflicts via rebase (8 Git branches)
01:03:51–01:21:43

Q: What command replays a local branch’s commits sequentially on top of an updated main branch to resolve conflicts locally? A: git rebase main replays the commits and triggers conflict resolution in the local text editor. (01:17:08)
Q: After resolving a conflict and finishing the rebase, why is a standard git push insufficient to update the remote branch? A: Because rebasing rewrites commit history, you must use a force push to update the remote. (01:19:47)
Q: What flag should you use with git push to safely force-push rewritten history to the remote repository? A: The --force-with-lease flag safely updates the remote branch only if no new, untracked commits were added by others. (01:19:47)

title: Git branches, pull requests and rebasing to fix conflicts: review questions, tier 2 — Understand
text:
Date: 2026-11-17
Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 2 of 5: Understand. Explain each answer in your own words before you read it; tier 1 (Remember) covers the facts, tiers 3 to 5 put them to use.

1. Course logistics: lab groups, attendance and interview week
00:00:01–00:04:04

Q: Why did the instructor insist that every student submit a correct GitHub username? A: The usernames build a main list of students that fills the GitHub username column of the lab sections repository. That list is metadata used “under the hood” everywhere else in the program, so a wrong username causes problems beyond this course. (00:02:01)
Q: Explain why lab attendance is mandatory in DSCI 522 this year. A: The course is built around a group project. During lab the TAs go around and talk to every single group, so you need to be there when a TA reaches your group. (00:02:19)
Q: Why can the seven-minute interview-week conversation cover anything in your group’s code base, not only Git? A: You are expected to know the code base you work in, “especially in the world of AI.” As at work, anything in the repository is fair game, so you should know what it does. The interview does not affect your grade. (00:03:15)



2. Why branches: escaping the 521 push/pull friction (8 Git branches)
00:06:49–00:09:43

Q: In the 521 shared slide-deck exercise, what friction did students hit even when there was no merge conflict? A: When you finished your part and tried to push, you often couldn’t, because someone else had pushed first. You had to pull before you could push again. Any time two people work on the same thing at the same time, that friction appears, whether or not there is a conflict. (00:07:06)
Q: Why will the push/pull friction from 521 still show up somewhere in every group project? A: Not every project can start with four parallel pieces of work. Early on, the whole group is blocked on one or two people getting the basics in place, so for a while everyone works on the same shared state. (00:07:50)
Q: How do parallel streams of work on branches let a teammate work from Tuesday to Friday without worrying about what others are doing? A: Each person works on a branch, “in your own little world,” and can push and pull it freely until the work is done. If the work is self-contained, other people’s pushes don’t matter. The group then reviews and coordinates everyone’s work at one point, for example on Friday. (00:08:46)



3. Review: the local–remote picture
00:09:46–00:11:47

Q: Why did the instructor say that work existing only on your laptop “effectively doesn’t really exist”? A: The GitHub remote is what gets graded and published. Work that isn’t pushed can’t be graded or used by the project, just as a product at work isn’t shipped if its code is only on your computer. (00:10:53)
Q: How does adding teammates change the local–remote picture? A: You still coordinate your computer with the GitHub remote, but each of your teammates must coordinate their own computer with that same remote. That makes a lot of coordination work, and the remote is the shared point that matters. (00:10:38)
Q: Compare the roles of clone, push and pull in the local–remote diagram. A: clone is a one-time command that brings the repository down to your computer. push sends your local commits up to GitHub. pull brings down commits that teammates pushed, so you can coordinate their work onto your computer. (00:11:33)



4. What a branch is: main, HEAD and origin/main (8 Git branches)
00:12:03–00:17:54

Q: What is the difference between main and origin/main in the output of git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all? A: main is your local branch, and it moves forward each time you commit while HEAD is attached to it. origin/main is what your computer thinks the state of GitHub is. If you commit on main without pushing, local main gets ahead of origin/main. (00:13:39)
Q: How does committing on a branch differ from committing on main? A: The workflow is the same: git add, then git commit. The difference is which name moves forward. On a branch, your commits advance a name you chose, such as b1, instead of advancing main. (00:14:25)
Q: Why should main be treated as the stable, “production” version of the project? A: A project has other moving pieces that should move at a steady rate. You don’t want an experiment that breaks on your computer to then break on all your teammates’ computers. On main, the code should at least work, even if the project isn’t finished. (00:15:24)
Q: Give the class’s example of what belongs on main and what stays on a branch during a data analysis. A: The cleaned dataset sits on main, and everyone bases their work on it. Exploratory data analysis, with plots still in progress, is not ready yet, so it stays on that person’s branch. (00:15:49)
Q: Why does the instructor use branches even in repositories where he is the only contributor? A: Branches section off work, so he can test and build things without main changing before he has reviewed everything. For example, he made textbook edits on branches while another instructor was teaching from the textbook, so pages wouldn’t move around mid-lecture. He merged them only after reviewing and testing them. (00:16:37)
Q: Explain why abandoning a failed idea is easier on a branch than undoing it on main. A: On a branch, you can say “that was a bad idea,” go back to main, and you are at your starting point; deleting a branch is easy. If you had written one commit that did twenty different things, you would have to dig through history and copy out the relevant parts. git reset and git revert from 521 also work, but branches make this easier. (00:17:22)



5. Creating and switching branches (8.1 Creating a branch using the command line)
00:17:54–00:26:29

Q: Why run git pull origin main before git switch -c when your work builds on coordinated work? A: It syncs your starting point with everything your teammates have pushed. The instructor has created branches on one computer and then realized he had already done half the work on another laptop. Syncing first would have saved him that time. (00:18:39)
Q: What does git switch actually do to the repository? A: It moves HEAD around the repository. You can tell which branch you are on because HEAD points to it in the log. git switch -c <name> creates a new branch and moves HEAD to it. (00:19:51)
Q: Why does the instructor start his branch names with his own name, as in dan-b1? A: In a group repository, the name tells others whom to talk to if something on that branch looks weird. (00:20:31)
Q: Interpret the log right after git switch -c dan-b1, which showed 145ff16 (HEAD -> dan-b1, origin/main, origin/HEAD, main). A: Nothing changed except a word. No new commit was made, so main, the remote references and the new dan-b1 all point to the same commit. The only difference is that HEAD is now attached to dan-b1 instead of main. (00:21:15)
Q: After committing on dan-b1, why is dan-b1 one commit ahead of both main and origin/main? A: Whichever branch HEAD is attached to gets dragged along when you commit. This time that was dan-b1, not main. origin/main would be behind in either case, because nothing had been pushed or synced with GitHub. (00:23:21)
Q: What happens to the files on disk after git switch main from dan-b1, and why is that useful? A: The files return to the state they have at main, and the branch you left stays where it was. This lets you move between parallel states of the project, for example to try a feature or to look at a teammate’s work on your own computer. (00:25:46)
Q: Why does the instructor always type --all in git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all? A: Without the --all flag, the log may not show your other branch names, only the history of where you are. (00:25:38)
Q: How does the graph in the Git tab of VS Code or Positron relate to the terminal log? A: It shows the same picture: origin/main, local main and the dan-b1 commit. Knowing the commands and how to draw the history helps you read that graph view. (00:24:09)



6. git checkout and git branch versus git switch (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:26:40–00:28:26

Q: How is the older git checkout related to git switch and to the restore and revert commands from 521? A: checkout used to do what switch does, moving HEAD around, but it also did much of what the restore and revert commands do. The newer commands were carved out of checkout, and checkout still has all of those behaviours. (00:27:09)
Q: Why should you ask an AI tool for the switch version when it tells you to run git checkout? A: checkout can do many different things. If you don’t know what a suggested command will do, and you are worried about losing work in your codebase, you should think about the commands you type rather than run whatever works. (00:27:48)
Q: How does git branch <name> differ from git switch -c <name> and git checkout -b <name>? A: git switch -c and its older equivalent git checkout -b both create the branch and move you onto it. git branch only creates the branch without moving you, so you still have to switch or check out afterwards. (00:28:13)



7. Pushing a branch and viewing it on GitHub (8.2 Useful things you can do with branches on GitHub)
00:28:31–00:33:40

Q: How did the class plan to get the dan-b1 commits onto main, rather than merging on the laptop? A: The easiest way is not to merge on your local computer, but through a review process, using a pull request (or merge request). That means pushing the branch to GitHub first, because push is the only command that links local work to the remote. (00:29:22)
Q: Why did a bare git push while on main print Everything up-to-date instead of sending dan-b1? A: With branches, where you push and what you push now matter; you are no longer pushing only main. Being on main, which had nothing new, a bare push didn’t send the new branch. You have to switch to the branch you want to push and name it. (00:29:50)
Q: Explain why the last word changes in git push origin dan-b1 compared with the git push origin main you typed for ten weeks. A: The last word names the branch you are pushing. Otherwise the behaviour is the same: you send your local work for that branch up to GitHub. (00:30:44)
Q: Interpret the log after git push origin dan-b1, where origin/dan-b1 appears next to dan-b1 but origin/main hasn’t moved. A: GitHub now has a branch called dan-b1 at the same commit as your local dan-b1. Pushing a branch doesn’t change main at all. (00:31:27)
Q: Why is it useful to view a pushed branch with the branch dropdown on GitHub before it is merged? A: You can confirm that your local work actually exists on GitHub. In a group, you can also read a teammate’s code, such as how they made a figure, without running it and before it is reviewed or merged into main. (00:32:36)



8. Opening a pull request (9.1 Creating a pull request)
00:33:40–00:41:16

Q: Why does the instructor open a pull request right away, even after one small commit? A: The “Compare & pull request” pop-up seems to disappear after a day or so. Starting the pull request immediately means he doesn’t risk losing it, and the pull request can still be marked as in progress. If the pop-up is gone, you can reach the same page from the Branches tab through “New pull request”. (00:35:15)
Q: Why should you check the line at the top of a new pull request that names the two branches? A: It says which branch is being merged into which. In this course that is your branch into main, but in DSCI 524 the target won’t always be main. With forks of open-source projects, you must also make sure your code goes to the right place. (00:36:20)
Q: Explain why the file list at the bottom of a pull request is a “second line of defence”. A: After reviewing on your own computer, you can review on GitHub every change from main. First, check that all the files you worked on are there; if not, you probably forgot to add, commit or push. Second, check that files that don’t belong, such as .ipynb_checkpoints, .DS_Store or Word backup files, aren’t there, because points are taken off for them even if the instructions don’t mention them. (00:39:42)
Q: How does a pull request’s title differ from its description, and when might the two be the same? A: The pull request is a report: the title names the change, and the description explains what is happening in the branch. For simple changes, like most group-project work, the two may be almost the same. Pull requests written by AI agents can “read like a novel.” (00:37:42)
Q: Why edit a pull request’s first comment instead of adding “now I’m also doing…” comments as the work grows? A: The very first message is what people are going to read. All your changes should be defined and explained there, which is why GitHub lets you edit it. (00:41:03)
Q: What changes once you click “Create Pull Request”? A: The pull request appears under the Pull requests tab. Anyone with access to the repository can see the branch and its changes, review them, and discuss them in the conversation. (00:40:01)



9. Code review and updating a pull request (10 Code review on GitHub)
00:41:16–00:45:41

Q: What does “code review” mean in terms of the Files changed tab? A: You look at the diff between the original code and the code being added or removed. You can comment on a line using the + that appears when you hover over it, as in “why are you using switch and not checkout?” Those comments are tracked in the main Conversation tab. (00:41:34)
Q: Explain the rule of thumb for who fixes problems found in a code review. A: If it’s your pull request, fixing it is your job. The reviewer’s job is to say “rewrite this” or “this doesn’t look right,” not to fix your code. (00:42:17)
Q: How do you change the code in an open pull request without closing it and opening a new one? A: Go back to the branch the pull request is working from, then add, commit and push to that same branch. The pull request is tied to the branch, so it updates. In class, committing “show you the long git log command” and running git push origin dan-b1 made a second commit appear in pull request #1, sometimes only after a page refresh. (00:44:43)
Q: Why might a reviewer’s comment collapse as “outdated” after you push a new commit? A: If you changed the line the comment was attached to, that comment probably isn’t relevant anymore. GitHub collapses it so you don’t end up looking at too much stuff. The comment isn’t necessarily deleted. (00:45:02)



10. AI reviewers and draft pull requests (9.2 Draft pull requests)
00:52:11–00:55:41

Q: How should you treat comments from a Copilot review on your pull request? A: Requesting one isn’t a bad thing, because more eyes on something is never really a bad idea. But you don’t have to keep every comment the LLM makes: you can push back on it, reject it or accept it. (00:53:05)
Q: What does “Convert to draft” communicate, and what does the grey bar mean? A: It turns an open pull request into a draft. The grey bar instead of a green one is the visual cue that people can look, but the work isn’t ready yet. You use it to tell yourself and others that this isn’t ready. (00:54:12)
Q: Why does greying out the merge button on a draft pull request matter? A: Nobody can accidentally merge something that explicitly says it isn’t working or isn’t ready. The instructor believes this also stops an agent from just merging everything that’s green. This is why he has kept drafts open for three or four months on long pieces of work. (00:55:03)
Q: How do you turn a draft pull request back into one that can be merged? A: At the bottom, where it says the pull request is a work in progress, click “Ready for review.” It becomes an open pull request again, with green merge buttons. (00:55:28)



11. Merging and deleting the branch on GitHub (8.2 Useful things you can do with branches on GitHub)
00:55:41–00:59:07

Q: Why does the instructor delete a branch on GitHub after its pull request is merged? A: A project creates many branches and pull requests over its lifetime. Without cleanup, the branch dropdown becomes a giant list, which he finds annoying. You don’t need to keep the branch name, because the commits are still there. (00:56:08)
Q: Why is no work lost when you delete dan-b1 after merging pull request #1? A: Deleting the branch removes only the marker. main’s history still contains the branch’s two commits plus a separate merge commit. You can find the commits related to the pull request and undo the feature later if you need to. (00:58:38)
Q: Why might a team not delete merged branches? A: Where law or compliance requires it, you can’t delete anything, and the branch list just gets long. Otherwise, your team’s workflow decides, but at least clean up your own work if it doesn’t affect other people. (00:57:34)



12. Syncing and cleaning up locally after a merge (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:59:07–01:03:51

Q: Why do merge conflicts still happen when each person works on their own branch? A: Even if you tell people which part you’re working on, other people or agents sometimes can’t help fixing a typo in your part. If you fix the same typo, there is still a conflict. This is why individual assignment 1 has you practise merge conflicts again. (00:59:39)
Q: Why do you need git pull origin main after a pull request is merged on GitHub? A: Local main doesn’t update itself. Pulling syncs it with GitHub. In class, the pull added new lines to README.md, which were the merged pull request’s changes. (01:00:17)
Q: How does git fetch differ from git pull? A: git pull does two things: it fetches, and then it merges on top. git fetch only coordinates the history with origin, so you run it alone when you don’t want the files on your computer to change. (01:01:52)
Q: Interpret what git fetch --prune did in class when it printed [deleted] (none) -> origin/dan-b1. A: The dan-b1 branch had been deleted on GitHub. The prune removed the matching origin/dan-b1 marker on the local computer. After that, the reference no longer appeared in the big git log command. (01:02:22)
Q: Why should you use lowercase git branch -d rather than capital -D, and why is the capital version dangerous? A: Lowercase -d deletes a local branch only if it has been merged. Git makes it harder to delete work, because deleting an unmerged branch in theory loses that work. Capital -D force-deletes even unmerged branches, and it’s only a one-character difference. Be very careful when copying commands from ChatGPT, which might give you -D and delete commits you’re still working on. (01:03:21)



13. Setting up two conflicting pull requests (8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?)
01:04:00–01:10:00

Q: What makes the dan-fetch and dan-delete branches conflict? A: A merge conflict happens when two changes are made to the same line of the same file. Both branches added text at the same place in README.md. (01:04:00)
Q: Why must you avoid merging the first pull request, dan-fetch, straight away when you practise conflicts on your own? A: Holding it open lets you create a second, conflicting set of changes from the same starting point. This stands in for what happens when two people each open a pull request and one of them conflicts with the other. (01:06:07)
Q: Why wasn’t the git fetch --prune line in README.md when the instructor started dan-delete? A: He switched to main before creating dan-delete, and that line had only been committed on dan-fetch. Both branches are therefore based on main without each other’s changes. (01:07:20)
Q: Interpret the git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate output in which two lines leave commit 3851b00. A: Both branches start from the same main commit and then split. The graph literally shows two parallel pieces of work: dan-fetch with 157c3cd and dan-delete with cb810d5. (01:09:00)
Q: Why doesn’t GitHub warn you about the coming conflict while both pull requests are still open? A: Each pull request is compared only with main, and on its own each one can be merged into main. Nothing in either pull request shows that they edit the same line, and it isn’t obvious that they share the same starting point. (01:09:53)



14. When a merge creates the conflict: resolving on GitHub
01:10:00–01:12:44

Q: How did pull request #3 go from mergeable to conflicting? A: When one pull request is merged, main changes. Every pull request that merges into main is then rechecked. After #2 was merged, #3 could no longer merge cleanly, and GitHub showed the conflict page. (01:10:31)
Q: Compare what “fixing” a conflict means for report prose and for code in this course. A: For report writing, whatever is left must be English that makes sense. For code, it isn’t enough to remove the <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> markers: the code must work from top to bottom again. (01:11:21)
Q: Why can resolving a conflict on line 13 still leave the code broken? A: The conflict only tells you which line has competing changes. Your resolution can affect code elsewhere, for example if you change a variable name that is used on line 50. Making that code work again is still your problem. (01:11:39)
Q: When did the instructor suggest the GitHub web editor, and when fixing the conflict locally? A: The web editor is fine for simple conflicts like the one in README.md. He showed the local fix because the commands are more involved. (01:12:33)



15. Resolving the conflict locally with rebase (8.3.2 Using rebase)
01:12:44–01:20:42

Q: What does git rebase main do to the dan-delete branch? A: It replays your branch’s commits on top of the existing changes on main. That replay is where the conflict surfaces on your computer, so you can fix it there. The instructor noted that there are many ways to fix conflicts and that people will have opinions; rebase is the one he uses. (01:14:31)
Q: Why must you run git switch main and git pull origin main before rebasing dan-delete? A: The merged dan-fetch commit was on GitHub’s main but not on your computer. Syncing main brings that commit down, so there is something to replay your branch on top of. (01:13:42)
Q: Explain what had to change about dan-delete’s history, in terms of the commit IDs from class. A: dan-delete’s previous commit was 3851b00. It needed to be one that contains 157c3cd, the fetch commit merged into main. Rebasing gives the branch that new parent. (01:16:00)
Q: How does triggering a conflict with git rebase main differ from week 3 of 521? A: Fixing the conflict is the same skill: open the file and resolve the markers. In 521 the conflict was triggered by git pull origin main. Here it is triggered by replaying your commits over another branch. (01:17:56)
Q: How does git status guide you through a rebase that stopped on a conflict? A: It tells you to use git add to mark the file as resolved. Once all conflicts are fixed, it tells you to run git rebase --continue, which asks you to confirm the commit message. If you’re scared that something got messed up, you can abort to get back to where you started. (01:18:44)
Q: Why did the instructor have to force-push, with git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete, after the rebase, and why should this be done with care? A: The rebase changed the branch’s history: the commit’s previous commit is no longer the old version of main. A simple push is no longer possible, so you can’t avoid force-pushing. GitHub records that a force push happened, and since you’ve “mangled history,” that matters in compliance settings. (01:20:21)

2. Why branches exist: escaping the pull-before-push friction (8 Git branches)
00:06:49–00:09:43

Q: Why did the shared slide deck exercise in DSCI 521 create friction even when no actual conflict occurred? A: Because even without a conflict, there was always the step of “I have to pull first because someone else pushed before I can push again.” If two people are working on the same thing at the same time, you always run into that coordination friction, whether or not a real conflict materializes. (00:07:06)
Q: What is the benefit of working in parallel streams with branches? A: You are in “your own little world” where you can push and pull until you are actually done, waiting for review from teammates. If the work is self-contained parallel work, it does not matter what other people are doing; you can work from Tuesday to Friday on your part of the project without being blocked. (00:08:46)
Q: Why does the instructor say the first week of the group project will “get a little bit weird”? A: Because not every project can start with four parallel pieces of work at the same time. There is always a part of a project where you are bound or stuck by one or two people getting the basics down first, and that problem exists in a project no matter what. (00:07:40)



3. Local repository versus remote origin (8 Git branches)
00:09:46–00:11:11

Q: Why does the instructor say that work existing only on your local computer “effectively doesn’t exist” for grading or project purposes? A: Because the remote is “the thing we grade” and “the thing that gets published.” If your code is only on your computer, “your product is not shipped because the code isn’t anywhere to be shipped.” The remote is the state that matters. (00:10:48)
Q: How does the remote origin serve as the coordination point when multiple teammates are working on the same repository? A: You coordinate with your GitHub remote, and your three other teammates also coordinate with the same remote. There is “a lot of coordination work that needs to happen” through that shared point, with git push sending your work up and git pull bringing others’ work down. (00:10:20)
Q: What does it mean that git clone is a “one-time command” in the local/remote relationship? A: Clone brings the repository down to your computer once; after that, the ongoing connection is maintained through git push (to send commits up) and git pull (to bring others’ commits down). You do not keep cloning; you push and pull to stay in sync. (00:11:25)



4. main, origin/main, HEAD, and what a branch is (8 Git branches)
00:11:11–00:16:05

Q: What is the difference between main and origin/main in the Git diagram? A: main is the local branch pointer that increments as you write commits on your computer. origin/main is “the remote, what your computer thinks the state of GitHub is at.” If you write commits on main without pushing, your local main moves ahead of origin/main. (00:13:30)
Q: How does a branch change the behaviour of git commit compared to committing on main? A: Instead of incrementing where main is when you write a commit, you increment “some other name that you give it yourself.” The same git add and git commit process applies, but the named branch moves forward while main stays where it is. (00:13:55)
Q: Why does the instructor compare main to a “production final” branch? A: Because in larger projects, you want other moving pieces to move at a steady rate. You do not want one person to try something on main and have it break on all of their teammates’ computers. Everything in main should be in working order and stable, even if not finished. (00:15:10)
Q: What does it mean that HEAD is “attached to” a branch? A: HEAD is the pointer into the Git history that shows which branch you are currently on. When HEAD is pointed to main, you are on the main branch; when you switch to a new branch, HEAD moves to point at that branch. It is the visual cue of your current location in the repository. (00:13:17)



5. Branches are useful even when working alone (8 Git branches)
00:16:05–00:17:54

Q: Why does the instructor say you can use branches even when working by yourself? A: To “section off work” and test a whole bunch of stuff without the main branch changing without reviewing everything. He gave the example of the course textbook, where he did all his work in a sequence of branches so the textbook would not “start things moving around like crazy in the middle of a teaching day.” (00:16:12)
Q: What is the advantage of abandoning a failed branch versus undoing a tangled set of commits on main? A: If something did not work, it is “really easy to delete a branch” and come back to main. Versus if you wrote one commit that did twenty different things on main, you would have to “go through the git history, start copying and pasting all the bits that are actually relevant,” which is really hard. (00:17:00)
Q: How do git reset and git revert relate to the undo capability that branches provide? A: The instructor acknowledged that you could use git reset and git revert (from DSCI 521) to undo commits on main, but branches “sort of just make that a little bit easier” because you can simply discard the whole branch and return to main as your starting point. (00:17:22)



6. Creating a branch with git switch -c (8 Git branches)
00:17:54–00:23:46

Q: Why should you synchronize with the remote (for example, git pull origin main) before creating a new branch for coordinated project work? A: So your starting point is “essentially up to date.” The instructor shared a personal example of creating a branch, forgetting he was working on three different computers, and realizing he had already done half the work on another laptop. Syncing first “could have saved [him] a bunch of time.” (00:18:09)
Q: What does git switch -c <branch> do that a plain git switch <branch> does not? A: The -c flag stands for create: it creates a new branch and immediately moves HEAD to it. Without -c, git switch just moves HEAD to an existing branch. The instructor summarized the -c version as “create and move head to the branch name.” (00:20:09)
Q: Why does the instructor sometimes prefix branch names with the owner’s name in group repositories? A: So that “other people know that if something’s going on around here and something’s weird, this is the person to talk to.” It is a signal about who owns that branch and who to contact if something looks off. (00:20:31)
Q: What happens to the Git log immediately after running git switch -c dan-b1 but before making any new commits? A: Not much changes: you still have main, the remote references, and a new branch called dan-b1 with HEAD on it. No new commit was made; the only difference is that HEAD is now attached to the new branch instead of main. (00:21:15)



7. Switching between branches and seeing the repository state (8 Git branches)
00:23:46–00:28:26

Q: Why does the instructor recommend using git switch rather than git checkout when teaching? A: checkout was doing what switch does (moving HEAD around) but also “did a lot of what revert and restore was doing.” If you are not comfortable with what checkout does, the instructor suggests asking tools to use switch instead, because switch has a narrower, more predictable behaviour. (00:27:09)
Q: What is the difference between git branch <name> and git switch -c <name>? A: git branch just creates the branch but “doesn’t move [HEAD] to it.” You still have to checkout or switch after creating it. git switch -c does both in one step: it creates the branch and moves HEAD to it. (00:28:13)
Q: Why does the --all flag matter when running git log --oneline --graph --decorate? A: Without it, you may not see your other branch names in the log output. The instructor noted that if you do not see your other branch names, that is why he has --all typed out; it ensures all branches appear in the graph. (00:25:38)



8. Pushing a branch to origin and viewing it on GitHub (8 Git branches)
00:28:31–00:33:40

Q: Why does the instructor say the easiest way to combine a branch into main is to “don’t do it on your local computer”? A: Because the class workflow uses a review process—pull requests—rather than local merges. The pull request is where you review your own work and your teammates’ work before incorporating it into the project. (00:28:58)
Q: What does it mean when origin/dan-b1 appears in the git log after running git push origin dan-b1? A: It means “GitHub also has a branch called dan b one and is in the same location as whatever exists on your local computer.” The local computer now knows that the remote has that branch, but main has not changed at all. (00:31:19)
Q: Why is it useful to view a teammate’s branch on GitHub before it is merged into main? A: You can see their code or work “even though it’s not combined into the main branch yet.” For example, if a teammate made a cool figure, you can look at their code without running it. It does not mean the work is completely reviewed and ready to merge, but you can look around. (00:32:36)
Q: Why do you need to change the last word in git push origin main when pushing a new branch? A: Because you are no longer pushing the main branch; you are pushing a different branch. The behaviour of push is “exactly the same,” but the target branch name changes from main to whatever branch you created, such as dan-b1. (00:30:44)



9. Opening a pull request and reviewing the changed files (9 Pull requests)
00:33:40–00:39:56

Q: Why does the instructor recommend opening a pull request immediately after pushing a branch, even if the work is not finished? A: Because the “Compare and Pull Request” popup disappears after a day or so. Starting the process right away means the pull request exists and updates as you keep pushing commits, so you do not lose the opportunity to begin the review workflow. (00:35:00)
Q: Why is the first comment in a pull request important, and why should you edit it rather than just appending new notes? A: “That’s what people are going to read.” All of your changes should be defined and explained in the very first comment. If you keep making changes to the pull request, you should edit the first message rather than just adding new ones, so the description stays coherent. (00:40:48)
Q: What two things should you check in the Files Changed tab before creating a pull request, and why does the second check matter? A: First, confirm that all the files and bits of code you thought you worked on actually exist. Second, check for files that “don’t really belong here,” like .ipynb_checkpoints, .DS_Store, or Word backup files, because in this course, if such unwanted files are visible in a repository, “we will take points off.” (00:38:44)
Q: Why does the instructor say to pay attention to where you are merging in the pull request? A: In DSCI 522, main is probably the target, but in 524, “main is not always going to be the branch that you’re going to be incorporating work into.” In large open-source projects with forks, you also need to make sure you are sending your code to the right repository and branch. (00:35:38)



10. Pull request conversation, code review, and updating the same branch (10 Code review on GitHub)
00:39:56–00:45:41

Q: What does the “Files Changed” tab in a pull request show, and how does it relate to what “code review” means? A: It shows “the diff between the original file and the new file.” Code review is literally looking at that diff and making comments on specific lines using the plus button, which then get tracked in the main conversation tab. (00:41:22)
Q: Why is it the pull request author’s job to fix issues rather than the reviewer’s job? A: The reviewer’s job is to say “rewrite this” or “this doesn’t look right.” It is the author’s job to “go and actually fix it” in the codebase. The instructor emphasized: “if it’s your pull request, it is your job to fix it all.” (00:42:17)
Q: How does a pull request update when the author makes additional commits, and why does the author not need to close and recreate it? A: The pull request is tied to the actual branch. You just go back to the branch, add, commit, and push to the same branch, and “the pull request will update.” You do not need to close the pull request and create a new one; it keeps track of all the information as you push. (00:43:15)
Q: What does it mean when GitHub “auto-collapses” a comment as outdated? A: It means you changed the line that the comment was attached to, so “that original comment, probably doesn’t exist anymore or is relevant anymore.” GitHub collapses it “just so you don’t end up looking at too much stuff.” (00:45:02)



11. Draft pull requests, merging, and deleting the remote branch (9 Pull requests)
00:52:11–00:58:51

Q: Why does the instructor create the pull request early and then convert it to a draft rather than waiting until the work is complete? A: To “make sure all the pipeline is working” and to signal to the team that work is in progress. The pull request updates as he keeps pushing the branch, and a draft communicates “we’re still working on this” without the risk of premature merging. (00:53:26)
Q: What is the purpose of disabling the merge button on a draft pull request? A: So “no one can actually accidentally merge something that is very explicitly saying this not working or this not ready yet.” The gray bar instead of a green one is the visual cue that the work is not finished. (00:54:30)
Q: Why does deleting the remote branch after merging not remove the commits from the project’s history? A: Because the commits have been merged into main; “the commits are still there. It’s not that the commits have been gone.” Even after deleting the branch marker, you can see the commits in the history, including a separate merge commit that says “this stuff got merged in.” (00:58:10)



12. Local cleanup after a merge: git pull, git branch -a, git fetch --prune, and git branch -d (8 Git branches)
00:58:53–01:03:51

Q: Why does your local main branch not automatically update after a pull request is merged on GitHub? A: Because “main doesn’t automatically update itself.” You need a synchronization step: switch to main and run git pull origin main to get the merged changes onto your local machine. (01:00:17)
Q: What is the difference between git pull origin main and git fetch --prune in terms of what happens to your local files? A: git pull does two things: it runs fetch and then merge on top, which changes your files. If you do not want the files on your computer to change, you only run git fetch, which “is coordinating the history” without modifying files. The --prune flag additionally removes local references to branches that were deleted on GitHub. (01:02:07)
Q: Why does git branch -d refuse to delete a branch that has not been merged? A: Because “if you delete it, in theory, you’ve lost work.” Git makes it harder to delete work that is kind of permanent. The lowercase -d only allows deletion if the branch has been merged; if it has not, the command will not delete it. (01:02:54)
Q: Why does the instructor specifically warn about capital -D when copying commands from tools like ChatGPT? A: Because capital -D force-deletes a branch even if it has not been merged. The instructor warned: “Be very careful if you’re copying and pasting commands from ChatGPT because it might just say capital D delete, force delete, and then you could delete the commits that you’re working on.” (01:03:21)



13. Creating a merge-conflict scenario with two branches (8 Git branches)
01:03:51–01:10:51

Q: Why did the instructor create two separate branches (dan-fetch and dan-delete) from the same main state to demonstrate a merge conflict? A: To simulate what happens when two people make changes to the same line of the same file. The conflict arises from “the same change to the same line of the same file,” which is what happens when two branches both modify a region that the other has already changed. (01:04:00)
Q: Why does looking at the two pull requests side by side not obviously reveal that they will conflict? A: Each pull request looks like it can merge into main individually. “It’s not very obvious that their starting point is from that main branch,” and “nothing here actually tells you that a merge conflict is going to happen.” The conflict only becomes apparent after one branch is merged. (01:09:17)
Q: What happens when the first pull request is merged that causes the second pull request to become conflicted? A: The main branch changes, and then “every single pull request that is merging into main is going to recheck to see if it can be merged.” The second pull request, even though it previously showed everything in green, now ends up on a conflict page because it can no longer merge cleanly. (01:10:19)



14. Resolving the conflict locally with git rebase main and git push --force-with-lease (8 Git branches)
01:10:51–01:20:42

Q: Why does the instructor say that “fixing” a merge conflict in this course means more than just removing the conflict markers? A: Because your code or report “needs to work from top to bottom again.” A conflict on line thirteen “doesn’t mean that’s the only place your code is going to affect.” If changing the conflict affects a variable used later in the file, that is still your problem to deal with. (01:11:21)
Q: What does git rebase main do, and why is it used to resolve the conflict on the dan-delete branch? A: It “replay[s] all of my commits in this branch back to the main branch over the main branch.” This moves the branch’s commit on top of the updated main, which is where the conflict appears on your computer so you can go and fix it in your text editor. (01:17:14)
Q: Why can you not use a normal git push origin dan-delete after rebasing, and why is a force push necessary? A: Because rebase “changed the history of that commit.” The previous commit is no longer the same version of main; the history is actually changed. “You have to force push to force update the branch” because a normal push will not accept the rewritten history. (01:19:34)
Q: How does the rebase approach to triggering a conflict differ from the DSCI 521 approach? A: In DSCI 521, the conflict was triggered by running git pull origin main on a branch that was behind. Now it is triggered by “replaying commits over another branch” with git rebase main. The resolution process—finding the markers, fixing the file, running git add, and continuing—is the same. (01:17:56)

title: Branches, Pull Requests, and Conflict Resolution: review questions, tier 3 — Apply
text:
Date: 2026-11-17

Generated by qwen3.6-35b-a3b, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 3 of 5: Apply. Work each situation through before you read the answer; tiers 1 (Remember) and 2 (Understand) cover the facts and reasons it relies on.

1. Creating and managing branches locally (8 Git branches)
00:09:43–00:25:12

Q: You are starting a new feature and want to work in isolation from the main branch. You have already synced your local copy with the remote. What command do you run to create a new branch named feature-x and immediately switch to it? A: Run git switch -c feature-x. This creates the new branch and moves the HEAD pointer to it in a single step, detaching it from origin/main so your subsequent commits only affect the new branch (00:20:18).
Q: After creating the branch, you want to verify that your HEAD is pointing to the new branch and visually confirm how the commit history diverges from origin/main. Which command produces this graph? A: Run git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all. This command renders a text-based visualization of all branches and commits, clearly showing the HEAD attached to your new branch while origin/main remains static (00:21:15).
Q: You are working in a group and create a new branch for your assigned task. What naming convention should you use to help teammates identify who is responsible for that specific line of development? A: Prefix the branch name with your username (e.g., dan-b1). This naming practice signals to collaborators who is actively developing on the branch, making it easier to coordinate and troubleshoot issues (00:20:48).



2. Pushing branches and initiating Pull Requests (9 Pull requests)
00:25:12–00:46:00

Q: You have finished adding commits to your local feature branch and need to send them to the remote repository so your teammates can begin reviewing your work. What command do you run? A: Run git push origin <branch_name>. This uploads your local branch’s commits to the remote, after which GitHub typically displays a prompt offering to create a Pull Request immediately (00:30:44).
Q: You are starting a task that will take several days, but you want your team to see your progress early and prevent anyone from accidentally merging incomplete code. How do you set up the Pull Request on GitHub? A: Click the dropdown arrow beside the “Create pull request” button and select “Create draft pull request”. This converts the PR into a draft, grays out the merge button, and signals to the team that the work is still in progress (00:53:52).
Q: After opening a Pull Request, you realize you forgot to add a file and need to make a small fix. How do you update the Pull Request on GitHub without closing it and creating a new one? A: Go back to your local computer, make the changes on the same branch, run git add, git commit, and git push origin <branch_name>. The GitHub Pull Request automatically updates to reflect the new commits (00:43:15).



3. Merging, cleanup, and local synchronization (8 Git branches)
00:52:17–01:03:51

Q: A teammate merges their Pull Request into main and deletes the branch on GitHub. You switch to your local main branch and synchronize your history, but your local terminal still lists the deleted branch. What command cleans up the tracking references for branches deleted on the remote? A: Run git fetch --prune. This synchronizes the local repository with the remote and automatically removes any local tracking references that correspond to branches deleted on GitHub (01:01:30).
Q: After synchronizing with the remote, you want to delete the merged branch from your local computer to keep your workspace tidy. Which command should you use to safely remove a branch that has already been merged, and why is this specific flag recommended? A: Run git branch -d <branch_name>. The lowercase -d flag is a safe deletion option that prevents you from accidentally deleting unmerged work, whereas uppercase -D would force delete and risk permanently losing commits (01:02:46).
Q: You just merged a Pull Request on GitHub and switched back to your local main branch. The local history is still one commit behind the remote. What command fetches and applies the new commits from the remote main branch to your local machine? A: Run git pull origin main. This retrieves the changes from the remote and fast-forwards your local main branch so it matches the current state on GitHub (01:00:27).



4. Resolving merge conflicts via rebase (8 Git branches)
01:03:51–01:21:43

Q: You have an open Pull Request, but another team member merges a different Pull Request into main that modifies the same lines of your README.md. When you try to merge your branch, GitHub reports a conflict. To resolve this locally using your preferred method, you switch to your branch and run a command that replays your commits on top of the updated main. What is this command? A: Run git rebase main. This replays your branch’s commits sequentially on top of the latest main, triggering the conflict resolution process locally where you can manually edit the conflict markers (01:14:04).
Q: After resolving the conflict markers in your text editor, you want to mark the resolution and continue the replay process. What sequence of commands do you run to finalize the rebase? A: Run git add <conflicted_file> to mark the conflict as resolved, then run git rebase --continue. This applies the resolved commit and completes the rebase process (01:17:32).
Q: Once the rebase is finished, your local commit history has been rewritten. What command do you use to push these changes to the remote branch, and why is a standard push insufficient? A: Run git push --force-with-lease origin <branch_name>. Because rebasing rewrites the commit history, a standard push will be rejected by the remote; force-with-lease safely updates the branch while checking that no other new commits were pushed by others in the meantime (01:19:34).
