title: Git branches, pull requests and rebasing to fix conflicts: review questions, tier 4 — Analyze
text:
Date: 2026-11-17
Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 4 of 5: Analyze. Take each one apart yourself before you read the answer; tiers 1 to 3 cover the facts, reasons and steps it relies on.

1. Git recap: setting up the demo repository
00:04:07–00:06:49

Q: Break down the review cycle Daniel ran on README.md in 2026-11-17-git: git status, git diff, git add README.md, git commit -m "intro and review", git push origin main. What does each step contribute, and which is the only one that touches GitHub? A: git status reported that README.md was modified but not staged. git diff showed the actual lines added: the review sentence and the Git branches link. git add staged the file, and git commit recorded it as commit 145ff16 in the local history only. git push origin main is the only step that reached GitHub; it moved the remote from 1360d7f to 145ff16. The log then showed HEAD -> main and origin/main on the same commit. (00:06:13)



2. Why branches: escaping the 521 push/pull friction
00:06:49–00:09:43

Q: Separate the phases of a group project as Daniel described them. Where does the 521 “pull before you can push” friction come from, which phase can’t avoid it, and how do branches change the later phase? A: The friction arises when two people push to the same place: even without a conflict, one of them has to pull first before pushing again. Early in a project, the work is blocked on one or two people setting up the basics, so that friction will exist somewhere no matter what. Later, each person owns a self-contained part. On their own branch, they can push and pull from Tuesday to Friday without caring what others do. Coordination is then moved to a review point, such as Friday, when the group reviews and merges the work. (00:08:46)



3. Review: the local–remote picture
00:09:46–00:11:47

Q: Take the 521 local–remote diagram apart. Which of clone, commit, push and pull happen on your computer and which move work between your computer and GitHub? Which side counts for grading, and how do teammates fit in? A: A commit happens only on your computer. clone is a one-time command that brings the repository down. push sends your commits up to the remote, and pull brings down commits that teammates pushed. Each teammate’s computer coordinates with that same GitHub remote. The remote is “the thing that matters”: it is what gets graded and published. Work that exists only on your laptop “effectively doesn’t really exist” for grading or project purposes. (00:11:19)



4. What a branch is: main, HEAD and origin/main (8 Git branches)
00:12:03–00:17:54

Q: Distinguish the three labels in git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all: HEAD, main (or a branch name such as b1), and origin/main. What does each represent, and what makes each one move? A: HEAD marks where you are. It is attached to a branch, and a commit moves whichever branch HEAD is attached to. main is the default branch. A branch like b1 is a name you choose, and it moves instead of main when HEAD is on it; the git add/git commit workflow itself is unchanged. origin/main is what your computer thinks the state of GitHub is. It does not move when you commit, so if you commit on main without pushing, local main gets ahead of origin/main. (00:13:30)



5. Creating and switching branches (8.1 Creating a branch using the command line)
00:17:54–00:26:29

Q: Trace dan-b1 through three snapshots of git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all: right after git switch -c dan-b1, after git commit -m "define swtich -c", and after git switch main. What moves at each step, and what stays put? A: After git switch -c dan-b1, no new commit existed. HEAD -> dan-b1 sat on 145ff16 alongside main and origin/main, so only a word had changed. After the commit, HEAD -> dan-b1 moved to the new commit 4a14a64, while main and origin/main stayed on 145ff16. After git switch main, HEAD moved back to main and README.md on disk returned to main’s version. dan-b1 stayed on 4a14a64, which is why the branch you left “never moved anywhere”. (00:22:58)



6. git checkout and git branch versus git switch (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:26:40–00:28:26

Q: Set git switch -c <name>, git checkout -b <name> and git branch <name> side by side. What does each create and move, and what did the failed git switch -b dan-delete in class reveal about mixing them up? A: git switch -c creates a branch and moves HEAD to it. git checkout -b is the older command that does the same thing; checkout also does much of what restore and revert now do. git branch <name> only creates the branch without moving you, so you still need switch or checkout afterwards. In class, git switch -b dan-delete failed with error: unknown switch `b', because -b belongs to checkout. The fix was git switch -c dan-delete. (00:28:13)



7. Pushing a branch and viewing it on GitHub (8.2 Useful things you can do with branches on GitHub)
00:28:31–00:33:40

Q: Break down how the dan-b1 commit reached GitHub. Why did the bare git push on main send nothing? What changed in the log after git push origin dan-b1, and where on GitHub did the work show up and not show up? A: On main, a bare git push printed Everything up-to-date, because the new commit lived on dan-b1 and not on main. After git switch dan-b1, running git push origin dan-b1 created the new branch on GitHub; the last word names what you push. The log then showed origin/dan-b1 beside dan-b1, while origin/main had not moved. On GitHub the repository’s main view still showed only main’s content. The work was visible only through the branch dropdown at the top left or the branches list. (00:30:36)



8. Opening a pull request (9.1 Creating a pull request)
00:33:40–00:41:16

Q: Break the “Compare & pull request” page down into its parts: the branch line at the top, the title and description, and the file list at the bottom. What should you check in each, and which check can cost points? A: The top line should name your branch and the branch it merges into, which is main in this course. That will not always be true in 524 or with forks. The title and description are a report of what changed and why, and later changes belong in an edit to that first comment. The file list shows every change relative to main. If a file you worked on is missing, you probably forgot to add, commit or push it. The file list is also your “second line of defence” against files that don’t belong, such as .ipynb_checkpoints, .DS_Store or Word backup files. Points are taken off for those even when the instructions don’t say so explicitly, which is why .gitignore still matters. (00:38:44)



9. Code review and updating a pull request (10 Code review on GitHub)
00:41:16–00:45:41

Q: Trace the second commit on pull request #1, from the local edit to GitHub. What did Daniel run, how did the pull request change, and what happens to a review comment on a line you then edit? A: On dan-b1, he added the git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all line to README.md. He then ran git add README.md, git commit -m "show you the long git log command" (commit b90e441) and git push origin dan-b1. The push moved the remote branch from 4a14a64 to b90e441. The pull request is tied to the branch, so #1 showed the second commit, sometimes only after a page refresh, without closing it or opening a new one. A comment on a line you changed may be auto-collapsed as outdated, because it no longer applies. (00:44:43)



10. AI reviewers and draft pull requests (9.2 Draft pull requests)
00:52:11–00:55:41

Q: Set a draft pull request and an open pull request side by side. How do they look, what can be done with the merge button, what does each signal to teammates and agents, and how do you move between them? A: “Convert to draft” at the top right turns an open pull request into a draft. A draft shows a grey bar instead of a green one, and its merge button is greyed out, so nobody can accidentally merge it. Daniel believes this also stops an agent from merging everything that’s green. A draft signals “you can look, but it’s not ready”. Daniel has kept drafts open for three or four months on long work. At the bottom of the page, “Ready for review” turns the draft back into an open pull request with green merge buttons. (00:54:30)



11. Merging and deleting the branch on GitHub (8.2 Useful things you can do with branches on GitHub)
00:55:41–00:59:07

Q: Separate what merging #1 and then clicking “Delete branch” removed on GitHub from what it kept. What happened to the counters, the branch list and main’s history? A: Merging closed #1, so the open pull request counter went down by one. Deleting the branch took the branch count from two to one, which keeps the dropdown from growing into a giant list. Only the branch label was removed. main’s history now holds dan-b1’s two commits plus a merge commit, “Merge pull request #1 from chendaniely/dan-b1”. You can still find the pull request’s commits and undo the feature later, so “nothing’s really lost”. (00:58:10)



12. Syncing and cleaning up locally after a merge (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:59:07–01:03:51

Q: Break down the local cleanup after #1 was merged and dan-b1 was deleted on GitHub: git pull origin main, git branch -a, git fetch --prune, git branch -d dan-b1. What does each one change or reveal on your computer? A: Local main doesn’t update itself. git pull origin main fast-forwarded it from 145ff16 to 3851b00, adding the 6 merged lines to README.md. git branch -a revealed that the computer still knew about the local dan-b1 and remotes/origin/dan-b1. git fetch --prune syncs history without changing your files (git pull is fetch plus merge). It also removed the stale reference, printing [deleted] (none) -> origin/dan-b1. Finally, git branch -d dan-b1 deleted the local label (was b90e441), while the commits stayed in the log. (01:02:22)
Q: Examine the one-character difference between git branch -d and git branch -D at the end of this cleanup. When does each one succeed, and what is at stake afterwards if you use the wrong one? A: Lowercase -d deletes a local branch only if it has been merged, as dan-b1 had been. For an unmerged experiment, it refuses, because deleting it would lose work. Capital -D force-deletes the branch regardless, so it can throw away commits you are still working on. Daniel warned that it is a very small change, and that ChatGPT may hand you the capital -D “force delete”. That is why he said to use lowercase -d for now. (01:03:21)



13. Setting up two conflicting pull requests (8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?)
01:04:00–01:10:00

Q: Deduce how dan-fetch and dan-delete were set up to conflict. Where did each start, what did each change, which step was the key to the setup, and why didn’t GitHub warn about the conflict at first? A: After git pull origin main, both branches started from the same main commit, 3851b00. dan-fetch added the fetch --prune definition (commit 157c3cd, pull request #2). Daniel then switched back to main, so that line wasn’t in the file, and dan-delete added the -d/-D definitions at the same spot in README.md (commit cb810d5, pull request #3). The key was not merging #2 right away. The log showed two lines leaving one commit. On GitHub, each pull request on its own looked mergeable into main, even though both edited the same line. (01:09:28)



14. When a merge creates the conflict: resolving on GitHub
01:10:00–01:12:44

Q: Trace how merging #2 caused the conflict on #3. Then break “fixing it” into what it means for report prose and what it means for code. A: Merging one pull request changes main. Every other pull request into main is then rechecked, so #3, which had looked green, showed a conflict. A simple conflict can be fixed in GitHub’s web editor by finding the <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> markers. For report prose, the remaining text must be English that makes sense. For code, removing the markers isn’t enough: the code must run from top to bottom again. A conflict on line 13 can affect line 50, for example through a renamed variable, and that is still your problem. (01:11:39)



15. Resolving the conflict locally with rebase (8.3.2 Using rebase)
01:12:44–01:20:42

Q: Break down Daniel’s local fix for dan-delete into its steps. What did each command do or print, and how does the trigger for the conflict differ from the one you met in 521? A: git switch main and git pull origin main brought in the merge of #2, fast-forwarding main to 3167d10. git switch dan-delete and git rebase main then replayed cb810d5 on top of that main and stopped with CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in README.md. In 521, git pull origin main triggered the conflict; here it is the replay. Daniel fixed the markers in his editor by keeping both definitions. git status then guided him: git add README.md marked the conflict resolved, and git rebase --continue finished with “Successfully rebased”. git rebase --abort was available as the escape hatch. (01:17:08)
Q: Examine why the rebased dan-delete could not be pushed normally. What changed in its history, what did the log and the push output show, and what does the forced update leave behind on GitHub? A: Before the rebase, the branch’s commit was cb810d5, whose parent was 3851b00. After the rebase, it was a new commit, 0e16503, sitting on 3167d10. The log still showed origin/dan-delete on the old cb810d5. Because the history had changed, a simple push won’t work: Daniel had to run git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete, which printed + cb810d5...0e16503 dan-delete -> dan-delete (forced update). You can’t get around force-pushing after a rebase, and GitHub records that the force push happened. As Daniel put it, “you’ve mangled history”, which matters in compliance settings. (01:19:47)

title: Git branches, pull requests, and merge conflicts: review questions, tier 4 — Analyze
text:
Date: 2026-11-17

Generated by qwen3.8-27b-sglang, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 4 of 5: Analyze. Take each one apart yourself before you read the answer; tiers 1 to 3 cover the facts, reasons and steps it relies on.

1. The first-README Git cycle in the demo repository
00:04:07–00:06:49

Q: Break the first-README.md workflow the instructor ran in the demo repository into the steps that happen only on the local computer and the one step that makes the change shared: what does each of git status, git diff, git add README.md, and git commit contribute, and why does git push origin main have to be the last one? A: git status reports that README.md is modified; git diff shows the added lines (the “we will review 521 git basics” text and the Git branches link); git add README.md stages that file; and git commit -m "intro and review" writes it locally as commit 145ff16. Those four steps all run on the instructor’s computer and only advance local main. The git push origin main that follows is the one step aimed at origin, so it must come last: it is what carries the new commit to the remote. The instructor framed the whole cycle as unchanged from DSCI 521, noting the new material only begins once a branch is introduced. (00:06:38)



2. Working on main together versus working on branches (8 Git branches)
00:06:49–00:09:43

Q: Set two ways of coordinating a group project side by side as the class discussed: everyone committing to main together versus each teammate committing to their own branch. On the points of whether you must pull before you can push, whether your unfinished work is visible to teammates, and what you are waiting on, how do the two line up? A: When everyone works on main, the DSCI 521 slide-deck pattern repeats: you often have to pull before you can push even without a real conflict, because a teammate pushed first, and your half-finished work is immediately exposed on the shared branch. On a branch you are in “your own little world” where you can push and pull against your branch until it is done, so the pull-before-push friction disappears for your own work and your unfinished piece stays out of main. In the first approach you are waiting on teammates’ pushes to land; in the second you are waiting only for the review that brings the finished branch back (for example a Friday review), so coordination happens through the pull request rather than through constant pulls. (00:09:19)



3. The local repository versus the remote origin
00:09:46–00:11:11

Q: Set the local repository and the remote origin side by side the way the instructor drew them: what kind of work lives on each, which commands move work between the two, and which of the two is the thing that actually gets graded and published? A: The local repository is where you edit, stage, and commit; origin (the cloud) is the shared copy every teammate coordinates through, reached once by git clone and then with git push sending your commits up and git pull bringing teammates’ commits down. Because a group routes all work through origin, it is the shared source of truth, and your local and remote copies can diverge until you push or pull. The instructor’s point is that the remote is what matters: if your work exists only on your local computer it “effectively doesn’t really exist” for grading or project purposes, so the remote is the state that gets graded and published. (00:11:05)



4. main, origin/main, and HEAD in the diagram (8 Git branches)
00:11:11–00:16:05

Q: Examine the Git diagram the instructor drew: what do the pointers main, HEAD, and origin/main each track, and what happens to each when you keep committing on main without pushing versus when you commit on a newly created branch? A: HEAD is the pointer to whichever branch you are on, so when it points at main your commits land on main; main then moves forward one commit at a time; and origin/main is your computer’s record of where the remote main actually is. If you only commit on local main and never push, local main pulls ahead of origin/main, so the two diverge until a push or pull closes the gap. When you create a branch and commit on it, the new branch name — not main — is the one that increments as HEAD moves onto it, leaving both main and origin/main where they were. (00:14:31)



5. Branching even when working alone (8 Git branches)
00:16:05–00:17:54

Q: Break down the reason the instructor gave for using branches even when a single person is working (as with the course textbook): what does committing on a branch contribute that committing on main does not, and what task becomes much easier afterward? A: Committing on a branch sections off a large set of changes so main stays stable and only changes after you have reviewed and tested everything, whereas committing directly on main mixes the new work into the shared state immediately. The benefit shows up in undo: if a branch was a bad idea you can abandon or delete the whole branch and return to main at your starting point, which is far easier than unwinding a tangled set of commits on main by copying and reverting bits through the history. So the branch trades a little setup for a clean, cheap way to keep main stable and to discard work that did not pan out. (00:17:22)



6. Creating a branch with git switch -c (8.1 Creating a branch using the command line)
00:17:54–00:23:46

Q: Break the branch-creation workflow the instructor ran in the demo repository into its steps and say what each contributes: git status, git pull origin main, git switch -c dan-b1, and then git add / git commit. Which step protects you from starting on an outdated local state, and which step is the one that actually moves HEAD? A: git status confirms you are on main and that the tree is clean, giving you a safe base; git pull origin main syncs your local main with whatever everyone has pushed so you do not branch from an old state (the instructor noted this saves time across multiple computers); git switch -c dan-b1 is the step that creates the new branch and moves HEAD onto it; and the later git add / git commit write your work so that dan-b1, not main, moves forward. The sync step and the switch step play different roles: one aligns your starting point with the remote, the other redirects where your future commits will land. (00:21:13)



7. Switching branches and reading the log (8.1.1 Switching to branches that already exist)
00:23:46–00:28:26

Q: Separate what git switch dan-b1, git switch main, and git switch -c <name> each do to HEAD as the class used them, and what adding --all to git log --oneline --graph --decorate changes about the branches you see in the graph. A: git switch dan-b1 and git switch main both move HEAD onto an existing branch, so switching back to main returns the working files to whatever main last stored while dan-b1 stays parked where it left off; git switch -c <name> is the different one, creating a brand-new branch and moving HEAD onto it in a single step. Because a branch you have not visited may not show up otherwise, the --all flag on the log makes every branch name appear in the graph — the instructor pointed out that if you do not see your other branch names, that is the flag you need. Together these let you move HEAD around the history and inspect where each branch actually points. (00:25:46)



8. Pushing dan-b1 to origin and viewing it on GitHub (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:28:31–00:33:40

Q: Trace what happens when dan-b1 is pushed to origin: why does a plain git push while you are on main report “Everything up-to-date,” what does git push origin dan-b1 add to your local log afterward, and how can a teammate view that branch’s code on GitHub before it is merged into main? A: A plain git push on main does nothing useful here because local main already matches origin/main, so Git just reports “Everything up-to-date”; the meaningful command is git push origin dan-b1, which changes only the last word from main to the branch name and sends that branch’s commit up. After it runs, your local log gains the origin/dan-b1 reference next to the commit, telling your computer that GitHub now holds that branch in the same place as your local copy, while main and origin/main stay where they were. On GitHub, the branch selector (the main dropdown) lets a teammate switch the view to dan-b1 and read its changes even though nothing has been merged, so the work is inspectable before review is complete. (00:31:39)



9. Opening the pull request and reviewing the changed files (9.1 Creating a pull request)
00:33:40–00:39:56

Q: Break the pre-merge review the instructor described for the dan-b1 pull request into its parts: what the “Compare and pull request” button starts, what the base-branch line at the top tells you, what the Files Changed tab is for, and where the danger of unwanted files (.ipynb_checkpoints, .DS_Store, Word backups) bites in the workflow. A: Clicking “Compare and pull request” (from the push banner, or from the branches tab if the banner has disappeared) opens the page where you set the title, description, and the branch you are merging into main. The base-branch line matters because in 522 the target is usually main, but in 524 or a fork it may not be, so you check that the words make sense before proceeding. The Files Changed tab is the review surface: you confirm every file you meant to change is present and that nothing stray is included. The danger of unwanted files bites right here — .ipynb_checkpoints, .DS_Store, or Word backup files that slipped in show up in this list, and the instructor warned that visible unwanted files in the repository can cost points, so this is the second line of defense before you click “Create pull request.” (00:39:56)



10. The pull request conversation versus the code review (10 Code review on GitHub)
00:39:56–00:45:41

Q: Set two surfaces of the open pull request side by side — the Conversation tab and the Files Changed tab: what each is for, where an inline code-review comment lands, and what happens to the pull request when the author commits and pushes again to the same branch versus when a reviewer would try to fix the code themselves. A: The Conversation tab holds the discussion and the first comment, which the instructor kept as the definitive explanation of all the changes (editing it rather than piling on new notes); the Files Changed tab is where code review actually happens, showing the diff between the original and new file, with the plus button by a line starting an inline comment. Those inline comments all get tracked back in the Conversation tab, so a review like “why switch and not checkout” lives on the diff but is logged in the conversation. The rule of thumb is that if it is your pull request, it is your job to fix it — the reviewer points out the problem, the author goes back to the branch, commits, and pushes to the same branch, and the pull request updates automatically (an edited commented line may collapse as “outdated”), rather than the reviewer rewriting the code. (00:44:51)



11. Draft pull requests, merging, and deleting the remote branch (9.2 Draft pull requests)
00:52:11–00:58:51

Q: Break the “not ready yet” workflow for a pull request into its parts: what “Convert to Draft” changes visually on the pull request, what it does to the merge button and why that matters, and what “Ready for review” reverses when the work is done. A: “Convert to Draft” turns an open pull request into a draft, which shows a gray bar instead of the green one — the visual cue that you can still look inside but the work is not ready for merge. It also grays out the merge button, so nobody can accidentally merge something that is explicitly marked not-working or not-ready, which is the protection the draft provides. Because of this, the instructor keeps draft pull requests open for days or months as a signal to the team that work is in progress, and it also stops an agent from auto-merging everything green. When the work is ready, “Ready for review” (at the bottom of the conversation) turns the draft back into an open pull request, restoring the green buttons. (00:55:03)
Q: Trace the outcome after dan-b1’s pull request #1 is merged and its remote branch is deleted on GitHub: what happens to the branch dropdown, and what remains in the commit history — including what the merge itself adds? A: After merging #1 and clicking delete branch, the branch dropdown on GitHub shrinks (from two branches to one) so the list does not grow into a long pile of finished branches, which is the cleanup the instructor recommended. But deleting the branch marker does not delete the commits: the two commits that were on dan-b1 are still in history, and the merge adds its own commit (“Merge pull request #1 from chendaniely/dan-b1”) on top of main. So the visible branch disappears while the work persists — you can still jump back to those commits or to the merge commit to inspect or undo the feature. (00:58:27)



12. Local cleanup after a merge (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:58:53–01:03:51

Q: Break the local cleanup sequence the instructor ran after dan-b1 was merged into its steps and say what each contributes: git switch main plus git pull origin main, git branch -a, git fetch --prune, and git branch -d dan-b1. Which step is where local main finally catches up, which step removes the now-deleted origin/dan-b1 reference, and where does the lowercase -d versus capital -D distinction bite? A: Switching to main and running git pull origin main is where local main catches up to the merged work, because local main does not update by itself after a GitHub merge. git branch -a lists local and remote-tracking branches (the star marks the current one) so you can see what is still around; git fetch --prune talks to origin and prunes the local reference to any branch deleted on GitHub, which is why origin/dan-b1 disappears from the log afterward. git branch -d dan-b1 then deletes the merged local branch, and the lowercase -d is the safety: it only deletes a branch that has been merged, protecting you from throwing away unmerged work. The warning is that a capital -D force-deletes even unmerged work, and copied-and-pasted AI advice might hand you -D when you meant the safe -d, so the distinction bites exactly at this final cleanup step where unmerged commits could be lost. (01:03:21)



13. How the two-branch merge conflict arises (8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?)
01:03:51–01:10:51

Q: Trace how a merge conflict arises in the two-branch demo: both dan-fetch and dan-delete start from the same main, so why does neither pull request show a conflict before either is merged, and what specifically happens to the second pull request after the first is merged into main? A: Because both dan-fetch and dan-delete branch from the same main and edit the same region of README.md, looking at the two pull requests side by side does not reveal a conflict — each just asks to merge into main and each looks green on its own. The conflict is latent until main itself moves: when the first pull request is merged, main advances, and GitHub rechecks every open pull request that targets main to see whether it can still be merged. The second pull request, which was based on the old main, now fails that recheck and surfaces as a conflict, so the outcome (a conflicted PR) is caused by the first merge changing the base branch rather than by anything visible in the second PR before that merge. (01:10:31)



14. Resolving the conflict with git rebase main and git push --force-with-lease (8.3.2 Using rebase)
01:10:51–01:20:42

Q: Break the local conflict-resolution workflow the instructor ran for dan-delete into its steps and say what each contributes: git switch main plus git pull origin main, git switch dan-delete, git rebase main, editing the file plus git add README.md plus git rebase --continue, and git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete. Why must main be synced before the rebase, and why is a force-with-lease push required instead of a plain push afterward? A: Syncing main first (git switch main then git pull origin main) is required because the rebase replays your branch’s commit on top of the current main; if local main still lacked the already-merged pull request, you would rebase onto the wrong base. git switch dan-delete moves HEAD back to the conflicting branch, and git rebase main replays that branch’s commit onto the updated main, which is exactly where the conflict in README.md surfaces and you resolve it by editing, then git add README.md and git rebase --continue to finish. The rebase rewrites the commit history of dan-delete (its base moves from the old main to the new one), so a plain git push origin dan-delete no longer works and git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete is what rewrites the remote branch to match, after which the pull request can be merged. The instructor’s caution is that fixing the visible conflict markers is not the whole job — the code or report must work from top to bottom afterward — and the force push is mandatory because the pushed history changed. (01:20:21)
Q: Distinguish resolving the dan-delete conflict in GitHub’s web editor from resolving it locally with git rebase main: what each approach requires, which one the instructor chose to show and why, and what extra local step the rebase path adds at the very end. A: The web-editor path is for simpler conflicts: you open the conflict in GitHub’s editor, fix the markers, and commit, keeping everything on the remote side. The local path is more involved but more general: you sync main, rebase the branch onto it, resolve the file, git add and git rebase --continue, and then you must also handle the remote. The instructor chose to show the local version “for complexity’s sake,” because the command-line process is the more general skill you will need when conflicts are not simple. The extra local step at the end is the git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete, which the web path does not require, because rebasing rewrote the already-pushed branch’s history. (01:12:33)

text:

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 5 of 5: Evaluate. Decide and justify your verdict before you read the answer; the criteria are the ones given in class.

1. Branching strategy and keeping main stable (8 Git branches)
00:04:04–00:09:43

Q: A teammate proposes committing their exploratory data analysis plots and messy intermediate datasets directly to main while still figuring out the data cleaning steps, arguing it’s just a quick addition to share their progress. Would you approve this plan for the group project, and what criterion decides the verdict? A: Verdict: No. Criterion: The main branch should be kept stable with working, finished code or cleaned foundational data, while exploratory and testing work belongs on separate branches to prevent breaking the project for other collaborators. (00:15:24)



2. Local branch management (8 Git branches)
00:09:43–00:25:12

Q: You are about to start a new feature for your group project. A classmate suggests skipping the synchronization step to save time and using git checkout -b because it’s a familiar command they saw in an older tutorial. Why is this plan risky for the group project, and what are the better alternatives the class recommended? A: Verdict: This plan is risky. Criterion: You should always run git pull origin main before branching to ensure you are building on the latest coordinated code. Additionally, git switch -c is preferred over git checkout because checkout also handles file restoration, which increases the risk of accidentally overwriting or losing work. (00:18:39, 00:27:09)
Q: In your group’s repository, you plan to create a branch to fix a typo in the README. Based on the class’s convention for group work, how should you name this branch to ensure your teammates know who to contact about it? A: Verdict: Name the branch with your username as a prefix (e.g., dan-fix-typos). Criterion: Prefixing branch names with a username in group projects lets teammates immediately identify the responsible person if issues arise or if they want to ask questions about that specific line of development. (00:20:31)



3. Draft Pull Requests and code review standards (9 Pull requests, 10 Code review on GitHub)
00:25:12–00:46:00

Q: You have made significant progress on a feature and want your teammates to see your work early, but you know it is not yet finished and might break the build. Would you create a standard open Pull Request or a Draft Pull Request, and what is the functional reason for this choice? A: Verdict: Create a Draft Pull Request. Criterion: A draft PR signals to the team that the code is still a work-in-progress and, functionally, it disables the merge button to prevent anyone from accidentally merging unready code. (00:53:59)
Q: While reviewing a teammate’s Pull Request, you notice their branch includes a .DS_Store file and a few temporary Jupyter checkpoint folders. Should you approve the request as-is, and what is your responsibility in the review process? A: Verdict: Do not approve it yet. Criterion: Reviewers must check for stray temporary or hidden files that should not be in the repository and ensure the author uses their .gitignore properly, as the reviewer’s job is to flag issues and ask for rewrites, not fix the code for the author. (00:39:16, 00:42:17)



4. Branch cleanup and safe deletion (8 Git branches)
00:52:17–01:03:51

Q: After merging your feature branch into main on GitHub, your local repository still lists the remote branch. You want to clean up your workspace. Is it safe to run git branch -D to delete your local branch, and what is a safer alternative the class demonstrated? A: Verdict: It is not safe if you want to avoid accidental data loss. Criterion: Use the lowercase d flag (git branch -d), which safely deletes only merged branches and prevents you from permanently losing work if you mistakenly target an unmerged branch. (01:02:46)
Q: A teammate asks why their local Git history still shows tracking references for branches that have already been merged and deleted on GitHub. Which single command would you recommend they run to clean up these stale local references before deleting the local branches themselves? A: Verdict: Run git fetch --prune. Criterion: This command synchronizes the local repository with the remote and automatically removes local tracking references for branches that no longer exist on the remote, keeping the workspace clean without altering local files. (01:01:30)



5. Resolving merge conflicts via rebase (8 Git branches)
01:03:51–01:21:43

Q: You encountered a merge conflict after rebasing your branch onto an updated main. You resolved the conflict markers for the specific line in question and ran git rebase --continue. Is your work considered complete for the Pull Request, and what criterion from the class ensures your code remains functional? A: Verdict: No, your work is not necessarily complete. Criterion: Fixing a conflict marker only resolves the immediate syntax clash; you must verify that the entire codebase still runs correctly, as dependencies, variable names, or logic may have shifted elsewhere during the merge. (01:11:21)
Q: After successfully rebasing your branch to resolve conflicts locally, you attempt to push the changes to the remote repository but receive an error rejecting the push. Why is a standard push failing in this situation, and what command must you use instead? A: Verdict: A standard push fails because rebasing rewrites the local commit history, which conflicts with the remote history. Criterion: You must force-push using git push --force-with-lease to safely update the remote branch with your rewritten history without overwriting concurrent work added by others. (01:19:47)

section: 1. Project advice: keep the analysis simple
text:
1. Project advice: keep the analysis simple

The analysis is not the point of the course: the course is about workflows, not model fitting. You will see almost no machine learning code in lectures.
Still required: code that downloads the data, any cleaning, EDA, modelling code, figures and tables. Keep each part very simple.
Correctness still matters: the score of the model does not matter (60% accuracy is fine), but the methods must be correct. For example, do not fit logistic regression to predict a numeric outcome.
Warning: do not use this project as your portfolio piece. Choosing something complicated such as a neural net will give you “a very bad time in about two weeks”. Do a portfolio project in parallel if you want one.
Same project throughout: you build on the same project for three or four weeks. This week is getting everything on Git; next week is containers.
Language choice: R projects are allowed, but class demos will be in Python. Package choices such as Altair, Plotly or Matplotlib may differ between groups, so each project must define its own minimal package list.

title: Introduction to Containers with Docker (plus Issues and Pull Request Workflow Review)
text:
2. Branch workflow habits

Check your branch before git add, and definitely before git commit: branch-based work is assumed from now on. Run git status and read the “On branch …” line.
Pull main before starting work: with several people working on several branches, this avoids building on out-of-date code.
Edited files while on main? If you have not committed yet, git switch -c <branch> takes your uncommitted changes onto the new branch. If you already committed on main, the textbook has a cheat sheet of commands to move the commits.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Introduction to Containers with Docker (plus Issues and Pull Request Workflow Review)
text:
3. GitHub issues as project management

Issues track what is happening in a project: you can use them for:

assigning responsibility (who is doing what);
meeting notes, from which separate action-item issues are created;
parking ideas and stretch goals (for example, “it would be nice to try a neural net”);
asking a coding agent to file an issue for a passing thought, which the instructor does himself.

Shared numbering: issues and pull requests use one counter. In the demo, issues #1 and #2 were followed by pull request #3.
#N references are two-way: writing “meeting from #1” in issue #2 also shows a link back on #1. This automatic cross-linking is a GitHub feature, not a Git one, and is a big reason GitHub became popular.
Assignees and reviewers: you usually assign yourself to your own pull request. You can request a teammate (or Copilot, as in the demo) as a reviewer. Some projects block merging until someone has reviewed the work.
Keep the first comment up to date: readers look at the first comment to learn why an issue or pull request exists, not at the whole conversation. Edit it when decisions change. Project owners can edit other people’s comments.
Task lists: Markdown checkboxes (- [ ], - [x]) in issues and pull requests show what is still unfinished. A draft pull request is the other way to signal “not done yet”.
For this course: you must create at least three issues. One pull request may handle all three. You are not graded on closing every issue, so feel free to record longer-term ideas as issues.
Demo artefacts: Issue #1, Issue #2, Pull request #3.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Introduction to Containers with Docker (plus Issues and Pull Request Workflow Review)
text:
4. Closing keywords in pull requests

fixes #N / closes #N: when a pull request containing these is merged, GitHub closes the referenced issues automatically.

The demo PR description was:
this is the fix for #2

- [x] item 1
- [ ] item 2

closes #1 fixes #2
In class the instructor briefly wondered whether closes worked, saying “fixes is the one I almost always use”. The demo repository shows both issue #1 and issue #2 were closed by PR #3, so both keywords work.

Write the message strategically: one pull request can close several issues, so you don’t have to close each one by hand. The keywords also work in commit messages, but they are harder to see there.
The instructor uses this for the textbook: he files issues, then lists fixes #… in the pull request, so his open-issues tab doubles as a to-do list.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Introduction to Containers with Docker (plus Issues and Pull Request Workflow Review)
text:
5. Cleaning up after a merge

Delete the remote branch on GitHub: use the “Delete branch” button on the merged pull request, or the trash-can icon on the repository’s Branches page.
Deleting branches is optional in this course: some people keep branches as a record. Teams and companies differ in how they use Git, so this is one workflow, not the only one.
git fetch --prune: removes local references to remote branches that no longer exist (here, origin/today).
git branch -d today: deletes the local branch label.
History is kept: the merge commit and the branch’s commit still show in git log --oneline --graph --all. Only the shortcut name disappears, so you would now need the hash (3c6d82a) instead of git switch today. Clean up when too many branch labels make the graph hard to read.

title: Introduction to Containers with Docker (plus Issues and Pull Request Workflow Review)
section: 6. Why containers? The problem a stable compute environment solves
text:
6. Why containers? The problem a stable compute environment solves
(Introduction to containerization)

Projects last a long time and involve other people: you need a stable environment for yourself over days, months or years, and one that also works for teammates.
Teammates’ machines differ: Mac vs Windows, and ARM vs Intel chips even among Windows machines. “It works on my machine” is not good enough when a teammate cannot run your code.
What virtual environments already cover: uv (Python) and renv (R), from 521, pin package versions through lock files.
What they don’t cover: the language version itself, and system tools.

Example: a container with a 2019 version of Git would not have git switch.
Lock files also assume the other person has uv installed. Installing it might disturb their setup.

A container is a virtual computer you build from scratch and hand to others: everyone runs code on “the same computer” even on different hardware.
Pharmaceutical example: clinical trial analyses can run for years, while R releases roughly every six months. Regulators reviewing a drug submission want the code and the full compute environment, so you give them the container that ran the analysis.
Other uses:

prototyping locally, then running the identical environment on a bigger machine that has the data;
giving someone a sandbox on a shared or remote machine without letting them install software directly on it.

Containers reset: if you break one, restart it and you get a fresh one. This makes them a safe place to learn Linux and the command line.
Cost: there is a performance hit from the extra layer, but this is often worth it.
Other container tools exist: LXC, LXD, Podman. Cloud compute mostly runs on containers, so you rarely get bare access to a machine.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Introduction to Containers with Docker (plus Issues and Pull Request Workflow Review)
text:
7. Containers vs virtual machines

Virtual machine: a full operating system, typically with the full graphical interface. A Windows VM is roughly a 50–80 GB install. The instructor still uses VMs, for example to test the MDS install instructions as if on Windows.
Container: only the minimum set of things you install, usually with no GUI. That is one reason 521 pushed typing commands in the terminal. Many containers are under 1–2 GB yet run a full computational stack.
Result: containers use less disk, memory and compute than VMs.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Introduction to Containers with Docker (plus Issues and Pull Request Workflow Review)
section: 8. Pulling and running other people’s images
text:
8. Pulling and running other people’s images
(Using and running containers)

Docker Desktop must be running before any docker command (on Mac and Windows). If you get a “can’t find Docker” error, Docker is not installed.
docker pull <image>: downloads an image, like git pull pulls code. Names look like a GitHub user and repository: rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 is the rocker organisation’s R-only image, with the tag 4.3.2 meaning R 4.3.2. If the image is already up to date, Docker says so and shows its digest (hash).
docker run: starts (turns on) a machine from an image. It also downloads the image first if you don’t have it.
--rm: a double-dash, multi-letter flag. It deletes the container when it stops; otherwise you have to delete it by hand.
-it: two single-letter flags chained together, the same way ls -alh chains -a, -l and -h.

-i: interactive, so what you type reaches the container.
-t: gives you a terminal (TTY) to interact with.

Demo result: rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 opened R 4.3.2, while R --version on the host showed R 4.6.2. Two versions of R ran side by side on one laptop.
Each container is a separate machine: library(tidyverse) failed in the container (“there is no package called ‘tidyverse’”) but worked on the host.
Know where you are typing: the prompt is often your only cue to whether you are on your laptop, in a container, or on a remote machine. Inside a container the prompt looks like root@<id>:/#. The instructor also showed a terminal on a machine at home, recognisable only by its hostname. Commands like whoami help confirm where you are.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Introduction to Containers with Docker (plus Issues and Pull Request Workflow Review)
section: 9. Web applications in containers: ports and environment variables
text:
9. Web applications in containers: ports and environment variables

Browser-based apps: many tools (Electron apps, JupyterLab, VS Code, GitHub Codespaces) run as browser applications. That is why they can run in a container or on a remote machine with the same interface. It is also why JupyterLab opens at a localhost address.
-p <host port>:<container port>: maps a port inside the container to a port on your computer.

RStudio Server listens on 8787, so -p 8787:8787, then open localhost:8787.
JupyterLab uses 8888.
These numbers are arbitrary choices by each tool.
To run two copies of the same app, map the container’s 8787 to a different free port on your computer.

RStudio login: the username is rstudio. Without a password set, the container prints a random one at startup, which is hard to remember.
-e VAR=value: passes an environment variable into the container, for example -e PASSWORD="apassword". Which variables an image understands depends on how its authors built it, so check its documentation.
Is a visible password a problem here? The port is only reachable from the instructor’s own machine, so a simple demo password is acceptable in this context.
Warning: every running container uses RAM. Use --rm so containers are removed when they stop. Otherwise you will wonder why your computer is slow and find you have “five computers” running.
Looking ahead: in DSCI 532 you can put a dashboard in a container. Users then only need Docker and one docker run command, with no renv or uv setup of their own.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Introduction to Containers with Docker (plus Issues and Pull Request Workflow Review)
section: 10. Building your own image with a Dockerfile
text:
10. Building your own image with a Dockerfile
(Customizing and building containers)

Containers don’t keep changes: the instructor installed cowsay inside a running rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 container. After exiting and starting a new container, library(cowsay) failed again. Every new container starts fresh from its image.

Good: this makes containers a safe place for dangerous experiments, including the destructive “delete the computer” command warned about in 521.
Bad: users should not have to follow README install steps every time. A tidyverse install on Linux can take about 15 minutes for a 30-second analysis.

Recommended workflow:

Start the base image with bash instead of its default program.
Try the install commands interactively until they work.
Write the working commands into the Dockerfile.

Installing from the terminal: Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')" runs an R expression from bash. Watch the quotes: double quotes outside, single quotes inside.
Dockerfile: a file with exactly that name, capital D and no extension, containing the build instructions for the machine. Published images such as RStudio have their own Dockerfile.
FROM: the starting-point machine. It is the first line, apart from optional metadata.

Starting from rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 skips steps such as installing compilers, which the image authors have already done.
Smaller, bare-bones Linux bases exist, but then you install everything yourself.

RUN: a shell command executed while the image is being built. Most Dockerfiles are mostly RUN and COPY lines, and sometimes port lines (for example, opening 8787).

Knowing the bash command for each install step is essential.
For Python, you would COPY in your lock files and run uv sync.

CMD: the default command when the container starts, written as a list (["Rscript", "-e", "..."]). Adding a command after the image name in docker run (for example bash) overrides it.
ENTRYPOINT: also exists, but the instructor called it pretty rare.
The class Dockerfile (in the demo repo):
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2

RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')"

CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "cowsay::say('Hello from my first image!')"]
docker build --tag hello-cowsay .: --tag names the image. The . is the current directory, where docker build looks for a file named Dockerfile.

This is “probably the first time a dot is actually something you have to type”.
Course instructions, including milestone 1, assume you run every command from the repository root, so commands can be copied and pasted without changing directories.

docker images: lists the images on your computer. The new hello-cowsay image appeared at 1.45 GB.
Pin versions: pin the language and tool versions (R, Python, Quarto) in the Dockerfile so nothing updates until you change that line.

Warning: in another class the instructor restarted a container with no pinned versions. Something had updated the day before and nothing worked. Fixing an unexpected update can take longer than the real work.

Next week: install your language, Quarto (copy-paste install steps will be provided) and your packages in a container, so the analysis runs both locally and in the container.

text:
What went wrong live

Edited README.md while still on main: git status reported On branch main with README.md modified, but the exercise asked for a branch. Nothing had been committed yet, so git switch -c today moved the uncommitted change onto the new branch. If you have already committed on main, use the textbook’s cheat sheet instead.
Stopping the RStudio container took several Ctrl+C presses: the first ^C started the container’s shutdown scripts. It then sat at [s6-finish] waiting for services. until two more presses forced it: got 3 SIGTERM/SIGINTs, forcefully exiting. Because of --rm, the container was removed either way.
Installed packages vanished between runs: cowsay installed in one rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 container was missing (there is no package called ‘cowsay’) in the next one, twice. This was the intended lesson. The fix was to put the Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')" line in a Dockerfile as a RUN step and build an image.

title: Git Pull Request Review and Intro to Docker Containers
text:
Date Time: 2026-11-19
Instructor: Daniel Chen
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Git Pull Request Review and Intro to Docker Containers
section: 1. Branch, issue, and pull-request workflow (Git review)
text:
1. Branch, issue, and pull-request workflow (Git review)

Before you commit, check your branch: run git status right before git add and definitely before git commit, and habitually git pull origin main first so you’re not branching from an out-of-date main. If you accidentally commit on main, the textbook has a set of recovery commands.
git switch -c <name>: create and switch to a new branch; uncommitted working-tree changes come along with you (the demo edited README.md on main, then created today before committing).
Pushing offers the PR: git push origin today prints a GitHub URL (.../pull/new/today) that opens the pull-request form.
Issues and pull requests share one numbering sequence: in the demo repo, issues #1 and #2 were followed by PR #3. You can reference any item by number (e.g. “meeting from #1”) and the reference is two-way — both items link to each other.
closes / fixes keywords: a sentence in the PR description that ends with closes #1 fixes #2 makes GitHub auto-close those issues when the PR is merged. This is a GitHub service feature, not a Git feature. One PR may deal with several issues (the lab task required three issues); referencing the same issue multiple times is fine.
Descriptions are editable and Markdown: keep the first comment of an issue or PR as the source of truth and edit it as decisions evolve; use checkboxes (- [ ] item 2) to track to-dos; assignees claim responsibility (“this is my responsibility, I’m claiming it”) while reviewers are requested separately — the instructor assigned Copilot as a reviewer.
Issues as meeting notes: record meeting notes on the issue board, then spawn action items out as separate issues. The instructor also files issues from an AI agent mid-work (“I just had this idea, can you file the issue?”) instead of tabbing away to a browser.
Cleanup after merging: delete the remote branch on GitHub (the “delete branch” button in the PR, or the trash can in the branches view), then git fetch --prune to drop the origin/today tracking ref and git branch -d today (lowercase -d) to drop the local ref. The merge commit remains visible in git log --oneline --graph --all. Deletion is not required in this class — keeping branches as a record is fine — and different teams use different Git conventions, so this is one valid workflow, not the only one.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Git Pull Request Review and Intro to Docker Containers
text:
2. Project scoping (the MDS group project)

Do not make your analysis difficult: this was the biggest tip of the session. If the model is a straight line, fit the straight line; do not say “it’s my time to shine” and build a neural net — “you’re going to have a very bad time in about two weeks.” This is not a model-fitting course; you will almost never see machine-learning code in the lectures.
Accuracy is not graded; correctness is: a 60%-accurate model is acceptable, but the technique must be right — “you shouldn’t be fitting logistic regression when you’re trying to predict a numeric outcome. That’s just wrong.”
Don’t turn it into a portfolio project: if you want a showcase project, do it in parallel, not inside this assignment.
Scope still includes: code that downloads the data, some cleaning, some EDA, modeling code, and figures/tables — just keep each part very simple. R or Python is fine, and per-project package choices (Altair, Plotly, Matplotlib, …) are expected; the instructor no longer provides one package list.
Milestone sequence: the same project is built on for three or four weeks. This week: getting everything on Git. Next week: containers. Follow the steps in the assignment in the student repository.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Git Pull Request Review and Intro to Docker Containers
text:
3. Why containers exist

The goal of the class: create a compute environment you can share with other people and run all of your code through — because “this works on my machine” doesn’t work when a teammate can’t run your code.
Lock files vs. containers: uv and renv lock files track package versions; containers go one level deeper and pin the tools themselves — the version of R, even the version of Git (joke: ship a 2019-era Git in the container and teammates can’t run git switch).
Real-world example: multi-year clinical-trial research needs a fixed R version even though R ships updates every six months; drug regulators ask for your code and your compute environment so they can reproduce the analysis. You hand over the container that ran the analysis, not your MacBook.
Hardware diversity: Mac vs Windows, ARM vs Intel chips — install paths differ, so a shared container is the same on all of them.
Containers vs. virtual machines: a VM installs a full OS (a Windows install is a 50–80 GB affair; the VM itself can take ~80 GB) with a GUI. A container is a stripped-down OS user-space with only what you install — the rocker images here are under 1–2 GB — so containers are lighter on disk, memory, and compute. They are less isolated than VMs, and there is a performance hit from the extra layer that there’s no way around.
Ephemeral by design: a running container has no save state; turn it off and it resets to the image. That’s a feature for experimenting: “if you blow it up, then you just restart it” — containers are a safe place to practice destructive commands and OS mucking-around. Remote machines also hand you containers as sandboxes when you can’t (or aren’t trusted to) install software directly.
Ecosystem: Docker is the tool in this course; LXC, LXD, podman, and cloud providers’ own options also exist. Cloud compute generally runs on containers — you get a container on a server, not bare access to a machine.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Git Pull Request Review and Intro to Docker Containers
text:
4. Pulling and running images

Docker Desktop must be open on macOS/Windows before any Docker command; a “can’t find Docker” error means the app isn’t running.
docker pull <registry>/<user>/<image>:<tag>: downloads an image from a registry without running it (Docker Hub by default; quay.io when the name says so). The rocker organization publishes images that only have R installed (rocker/r-ver), plus R+RStudio (rocker/rstudio).
The three class images (pulled from the commands posted in Slack; ~13 GB of disk space, ~3 GB to download in total): rocker/r-ver:4.3.2, rocker/rstudio:4.4.2, and quay.io/jupyter/datascience-notebook:2025-03-14 (the largest, ~9 GB). Pulling them before class avoids waiting ~20 minutes mid-lecture; docker run will also pull a missing image on the fly.
docker run --rm -it <image>: --rm deletes the container when it stops, so stopped containers don’t pile up and eat RAM; -i (--interactive) passes your typing in, and -t (TTY) gives you a terminal to interact with — “you don’t have to know what that is, but you’ll see it everywhere.”
The image’s default command runs automatically: rocker/r-ver’s Dockerfile sets CMD ["R"], so the run command dropped straight into an R session — R 4.3.2 (2023-10-31) “Eye Holes” on Linux, versus the host’s R 4.6.2, proven by running R --version first.
Proof it’s a different machine: library(tidyverse) failed inside the fresh container with Error in library(tidyverse) : there is no package called 'tidyverse' while the same command works on the host. Pay attention to where you’re typing — the prompt changes when you’re inside a container or on a remote machine (the instructor’s “machine in the closet” example), and whoami-style commands from DSCI 521 help confirm which machine you’re on. q() quits R and exits the container.

title: Git Pull Request Review and Intro to Docker Containers
section: 5. Web apps in containers: ports and environment variables
text:
5. Web apps in containers: ports and environment variables

Browser-first applications: RStudio Server, JupyterLab, and VS Code are built as web apps so the same interface can run on a remote machine with more cores and memory — JupyterLab lives at localhost:8888 for the same reason, and GitHub’s Codespaces button is VS Code in a browser. Electron apps follow the same “the browser is the application” pattern.
Port mapping with -p: -p <host_port>:<container_port> forwards a port on your computer to the app’s port inside the container. RStudio listens on 8787 inside the image, so docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 puts it at http://localhost:8787. To run a second RStudio at the same time, map a different host port to the same container port. These port numbers are arbitrary conventions (Jupyter’s is 8888); the container-side port is documented per image.
Authentication: the first run prints a random password to the terminal (The password is set to ...). Set your own with an environment variable: -e PASSWORD="apassword" (multiple -e flags allowed). Sign in at http://localhost:8787 with username rstudio.
Stopping it: the web app runs in the foreground, so Ctrl+C in that terminal stops the container.
Security note confirmed in class: even with the port number known, the app is only reachable from the host machine — without access to the physical machine, port 8787 is not available to you.
DSCI 532 preview: a dashboard can be shipped as a container; the end user only needs Docker, not your whole install process.

section: 6. Building your own image: the Dockerfile
text:
6. Building your own image: the Dockerfile

The problem it solves: packages installed in a running container disappear when it restarts (demonstrated live with cowsay), and teammates shouldn’t have to follow your README’s install steps every time — tidyverse on a bare Linux machine can be a 15-minute install for a 30-second script.
Rscript -e "<R expression>": runs R non-interactively from the shell — Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')" — which is the form a RUN line needs. Mind the nested quotes: double on the outside, single on the inside.
Dockerfile (capital D, no extension, lives in the project root): the plain-text build recipe, version-controlled in Git alongside your analysis code.

FROM <base>: the starting machine. rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 already has R 4.6.2 plus the system packages R needs; you could start from a bare-minimum Linux image and install everything by hand.
RUN <bash command>: shell commands executed during the build.
CMD [...]: the default command a container runs when it starts (JSON-list form); it replaces the base image’s own CMD ["R"]. ENTRYPOINT exists but is “pretty rare”.
The file the class wrote, committed to main in the demo repository’s Dockerfile:
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2

RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')"

CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "cowsay::say('Hello from my first image!')"]

Recommended workflow: try the install commands interactively first — docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash gives you the container’s shell instead of R (a command after the image name replaces the default CMD) — verify they work, then write them into the Dockerfile; add every couple of lines and rebuild while you go.
docker build --tag hello-cowsay .: --tag names the image (no version given → latest); . means “the Dockerfile in the current directory” — the first time a dot is something you actually type. Docker by default looks for a file named exactly Dockerfile; you can also point it at a full path to another file. Assume all commands run from the project root — that’s what milestone-one instructions will say. The build prints each step, and unchanged steps show as CACHED (the class’s build reused the already-run install layer).
docker images: lists local images with their disk usage — hello-cowsay:latest came out at 1.45 GB on disk.
Running the result: docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay executed the CMD — the ASCII-art “Hello from my first image!” — while docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay bash opened a shell where library(cowsay) now works because the install is baked into the image.
Pin your versions (flagged as a real pain point): pin the base-image tag and any tool versions — Quarto is at 1.11; the instructor suggested building on 1.10 if you want to stay there. Anecdote: a container restarted without hard version pins picked up an upstream update the day before and “nothing worked” — hours spent fixing the update instead of doing the work.
Coming up: next week’s milestone builds an image that installs R or Python, Quarto, and your packages (materials sketch COPY-ing lock files plus uv sync / renv restore in the image); Docker Compose (chapter 33) is next class, not covered today.

title: Course materials: 2026-11-19 lecture
text:
27.2 What is a container?
Containers are another way to generate (and share!) isolated computational environments. They differ from virtual environments (which we discussed previously) in that they are even more isolated from the computer’s operating system, and they can be used to share many other types of software, applications, and operating system dependencies.
Before we can fully define containers, however, we need to define virtualization. Virtualization is a process that allows us to divide the elements of a single computer into several virtual elements. These elements can include computer hardware platforms, storage devices, computer network resources, and even operating system user spaces (e.g., graphical tools, utilities, and programming languages).
Containers virtualize operating system user spaces so that they can isolate the processes they contain, as well as control the processes’ access to computer resources (e.g., CPUs, memory, and disk space). What this means in practice is that an operating system user space can be carved up into multiple containers running the same or different processes in isolation. Below we show the schematic of a container whose virtual user space contains the:

R programming language, the Bioconductor package manager, and two Bioconductor packages
Galaxy workflow software and two toolboxes that can be used with it
Python programming language, IPython interpreter, and Jupyter notebook package


Schematic of a container for genomics research. Source: https://doi.org/10.1186/s13742-016-0135-4
Exercise
Running a simple container
To further illustrate what a container looks like, and feels like, we can use Docker (containerization software) to run one and explore. First we will run a Linux (Debian-flavored) container that has R installed. To run this, type:
Terminal
docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2
Here is what each part of the command does:

docker run starts a new container from an image. If the image is not on your computer yet, Docker first downloads (pulls) it from a container registry.
--rm deletes the container when it stops, so that stopped containers do not pile up on your computer.
-it is two flags written together. -i (--interactive) keeps the container’s input open, so that what you type reaches R. -t (--tty) connects R to a terminal, so that R runs as an interactive session. Without -t, R stops with Fatal error: you must specify '--save', '--no-save' or '--vanilla'.
rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 is the image to run, rocker/r-ver from Docker Hub with the tag 4.3.2, which picks R 4.3.2.

More information
R starts because the image’s Dockerfile sets CMD ["R"], the command a container runs when it starts. Building images explains CMD.
Running containers covers these flags in more detail, and Docker’s docker run reference lists them all.
When you successfully launch the container, R should have started. Check the version of R - is it the same as your computer’s version of R? Use getwd() and list.files() to explore the container’s filesystem from R. Does this look like your computer’s filesystem or something else?
Type q() to quit R and exit the container.
Compare this version of R that is running in the container to the version of R you have on your computer.
Exercise
Running a container with RStudio as a web app
Next, try to use Docker to run a container that has the RStudio Server web application installed:
Terminal
docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 -e PASSWORD="apassword" rocker/rstudio:4.4.2
Then open a web browser on your computer and type: http://localhost:8787
If it worked, then you should be at an RStudio Sign In page. To sign in, use the following credentials:

username: rstudio
password: apassword

The RStudio Server web app being run by the container should look something like this:

Type Ctrl + C in the terminal where you launched the container to quit R and RStudio and exit the container.
We can pass in multiple environment variables by using multiple -e flags. For example, we can set the password for the rstudio user with the PASSWORD environment variable, but we can also disable the login screen with the DISABLE_AUTH=true variable.
Terminal
docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 -e PASSWORD="apassword" -e DISABLE_AUTH=true rocker/rstudio:4.4.2
Each container will have its own set of environment variables to control its behavior. For the rocker/rstudio project, you can find the environment variable documentation here: https://rocker-project.org/images/versioned/rstudio.html#environment-variables.
Exercise
Running a container with Jupyter as a web app
Next, try to use Docker to run a container that has the Jupyter web application installed:
Terminal
docker run --rm -p 8888:8888 quay.io/jupyter/datascience-notebook:2025-03-14
In the terminal, look for a URL that starts with http://127.0.0.1:8888/lab?token= (for an example, see the highlighted text in the terminal below). Copy and paste that URL into your browser.
Important
Do not forget to copy the token= portion of the URL. If you only go to localhost:8888 or http://127.0.0.1:8888, it will ask you for the password/token.

The Jupyter web application being run by the container should look something like this:

Type Ctrl + c in the terminal where you launched the container to quit Jupyter and exit the container.

title: Course materials: 2026-11-19 lecture
text:
27.3 Contrasting containers with virtual machines
Virtual machines are another technology that can be used to generate (and share) isolated computational environments. Virtual machines emulate the functionality of an entire computer on another physical computer. With virtual machines, the virtualization occurs at the layer of software that sits between the computer’s hardware and the operating system(s). This software is called a hypervisor. For example, on a Mac laptop, you could install a program called Oracle VirtualBox to run a virtual machine whose operating system was Windows 8.1, as the screenshot below shows:

A screenshot of a macOS computer running a Windows virtual machine. Source: https://www.virtualbox.org/wiki/Screenshots
Below, we share an illustration that compares where virtualization happens in containers compared to virtual machines. This difference leads to containers being more lightweight and portable compared to virtual machines, and also less isolated.

Source: https://www.docker.com/resources/what-container
Key take-home: Containerization software shares the host’s operating system, whereas virtual machines have a completely separate, additional operating system. This can make containers lighter (smaller in terms of size) and more resource- and time-efficient than using a virtual machine.

section: 27.5 Virtualization strategy advantages and disadvantages for reproducibility
text:
27.5 Virtualization strategy advantages and disadvantages for reproducibility
Let’s collaboratively generate a list of advantages and disadvantages of each virtualization strategy in the context of reproducibility:

27.5.1 Virtual environment
A virtual environment, such as a uv or renv project, isolates the packages for one programming language.

Advantages

Extremely small size
Porous (less isolated) - makes it easy to pair the virtualized computational environment with files on your computer
Specify these with a single text file



Disadvantages

Not always possible to capture and share operating system dependencies, and other software your analysis depends upon
Computational environment is not fully isolated, and so missed dependencies can go unnoticed




27.5.2 Containers
A container isolates an operating system user space, with its programming languages, packages and other software.

Advantages

Somewhat lightweight in size (manageable for easy sharing - there are tools and software to facilitate this)
Possible to capture and share operating system dependencies, and other software your analysis depends upon
Computational environment is fully isolated, and errors will occur if dependencies are missing
Specify these with a single text file
Can share volumes and ports (advantage compared to virtual machines)



Disadvantages

Possible security issues - running software on your computer that you may allow to be less isolated (i.e., mount volumes, expose ports)
Takes some effort to share volumes and ports (disadvantage compared to virtual environments)




27.5.3 Virtual machine
A virtual machine isolates a whole computer, including its operating system.

Advantages

High security, because these are much more isolated (filesystem, ports, etc.)
Can share an entirely different operating system (might not be so useful in the context of reproducibility however…)



Disadvantages

Very big in size, which can make it prohibitive to share them
Takes great effort to share volumes and ports - which makes it hard to give access to data on your computer

title: Course materials: 2026-11-19 lecture
text:
27.6 Container usage workflow
Below is a schematic of a typical container usage workflow from a blog post by Arnaud Mazin. The source code for container images is stored in a file called a Dockerfile. Like a pyproject.toml or an renv.lock file, you would typically version control this with Git and store this in your GitHub repository with your analysis code. From the source Dockerfile we can build a Docker container image. This image is a binary file, from which we can run one, or more, container instances. Container instances are the computational environment in which you would run your analysis. Containers are usually ephemeral - we create them from the image when we want to run the analysis and then stop and remove/delete them after it has run. Docker images can (and should) be versioned and shared via container registries (which are akin to remote code repositories).

Source: OctoTalks
