section: 28.1 Launching containers using Docker at the command line
text:
28.1 Launching containers using Docker at the command line
Docker has many ways we can run containers (GUI, command line, Docker Compose configuration files). Here we will learn how to use the command-line interface for running container instances from container images. We will then build on this knowledge to move to using Docker Compose configuration files for increased efficiency. We are opting to use command-line and configuration file tools so that we can automate and scale the running of containers. It is also more reproducible.

28.1.1 Launch and run containers
Below we demonstrate how to launch and run containers using the ubuntu image as an example, which is Ubuntu Linux with almost nothing else installed. We will slowly walk through the 4 basic steps needed to run a container:

Step 1 - launch the Docker app (for OSX & Windows only)
On Mac and Windows, Docker runs in a virtual machine managed by the Docker Desktop app. To run a Docker container, you must have this running. To do this, use Launchpad/Finder/Start menu/etc. to find and launch Docker Desktop.

Note: Docker might already be running. If so, great, but if it’s not, the commands below will not work. So it is always good to check!



Step 2 - get container image from Docker Hub
To run a container instance, you need to have a container image locally. One way to get a container image locally is to pull (i.e., download) one from a container registry like Docker Hub. To do this we use the docker pull <CONTAINER> command. You will commonly see the container to pull written as: container_registry/container_user/container_image:container_image_version_tag.
If you only see container_user/container_image:container_image_version_tag, Docker will assume you are using Docker Hub as the container registry (this is the default). In the previous chapter, we ran the quay.io/jupyter/datascience-notebook:2025-03-14 container from the quay.io registry, and rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 from Docker Hub.
Sometimes the container_image_version_tag is omitted. When this happens, the most recent container is pulled, and it has the version tag latest. In data analysis projects, we try to avoid using this strategy because Docker is lazy, and if you already have a latest image on your local host machine, docker run container_user/container_image will use it without checking whether there is a newer version of the container image on the remote container registry. Only docker pull checks the registry for a newer latest.
We will now pull the ubuntu Docker image, container image version 24.04, which is hosted on Docker Hub, by running the following in the terminal:
Terminal
docker pull ubuntu:24.04
We can verify that it successfully pulled by typing docker images ubuntu:24.04, or docker images to list all of your images. When you do that, you should see something like:
Terminal
docker images ubuntu:24.04
Output
IMAGE          ID             DISK USAGE   CONTENT SIZE   EXTRA
ubuntu:24.04   008173c23f95        141MB         30.9MB        
Note

You can skip this step and just go on to docker run ... as that command will pull the image if you do not have it locally.
If you ever need to delete a container image from your computer, you can run docker rmi <IMAGE_ID> to do so.



Step 3 - launch a container from the image and poke around!
We use docker run to launch a container instance from a container image. By default, the container instance will execute its programmed launch behavior and immediately stop. Thus, if we want to use the container in a more interactive way, we need to tell Docker that by adding the -it flag to our docker run command.
Terminal
docker run -it ubuntu:24.04
If it worked, then your command line prompt should now look something like this, which says that you are the user root in the container whose ID starts with 8f04536bf43d, in its folder /:
Output
root@8f04536bf43d:/#
You can use standard Bash shell commands like ls, cd, and pwd to explore the container:
Terminal
pwd
ls
Output
/
bin  boot  dev  etc  home  lib  media  mnt  opt  proc  root  run  sbin  srv  sys  tmp  usr  var
You can type exit to leave when you are done (your prompt will look normal again)!


Step 4 - clean up your container!
After you close a container, it still “hangs” around… It has stopped running, but the container instance still exists on your computer. You can view the containers on your computer, including the stopped ones, using docker ps -a. It may list other containers too:
Terminal
docker ps -a
Output
CONTAINER ID   IMAGE          COMMAND       CREATED          STATUS                     PORTS     NAMES
8f04536bf43d   ubuntu:24.04   "/bin/bash"   15 seconds ago   Exited (0) 3 seconds ago             ecstatic_hoover
You can remove the container by typing docker rm <container_id>:
Terminal
docker rm 8f04536bf43d
Output
8f04536bf43d
After you remove the container, you can prove to yourself that the container is no longer “hanging around” via docker ps -a, but that you still have the image installed (which you can see via docker images).

Note: to remove running containers, you will need to first stop them via docker stop <container_id>.



That’s a lot of work…
We walked through those steps slowly so that you understand how everything is working. However, it is not the most efficient way to work with Docker container instances when using docker run. What we typically do is tell Docker to delete the container upon exit using the --rm flag in the run command.
The command below runs a new container instance from the same image. This one command is equivalent to steps 2–4 above!
Terminal
docker run \
    --rm \
    -it \
    ubuntu:24.04
Note
We are using \ above to split a Bash command across lines to make it more readable. You will see that throughout this chapter.



28.1.3 Mapping ports to containers with web apps
Docker documentation on Container networking
If we want to use a graphical user interface (GUI) with our containers, for example to be able to use the computational environment in the container in an integrated development environment (IDE) such as RStudio or JupyterLab, then we need to map the correct port from the container to a port on our computer.
Note
In computer science, ports are points where network connections start and end. They can be physical (e.g., USB ports, Ethernet ports) or virtual. In the case of virtual ports, they are really a software-based addressing mechanism that identifies points to connect specific processes or types of network services. When we are discussing ports in the context of containerization, we are referring to virtual ports.
To do this, we use the -p flag with docker run, specifying the port in the host (your computer) on the left-hand side, and the port in the container on the right-hand side of :. For example, to run the rocker/rstudio container image we would type -p 8787:8787 to map the ports as shown in the docker run command below:
Terminal
docker run \
    --rm \
    -p 8787:8787 \
    -e PASSWORD="apassword" \
    rocker/rstudio:4.4.2
Then to access the web app, we need to navigate a browser URL to http://localhost:<HOST_PORT>. In this case, we would navigate to http://localhost:8787 to use the RStudio Server web app from the container.
Note that we can only map one port on our computer (the container/Docker host) to a container at any given time. However, our computer (the container/Docker host) has many ports we can choose from to map. So if we wanted to run a second rocker/rstudio container, then we could map it to a different port as shown below:
Terminal
docker run \
    --rm \
    -p 8788:8787 \
    -e PASSWORD="apassword" \
    rocker/rstudio:4.4.2
When we do this, to run the app in a browser on our computer, we need to go to http://localhost:8788 (instead of http://localhost:8787) to access this container as we mapped it to the 8788 port on our computer (and not 8787).
Another important note is that the container port is specific to the container, and the web app installed therein. So we cannot change that without changing the container image and/or the application installed therein. Where do you learn what port is exposed in a container image? The image documentation should specify this. For example, in the rocker/rstudio container image documentation it states:

Source: https://hub.docker.com/r/rocker/rstudio


28.1.4 Changing the containers default command
When we launch containers, they execute the command at runtime that was specified in their Dockerfile. For example, in the case of the Rocker and Jupyter images, this default behavior is to run a web app. Sometimes the default container behavior is not what we want to do. Instead, we want to do something different, like run the container as a Bash shell to test out some installation commands (common when we are building and customizing our own containers) or use the container to run a script non-interactively (like executing a data analysis pipeline from beginning to end).
To do this, we can append a new command to the end of our docker run commands. For example, to open the rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 image in an interactive Bash shell, we would run:
Terminal
docker run \
    --rm \
    -it \
    rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 \
    bash
Notice the command above does not specify the ports, nor does it set the password. This is because, in this instance, we are not using this container to run it as a web app; we are just running it as a Bash shell (which needs no ports or authentication).
The general form for running things non-interactively is this:
Terminal
docker run \
    --rm \
    -v PATH_ON_YOUR_COMPUTER:VOLUME_ON_CONTAINER DOCKER_IMAGE PROGRAM_TO_RUN \
    PROGRAM_ARGUMENTS

title: Course materials: 2026-11-19 lecture
text:
29.1 Building container images from Dockerfile’s

A Dockerfile is a plain-text file that contains commands primarily about what software to install in the Docker image. This is the more trusted and transparent way to build Docker images.
Once we have created a Dockerfile, we can build it into a Docker image.
Docker images are built in layers, and as such, Dockerfiles always start by specifying a base Docker image that the new image is to be built on top of.
Docker containers are all Linux containers and thus use Linux commands to install software. However, there are different flavors of Linux (e.g., Ubuntu, Debian, CentOS, Red Hat), and thus you need to use the right Linux install commands to match your flavor of container. For this course, we will focus on Ubuntu- or Debian-based images (and that means if we need to install software outside of R and Python packages, we will use apt-get as our installation program). However, most of what we’ll be doing for installation is R, Python, and their packages. For those, an image uses the same tools as your laptop, uv for Python and renv for R, which the next chapters put into an image.

apt or apt-get?
Ubuntu has two commands for its package manager. apt is designed for people typing at a terminal, and its behavior may change between versions. apt-get is the older command, which keeps working the same way, so Ubuntu’s apt manual page recommends apt-get for scripts. The RUN lines in a Dockerfile are a script, so this book uses apt-get in them. apt even prints a warning when a script runs it:
Output
WARNING: apt does not have a stable CLI interface. Use with caution in scripts.
At a container’s prompt either command works, but using apt-get there too means you can copy the command that worked straight into the Dockerfile.

29.1.1 Workflow for building a Dockerfile
It can take a LOOOOOOOONNNG time to troubleshoot the building of Docker images. Thus, to speed things up and be more efficient, we suggest the workflow below:

Choose a base image to build off (from https://hub.docker.com/).
Create a Dockerfile named Dockerfile and save it in an appropriate project repository. Open that file and type FROM <BASE_IMAGE> on the first line. Add any files that need to be accessed at build time via the COPY command.
In a terminal, type docker run --rm -it <BASE_IMAGE> bash and interactively try the install commands you think will work. Edit and try again until the install command works. The bash at the end starts a Bash shell in place of the image’s default command.
Write working install commands in the Dockerfile, preceding them with RUN, and save the Dockerfile.
After adding every 2–3 commands to your Dockerfile, try building the Docker image via docker build --tag <TEMP_IMAGE_NAME> <PATH_TO_DOCKERFILE_DIRECTORY>.
Once the entire Dockerfile works from beginning to end on your laptop, then you can finally move to building remotely (e.g., creating a trusted build on GitHub Actions).



29.1.2 Build your first image
Let’s follow the workflow to build a small image with R and the R package cowsay, which draws an animal saying whatever you give it.
For step 1, the base image is rocker/r-ver:4.6.2, Ubuntu Linux with R 4.6.2 installed. For step 2, make a folder for the project and move into it:
Terminal
mkdir hello-cowsay
cd hello-cowsay
In a text editor, create a file in that folder named Dockerfile, with no file extension, that has one line:
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2
For step 3, start a container from the base image with a Bash shell:
Terminal
docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash
Inside R, you would install the package with install.packages("cowsay"). At the container’s Bash prompt, Rscript -e runs a line of R code instead, which is the form a RUN line needs:
Terminal
Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')"
Output
Installing package into ‘/usr/local/lib/R/site-library’
(as ‘lib’ is unspecified)
also installing the dependencies ‘crayon’, ‘rlang’

trying URL 'https://p3m.dev/cran/__linux__/resolute/latest/src/contrib/crayon_1.5.3.tar.gz'
trying URL 'https://p3m.dev/cran/__linux__/resolute/latest/src/contrib/rlang_1.3.0.tar.gz'
trying URL 'https://p3m.dev/cran/__linux__/resolute/latest/src/contrib/cowsay_1.2.2.tar.gz'
* installing *binary* package ‘crayon’ ...
* package ‘crayon’ successfully unpacked and SHA256 sums checked
* DONE (crayon)
* installing *binary* package ‘rlang’ ...
* package ‘rlang’ successfully unpacked and SHA256 sums checked
* DONE (rlang)
* installing *binary* package ‘cowsay’ ...
* package ‘cowsay’ successfully unpacked and SHA256 sums checked
* DONE (cowsay)

The downloaded source packages are in
    ‘/tmp/RtmpAypckK/downloaded_packages’
Then try it:
Terminal
Rscript -e "cowsay::say('Hello')"
Output
 _______ 
< Hello >
 ------- 
      \
       \

        ^__^ 
        (oo)\ ________ 
        (__)\         )\ /\ 
             ||------w|
             ||      ||
Type exit to leave the container.
For step 4, write the commands that worked into the Dockerfile:
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2

RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')"

CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "cowsay::say('Hello from my first image!')"]
RUN runs the install while the image is built. It is the same command you typed at the container’s Bash prompt, which is one reason this book works at the command line (see Introduction to the Bash Shell). CMD sets the command a container from this image runs when it starts. It replaces the base image’s own CMD ["R"] (see Introduction to containerization), so a container runs our line of R code instead of starting R.
A misspelled package does not stop the build
install.packages() only warns when it cannot find a package, and Rscript still finishes with exit status 0, which tells the shell that the command worked. echo $? prints the exit status of the last command:
Terminal
Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsya')"
echo $?
Output
Installing package into ‘/usr/local/lib/R/site-library’
(as ‘lib’ is unspecified)
Warning message:
package ‘cowsya’ is not available for this version of R

A version of this package for your version of R might be available elsewhere,
see the ideas at
https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-patched/R-admin.html#Installing-packages 
0
So a RUN line with a misspelled package builds without an error, into an image without the package. Adding library() after the install makes R stop with an error, which stops the build at that step:
Terminal
Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsya'); library(cowsya)"
echo $?
Output
Installing package into ‘/usr/local/lib/R/site-library’
(as ‘lib’ is unspecified)
Warning message:
package ‘cowsya’ is not available for this version of R

A version of this package for your version of R might be available elsewhere,
see the ideas at
https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-patched/R-admin.html#Installing-packages 
Error in library(cowsya) : there is no package called ‘cowsya’
Execution halted
1
For step 5, build the image from the folder that has the Dockerfile:
Terminal
docker build --tag hello-cowsay .

--tag hello-cowsay names the image. You can add a version after a colon, such as hello-cowsay:0.1; without one, Docker uses the tag latest.
. is the build context, the folder Docker reads the Dockerfile and any copied files from, here the current folder.

Output
[+] Building 4.0s (6/6) FINISHED                                               docker:desktop-linux

 => CACHED [1/2] FROM docker.io/rocker/r-ver:4.6.2@sha256:8739c76d2d9316698a7145b032601f1e822  0.0s

Each [1/2] and [2/2] is a step of the Dockerfile. If you have not pulled rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 before, the FROM step downloads it first.
Run a container from the new image. It needs no -it, because our R code prints its message and exits:
Terminal
docker run --rm hello-cowsay
Output

< Hello from my first image! >
 ---------------------------- 
      \
       \

        ^__^ 
        (oo)\ ________ 
        (__)\         )\ /\

29.2 Dockerfile command summary
The most common Dockerfile commands I use:







Command
Description




FROM
States which base image the new Docker image should be built on top of


RUN
Specifies that a command should be run in a shell


ENV
Sets environment variables


EXPOSE
Specifies the port the container should listen to at runtime


COPY or ADD
Adds files (or URLs in the case of ADD) to a container’s filesystem


CMD
Sets the default command a container runs when it starts; a command after the image name in docker run replaces it


ENTRYPOINT
Sets a command that always runs when a container starts; anything after the image name in docker run is passed to it as arguments


WORKDIR
Sets the working directory for any RUN, CMD, ENTRYPOINT, COPY and ADD instructions that follow it in the Dockerfile



And more here in the Dockerfile reference.

text:
29.4 Dockerfile FAQ
These questions come up when you start writing your own Dockerfile.

29.4.1 1. Where does the Dockerfile live?
The Dockerfile should live in the root directory of your project.


29.4.2 2. How do I make an image from a Dockerfile?
There are 2 ways to do this! I use the first when developing my Dockerfile (to test quickly that it works), and then the second when I want a build that others can check, made from the Dockerfile in the repository.

Build a Docker image locally on your laptop
Build a Docker image on GitHub Actions (see Building images for several platforms)



29.4.3 3. How do I build an image locally on my laptop?
From the directory that contains your Dockerfile (usually your project root):
Terminal
docker build --tag IMAGE_NAME:VERSION .
Note
--tag lets you name and version the Docker image. You can call this anything you want. The version number/name comes after the colon.
After I build, I then try to docker run ... to test the image locally. If I don’t like it, or it doesn’t work, I delete the image with docker rmi {IMAGE_NAME}, edit my Dockerfile, and try to build and run it again.

text:
1. Project Advice and Course Logistics (00:00:14–00:05:43)

Keep analysis simple: Fit a straight line if a straight line is appropriate; avoid complex models like neural networks for this milestone.
Results do not matter: The grade focuses on technically correct data science practices and reproducibility workflows, not model accuracy.
Workflow over report: The written report is not the main point; the code, data downloading, cleaning, and EDA are what matter.
Timeline: This week focuses on Git branching and pull requests. Next week introduces containers. Lab 3 is an individual assignment to practice the main assignment workflow.


[!WARNING]
Don’t overcomplicate your analysis. Fitting a complex model unnecessarily will make the workflow and reproducibility aspects significantly harder to manage.

title: Introduction to Containers and Git Workflow Review
text:
2. Git Branching and Pull Requests (00:06:05–00:25:29)

Branch workflow: Always ensure you are on the intended branch before committing. Use git switch -c <branch-name> to create and switch to a new branch.
GitHub Issues as project management: Use issues to track tasks, meeting notes, and action items. Assign people to issues to clarify responsibility.
Cross-referencing: Issues and pull requests share a single numbering sequence. Use #<number> in descriptions or commit messages to create two-way links.
Closing issues automatically: Use keywords fixes #<number> or closes #<number> in a pull request description. Merging the PR will automatically close the referenced issue(s).
Cleaning up branches: After merging a PR, delete the remote branch via the GitHub UI. Locally, run git fetch --prune to remove remote tracking references, then git branch -d <branch-name> to delete the local branch.


[!WARNING]
Keep your first pull request or issue comment updated. It serves as the primary summary for reviewers and future team members; the rest of the conversation is secondary.

title: Introduction to Containers and Git Workflow Review
section: 3. Introduction to Containers and Docker (27 Introduction to containerization) (00:25:33–00:46:44)
text:
3. Introduction to Containers and Docker (27 Introduction to containerization) (00:25:33–00:46:44)

Why containers?: Virtual environments (uv, renv) manage packages but not the underlying OS or system dependencies. Containers isolate the entire operating system user space, solving compatibility issues across different machines and operating systems.
Containers vs. Virtual Machines: Virtual machines emulate full hardware and OS, making them heavy (gigabytes). Containers are stripped-down, share the host OS, and are lightweight (often <1 GB), making them faster to start and share.
Pulling and running images: docker pull <image> downloads an image. docker run --rm -it <image> starts an interactive session. --rm deletes the container when it exits, preventing clutter. -it enables interactive terminal mode.
Version isolation: Containers allow running specific software versions (e.g., R 4.3.2 inside a container while the host has R 4.6.2) without interfering with the host system.


[!WARNING]
Containers reset to their initial state when stopped. Any packages or changes installed interactively are lost upon exit unless explicitly saved via a Dockerfile or volume mount.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Introduction to Containers and Git Workflow Review
section: 4. Running Web Applications in Containers (28.1.3 Mapping ports to containers with web apps) (00:46:47–01:03:00)
text:
4. Running Web Applications in Containers (28.1.3 Mapping ports to containers with web apps) (00:46:47–01:03:00)

Browser-based apps: Tools like JupyterLab, RStudio Server, and VS Code run inside containers and are accessed via a web browser.
Port mapping: Use -p <host_port>:<container_port> to map a container’s port to your local machine. RStudio defaults to port 8787. You can run multiple containers by mapping them to different host ports (e.g., 8788:8787).
Environment variables: Pass configuration using -e VARIABLE_NAME="value". For RStudio, you can set a custom password with -e PASSWORD="yourpassword" to avoid the default generated one.
Security note: Port mapping only exposes the app to your local machine. External access depends on your network configuration, but locally it is restricted to localhost.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Introduction to Containers and Git Workflow Review
section: 5. Building Custom Containers with Dockerfile (29 Customizing and building containers) (01:03:00–01:20:39)
text:
5. Building Custom Containers with Dockerfile (29 Customizing and building containers) (01:03:00–01:20:39)

Dockerfile structure: A plain-text file (named Dockerfile) that defines the steps to build a container image. It always starts with a base image.
FROM: Specifies the starting base image (e.g., rocker/r-ver:4.6.2).
RUN: Executes shell commands during the image build process (e.g., RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')") to install software permanently into the image layers.
CMD: Sets the default command a container runs when started from this image. It replaces the base image’s default. Syntax uses JSON array format: CMD ["executable", "param1"].
Building and running: Use docker build --tag <image_name> . to build the image from the current directory. Run it with docker run <image_name>. You can override the default CMD by appending a command like bash to the run command.


[!WARNING]
Always pin software versions in your Dockerfile (e.g., FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2). Relying on latest can cause unexpected breaks if upstream packages update outside your control.

title: Introduction to Containers and Git Workflow Review
text:
Git branch workflow
git switch -c today                  # Create and switch to a new branch
git add README.md                    # Stage changes
git commit -m "today we are talking about containers" # Commit with message
git push origin today                # Push branch to remote
git switch main                      # Switch back to main
git pull origin main                 # Ensure main is up to date
git fetch --prune                    # Remove deleted remote branch references
git branch -d today                  # Delete local branch
The instructor demonstrated moving a change from main into an isolated branch, pushing it, and then cleaning up local and remote tracking references after the pull request was merged.

title: Introduction to Containers and Git Workflow Review
section: Pulling and running base R container
text:
Pulling and running base R container
docker pull rocker/r-ver:4.3.2       # Download a specific R version image
docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 # Start interactive session, auto-delete on exit
This command downloads the R 4.3.2 image if missing and launches an interactive R session. The container’s R version runs independently of the host machine’s R installation.

title: Introduction to Containers and Git Workflow Review
text:
Running RStudio container (web app)
docker pull rocker/rstudio:4.4.2     # Download RStudio Server image
docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 # Run with port mapping
docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 -e PASSWORD="apassword" rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 # Set custom password
Web applications inside containers must be accessed via the host’s browser. Port mapping exposes the container’s port 8787 locally, while -e PASSWORD overrides the auto-generated login credentials.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Introduction to Containers and Git Workflow Review
text:
Building a custom container
docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash # Start base R image with bash shell
Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')" # Install package inside container
docker build --tag hello-cowsay .      # Build image from current Dockerfile
docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay       # Run custom image
docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay bash  # Override default CMD to get bash shell
Because interactive changes are lost when a container stops, a Dockerfile is used to bake the installation into the image layers. The CMD instruction defines the default startup behavior, which can be overridden by appending a command to docker run.

title: Summary
text:
1. Project scope and data analysis

Keep the analysis simple and technically correct

This is not primarily a model-fitting course, so avoid unnecessary complexity. If a straight-line model fits the task, use one rather than adding a neural network just for complexity.
Simple linear or logistic regression is acceptable, but the method must match the outcome. For example, logistic regression is not appropriate for predicting a numeric outcome.
Model performance is not the main focus. A model that is 60% accurate is not automatically a problem if the data science and machine-learning techniques are technically correct.
Do not turn the assignment into a portfolio project. Students who want a portfolio project can work on one separately.

Complete the requested components without overbuilding

The work may include code to download data, data cleaning, exploratory data analysis (EDA), modeling, figures, tables, and a report. Keep these components straightforward and follow the assignment’s instructions for the requested report detail.
The project is developed over approximately three or four weeks. Students should begin with a machine-learning project even though the lectures contain relatively little machine-learning code.
The lecture described the week of November 19, 2026, as focused on getting everything on Git, and the following week, November 26, 2026, as focused on containers. Individual assignments provide short practice for the main assignment; a later assignment includes a very simple data analysis.

title: Summary
text:
2. Git and GitHub workflows

Use branches to make changes

The practical exercise is to create or use a repository, bring it onto the local computer, edit a file, and open a pull request. The example adds “Today we will talk about containers” to the README.
Check the active branch with git status before staging or committing, especially to avoid making changes directly on main. If work has already been committed on main, the textbook includes a cheat sheet with commands for moving it.
The demonstrated workflow is to create a branch with git switch -c today, check the branch and working tree with git status, review changes with git diff, stage the README with git add README.md, commit with a descriptive message, and push the today branch.
In an active collaboration, pull the latest main branch before beginning work so that changes are based on an up-to-date version.

Use GitHub issues to plan and track work

Issues can record tasks, ideas, plans, meeting notes, and responsibilities. Meeting action items can be recorded in notes and split into issues assigned to individuals.
Issues are also useful for longer-term ideas or stretch goals that are not part of the immediate assignment.
Students are expected to create three issues to practice using the project-board system. Not every issue needs to be closed by the end of class.

Connect issues and pull requests

Issues and pull requests share one numbering sequence. Referencing an item by number, such as #2, creates a link that can be navigated in both directions.
A pull request can address one or several issues; the relationship is not necessarily one issue, one branch, and one pull request.
GitHub recognizes closing keywords in pull-request text. For example, fixes #2 links a pull request to issue 2 and automatically closes the issue when the pull request is merged. The instructor also mentioned closes, while recommending fixes as the keyword they regularly use.
Issues may remain open for future exploration or stretch goals. The course does not require every issue to be closed.

Maintain useful pull-request information

Issues and pull requests can be assigned to people. Pull requests can also have reviewers, such as a teammate asked to inspect the work.
The main pull-request description should explain what the change does and include relevant issue references. Keep it current so readers can understand the work without reconstructing it from later discussion.
Markdown checkboxes can track remaining tasks. A draft pull request can indicate that work is not yet ready.

Update and optionally clean up branches after merging

After a pull request is merged, check the state with git status, switch to main using git switch main, and pull the latest changes.
GitHub offers an option to delete the remote branch after merging, or it can be deleted from the branches view. This cleanup is optional; teams may have different workflows, and retaining branches can provide convenient references to past work.
Deleting a remote branch does not automatically remove its local reference. Use git fetch --prune to remove references to remote branches that no longer exist, then optionally remove a local branch with git branch -d <branch-name>. This does not erase the merged history.
Keeping a local branch name can be more convenient than navigating to a commit hash. Cleanup may help when many branches make Git output difficult to follow.

title: Summary
text:
3. Why containers are useful

Projects need tailored, minimal environments

Projects may last weeks, months, or years and may use different languages and tools. Students can choose R or Python, and visualization tools might include Altair, Plotly, or Matplotlib.
Package lists should include only what the project needs. Unused packages waste disk space, and installing many packages can lead to compatibility problems as packages update on different schedules.
In real-world projects, users need to adapt the environment to the project rather than rely on one standard package set.

Reproducibility across people, computers, and time

A project that runs on one person’s machine may fail on another’s because collaborators use different operating systems, hardware, or processor architectures, such as ARM or Intel.
UV and “RM,” as referenced in the lecture, help keep required packages consistent. Lock files record package versions, but do not necessarily include all the instructions, tools, or system components needed to reproduce the environment on another computer.
Containers provide a broader, shareable environment. They can also support modular pipelines so collaborators can use different parts of an analysis, not just its final report.
Containers bridge local development and remote computing environments that may have more memory, processor cores, or access to project data.

Containers compared with virtual machines

A container is a stripped-down computing environment containing the software and tools needed for a task. It typically does not include a full graphical operating system.
A virtual machine typically runs a full operating system, such as Windows, with a graphical interface. Containers are generally lighter and more resource-efficient, though they still add a layer and can incur a performance cost.
The lecture contrasted virtual-machine installations that might use 50 or 80 GB with class containers that may be under 2 GB or even under 1 GB. Virtual machines remain useful for some purposes, such as testing an MDS installation in Windows.
Containers can act as sandboxes: if an environment is damaged, it can be restarted or replaced. They are also useful for experimenting with operating systems or command-line tools without changing the local computer.
Docker is the container tool used in class. LXC, LXD, and Podman were mentioned as alternatives. Cloud computing commonly uses containers or similar environments rather than providing unrestricted access to a physical machine.

Pinning tools and preserving long-running analyses

Docker can preserve specific tool versions, not just project package versions. For example, a Docker image can provide R 4.3.2 even if the host has a different version, allowing multiple R versions to be used without installing each directly on the computer.
The lecture also noted that system-tool versions affect available commands: a container with a 2019 version of Git, for example, would not support git switch.
Stable environments can be important for long-running or regulated research. A clinical-trial analysis may span several years while R updates about every six months. Repeatedly changing or revalidating the environment may be undesirable.
For a drug submission to the relevant Canadian regulator, described in the lecture as the Canadian equivalent of the FDA, submitted materials may need to include code and the computing environment so the work can be reproduced.
Lock files preserve package versions; containers can additionally preserve the tool itself and potentially system-level tools.

title: Summary
text:
4. Docker commands and running containers

Pulling and running images

docker pull <image> downloads a container image to the local computer. Image names resemble a username and repository, such as images provided by Docker for R. Docker may report that an image is already up to date and can identify a specific image version with a hash.
The word pull is similar to git pull: both retrieve something onto the computer.
docker run <image> starts a container. If the image is not available locally, Docker downloads it. Additional flags can determine how the container runs.
Docker Desktop must be open before running the class commands. If Docker cannot be found, install Docker; if it is installed but not running, the commands will prompt the user to start it.
The instructor directed students to find three Docker commands in Slack and run them; the setup was expected to take about ten minutes.

Flags, terminals, and host-versus-container behavior

Double-dash options introduce longer flags. In the example, --rm removes a container when it stops. Without it, the container may need to be removed manually.
Single-dash flags are typically single-letter options and can be combined. For example, ls -a -l -h shows all files, lists them, and uses human-readable sizes.
-i enables interactive input and -t allocates a TTY; they are often used together for an interactive terminal. docker run --rm -it <image> is a demonstrated pattern.
A container behaves like a separate computer on the same physical hardware. An R container with R 4.3.2 runs that version rather than the host’s version. Typing R in a separate host terminal starts the host’s version, if installed and available on its path. Windows may require different path handling.
The R container initially did not have tidyverse, so library(tidyverse) failed there even though it worked in the host’s R environment. This demonstrates that the host and container have separate software and packages.
Check the terminal prompt or other interface cues to determine which machine is active. Commands such as who am I? can help identify the current username. Confirm the active environment before running commands, especially on remote systems.
Running containers use memory and other resources. Shut down containers that are no longer needed; several running containers can make a computer unresponsive.

title: Summary
section: 5. Browser-based applications, ports, and environment variables
text:
5. Browser-based applications, ports, and environment variables

Accessing applications through a browser

Applications such as RStudio and Jupyter Lab can run inside containers and be accessed through a browser. The browser provides a familiar interface while computation runs in a separately configured environment, locally or remotely.
Jupyter Lab was described as commonly running at localhost:8 in the lecture. VS Code and GitHub Codespaces were also mentioned as examples of familiar interfaces connected to separate computing environments.
The instructor demonstrated rocker/rstudio:4.2, accessing its browser-based RStudio through localhost:8787. This was separate from RStudio installed on the host.

Mapping ports

Docker’s -p option maps a host port to a port inside the container. Mapping host port 8787 to container port 8787 allows a browser to connect through localhost:8787.
Port numbers are selected by the application and are not inherently special. RStudio and Jupyter Lab use different ports; other tools use others.
Multiple instances can run concurrently if they use different host ports. The lecture gave an alternate host-port example transcribed as 61.11; users must connect through whichever host port they map.

Passing environment variables and sharing applications

Docker’s -e option passes environment variables into a container. In the RStudio example, PASSWORD was set to a chosen password. The available variables and default username depend on how the image was configured and documented.
A containerized dashboard or other application can be shared through a port, allowing end users to run it without separately installing all its dependencies. Users still need Docker but can run the prepared application with the relevant docker run options.
The lecture noted that containerized browser-based applications may be useful when a graphical interface is desired, though students may not need to install Jupyter Lab independently for the current course.

title: Summary
text:
6. Building a customized container

Interactive changes are temporary

The instructor demonstrated installing the R package cowsay, which provides ASCII-art output, and loading it with library(cowsay).
Packages installed interactively are not retained when a container is stopped and restarted. A fresh start returns the container to its configured state unless the setup instructions preserve the changes.
This reset behavior is useful for experimentation, but manually reinstalling dependencies every time is inconvenient. The instructor contrasted a potentially 15-minute tidyverse installation on an improperly configured Linux machine with an analysis that may take only 30 seconds.

Dockerfile instructions

A Dockerfile (capital D) contains instructions for setting up an environment. Existing R and RStudio images already have their own setup instructions.
FROM specifies the base image and is typically the first Docker instruction. The example FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 starts from an image with R 4.6.2 installed.
Smaller, minimal Linux images are possible but require more components to be installed manually. A somewhat larger base image can be a reasonable choice.
RUN executes shell or Bash commands while the image is being built. Rscript -e can run an R expression from the terminal. The instructor demonstrated using it to install cowsay; the shell example used double quotes outside and single quotes inside.
CMD specifies the default behavior when the image runs without an overriding command. The example printed “hello from my first image.” ENTRYPOINT is another instruction, described as less common and suited to specific cases.
Dockerfiles can also use instructions such as COPY and multiple RUN steps. For a Python environment, for example, files such as lock files could be copied in and uv sync run to install packages. Depending on the image, port instructions may also be needed; port 8787 was given as an example.

Building and testing an image

docker build creates an image from a Dockerfile. The -t option assigns a name or tag. The example command was docker build -t hello-cowsay .; the final . tells Docker to look in the current directory for the file named Dockerfile.
A full path can be supplied, but commands are commonly run from the project root, consistent with course working-directory conventions.
docker images lists images available locally. docker run --rm hello-cowsay runs the image. Adding bash opens a terminal inside the container for testing or investigation.
The instructor also demonstrated docker run --rm -it with an R image intended to use R 4.6.2, opening a shell rather than launching R automatically. From the shell, users can test setup steps and start R by typing R.
The general workflow is to start from a base image, add the commands and files needed to configure it, and build the result. Testing setup steps interactively first can help before documenting them in the Dockerfile.

Version pinning and upcoming setup

Specifying versions in a Dockerfile keeps tools and packages consistent until the setup instructions are deliberately changed. The lecture gave a “Cordova” example: a project using version 1.11 could instead select version 1.10 and continue using it while the instruction remains unchanged.
Pinning helps prevent unexpected updates from breaking a project. The instructor described another project where a tool updated shortly before work, causing the project to stop working because versions had not been pinned.
In the next class, students will set up a container for the language they use (R or Python), install Quarto and project packages, and configure the environment so the analysis can run locally and inside the container. Copy-and-paste setup instructions will be provided. The lecture also mentioned an “RM setup” placeholder for installing, snapshotting, and loading packages.
Container material will continue in the next class, including connecting multiple containers. No container work is required for this week’s lab assignment.

title: Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers: review questions, tier 2 — Understand
text:
Date: 2026-11-19
Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 2 of 5: Understand. Explain each answer in your own words before you read it; tier 1 (Remember) covers the facts, tiers 3 to 5 put them to use.

1. Opening: pull the Docker images and start the branch exercise
00:00:14–00:01:41

Q: Why were students asked to run the three docker pull commands from Slack at the very start of class, before anything else? A: The downloads take about ten minutes. Starting them at the beginning meant they would finish while the class was checking everything else, so nobody would wait for them later. (00:00:18)
Q: Docker can fail in two ways at the start: with an error that it “can’t find Docker”, or by asking you to turn it on. What does each one mean? A: An error that Docker can’t be found means Docker isn’t installed, so you need to install the Docker application. If Docker is installed but Docker Desktop isn’t running, the commands tell you to turn it on. That is why you open Docker Desktop before running them. (00:00:33)
Q: Why did the warm-up exercise practise making a branch, opening a pull request and merging it, together with issues? A: Branches, pull requests and issues are part of how students will work on all their project-based courses from now on. The exercise gets them practising that workflow right away. (00:00:57)



2. Project advice: keep the analysis simple
00:01:41–00:05:57

Q: Why did the instructor say to keep the group project’s analysis simple, for example a straight-line model rather than a neural net? A: This is not a model-fitting course. The course title is about workflows, and there is almost no machine learning code in the lectures. The report is not the point of the class, and there is a lot more to do, so an ambitious model means “a very bad time in about two weeks.” (00:02:16)
Q: What is the difference between a model that is “simple” and one that is “incorrect”, in terms of how the project is judged? A: A simple model is fine: the results don’t matter, so 60% accuracy is acceptable, and linear or logistic regression won’t be penalised. The techniques must still be technically correct data science. Fitting logistic regression to predict a numeric outcome, for example, is just wrong. (00:03:08, 00:05:24)
Q: Why did the instructor advise against turning this group project into a portfolio piece? A: A lot is happening in this class, and you don’t want to deal with a complicated report at the same time. If you really want a portfolio project, build it separately, in parallel. (00:03:27)
Q: Explain why the project needs a machine learning analysis even though the lectures show almost no machine learning code. A: The class teaches the workflow around an analysis, not the modelling. You still need a machine learning project to start with, because that analysis is what you build the workflow on over three or four weeks. (00:05:37, 00:05:43)



3. Git review: working on a branch
00:06:16–00:09:50

Q: The instructor edited README.md while still on main. Why could he fix this just by running git switch -c today? A: He had only edited the file and had not committed anything yet, so he could still create the new branch. After git switch -c today, git status showed “On branch today” with the same modified README.md, ready to commit there. (00:08:57, 00:09:17)
Q: Why should you look at which branch you are on right before git add, and especially before git commit? A: From now on the course assumes a branch workflow, so commits belong on a branch, not on main. Once you have committed on main, you need extra commands to move the work around; the textbook has a cheat sheet for this. Checking first avoids the problem. (00:07:44, 00:08:08)
Q: Why pull main before starting new work when you are actively collaborating? A: It keeps your copy up to date, so you aren’t making changes to something that is out of date. With several people working on several branches, this is something you now have to pay attention to. (00:08:27, 00:08:41)
Q: What did the git diff output on the today branch show before staging? A: It showed the uncommitted change to README.md: the lines starting with + were the new blank line and the added line “- today we will talk about containers”. That is the change he then staged with git add README.md and committed. (00:09:25)



4. GitHub issues as a project board
00:09:50–00:16:17

Q: What are GitHub issues for, beyond reporting bugs? A: They track what is happening in a project, as a simple project board, including who is responsible for what. MDS uses one internal repository’s issues for meeting notes. Action items assigned to people are then spawned as separate issues from the notes issue. (00:10:08, 00:10:28, 00:10:49)
Q: Why do issues and pull requests in the demo repository 2026-11-19-docker share one numbering sequence, so that after issues #1 and #2 the pull request was #3? A: Because they share one counter, any issue or pull request can refer to any other item just by its number. (00:12:07, 00:12:20)
Q: What does it mean that a # reference is “two-way”, as when issue #2 said “meeting from #1”? A: Writing #1 in issue #2 links to issue #1, and issue #1 automatically shows a reference back to #2. Everything links to everything else without extra work. The instructor called this one of the reasons GitHub, rather than just Git, became so popular as a project management system. (00:13:34, 00:13:47)
Q: Why does the instructor sometimes ask a coding agent to file an issue for a passing idea instead of opening GitHub himself? A: Switching to a browser risks ending up on a site he doesn’t need and losing track of his work. Asking the agent to file the issue records the idea without breaking his focus. (00:13:06, 00:13:24)
Q: What is the difference between being an assignee and being a reviewer on a pull request? A: Assigning yourself claims the pull request as your responsibility. A reviewer is a teammate asked to look over your work. Some projects block changes until someone has actually reviewed them. In the demo, the instructor added Copilot as a reviewer. (00:14:47, 00:15:14)
Q: Why is it acceptable for one pull request to deal with all three issues the lab asks for? A: One issue, one branch and one pull request is only one extreme, and it isn’t always how work happens. The lab asks for issues so you gain experience with the project board system, not to force a one-to-one match. (00:14:23)



5. Pull request descriptions, checkboxes and closing keywords
00:16:17–00:22:18

Q: Why did the instructor edit the first comment of the pull request instead of adding new comments as the work changed? A: People coming to an issue or pull request want to know what is happening and why it exists, and they won’t read the whole conversation. The first comment should hold all the references and any big decisions. It is editable because the work evolves, and project owners can usually edit others’ comments too. (00:16:40, 00:16:56)
Q: How do Markdown checkboxes in a pull request description compare with marking the pull request as a draft? A: Both show teammates that the work isn’t done yet. Checkboxes such as - [ ] item 2 also let you track your own remaining to-dos as you fix things. They show what is still unchecked even if you never use the draft button. (00:17:49, 00:18:21)
Q: How does writing fixes #2 in pull request #3’s description close issue #2? A: fixes (and closes) followed by an issue number is a special pattern that GitHub recognises. When that pull request is merged, the issues it says it fixes are closed automatically. This is a GitHub feature, not a feature of Git itself. (00:18:33, 00:18:54, 00:19:30)
Q: Why write closing keywords in the pull request message rather than in a commit message? A: They also work in a commit message, but they are harder to see there. Putting them in the pull request message makes it visible which issues the work deals with. (00:19:55)
Q: Why does auto-closing issues help with project management? A: As pull requests merge, the issues tab gets smaller, so you don’t have to think about finished items again or click close on each one. The instructor works this way on the textbook: file an issue, do the work, write “fixes” in the pull request, then take the next item from the issues list. (00:20:12, 00:20:28, 00:21:02)
Q: Why is it fine to leave stretch-goal issues open at the end of the course? A: Closing all your issues is not what the course grades. Issues are a place to keep longer-term ideas and things to explore, so creating them is good practice even if they stay open. (00:21:50)



6. Cleaning up after a merge
00:22:18–00:25:19

Q: What is the difference between what git fetch --prune and git branch -d today each removed? A: git fetch --prune removed the local reference to the branch that had been deleted on GitHub, origin/today. git branch -d today then deleted the local today branch. Both only clean up references. (00:24:30)
Q: After both cleanup commands, what did git log --oneline --graph --all still show, and what had been lost? A: Commit 3c6d82a and the merge commit were still in the graph, so you could still tell a merge had happened. Only the branch labels were gone: the quick shortcut reference to that commit. (00:24:30)
Q: Why do some people prefer not to delete merged branches? A: Deleting a branch loses the convenient reference to that point in history. With the branch kept, you can type git switch today instead of git switch 3c6d82a. (00:24:05, 00:25:05)
Q: Why might you clean up branch references anyway? A: Leftover references can leave you in weird Git states where the graph has too many colours and labels to see what is happening. Cleaning up makes the history readable again. (00:24:05)
Q: Why is deleting branches optional in this course? A: You may want to keep branches as a record. Teams and companies handle Git very differently, even within one company. The course shows one way, and others are modifications of it. (00:23:16, 00:23:22)



7. Why data science workflows need stable environments (27.1 Documenting and loading dependencies)
00:25:29–00:30:13

Q: How does working on a project differ from earlier MDS homework when it comes to packages? A: In homework, the instructors gave you the package file. In projects, each group chooses its own tools, such as R or Python, or Altair, Plotly or Matplotlib, so you must adapt the environment to your project. That is also how it works at a company. (00:25:52, 00:27:06, 00:27:38)
Q: Why keep a project’s package list to the bare minimum instead of installing everything? A: Installing packages you don’t use wastes disk space. Packages also have different update cycles, so updating a big environment in one go can make things incompatible. You can end up unable to install everything. (00:27:38, 00:28:04)
Q: Explain the two kinds of stability a long-running group project needs. A: You need your own environment to stay stable over days, weeks, months or even years. It also has to work for someone else, because “this works on my machine” doesn’t help a teammate who can’t run your code. (00:28:20, 00:28:34, 00:29:39)
Q: Why is reproducing an environment on a teammate’s computer harder than copying it to “just another Mac”? A: The teammate may be on Windows, and the CPU chips differ between machines, so software is installed differently. Even two Windows machines can differ, because Windows now runs on both ARM and Intel chips. (00:28:53)
Q: Why does the course care about modular pipelines, not just a finished report? A: Other people may need different parts of your analysis, not only the report. The pipeline has to be built so those parts can be used separately. (00:29:55)



8. What a container is (27.2 What is a container?)
00:30:13–00:34:28

Q: If you can hand a teammate a uv lock file, what problem is still left over? A: The lock file lets them install the Python packages, but their computer may be set up differently. They may not use uv at all, and installing it might mess up other things on their computer. (00:30:40, 00:31:06, 00:31:17)
Q: Explain the idea of a container in the instructor’s “here’s my computer” terms. A: Instead of giving you his physical computer, he builds a virtual computer from scratch and gives you that. You do your work on that virtual computer instead of directly on your own. Everyone is effectively sharing the same computer while sitting at different physical machines. (00:31:17, 00:31:49, 00:31:56)
Q: Why are containers useful when you prototype on a laptop but run the full analysis on a bigger machine? A: The bigger machine may be the one with access to all the data. A container makes the compute environment exactly the same on your machine and on that machine, and on any number of other machines. (00:32:06, 00:32:15)
Q: What is the cost of a container, and why might it be worth paying on a remote machine? A: There is a performance hit, because a container adds an extra layer. However, you often can’t install things directly on a shared remote machine, or the admins don’t trust what you’d install. A container gives you a sandbox to play in instead. (00:32:34)
Q: Why is a container a good place to learn by “mucking around” with an operating system? A: If you break the sandbox, you restart it and get a new one. Blowing up a container costs nothing, unlike blowing up your own computer. (00:33:05, 00:33:13)
Q: How do containers relate to the “instances” you get from cloud providers? A: Containers are almost like instances. A provider such as Google usually gives you a container on one of its servers, not bare access to a machine. Pretty much all cloud compute runs on some version of containers. (00:33:30)
Q: How does a container deal with two versions of software that can’t be installed side by side? A: A container is a little machine with everything it needs installed inside it. Each version can live in its own container, separate from your computer. (00:34:03)



9. Containers versus virtual machines (27.3 Contrasting containers with virtual machines)
00:34:31–00:36:40

Q: What is the main difference between a virtual machine and a container? A: A virtual machine is a full-blown operating system, such as all of Windows, with the graphical interface and all the buttons to click. A container is stripped down: it typically has no graphical interface and contains only the bare minimum you install. (00:34:48, 00:35:00, 00:35:33)
Q: Why are containers more performant than virtual machines? A: A container has less in it and no visual parts, so it uses fewer resources. A Windows virtual machine can take 50–80 GB. Some containers used in class are under one or two gigabytes and still run a full computational stack, using less disk, memory and compute. (00:35:33, 00:36:16, 00:36:32)
Q: How does the container’s lack of a graphical interface explain why DSCI 521 pushed you to type commands in the terminal? A: In a container, and in many other places, the terminal may be the only interface you have. You can’t double-click through folders, so you have to type commands such as cd to get around. (00:35:00)
Q: Why does the instructor still use virtual machines? A: When testing the MDS installation instructions, he has to pretend to be on a Windows machine. That needs a whole different operating system, which is what a virtual machine provides. (00:36:01)



10. Pulling and running a container: R 4.3.2 beside local R (28.1.1 Launch and run containers)
00:36:40–00:45:01

Q: Explain what each part of the image name rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 means. A: The name looks like a GitHub username and repository because it works similarly. rocker is the organisation, which makes machines that have only R installed. The tag after the colon picks the version, here a machine with R 4.3.2. (00:37:05, 00:37:22, 00:37:26)
Q: Why would anyone want R 4.3.2 in a container when R --version on the laptop shows R 4.6.2? A: Some work needs an older, fixed version, as in pharmaceutical clinical trials research that runs for years while R updates every six months. You don’t want to redo or check your work every six months. Regulators may also require your code and the full compute environment, so you hand over the container that ran the analysis. (00:37:54, 00:38:10, 00:38:23)
Q: How does what a container pins differ from what a uv or renv lock file pins? A: Lock files track package versions only. A container goes one level deeper and fixes the tools on the system as well, such as the version of R itself or of Git. For example, a container with a 2019 Git would prevent anyone from running git switch. (00:38:46, 00:39:02)
Q: What does the output “Status: Image is up to date” with a Digest: sha256:... line mean after docker pull rocker/r-ver:4.3.2? A: The image was already downloaded and no newer version exists, so nothing new was pulled. The hash identifies the exact version of the image you have. (00:39:47, 00:39:51)
Q: Why does docker pull sound so much like git pull? A: Tools in the data science and compute stack borrow words from one another. Both commands pull something onto your computer. (00:40:22, 00:40:33)
Q: What does --rm do in docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2, and what does its double dash tell you? A: Two dashes mark a flag that is several letters long. --rm deletes the container automatically when you turn it off; otherwise you would have to delete it by hand. (00:40:55)
Q: Explain -it in docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2. A: It is two single-letter flags chained together, the same way ls -alh chains three. -i (interactive) lets you type into the container, and -t (TTY) gives you an actual terminal to interact with. (00:41:20, 00:41:48)
Q: Why did library(tidyverse) fail inside the rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 container but load in a local terminal on the same laptop? A: The container has only R in it; nobody had told it to install tidyverse. The laptop has tidyverse installed. The two terminals behave like two different machines because the container effectively is a different machine. (00:43:49, 00:44:09)
Q: How is running a Docker container like connecting to a cloud machine? A: In both cases you are connected to another machine, through pretty much the same interface. With Docker, that other machine just happens to run on the same hardware you’re typing on. (00:44:31)



11. Know which machine you are typing on
00:45:01–00:46:44

Q: Why does paying attention to your terminal prompt matter once you use containers and remote systems? A: The prompt is often your only visual cue about which machine you are on. After quitting the container, the laptop’s own prompt came back, which showed he was on his actual computer again. (00:45:04)
Q: What did the instructor’s terminal on a computer in his closet at home show about remote work? A: Commands typed there ran on that other computer. The only visual cue was the hostname he had given it, a Game of Thrones sword name. Sometimes you get nothing but a blinking cursor, so these cues are what tell you where you are. (00:45:45, 00:45:48, 00:46:08)
Q: Explain why a command like whoami exists, as discussed in DSCI 521. A: It reports the username on that computer. That is another way to check that you are on the machine you think you’re working on. (00:46:08, 00:46:29)



12. Why so many data science tools run in a browser
00:46:44–00:49:11

Q: Why are so many applications built on Electron as “browser-first” apps? A: Electron makes a browser into the application. An app built that way can run in a container, or on another machine, and be opened in a browser. (00:47:39)
Q: Why do you open Jupyter Lab at a localhost address instead of double-clicking an app? A: Jupyter Lab was made to run on a remote container that can have many more cores and much more memory than your laptop, while keeping the same interface. Building it as a browser app means you just connect your browser to wherever it is running. (00:48:04, 00:48:33)
Q: What does GitHub’s Codespaces button show about running tools in a browser? A: It opens VS Code in a browser on another machine whose whole compute environment someone has set up. You get the same interface while working on the same versions of all the software. (00:48:49, 00:49:00, 00:49:07)



13. Running RStudio in a container and mapping ports (28.1.3 Mapping ports to containers with web apps)
00:54:10–00:58:59

Q: Why keep --rm when running rocker/rstudio:4.4.2, especially while practising with several containers? A: --rm shuts the machine down and cleans it up when you exit; otherwise it keeps running. Every running container takes up RAM. Leave several running and your computer stops working well, because you’ve turned on “five computers” that each use resources. (00:55:06, 00:55:17, 00:55:24)
Q: Why does running RStudio in a container need a port at all? A: As with Jupyter Lab, the application is running somewhere else, inside the container. You have to connect your browser on your machine to the place where it is running, and the port is that connection point. (00:55:41, 00:55:56)
Q: In docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 rocker/rstudio:4.4.2, what do the numbers on each side of the colon mean? A: The left number is the port on your local computer. The right number is the port inside the container, where RStudio is running. -p 8787:8787 takes the container’s 8787 and puts it on the Mac’s 8787. (00:56:38, 00:57:05)
Q: How can you run two RStudio containers at the same time if both listen on 8787? A: The container side stays 8787, but you redirect each container to a different port on your machine. Things can run side by side as long as they use different local ports, which you specify with -p. (00:56:38, 00:57:29)
Q: Why does RStudio Server use 8787 when Jupyter Lab uses a different number? A: The numbers are arbitrary. Each tool’s developers picked one, and you could pick whatever you want. (00:55:56, 00:56:19)
Q: What did comparing RStudio at localhost:8787 with the desktop RStudio show? A: The desktop RStudio runs the laptop’s R 4.6.2. The browser RStudio runs R 4.4.2 inside the container, which also differs from the R 4.3.2 in the earlier r-ver container. You can treat them as completely different machines: one terminal-only, one an application running in a browser. (00:58:41, 00:58:51, 00:58:59)



14. Passing environment variables into a container
00:59:20–01:02:53

Q: Why did the instructor rerun RStudio with -e PASSWORD="apassword"? A: Without it, the container generates a password that is very annoying to remember. The start-up output itself says you can set your own by setting the PASSWORD environment variable. Passing -e with the same docker run command sets that variable, and the container used it as the login password. (00:59:45, 01:00:05, 01:00:39)
Q: Why can’t you assume every container understands a variable like PASSWORD? A: Whether a container reads certain variables depends on how whoever built it set it up. Containers behave differently depending on how they were built. (01:00:05, 01:01:08)
Q: Why was it acceptable for the instructor to show his RStudio password on screen? A: The container’s port is only reachable through his physical machine. If you can’t log into his laptop, port 8787 on it isn’t available to you. (01:00:16, 01:00:28)
Q: Explain the benefit of putting a dashboard (as in DSCI 532) into a container. A: You’ve done all the installation, so the end user doesn’t have to install renv, restore a snapshot or go through the setup at all. If they have Docker, they docker run it with some flags and open the port. You’ve essentially given them a computer you built from scratch. (01:01:47, 01:02:20)



15. Starting from a base image and working inside it (29.1.1 Workflow for building a Dockerfile)
01:03:00–01:08:19

Q: Why start your own container from rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 instead of a completely blank machine? A: Whoever designed that image has already installed R and probably the system pieces a brand-new computer needs for R to work. Those are like the Xcode or compiler tools students installed on their own laptops. Starting there lets you skip steps. (01:04:00, 01:04:29)
Q: What does adding bash to the end of docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash change? A: It tells the container not to start its default program, R, and to give you a terminal instead. The prompt changes to the container’s own, and you can do anything there. You can still type R to start R. (01:04:53, 01:05:20)
Q: Why try install steps interactively in a shell before writing them down? A: You go through the steps first, and once they work you document them. You end up with instructions for building the machine from scratch that you know succeed. (01:05:43, 01:05:48)
Q: Why did library(cowsay) fail after the instructor exited the container and started it again, right after installing the package? A: A container has no saved state. Each time it starts, it resets back to how its image was set up. Anything installed by hand in the previous session was gone. (01:07:10, 01:08:11)
Q: Why is a container a safe place to run destructive commands, like the “delete the computer” command warned about in DSCI 521? A: The damage only happens inside the container. Once you turn it off and on again, it is as if you never ran the command. That makes containers a good place to try packages and learn Linux without messing up your own computer. (01:07:25, 01:07:37)
Q: Why is the reset also a problem when sharing an analysis? A: Users would have to follow your README install steps every time they load the container. Installing tidyverse on Linux can take 15 minutes, and spending that before every 30-second analysis is really painful. (01:08:19)



16. Running R from the command line with Rscript -e (29.1.2 Build your first image)
01:08:19–01:10:18

Q: Why did the instructor need a terminal command for installing cowsay rather than install.packages() typed inside R? A: Saving the setup comes down to knowing the terminal command that makes it happen. He needed R to execute the install from the command line, not to open an interactive R session where he types it. (01:08:54, 01:08:59)
Q: Explain each part of Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')". A: Rscript is how R runs commands from the terminal. -e means “here is an R expression”, and the expression is the install.packages call. The quoting matters: double quotes on the outside and single quotes inside. (01:09:23, 01:09:27, 01:09:41)
Q: After Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')" worked, why was cowsay missing again in the next container? A: The install happened only in that running container, and exiting threw it away. Knowing the command isn’t enough: the information has to be saved somewhere, which is what the Dockerfile is for. (01:10:01, 01:10:13, 01:10:18)



17. The Dockerfile: FROM, RUN, CMD (29.2 Dockerfile command summary)
01:10:18–01:15:01

Q: What is a Dockerfile, and how does it explain why the RStudio container works as soon as you run it? A: A Dockerfile, named with a capital D by convention, holds the instructions for installing and setting up a computer. The RStudio image has its own Dockerfile that installs RStudio and opens the ports. That is why RStudio is ready when you load the container. (01:10:22, 01:10:41, 01:10:45)
Q: What does the FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 line do, and why is a fairly large base image acceptable? A: FROM names the starting-point machine, here one with R 4.6.2 already installed. You could start from a bare-minimum Linux and install everything by hand. Disk space is relatively cheap compared with other costs, so a beefier starting machine is fine. (01:11:25, 01:11:30, 01:12:02, 01:12:15)
Q: What is the difference between RUN and CMD in the class’s Dockerfile? A: RUN holds the bash commands the container executes while it is being built, here installing cowsay with Rscript. CMD is the last thing, the default the machine runs when you turn it on: printing “Hello from my first image!”. (01:12:44, 01:13:52, 01:14:05)
Q: How does CMD relate to adding bash at the end of docker run? A: CMD is only the default behaviour, used when you don’t say something like bash. Naming a command when you run the container overrides it. (01:13:52, 01:14:05)
Q: How is CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "cowsay::say('Hello from my first image!')"] written differently from the same command typed in a shell? A: It looks like a bash command, but instead of separating terms with spaces it writes them as a list. (01:13:40)
Q: Explain how the middle of a Dockerfile would differ for a Python project. A: In place of the Rscript install, you’d run the command that installs uv and use a copy command to bring in your lock files. Then you’d run uv sync. The packages are then installed in the container, so the machine has your compute environment ready. (01:14:15)



18. Building and running your own image (29.4.3 3. How do I build an image locally on my laptop?)
01:15:01–01:18:44

Q: Explain each part of docker build --tag hello-cowsay .. A: --tag gives the new machine the name hello-cowsay. The . tells Docker where to look for the Dockerfile: the current directory. It may be the first time a lone dot is something you must type. By default, docker build looks there for a file named exactly Dockerfile. (01:15:11, 01:15:38)
Q: Why does the course assume docker build and other project commands are run from the repository root? A: Then every command in the instructions can just be copy-pasted. Nobody has to worry about changing directories in the middle of something. Milestone instructions make the same assumption. (01:16:11, 01:16:29)
Q: What is the difference between docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay and docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay bash? A: Without bash, the container runs its CMD and prints the cow saying “Hello from my first image!”. With bash, the default is overridden and you get a terminal inside the machine instead. (01:17:14, 01:17:28, 01:17:30)
Q: Why does library(cowsay) work inside hello-cowsay when it kept failing in containers from rocker/r-ver:4.6.2? A: The install instructions are now in the Dockerfile, and the machine was built from them. Every container started from hello-cowsay therefore begins with cowsay installed, instead of resetting to a machine without it. (01:17:52)
Q: Why is shell access to your own image useful? A: When code works on your machine but not in the container, you can play inside the container directly to find out why. (01:17:30)
Q: Why does writing a Dockerfile depend so much on knowing bash? A: Apart from the starting point, the middle of a Dockerfile is all commands, such as RUN and copy commands. You have to give it the exact shell commands it needs to install whatever you need. (01:18:07)



19. Pinning versions, and what comes next
01:18:44–01:20:39

Q: Why should a project container pin the versions of its tools? A: Things updating without you being explicit, and without you knowing an update happened, is very annoying. Pinning in Docker means a version doesn’t change until you change that line. You control what gets updated and when. (01:19:35, 01:19:46, 01:20:27)
Q: What went wrong when the instructor restarted a container in another class, and what does it show? A: He hadn’t hard-pinned any versions, and something had updated the day before, so nothing worked. On a real job you’d spend hours fixing the broken update instead of doing the actual work. That is the reason to pin. (01:19:55)
Q: How does a Dockerfile keep a project on the same versions a year from now? A: The FROM line fixes the version of R. The install lines can name specific versions of other tools, even an older Quarto than the latest. As long as you don’t change those install commands, a year later you are still on the same versions. (01:18:53, 01:19:14, 01:19:35)
