title: Containers: running and building a shareable compute environment: review questions, tier 2 — Understand
text:
Date: 2026-11-19

Generated by qwen3.8-27b-sglang, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 2 of 5: Understand. Explain each answer in your own words before you read it; tier 1 (Remember) covers the facts, tiers 3 to 5 put them to use.

1. Class setup: Docker Desktop and pre-lecture Docker pulls (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:00:14–00:01:41

Q: Why does the instructor ask students to run the three docker pull commands from Slack before the session starts? A: Pulling the images takes a while, about ten minutes, so doing it before means they should be downloaded by the time the class is checking everything. The instructor put the commands in Slack so students could start that download before the session began. (00:00:18)
Q: What does an error like “can’t find Docker” mean when you run the pre-lecture Docker commands? A: It means Docker is not available to the shell. You need to install the Docker application and have Docker Desktop open before running the commands. (00:00:33)
Q: Why is the day’s Git exercise framed as practising a branch, pull request, and merge? A: It gives everyone a chance to practice the branch, pull-request, and merge workflow. That is the same workflow they will use in project-based courses and future assignments. (00:00:43)



2. Project advice: keep the analysis simple and correct
00:01:41–00:06:05

Q: Why does the instructor tell students not to make the group-project analysis difficult? A: This course is about workflows, not model fitting. If you turn a simple task into a complicated model now, you will have a bad time in about two weeks because there is a lot more workflow work to do. (00:02:03)
Q: What does the instructor mean when saying the accuracy of the model does not matter? A: A model can be only sixty percent accurate and that is acceptable. What matters is that the data science and machine-learning techniques are technically correct. (00:03:04)
Q: Why is it okay to fit a linear or logistic regression rather than a fancier model? A: The class will not penalize simplicity. The requirement is correctness, so you should not, for example, fit logistic regression to a numeric outcome. (00:05:12)



3. Git review: branch, commit, and push for the pull-request task
00:06:05–00:09:50

Q: Why does the instructor say to run git status right before git add and definitely before git commit? A: In a branch workflow you need to confirm which branch you are on. If you accidentally commit on main, the textbook has a cheat sheet of commands that can move the commits. (00:08:08)
Q: Why should you pull main before starting work on a new branch in a collaborating environment? A: You want to start from an up-to-date main. That prevents you from making changes based on something that is out of date while multiple people are working on multiple branches. (00:08:27)
Q: Why could the instructor create the today branch after already editing README.md on main? A: He had not committed anything yet. git switch -c today created the new branch and kept the uncommitted README.md change on today instead of main. (00:08:57)
Q: What does git push origin today make possible on GitHub? A: It uploads the today branch to the remote. GitHub can then show the pull-request button so you can open a pull request for that branch. (00:09:44)



4. Issues as a project board
00:09:50–00:16:17

Q: Why does the instructor recommend using GitHub issues to track a project? A: Issues give a simple project-board view of what is happening in the project. They can also record who is responsible for what and can hold meeting notes and action items. (00:10:08)
Q: How can an issue board be used as meeting notes in the MDS workflow? A: You can write a big note in an issue during a meeting. Then you create separate issues for the action items or to-do items that spawn out of that meeting note. (00:10:49)
Q: Why do issues and pull requests share the same numbering sequence? A: The shared number lets you refer to any issue or pull request from another item with a hash number. For example, you can refer to issue #1 from a pull request. (00:11:54)
Q: What does a “two-way reference” between an issue and a pull request mean? A: When one item references another by number, the referenced item also gets a back-reference. That makes the items link to each other automatically. (00:13:34)
Q: Why is it acceptable for one pull request to deal with all three required issues? A: The instructor says the point is to gain experience with the project-board system. A single pull request can therefore deal with multiple issues, even though one issue, one branch, and one pull request is the clean extreme. (00:14:23)



5. Pull-request descriptions, checkboxes, and auto-close keywords
00:16:17–00:22:18

Q: Why should the first comment on an issue or pull request be kept up to date? A: Other people typically look at the first comment to understand what is happening and why the item exists. Project owners can edit it because issues and pull requests evolve over time. (00:16:40)
Q: What are Markdown checkboxes in a pull request used for? A: They let you track items that are done or not done in the pull request. If the pull request is not marked as a draft, teammates can see that work is still unfinished. (00:17:37)
Q: What do the keywords closes and fixes do when they appear in a pull-request message? A: A sentence such as closes #1 or fixes #2 references those issues. When the pull request is merged, GitHub automatically closes the referenced issues. This is a GitHub service feature rather than part of the Git version-control system. (00:18:33)
Q: Why does the instructor prefer putting fixes #N in the pull-request message rather than relying on a commit message? A: It is easier to see in the pull request than in a commit message. When the merge happens, the issue tab gets smaller automatically, so you do not have to manually close several issues. (00:19:55)



6. Merging the pull request and cleaning up branches
00:22:18–00:25:29

Q: What does git switch main followed by git pull origin main accomplish after pull request #3 is merged? A: It moves the local checkout to main. Then git pull origin main brings the merged pull-request commit down from origin/main so the local README.md change is present. (00:22:25)
Q: Why is deleting the merged today branch on GitHub optional in this course? A: The instructor says you do not have to delete branches in this course. Some people keep branches as a record, and different teams or companies have different Git conventions. (00:23:16)
Q: Why run git fetch --prune and then git branch -d today after the remote today branch is deleted? A: The local machine still has branch references that show up in git log --oneline --graph --all. git fetch --prune removes the remote-tracking reference, and git branch -d today deletes the local branch reference while the merge commit remains. (00:24:30)



7. Why containers: a stable, shareable compute environment (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:25:29–00:33:21

Q: Why does DSCI 522 move from a single supplied package file to projects that need their own environments? A: Data-science projects can last days, weeks, or years and are often team-based. Each project may need a stable compute environment that more than one person can share. (00:26:11)
Q: Why does the instructor say “this works on my machine” is not good enough? A: A teammate may have a different operating system or CPU architecture, such as a Windows ARM machine versus your Mac. The course goal is a shared compute environment where all the code can run. (00:29:32)
Q: Why does the instructor advise keeping the package list to the bare minimum? A: Installing packages you do not use wastes disk space. Later, updating everything in one go can fail because different packages have different update cycles and may become incompatible. (00:27:38)
Q: Why can a container act as a sandbox for learning operating-system commands? A: It adds an extra layer between you and your real machine. If you break the sandbox, you can restart it and get a new one rather than damaging your computer. (00:33:05)



8. Containers versus virtual machines (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:33:21–00:36:47

Q: What is the difference between a virtual machine and a container? A: A virtual machine installs a full operating system with a graphical interface you can log into. A container is a stripped-down environment containing only the bare minimum software you need and usually just a terminal. (00:34:48)
Q: Why are containers more performant than virtual machines? A: They do not include a full visual operating system. That makes them use less disk space, memory, and compute. (00:35:33)
Q: Why does the instructor still use virtual machines? A: He uses them when he needs to test the MDS install by pretending he is on a Windows machine. In that case, having a full operating system is the point. (00:36:01)



9. Running the R container: docker pull and docker run (28 Using and running containers)
00:36:47–00:45:01

Q: What does the tag 4.3.2 mean in docker pull rocker/r-ver:4.3.2? A: It selects the image whose R version is 4.3.2. That lets the container run R 4.3.2 even when the host machine has a different R version. (00:37:26)
Q: Why is running rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 a useful example for a stable analysis environment? A: It shows you can keep a fixed R version for a long-running analysis, such as clinical-trial or drug-submission work. The host’s R can keep upgrading without changing the analysis environment. (00:37:54)
Q: What do the flags --rm and -it do in docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2? A: --rm deletes the container when it stops so stopped containers do not pile up. -it gives an interactive terminal, with -i keeping input open and -t attaching a TTY. (00:40:55)
Q: Why does library(tidyverse) fail inside the bare rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 container but work on the host? A: The bare container only has R installed, not tidyverse. The host has its own packages, which shows that the two terminals are effectively different machines. (00:43:49)
Q: Why does the instructor emphasize paying attention to the prompt when working in a container? A: The prompt is often the only visual cue that you are typing in the container rather than on your local machine. This is similar to connecting to a remote machine, where you need to know which machine you are on. (00:45:04)



10. Web-app containers: RStudio and browser-first tools (28 Using and running containers)
00:45:01–00:54:10

Q: Why can applications such as RStudio, Jupyter Lab, and VS Code be run in a container and opened in a browser? A: Many of these tools are browser-first applications. They can run on a remote or container machine while still giving the user the same application interface. (00:47:15)
Q: What does it mean that Jupyter Lab is built to run in a browser? A: It means you can connect to Jupyter Lab that is running in a container or on a bigger machine. You still use the familiar browser interface even though the compute is elsewhere. (00:48:04)
Q: Why does the instructor choose the RStudio container as the example for running “an actual application”? A: The instructor calls the RStudio example the easier one to teach. RStudio can be run as a web app inside a container and then accessed through a browser. (00:46:47)



11. Port mapping the RStudio container (28 Using and running containers)
00:54:10–00:59:14

Q: What does -p 8787:8787 do in docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 rocker/rstudio:4.4.2? A: It maps port 8787 on the local computer to port 8787 inside the container. RStudio is listening on that internal port, so the browser can reach it at localhost:8787. (00:56:31)
Q: Why can you run the RStudio container more than once at the same time? A: The container’s internal port is fixed at 8787, but you can map it to a different local port. That lets multiple RStudio containers run at the same time on different local ports. (00:56:38)
Q: What does the instructor mean by saying port numbers are “very arbitrary”? A: The number is chosen by the tool or image, and you can map to many different local ports. Numbers like 8787 or 8888 are common conventions rather than required Docker rules. (00:56:19)
Q: Why is --rm useful when running several RStudio containers? A: Each running container uses RAM on the computer. --rm shuts down and removes the container when you exit, so you do not leave many machines running. (00:55:06)



12. Environment variables and running dashboards in containers (28 Using and running containers)
00:59:20–01:03:00

Q: What does -e PASSWORD="apassword" do when running the rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 container? A: It passes the environment variable PASSWORD into the container. The RStudio image uses that value to set the login password instead of generating a random one. (00:59:29)
Q: Why did the instructor check whether port 8787 is available to someone who cannot log into the host machine? A: He wanted to verify what the port mapping actually exposes. If you cannot log into the physical host machine, the local port is not available to you. (01:00:16)
Q: Why can a dashboard be deployed as a container in a course like DSCI 532? A: The container can include all the installation and environment setup. An end user only needs Docker, then runs the container and opens the dashboard’s port. (01:01:47)



13. Building interactively: base image and the cowsay package (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:03:00–01:08:46

Q: Why does the instructor start from rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 instead of an empty machine? A: The base image already has R and some of the system setup needed for R to work. It can skip several low-level installation steps, such as compiler setup that Windows and Mac users otherwise had to do by hand. (01:03:42)
Q: Why run docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash rather than letting the container start R? A: The bash command overrides the image’s default start-up, which would otherwise open R. It gives a terminal where you can test installation commands before writing them into a Dockerfile. (01:04:44)
Q: Why does cowsay disappear after you exit and restart the rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 container? A: A container has no saved state for interactive changes. When you turn it off and start the image again, it resets to the original image without the package you installed. (01:06:49)
Q: Why is a container a safe place to practice destructive command-line operations? A: If you “delete the computer,” you are only deleting the container. You can restart from the image and get a clean machine without affecting your real computer. (01:07:25)



14. Writing the Dockerfile: FROM, RUN, and CMD (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:08:46–01:15:01

Q: What is the role of a Dockerfile in the class’s workflow? A: It is the plain-text file that records the instructions for building the container machine. It specifies which base image to start from and which packages or setup commands to run. (01:10:18)
Q: What does the FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 line tell Docker? A: It sets the starting-point image for the new image. The build therefore begins with a machine that already has R 4.6.2 installed. (01:11:17)
Q: Why is Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')" the form used in the Dockerfile instead of starting R interactively? A: RUN lines need terminal commands, and Rscript -e runs an R expression from the command line. The outer double quotes and inner single quotes keep the shell quoting correct. (01:09:07)
Q: What does CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "cowsay::say('Hello from my first image!')"] control? A: It sets the default command that runs when a container from the new image starts. The container prints the cowsay message unless you override it with another command such as bash. (01:13:25)



15. Building and running the hello-cowsay image (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:15:01–01:18:44

Q: What does docker build --tag hello-cowsay . do? A: It builds an image named hello-cowsay from the Dockerfile in the current directory. The . tells Docker where to look for that file. (01:15:06)
Q: Why does the instructor use . as the build context in the build command? A: It assumes you are running the command from the project root, where the Dockerfile lives. That matches the milestone instruction to assume commands are run from the directory root. (01:16:29)
Q: Why does docker images matter after running the build? A: It lists the local images so you can confirm that the new hello-cowsay image exists. It also shows the image’s disk usage. (01:17:01)
Q: Why does docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay bash show that library(cowsay) works? A: The image’s RUN step installed cowsay at build time. A shell started from the new image therefore has the package already present. (01:17:52)



16. Version pinning and wrap-up (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:18:44–01:20:39

Q: Why does the instructor advise pinning tool versions, such as Quarto, in a Dockerfile? A: Pinning the install line means the image will install the exact versions you chose. As long as you do not change that line, a year later you can still be on the same tool versions. (01:19:25)
Q: What problem did the instructor report when a container was restarted without hard-version-pinning its tools? A: An update had happened the day before the instructor restarted the container. After that, nothing worked, so time was spent fixing the update instead of doing the actual project work. (01:19:50)
Q: What is the purpose of the placeholder for the language and package setup that the instructor mentions for the Dockerfile? A: It is where the Dockerfile will install the programming language, Quarto, and the package environment. That lets the image contain the full compute environment, not just the base language. (01:19:02)

Tier 3 of 5: Apply. Work each situation through before you read the answer; tiers 1 (Remember) and 2 (Understand) cover the facts and reasons it relies on.

1. Git Branching and Pull Requests
00:06:05–00:25:29

Q: You edit a file on main by mistake and want to move your uncommitted changes to a new branch called feature before committing. Which command do you run to create the new branch and switch to it? A: Run git switch -c <branch-name> to create a new branch and immediately switch your working directory to it, preserving your unstaged changes on the new branch instead of committing them to main. (00:09:17)
Q: After finishing work on a feature branch and merging it to main on GitHub, you want to completely remove the remote branch reference from your local machine. What two commands do you run to prune the remote tracking reference and delete the local branch? A: Run git fetch --prune to remove the deleted remote tracking references, then run git branch -d <branch-name> to delete the local branch reference. (00:24:30)
Q: You create a pull request to fix two open issues. How should you write the pull request description so that merging the pull request automatically closes both issues? A: Include the keywords fixes #<number> or closes #<number> at the end of a sentence in the pull request description, which triggers GitHub to automatically close the referenced issues when the pull request is merged. (00:18:33)



2. Introduction to Containers and Docker (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:25:33–00:46:44

Q: You need to run R version 4.3.2 on your Mac, but your system has R version 4.6.2 installed. Which Docker command runs the older R version interactively without leaving stopped containers cluttering your machine? A: Run docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2, which downloads the specific versioned image if missing, starts an interactive R session, and automatically deletes the container instance when you quit. (00:40:41)
Q: You are exploring a newly started container and notice the terminal prompt shows root@<container_id>:/#. How do you verify that the R version running inside matches the one you requested in the docker run command, rather than the one on your host machine? A: Type R --version inside the R session to verify the version matches the requested tag, while noting that your host terminal remains on the system’s default R version. (00:43:10)
Q: You accidentally install a package inside an interactive container session, but when you stop the container and restart it, the package is gone. Why does this happen, and what is the intended use case for this behavior? A: Containers do not save state between runs; they reset to the exact configuration defined in the image each time, which is intentionally designed so you can safely experiment or test commands without risking your host machine. (00:08:10)



3. Running Web Applications in Containers (28 Using and running containers)
00:46:47–01:03:00

Q: You want to run RStudio Server inside a container and access it through your web browser. Which flag and syntax do you use in the docker run command to map the container’s default port to your local machine? A: Use the -p flag with the format -p <host_port>:<container_port> (e.g., -p 8787:8787), which forwards network traffic from a specified port on your local machine directly to the web application inside the container. (00:56:55)
Q: The RStudio container you just started generates a random default password for login. How can you modify your docker run command to set a custom password instead? A: Append -e PASSWORD="yourpassword" to your run command, which passes the environment variable to the container to override the default auto-generated login credentials. (01:00:05)
Q: You try to run two separate RStudio containers simultaneously, but both fail to start on port 8787. What modification do you make to the port mapping for the second container to allow both to run? A: Change the host port number in the -p flag for the second container (e.g., -p 8788:8787), which maps the container’s internal port to a different available port on your local machine to prevent conflicts. (00:57:29)



4. Building Custom Containers with Dockerfile (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:03:00–01:20:39

Q: You are designing a custom R container and have just tested an installation command at the Bash prompt. How do you translate that command into a Dockerfile so it executes during the image build process? A: Prefix the tested command with RUN in the Dockerfile (e.g., RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')") so that it executes as a step during the image build sequence rather than at runtime. (01:12:41)
Q: You have finished writing a Dockerfile in your project root that installs a package. Which command do you run to compile this file into a named Docker image named hello-cowsay? A: Run docker build --tag hello-cowsay ., which reads the Dockerfile in your current directory and compiles the specified instructions into a named Docker image on your local machine. (01:15:38)
Q: After building a custom image, you want it to automatically run a specific R script every time it starts, instead of opening an interactive terminal. Which Dockerfile instruction do you use to define this default startup behavior? A: Use the CMD instruction with JSON array syntax (e.g., CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "cowsay::say('Hello')"]) to specify the command that runs by default when a container starts from this image. (01:13:36)

title: Git issues and pull requests, then Docker containers: review questions, tier 4 — Analyze
text:
Date: 2026-11-19
Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 4 of 5: Analyze. Take each one apart yourself before you read the answer; tiers 1 to 3 cover the facts, reasons and steps it relies on.

1. Git review: working on a branch
00:06:16–00:09:50

Q: In the 2026-11-19-docker demo repository, the instructor edited README.md before he made a branch. Break down the sequence from that edit to git push origin today. What did git status report at each point, and why did creating the branch late still work? A: The first git status reported On branch main, with README.md modified but not staged, so the edit existed only in the working directory. Nothing had been committed yet, so git switch -c today created the today branch and carried the uncommitted edit with it. The second git status showed On branch today with the same modification. git diff then showed the added line, git add README.md staged it, git commit recorded it on today as 3c6d82a, and git push origin today sent the branch to GitHub. Had he already committed on main, he would have needed the textbook’s cheat sheet to move the commits, which is why he says to look at your branch right before add, and definitely before commit. (00:08:57)



2. GitHub issues as a project board
00:09:50–00:16:17

Q: The 2026-11-19-docker repository ended up with issue #1 “what are we doing today?”, issue #2 “edit the readme with today’s topic” and pull request #3. Relate these three items: why did the pull request get number 3, and how do the references among them link up? A: Issues and pull requests share one counter, so after two issues the pull request from today became #3. Issue #2 points back to #1 with “meeting from #1”, the way an action item spawns from a meeting-notes issue. The pull request’s description refers to #2 and names both issues. Every # reference is two-way: the item referred to automatically shows a link back. As a result, #1 lists #2, and both issues show the pull request that deals with them. (00:12:07)
Q: On a GitHub pull request such as #3 in 2026-11-19-docker, distinguish the assignee role from the reviewer role. Who normally fills each one, and what does each contribute to the project? A: Being an assignee means claiming the work as your responsibility. You normally assign yourself to your own pull request, and you can also assign people to issues. The reviewer section is separate, and it is where you add a teammate to look over your work. Some larger projects block changes until someone has actually reviewed them. In the demo the instructor added Copilot as the reviewer. (00:14:47)



3. Pull request descriptions, checkboxes and closing keywords
00:16:17–00:22:18

Q: Pull request #3 in 2026-11-19-docker had a description in three parts: “this is the fix for #2”, a checklist (- [x] item 1, - [ ] item 2), and “closes #1 fixes #2”. Separate these parts: what does each do, and which one acts when the pull request is merged? A: “this is the fix for #2” is a plain reference. It links the pull request and issue #2 both ways but closes nothing. The checklist uses Markdown checkboxes to track what is still to do, which shows teammates that the work isn’t finished, much like the draft button does. The last sentence uses closing keywords. When the pull request is merged, GitHub auto-closes the issues named after closes or fixes, and this is a GitHub feature, not a Git one. In class the instructor wasn’t sure closes had worked and said he almost always uses fixes, but the demo repository lists both #1 and #2 as closed by #3. (00:19:30)
Q: Break down the issue-to-merge workflow the instructor uses for the textbook. How does it explain why one pull request can satisfy the lab’s three issues? A: He files an issue, works on it, and writes “fixes #N” in a comment or in the pull request message. When the pull request is merged, the issue closes at the same moment, the issues tab shrinks, and he picks the next item from the list. One refactor of the containers and virtual environments chapters covered two separate issues, moving the old material and writing the new, and a single pull request fixed both. In the same way, one pull request whose message names all three lab issues closes them on merge, so you don’t have to close each one by hand. Keywords also work in commit messages, but they are harder to see there. (00:20:28)



4. Cleaning up after a merge
00:22:18–00:25:19

Q: After pull request #3 was merged, the instructor ran git log --oneline --graph --all three times while cleaning up. Break down how the labels on commit 3c6d82a changed after each step, which steps acted on GitHub and which on the laptop, and what stayed the same throughout. A: git switch main and git pull origin main fast-forwarded the local main to the merge commit d25ddfa. At that point 3c6d82a was labelled (origin/today, today), even though the branch had already been deleted on GitHub with the delete button. git fetch --prune reported [deleted] origin/today and dropped the stale remote-tracking reference, leaving (today). git branch -d today then deleted the local branch, and the commit had no label at all. Throughout, the merge commit and the history stayed in the graph: only the shortcut names disappeared, which is why some people keep branches, since git switch today is easier than switching to a hash. (00:24:30)



5. Why data science workflows need stable environments (27.1 Documenting and loading dependencies)
00:25:29–00:30:13

Q: The instructor described two stability goals for a project that lasts weeks or years. Separate them: what threatens each one, and why does “it works on my machine” fail? A: The first goal is keeping your own environment stable over time. Packages update on different cycles, so an environment that installs everything can become impossible to install all at once, which is one reason to keep the package list to the bare minimum. The second goal is reproducing the environment on a teammate’s computer, which may run a different operating system or even a different chip. Mac and Windows machines differ, and Windows now ships on both ARM and Intel, so the way software gets installed differs too. Code that runs only on your machine therefore fails as soon as a teammate tries to run the same analysis. (00:28:53)



6. What a container is (27.2 What is a container?)
00:30:13–00:34:28

Q: Set handing a teammate a uv.lock file side by side with handing them a container. Compare what each one carries, what the teammate must already have set up, and where the teammate’s code actually runs. A: A uv.lock file records the Python packages, so the teammate can at least install the same package versions. To use it, though, they must install uv themselves, which might interfere with how their computer is already set up, and their computer may still differ from yours. A container is a virtual computer built from scratch and handed over whole. The teammate runs their code on that computer instead of directly on their own, so everyone shares the same computer even on different physical machines. (00:31:17)
Q: Break down what a container offers in three settings the instructor described: prototyping on your laptop, running on a bigger machine that holds the data, and working on a remote machine whose administrator won’t let you install software. What is the cost? A: The same container gives an identical compute environment on your laptop and on the bigger machine, so work prototyped locally runs unchanged where the data lives. On a remote machine, the administrator can hand you a container as a sandbox instead of letting you install Python directly. If you break the sandbox, you restart it and get a fresh one, which also makes a container a safe place to muck around with an operating system. The cost is a performance hit from the extra layer, which can’t be avoided. (00:32:34)



7. Containers versus virtual machines (27.3 Contrasting containers with virtual machines)
00:34:31–00:36:40

Q: Set a virtual machine and a container side by side. Compare what each contains, how you interact with it, its size, and what the instructor still uses virtual machines for. A: A virtual machine is a full-blown operating system, such as all of Windows, with its graphical interface and buttons. A container holds only the bare minimum you install and typically has no graphical interface, so you work in it by typing commands. That makes containers far lighter: a Windows VM takes 50 to 80 GB, while the containers used in class are around a couple of gigabytes or less and still run a full computational stack. They also use less memory and compute. The instructor still uses a VM to test the MDS installation instructions as if he were on Windows. (00:35:33)



8. Pulling and running a container: R 4.3.2 beside local R (28.1.1 Launch and run containers)
00:36:40–00:45:01

Q: Break down docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 into its parts. What does each part contribute? A: docker run turns on the machine named at the end, and it downloads the image first if it isn’t already on your computer. --rm has two dashes because it is a multi-letter flag, and it deletes the container when it stops; otherwise you would have to delete it by hand. -it chains two single-letter flags: -i for interactive and -t for a TTY, a terminal you can type in. rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 names the image: rocker is the organisation, whose r-ver images have only R installed, and the tag 4.3.2 picks the R version. (00:41:48)
Q: Distinguish the two terminals the instructor had open on his laptop: one running local R, one running rocker/r-ver:4.3.2. What did each show for the R version, the platform and library(tidyverse), and what does the contrast demonstrate? A: Local R --version reported R 4.6.2 on aarch64-apple-darwin23, the Mac, and there library(tidyverse) loaded. The container started R 4.3.2 on aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu, and library(tidyverse) failed with “there is no package called ‘tidyverse’”, because the image has only R installed. The two terminals run on the same hardware but behave like two different machines. That is how you can run a second version of R even though your computer has another version installed. (00:44:09)
Q: Using the instructor’s clinical-trials example, separate what lock files pin from what a container pins, and relate each layer to what a regulator asks for. A: Lock files such as uv.lock and the renv lock track only package versions. A container goes one level deeper and fixes the tools on the system: the version of R itself, and even system tools such as Git. A container with a 2019 Git, for example, would stop anyone from using git switch. Clinical trials research can run for years while R updates every six months. The regulator wants your code and the full compute environment so they can reproduce your work, and the container that ran the analysis provides both. (00:39:02)



9. Know which machine you are typing on
00:45:01–00:46:44

Q: In the terminal log, separate the prompts that appear: dan@Heartsbane 2026-11-19-docker %, root@95765251a970:/# and >. What does each one tell you about where you are typing, and why did the instructor stress reading them? A: dan@Heartsbane 2026-11-19-docker % is the laptop’s own prompt, showing the user, the machine and the current folder, and it returned after each container exited. root@95765251a970:/# is a Bash shell inside a container: the user root, a container ID, and the folder /. > is R’s own prompt, whether on the laptop or inside a container. With containers and remote machines, the prompt is sometimes the only cue you get, as on the machine in the instructor’s closet. Check it, or run whoami, before running commands, so you don’t run something on the wrong machine. (00:45:04)



10. Why so many data science tools run in a browser
00:46:44–00:49:11

Q: Relate Electron, Jupyter Lab, VS Code and GitHub Codespaces. What design do they share, and what does that design make possible with containers? A: Electron is essentially a browser packaged as an application, and many applications are built on it. Jupyter Lab opens at a localhost address because it was designed to run on a remote machine with more cores and memory while keeping the same interface. VS Code is likewise a large browser application, and the Codespaces button gives you VS Code in a browser on a machine someone else has set up. All of them are browser-first, so the application can run in a container or on another machine while you use it in your local browser, with the same versions of all the software as everyone else. (00:48:04)



11. Running RStudio in a container and mapping ports (28.1.3 Mapping ports to containers with web apps)
00:54:10–00:58:59

Q: Break down docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 rocker/rstudio:4.4.2. How does each part get RStudio into your browser, and what would you change to run a second RStudio at the same time? A: --rm deletes the machine when you exit. Without it, every container you started keeps using RAM, and you end up with “five computers” running and a computer that stops working. -p maps ports: the left number is the port on your machine and the right number is the port inside the container, where RStudio Server listens on 8787. You then open localhost:8787 in your browser and log in as rstudio with the password printed in the start-up output. To run a second copy, keep the container side at 8787 and map it to a different host port on the left. (00:57:05)
Q: By the end of the RStudio demo, three versions of R were in play on one laptop. Distinguish them by where each one runs and how you interact with it. A: The desktop RStudio uses the laptop’s installed R 4.6.2. The rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 container runs its own R inside the container and serves RStudio to the browser at localhost:8787. The earlier rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 container ran R 4.3.2 with only a terminal. The instructor described them as effectively completely different machines: one is terminal-only, and one is an application that runs in a browser. (00:58:59)



12. Passing environment variables into a container (27.2 What is a container?)
00:59:20–01:02:53

Q: Compare the start-up output of the two rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 runs, one without -e and one with -e PASSWORD="apassword". What differs, what caused the difference, and why was it acceptable to show the password in class? A: The first run printed “The password is set to ooph3Aef2Ohcahcu”, followed by a hint to set the PASSWORD environment variable. In the second run, skipping /var/run/s6/container_environment/PASSWORD appears among the environment entries, no generated password is printed, and you log in with the password you chose. The difference exists because this image was built to read PASSWORD; not every container reads the same variables, since that depends on how its builder set it up. Showing the password was fine because port 8787 is reachable only from the instructor’s own machine. (01:00:39)
Q: Break down the dashboard handoff the instructor described for DSCI 532. What does the builder do, what does the end user do, and which steps does the user skip? A: The builder puts the dashboard code into a container and does all of the installation in it. The end user needs only Docker. They run docker run with the right flags, then go to the port in their browser to reach the dashboard. They skip the whole installation process, such as setting up renv and the snapshot. In effect, the builder has given them a computer built from scratch. (01:02:20)



13. Starting from a base image and working inside it (29.1.1 Workflow for building a Dockerfile)
01:03:00–01:08:19

Q: The instructor ran docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash three times. Trace what happened to the cowsay package across the three sessions, and point out what in the terminal log shows that each session was a new machine. A: In the first session (root@95765251a970), install.packages("cowsay") inside R installed it, and cowsay::say('hello') drew the cow. After exit, the second session (root@97a536175dca) started with library(cowsay) failing again, and the package was installed once more with Rscript -e. The third session (root@a642984ec391) failed on library(cowsay) once more. A different container ID in each prompt shows a fresh machine each time. A container resets to how its image was built, with no saved state, so following README install steps on every start is painful. (01:07:10)



14. Running R from the command line with Rscript -e
01:08:19–01:10:18

Q: Distinguish install.packages("cowsay") typed at R’s > prompt from Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')" typed at the container’s Bash prompt. Where does each run, what does the quoting do, and why did the class need the second form? A: The first form only works once you have started R interactively. The second runs from the shell: Rscript executes R code from the terminal, and -e passes it an R expression. The double quotes wrap the whole expression for the shell and the single quotes go around the package name inside it. Both installed cowsay, and both installs vanished when the container restarted. The class needed the shell form because saving the setup depends on knowing the terminal command that performs the install. (01:09:27)



15. The Dockerfile: FROM, RUN, CMD (29.2 Dockerfile command summary)
01:10:18–01:15:01

Q: Break down the class’s three-line Dockerfile (FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2, RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')", CMD [...]). What does each line contribute, and when does it take effect? A: FROM names the starting machine. Here it already has R 4.6.2 and the system pieces R needs, which skips steps you would otherwise do by hand. RUN holds the shell commands to run while the machine is being built, and here it is the same Rscript -e line that was tested by hand. CMD, written as a list instead of space-separated words, is what a container from the image runs by default when it starts: it prints “Hello from my first image!”. You can override it, for example with bash. For a Python project, the middle section would instead install uv, COPY in the lock files and run uv sync. (01:14:05)

That is why commands assume you run them from the repository root. The build output lists [1/2] FROM docker.io/rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 and [2/2] RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')", and ends with naming to docker.io/library/hello-cowsay:latest. docker images then lists hello-cowsay:latest among the images on the machine. In docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay bash, R loads cowsay, because the build installed it into the image itself. (01:17:52)
Q: Distinguish docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay from docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay bash. What does each run, what did each produce, and when is the second one useful? A: Without a command after the image name, the container runs the Dockerfile’s CMD, so the cow printed “Hello from my first image!” and the container exited. Adding bash replaces that default and drops you at the container’s shell, where you can open R and check that library(cowsay) loads. 17. Pinning versions, and what comes next

Q: Break down where each layer of a project’s environment gets pinned in a Dockerfile, following the instructor’s plan for next week’s project container. Then relate that plan to the failure he described from another class. A: The FROM line pins the language: rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 fixes the R version. A section after it holds the renv or uv setup that installs the packages. Tools such as Quarto get an explicit version in their install line, even an older one, so a year later you are still on the same versions as long as you don’t touch that line. In another class a few weeks earlier, the instructor restarted a container that had no hard-pinned versions. Something had updated the day before, nothing worked, and fixing it could cost hours that should have gone to the actual work. Pin every version, and change one only when you mean to. (01:19:55)

title: Containers: running and building a shareable compute environment: review questions, tier 4 — Analyze
text:
Date: 2026-11-19

Generated by qwen3.8-27b-sglang, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 4 of 5: Analyze. Take each one apart yourself before you read the answer; tiers 1 to 3 cover the facts, reasons and steps it relies on.

1. Class setup: Docker Desktop and pre-lecture pulls (Download the images before you start)
00:00:14–00:01:41

Q: In the opening Docker setup, break down the roles of Docker Desktop, the three pre-lecture docker pull commands, and the image names rocker/r-ver:4.3.2, rocker/rstudio:4.4.2, and quay.io/jupyter/datascience-notebook:2025-03-14. A: Docker Desktop must be open because it provides the Docker engine that later commands talk to; if Docker cannot be found, the commands will fail or tell you to turn it on. Each docker pull downloads one image to the local machine before the lecture’s docker run commands need it. The registry/organization part selects where the image lives, the image name selects the software, and the tag selects the version. Pulling them first avoids waiting for long downloads during the live exercise. (00:00:43)



2. Project advice: simple but technically correct
00:01:41–00:06:05

Q: Examine the instructor’s warning about making the project analysis difficult: where in the group-project workflow does over-scoping bite, and what downstream pieces does it affect? A: The warning bites at the start of the project because the same project is built on for three or four weeks, so an early complicated model stays in the workflow. The instructor says a straight-line model is acceptable if that is the analysis, while adding a neural network for show creates a harder project two weeks later. Even a short analysis still includes code that downloads data, some cleaning, EDA code, modelling code, and figures/tables. Model accuracy is not the point; the data science and machine-learning technique must be technically correct, such as not fitting logistic regression to a numeric outcome. (00:02:59)



3. Git review: branch, commit, and push
00:06:05–00:09:50

Q: Follow the today branch in the 2026-11-19-docker demo repository from the modified README.md to the pushed remote branch: which local commands change the local state, which command creates the remote branch, and how does that make GitHub’s pull-request path possible? A: git switch -c today creates and moves to today, so the subsequent commit will not go to main. git add README.md stages the one-line change shown by git diff, and git commit -m "today we are talking about containers" creates the local commit on today. git push origin today sends that commit to GitHub and creates the remote today branch. The push response prints a GitHub URL for creating a pull request from that remote branch. (00:09:25)



4. Issues as a project board
00:09:50–00:16:17

Q: Examine issue #1, issue #2, and pull request #3 in the 2026-11-19-docker demo repository: how do GitHub’s shared numbering and two-way hash references turn a meeting note, an action item, and a code change into one tracked project thread? A: Issues and pull requests use one shared counter, so the meeting note is #1, the action item is #2, and the branch change becomes #3. Referencing #1 in issue #2 creates a back-link, so the action item points to the meeting that produced it. Put the same references in the pull request description, and the pull request links back to the issues it addresses. This makes the project board show responsibility, progress, and related work without a separate document. (00:13:34)



5. Pull-request descriptions and auto-close keywords
00:16:17–00:22:18

Q: Separate the parts of pull request #3’s description in the 2026-11-19-docker demo repository that provide context, that track task status, and that make GitHub close issues automatically when the pull request is merged. A: The first comment’s “this is the fix for #2” tells readers the purpose and links the related issue. The Markdown checkboxes - [x] item 1 and - [ ] item 2 show which tasks are done and which remain. The sentence closes #1 fixes #2 uses GitHub keywords that reference issue #1 and issue #2. When the pull request merges, those referenced issues are closed automatically. (00:19:30)



6. Merging the pull request and cleaning up branch references
00:22:18–00:25:29

Q: Trace what happens to the 2026-11-19-docker demo repository after pull request #3 is merged: what main receives, what deleting the GitHub branch removes, and what git fetch --prune and git branch -d today remove locally. A: After the merge, git switch main and git pull origin main bring the merge commit into local main, updating the README with the merged change. Deleting the today branch on GitHub removes the remote branch, but the merge still exists in main’s history. git fetch --prune drops the stale origin/today reference from the local remote-tracking branches. git branch -d today deletes the local today shortcut, while git log --oneline --graph --all still shows the merged commit. (00:24:30)



7. Why containers: a stable, shareable compute environment (27.1 Documenting and loading dependencies)
00:25:29–00:33:21

Q: Break down the course’s “stable, shareable compute environment” goal into package lock files, operating-system/architecture differences, and the container. A: The class moves from instructor-supplied package lists to team projects where package needs differ by project and language. A lock file such as uv.lock or renv.lock keeps package versions consistent on one machine, but a teammate may have a different operating system or CPU architecture, such as Mac versus Windows or ARM versus Intel. The instructor’s solution is to build a virtual computer and share that container instead of asking everyone to replicate the local machine. This lets everyone run the same code through one shareable compute environment instead of depending on a private local machine. (00:31:17)



8. Containers versus virtual machines (27.3 Contrasting containers with virtual machines)
00:33:21–00:36:47

Q: Set a virtual machine and a container side by side on interface, operating system, and resource use, using the instructor’s comparison from class. A: A virtual machine installs a full operating system, such as Windows, and gives a graphical interface you log into. A container is stripped down to the bare minimum needed for the task and normally has only a terminal, not a graphical interface. The instructor contrasts a virtual machine’s 50 to 80 GB size with containers used in class that can be under about one to two gigabytes. Because containers carry fewer resources, they are lighter in disk, memory, and compute. (00:36:16)



9. Running the R container (28 Using and running containers)
00:36:47–00:45:01

Q: Deduce from the host R --version, docker pull rocker/r-ver:4.3.2, docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2, and the failed library(tidyverse) why the container is a separate machine rather than just another terminal on the host. A: The host reports R 4.6.2, while the pulled rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 image supplies a Linux container with R 4.3.2. docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 starts that container and gives an interactive R session from the container’s own environment. library(tidyverse) fails in the container because the image only has R, while the host terminal can load tidyverse from the host’s installed packages. The different version and different package availability show that the two terminals are operating in different machines. (00:44:09)



10. Web-app containers: RStudio and browser-first tools (27.2 What is a container?)
00:45:01–00:54:10

Q: Examine the instructor’s point that RStudio, JupyterLab, and VS Code are browser-first applications: what does that make possible when such an application is placed in a container, and where does the user’s interface actually run? A: Browser-first tools are built to serve their interface over a browser instead of requiring a local desktop double-click. Placing one in a container lets the application run inside the container while the user still opens the familiar interface in a local browser. The container supplies the compute environment and the application server, while the browser provides the graphical front end. This is the same idea as connecting to a remote cloud machine: the interface is local, but the work is done on another machine. (00:48:33)



11. Port mapping the RStudio container (28.1.3 Mapping ports to containers with web apps)
00:54:10–00:59:14

Q: Break down docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 into the container-side port, the host-side port, and the browser address that makes RStudio reachable. A: Inside rocker/rstudio:4.4.2, RStudio listens on port 8787. The -p 8787:8787 flag maps a port on the local host to that container port, so the container’s service becomes reachable from the host. The user then opens localhost:8787 in a browser to get the RStudio sign-in page. To run another RStudio container at the same time, the container side can stay 8787 while the host side is mapped to a different available port. (00:57:05)



12. Environment variables and running dashboards in containers (27.2 What is a container?)
00:59:20–01:03:00

Q: Distinguish the first RStudio container run from the second run with -e PASSWORD="apassword" in terms of what the terminal shows and what password the browser login accepts. A: In the first run, the container prints that it has set a generated password and suggests setting the PASSWORD environment variable to choose one. The second run passes -e PASSWORD="apassword", so the container is told to use that supplied password instead of a random one. The browser login then uses the rstudio user name and the password set on the command line. The mapped port still does not expose the app to anyone who cannot reach the host machine. (01:00:39)



13. Building interactively: base image and the cowsay package (29.1.1 Workflow for building a Dockerfile)
01:03:00–01:08:46

Q: Trace why installing cowsay inside an interactive rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 container disappears after exit, and why the class runs docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash before writing the Dockerfile. A: The command ends with bash, which replaces the image’s default startup command, so the user gets a shell instead of immediately starting R. Inside that shell, Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')" can be tested as a non-interactive command that later fits a RUN line. When the container exits, --rm removes the running container, and the image has no saved state for packages installed only in that run. Starting the container again returns to the original image, so cowsay is missing until it is installed at build time. (01:07:25)



14. Writing the Dockerfile: FROM, RUN, and CMD (29.2 Dockerfile command summary)
01:08:46–01:15:01

Q: Break down the class Dockerfile into its FROM, RUN, and CMD lines, and say what each contributes to the behavior of the hello-cowsay image. A: FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 chooses the base image and supplies R 4.6.2 as the starting machine. RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')" installs cowsay while the image is built, so the package is baked into the image. CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "cowsay::say('Hello from my first image!')"] sets the default command that runs when a container starts from this image. A command after the image name in docker run, such as bash, can override that default for a one-time run. (01:13:40)



15. Building and running the hello-cowsay image (29.1.2 Build your first image)
01:15:01–01:18:44

Q: Trace how docker build --tag hello-cowsay ., docker images, docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay, and docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay bash together prove that the Dockerfile was built and that the image’s CMD can be overridden. A: docker build --tag hello-cowsay . reads the Dockerfile from the current directory and builds an image named hello-cowsay. docker images shows that local image, confirming it exists after the build. docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay runs without an extra command, so it executes the CMD and prints the cowsay message. docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay bash replaces the CMD with a shell, where library(cowsay) works because the RUN step installed it. (01:17:14)



16. Version pinning and wrap-up (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:18:44–01:20:39

Q: Examine where unpinned tool versions can break the Dockerfile-based workflow the class just built, and identify which Dockerfile lines act as the control point for keeping versions stable. A: The warning bites when a Dockerfile installs tools with floating or latest versions, so an external update can change the image without the user changing the project. The instructor’s example was restarting a container after an unpinned tool updated, after which nothing worked and hours were spent fixing the update. A pinned FROM line fixes the base language/tool version, and pinned RUN install lines fix the versions of later tools such as Quarto, uv, or renv. As long as those lines are not changed, rebuilding should keep the same tool versions instead of silently updating them. (01:20:27)

1. Project Advice and Course Logistics
00:00:14–00:05:43

Q: A teammate suggests building a complex neural network for the group project’s milestone to showcase advanced modeling skills. Based on the class guidance, should you approve this plan, and what is the reasoning? A: No, you should not approve this plan. 2. Git Branching and Pull Requests (Documenting and loading dependencies)
00:06:05–00:25:29

Q: Your team decides to keep all historical Git branches in the repository as a permanent record of every task completed, even after the pull requests are merged. Based on the class demonstration, would you approve of this practice for a class project, and what is the reason? A: You would find it acceptable, though it is not required. The class explicitly stated that deleting branches after merging is optional and depends on the specific team or company’s workflow; while cleaning up references with git fetch --prune and git branch -d helps avoid confusing Git states, keeping them as a record is also valid. (00:23:22)
Q: A pull request description consists entirely of a brief, evolving back-and-forth conversation between two reviewers, with no summary or checklist in the first comment. Would you approve this PR based on the class’s advice on PR descriptions, and what criterion decides this? A: No, you should not approve it in this state. The instructor advised keeping the first comment up to date as the primary summary of what is happening, because reviewers and future team members will focus on that initial description rather than scrolling through the entire conversation thread. (00:16:40)
Q: A teammate submits a pull request to fix three separate issues but omits the fixes #1 fixes #2 fixes #3 keywords in the description, instead closing each issue manually after the merge. Is this an acceptable workflow according to the instructor’s recommendation, and why? A: No, this is not the recommended workflow. The instructor emphasized writing the message strategically with closes or fixes keywords so that GitHub automatically closes the referenced issues upon merge, which streamlines project management and avoids manually clicking to close issues one by one. (00:20:23)



3. Introduction to Containers and Docker (What is a container?)
00:25:33–00:46:44

Q: A student runs a container to test a new R package, manually installs it inside the interactive session, and exits without building an image. They then restart the same container image expecting the package to be available. Would you consider this a reliable workflow for setting up a shared analysis environment, and what criterion decides this? A: No, you should not consider it reliable. The instructor explained that containers reset to their initial base state when stopped; any interactive changes or installations are lost upon exit unless explicitly saved via a Dockerfile or volume mount. (00:08:10)
Q: A teammate argues that using a full virtual machine is better than a container for this course because VMs are heavier and provide better isolation. Based on the class comparison, would you agree, and what criterion weighs against their argument? A: No, you would not agree. The class emphasized that containers are significantly lighter in size and resource usage, start faster, and are more portable because they share the host OS, making them preferable for sharing compute environments without the massive storage and performance overhead of emulating an entire OS like a VM. (00:36:01)



4. Running Web Applications in Containers (Mapping ports to containers with web apps)
00:46:47–01:03:00

Q: A student wants to run two separate RStudio containers simultaneously for testing purposes but only specifies port 8787 for both in their docker run commands. Would you approve this configuration for simultaneous access, and what criterion decides this? A: No, you should not approve this configuration. The instructor explained that you must map different host ports to each container (e.g., -p 8787:8787 for the first and -p 8788:8787 for the second) to avoid port conflicts and allow simultaneous local access. (00:57:19)
Q: For a containerized RStudio setup used by an external collaborator, a teammate proposes leaving the default auto-generated password in the terminal output instead of passing a custom one via -e PASSWORD="securepass". Is this a practical recommendation for sharing the container, and what is the reasoning? A: It is not a practical recommendation. The class noted that the default password is randomly generated and cumbersome to remember or securely share; using the -e flag to set a predictable password is a better workflow, provided access to the host machine itself is controlled. (00:59:34)



5. Building Custom Containers with Dockerfile (Build your first image)
01:03:00–01:20:39

Q: A developer writes a Dockerfile to set up an analysis environment and relies on the base image’s default command CMD ["R"] to run their analysis script instead of defining a custom CMD. Would you approve this approach for automating the workflow, and what criterion decides this? A: No, you should not approve this approach for automation. The class demonstrated that CMD defines the startup command, so relying on the base image’s default will only launch an interactive R session; they must define a custom CMD to execute the analysis script automatically. (01:13:36)
Q: During a container build, a student accidentally misspells a package name in the RUN instruction, e.g., install.packages('cowsya'). The build completes without returning an error. Would you assess this behavior as a safe way to validate dependencies during the build process, and what criterion decides this? A: No, you should not assess it as safe. The class demonstrated that install.packages() only throws a warning and exits with status 0, which Docker interprets as success; to properly validate dependencies, they should append library(misspelled_package) to halt the build with a fatal error on failure. (01:12:44)
